Study in Australia from Your Country — Document Prep Guides | YouSafe 
Skip to main content Country of citizenship
Study in Australia from your country — document prep
Hub only. We are not shipping two hundred thin /from/[slug]/ pages. The notes below cover frequent sending countries: funds-proof patterns, police certificates, and Genuine Student issues. Procedure checklists stay on the legal panel.
India
Funds often mix education-loan sanction letters, sponsor ITR, and bank statements. Genuine Student answers should explain why this CRICOS course, not a US F-1 SOP. Police certificates and name-variation on passports are common upload issues.
Nepal
Sponsor capacity and relationship evidence get read closely. Keep CoE, OSHC, and the GS answers consistent with the same sponsor. We do not promise processing times; Home Affairs publishes those.
China
Notarial translations and hukou / relationship documents for dependants are frequent extras. English-test timing must match the CoE. GS is not a personal-statement essay.
Philippines
NBI clearance timing and employment certificates for GS work-history answers. Packaged English plus a VET or degree CoE should sit in one folder.
Vietnam
Sponsor bank books and relationship evidence. Translate consistently. Genuine Student should address why Australia and why this provider, not a recycled Canada study-permit SOP.
Nigeria
Funds source, name consistency across WAEC / degree certificates, and police character documents. GS answers must match the occupation story if the course is vocational.
Continue to Subclass 500 prep , GS workshop , or the study sequence .
Book country-specific prep

Privacy Policy
Last updated: January 1, 2026
1. Introduction
YouSafe Consultancy, operated by Youssef Hammoud and based in Online, Australia, is committed to protecting your privacy. This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, disclose, and safeguard your personal information when you use our study document preparation, education planning, and settlement support services. We comply with the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) and applicable Australian privacy laws.
2. Information We Collect
We collect information that you provide directly to us, including:
Personal identification information (name, date of birth, nationality, passport details)
Contact information (email address, phone number, mailing address)
Educational background and employment history
Immigration history and travel documents
Financial information for proof of funds documentation
Payment information for processing fees
Communications between you and our team
3. How We Use Your Information
We use the information we collect to:
Provide study document preparation, education planning, and settlement support services
Communicate with you about your case and our services
Process payments and maintain financial records
Help organize materials for Department of Home Affairs and educational institutions when requested by you
Comply with legal obligations and regulatory requirements
Improve our services and client experience
4. Information Sharing and Disclosure
We do not sell, trade, or rent your personal information to third parties. We may share your information only in the following circumstances: with government agencies (such as Department of Home Affairs) when you authorize us to help with document submission or support; with educational institutions as part of your admission applications; with service providers who assist us in operating our business (subject to confidentiality agreements); and when required by law, court order, or government regulation.
5. Data Security
We implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect your personal information against unauthorized access, alteration, disclosure, or destruction. This includes encrypted storage of sensitive documents, secure communication channels, and restricted access to client files. However, no method of transmission over the Internet is 100% secure, and we cannot guarantee absolute security.
6. Data Retention
We retain your personal information for as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes for which it was collected, typically for seven (7) years after the conclusion of your case. This retention period allows us to comply with legal requirements, resolve disputes, and enforce our agreements. After this period, your information will be securely deleted or anonymized.
7. Your Rights
Under Australian privacy law, you have the right to:
Access the personal information we hold about you
Request correction of inaccurate or incomplete information
Withdraw consent for certain uses of your information
Request deletion of your information (subject to legal retention requirements)
File a complaint with the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
8. Cookies and Website Analytics
Our website may use cookies and similar technologies to enhance your browsing experience and analyze website traffic. You can control cookie settings through your browser preferences. We use analytics tools to understand how visitors interact with our website, but this data is aggregated and does not identify individual users.
9. International Transfers
As we serve clients from around the world, your information may be transferred to and processed in countries other than your country of residence. When we transfer information internationally, we ensure appropriate safeguards are in place to protect your privacy in accordance with this policy and applicable laws.
10. Changes to This Policy
We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time to reflect changes in our practices or legal requirements. We will notify you of any material changes by posting the updated policy on our website with a new Last updated date. We encourage you to review this policy periodically.

1. Overview
At YouSafe Consultancy, operated by Youssef Hammoud in Online, Australia, we are committed to providing high-quality study document preparation, education planning, and settlement support services. We understand that circumstances may change, and we have established this Refund Policy to ensure fair treatment for all our clients.
2. Consultation Fees
Initial consultation fees are non-refundable once the consultation has taken place. If you cancel a scheduled consultation at least 48 hours in advance, you may reschedule at no additional cost or receive a full refund. Cancellations made less than 48 hours before the scheduled consultation are non-refundable.
3. Service Package Refunds
Refunds for service packages are calculated based on the work completed at the time of cancellation:
Before work begins: 90% refund (10% administrative fee) 
Document review stage: 70% refund 
Application preparation stage: 50% refund 
After application submission: No refund 
4. Government Fees
Government fees paid to Australian Department of Home Affairs (immigration authority) or other government agencies are non-refundable through YouSafe Consultancy. These fees are paid directly to the government and are subject to their own refund policies. We are not responsible for refunding any government fees.
5. Application Refusals
If your visa, student visa, or immigration application is refused by Department of Home Affairs or any other government authority, you are not entitled to a refund of our consulting fees. Our services involve preparing and submitting your application according to best practices, but the final decision rests with the government. However, we offer discounted rates for re-applications if you choose to apply again with our assistance.
6. Mentorship Packages
Monthly mentorship packages may be cancelled at any time with 14 days written notice before the next billing cycle. No refunds will be issued for partial months. Quarterly mentorship packages are non-refundable once the quarter has begun, but unused sessions may be credited toward future services at our discretion.
7. How to Request a Refund
To request a refund, please contact us in writing with the following information:
Your full name and contact information
The service package or consultation purchased
Date of purchase and payment method
Reason for requesting a refund
8. Processing Time
Refund requests will be reviewed within 5 business days. Approved refunds will be processed within 10 business days and returned to the original payment method. Please allow additional time for your bank or payment provider to process the refund.
9. Exceptions
We reserve the right to make exceptions to this policy on a case-by-case basis in extraordinary circumstances. Any exceptions are at the sole discretion of YouSafe Consultancy and do not create precedent for future refund requests.
10. Disputes
If you are unsatisfied with our refund decision, you may contact us to discuss your concerns. We are committed to resolving disputes fairly and amicably. Any further dispute process will be stated in the written service agreement.

body:
Source site: https://ca.yousafeconsultancy.com
Source URL: https://ca.yousafeconsultancy.com/canada-express-entry-crs-international-student-graduates/

Canada Express Entry CRS for Graduates: 2026 Guide 
Skip to main content Your CRS profile after a Canadian credential is a ranking tool, not a visa. IRCC still decides every invitation and every file.
In 60 seconds
CRS ranking: canada express entry crs international student graduates profiles sit in a pool; invitations are not automatic.
Programs first: you still need FSW, CEC, or FST eligibility before a CRS number matters.
Study help: a Canadian degree can add points; a study permit is not permanent residence.
Next step: use this canada express guide to list tests, transcripts, and work proof before you create a profile.
Table of contents
Canada Express Entry CRS for International Student Graduates 
Eligibility for Express Entry After Graduation 
CRS Score Factors and Provincial Nominee Options 
Documents and Language Tests for Express Entry 
Application Timeline After a Canadian Study Permit 
Official sources 
FAQ 
Canada Express Entry CRS for International Student Graduates
CRS is IRCC’s Comprehensive Ranking System. Officers use it only after you enter the Express Entry pool.
Study is not PR. Graduation from a designated school does not create a permanent resident grant.
Programs still apply. You must first meet Federal Skilled Worker, Canadian Experience Class, or Federal Skilled Trades rules.
Credentials from a DLI can raise education and Canadian-study factors. Language, age, and skilled work still move the number.
PGWP work can support CEC if duties match a skilled NOC. Job titles alone do not prove skill level.
Job Bank listings help you map duties. Confirm the occupation against Job Bank .
Study planning starts on EduCanada . Campus pages do not replace IRCC program text.
Why graduates ask now: canada express entry crs international student graduates 2026 cut-offs shift with each round. Rounds also change by category.
Where files live: you create the profile online. You only submit a full canada express entry crs international student graduates application after an invitation.
Cost caution: canada express entry crs international student graduates cost includes language tests, ECA if needed, biometrics, and right-of-permanent-residence fees. IRCC sets those amounts; they change.
Fees vs extras: medical exams and police certificates sit outside the government PR fee table.
Mistakes to avoid: expired tests, unpaid work claimed as skilled, and missing hours on letters.
Compare your number on the Express Entry: CRS & Application Timeline page before you pay extra tests.
> Note: Category-based rounds can ignore a high general CRS. Read the round notice, not last month’s rumour.
Next, confirm program canada express eligibility, not only your score.
Worked Example: Priya after a Toronto master’s
Example: Priya finished a one-year master’s, then a PGWP software job. She booked IELTS, aligned duties to a TEER 1 NOC, and entered the pool.
IRCC later invited her in a CEC-focused round. Her result was an invitation to apply, not a visa grant.
For example, her unused French test stayed off the file.
Eligibility for Express Entry After Graduation
canada eligibility after study still tracks one of three federal programs. Graduation is evidence, not a separate class.
CEC path: skilled Canadian work in the last three years, plus language at the program CLB. Hours must be paid and documented.
FSW path: foreign skilled work, language, education, and settlement funds unless you are already authorised to work.
Trades path: qualifying trade experience and a certificate or job offer where the program requires one.
canada requirements also include admissibility. Police, medical, and misrepresentation rules still apply.
Study permit status is not CEC. You need qualifying work after studies, usually on a PGWP or other work permit.
Hours: part-time study jobs often fail CEC if they were not skilled or not enough hours.
NOC match: compare daily duties, not the employer’s marketing title.
Age: CRS age points fall after 29. Program eligibility can remain even when CRS drops.
Spouse factors: a partner’s language and education can add CRS points if you include them.
Funds: CEC usually does not need proof of funds. FSW often does unless you have valid work and a qualifying offer.
Credential assessment: foreign degrees may need an ECA. Alberta’s IQAS is one designated option.
canada express requirements are program rules plus CRS ranking. Meeting one without the other is not enough.
Read the Canada Immigration — Complete Guide for how to study, work, and PR stages connect.
> Note: Provincial nominee streams have extra tests. A nomination is separate from the federal pool.
If you meet a program, next model CRS and any PNP add-on.
CRS Score Factors and Provincial Nominee Options
Core human capital covers age, education, official language, and Canadian work. A second language can add more.
Spouse factors apply if you include a partner. Leaving a partner out changes both CRS and later sponsorship risk.
Skill transferability pairs education or foreign work with language or Canadian work. Weak language caps this block.
Canadian study can add extra CRS if the credential and length meet IRCC’s extra-points rules.
Job offers under genuine LMIA or qualifying arrangements can add points. Many graduate files have none.
PNP: a provincial nomination can add 600 CRS points. Provinces run their own intakes and occupations.
how to apply for canada through a PNP still starts with Express Entry if the stream is aligned. Non-aligned streams use different forms.
Occupation lists change. Check Job Bank and the province’s current notice.
Labour context from the OECD and ILO explains shortages. Those papers do not replace IRCC draws.
Housing costs affect settlement planning. CMHC publishes market data, not visa criteria.
IOM and UNHCR pages help if you have prior displacement history. Disclose that history on the forms.
In this case, canada express ranking is relative. A 500 CRS can be high one month and unused the next.

France is one of Canada's largest Western European source countries for international students, with consistently strong study permit volumes, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from France sits at the centre of Canada's francophone-recruitment strategy. Canada actively courts French-speaking students, and that shapes the experience for French applicants in a way it does not for many other countries. France was never part of the Student Direct Stream, so its closure in November 2024 had little practical effect; French applicants have always used the standard study permit stream. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides the case on your documents.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. If you plan to study in Quebec, you also need a Quebec Acceptance Certificate, the CAQ, before the federal study permit.

Canada Study Permit Guide for Hong Kong
This page gives Hong Kong students the full Canada study permit path, from letter of acceptance to IRCC decision, with checks that reduce delays.
Hong Kong is a consistent source of Canadian study permit holders, supported by deep migration ties and dedicated immigration measures, according to IRCC.
A Canada study permit from Hong Kong runs through the standard study permit stream, but it sits within a wider set of options. Canada has dedicated immigration measures for Hong Kong residents, including permanent-residence pathways and an open work permit for recent graduates, which makes a study permit a recognised first step toward working and settling in Canada. Hong Kong was never part of the Student Direct Stream, so its closure in November 2024 changed nothing procedural. There is no interview; an IRCC officer decides on your documents.
The steps are clear. You receive a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution, obtain the Provincial Attestation Letter your province issues, prepare proof of funds, complete the online application, and give biometrics. Privacy Policy | YouSafe Canada

Privacy Policy
Last updated: January 1, 2026
1. Introduction
YouSafe Consultancy, operated by Youssef Hammoud and based in Toronto, Canada, is committed to protecting your privacy. This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, disclose, and safeguard your personal information when you use our study document preparation, education planning, and settlement support services. We comply with the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) and applicable Canadian privacy laws.
2. Information We Collect
We collect information that you provide directly to us, including:
Personal identification information (name, date of birth, nationality, passport details)
Contact information (email address, phone number, mailing address)
Educational background and employment history
Immigration history and travel documents
Financial information for proof of funds documentation
Payment information for processing fees
Communications between you and our team
3. How We Use Your Information
We use the information we collect to:
Provide study document preparation, education planning, and settlement support services
Communicate with you about your case and our services
Process payments and maintain financial records
Help organize materials for IRCC and educational institutions when requested by you
Comply with legal obligations and regulatory requirements
Improve our services and client experience
4. Information Sharing and Disclosure
We do not sell, trade, or rent your personal information to third parties. We may share your information only in the following circumstances: with government agencies (such as IRCC) when you authorize us to help with document submission or support; with educational institutions as part of your admission applications; with service providers who assist us in operating our business (subject to confidentiality agreements); and when required by law, court order, or government regulation.
5. Data Security
We implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect your personal information against unauthorized access, alteration, disclosure, or destruction. This includes encrypted storage of sensitive documents, secure communication channels, and restricted access to client files. However, no method of transmission over the Internet is 100% secure, and we cannot guarantee absolute security.
6. Data Retention
We retain your personal information for as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes for which it was collected, typically for seven (7) years after the conclusion of your case. This retention period allows us to comply with legal requirements, resolve disputes, and enforce our agreements. After this period, your information will be securely deleted or anonymized.
7. Your Rights
Under Canadian privacy law, you have the right to:
Access the personal information we hold about you
Request correction of inaccurate or incomplete information
Withdraw consent for certain uses of your information
Request deletion of your information (subject to legal retention requirements)
File a complaint with the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
8. Cookies and Website Analytics
Our website may use cookies and similar technologies to enhance your browsing experience and analyze website traffic. You can control cookie settings through your browser preferences. We use analytics tools to understand how visitors interact with our website, but this data is aggregated and does not identify individual users.
9. International Transfers
As we serve clients from around the world, your information may be transferred to and processed in countries other than your country of residence. When we transfer information internationally, we ensure appropriate safeguards are in place to protect your privacy in accordance with this policy and applicable laws.
10. Changes to This Policy
We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time to reflect changes in our practices or legal requirements. We will notify you of any material changes by posting the updated policy on our website with a new Last updated date. We encourage you to review this policy periodically.
11. Contact Us
If you have questions about this Privacy Policy or wish to exercise your privacy rights, please contact us:

If you cancel a scheduled consultation at least 48 hours in advance, you may reschedule at no additional cost or receive a full refund. Cancellations made less than 48 hours before the scheduled consultation are non-refundable.
3. Service Package Refunds
Refunds for service packages are calculated based on the work completed at the time of cancellation:
Before work begins: 90% refund (10% administrative fee) 
Document review stage: 70% refund 
Application preparation stage: 50% refund 
After application submission: No refund 
4. Government Fees
Government fees paid to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) or other government agencies are non-refundable through YouSafe Consultancy. These fees are paid directly to the government and are subject to their own refund policies. We are not responsible for refunding any government fees.
5. Application Refusals
If your visa, study permit, or immigration application is refused by IRCC or any other government authority, you are not entitled to a refund of our consulting fees. Our services involve preparing and submitting your application according to best practices, but the final decision rests with the government. However, we offer discounted rates for re-applications if you choose to apply again with our assistance.
6. Mentorship Packages
Monthly mentorship packages may be cancelled at any time with 14 days written notice before the next billing cycle. No refunds will be issued for partial months. Quarterly mentorship packages are non-refundable once the quarter has begun, but unused sessions may be credited toward future services at our discretion.
7. How to Request a Refund
To request a refund, please contact us in writing with the following information:
Your full name and contact information
The service package or consultation purchased
Date of purchase and payment method
Reason for requesting a refund
8. Processing Time
Refund requests will be reviewed within 5 business days. Approved refunds will be processed within 10 business days and returned to the original payment method. Please allow additional time for your bank or payment provider to process the refund.
9. Exceptions
We reserve the right to make exceptions to this policy on a case-by-case basis in extraordinary circumstances. Any exceptions are at the sole discretion of YouSafe Consultancy and do not create precedent for future refund requests.
10. Disputes
If you are unsatisfied with our refund decision, you may contact us to discuss your concerns. We are committed to resolving disputes fairly and amicably. If a resolution cannot be reached, disputes shall be governed by the laws of the Province of Ontario, Canada.

About
Real legal help, without the law-firm bill.
What MyCaseworks does
MyCaseworks is a document-preparation and attorney-matching platform built for international students and immigrants navigating the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom. We prepare the paperwork — visa forms, tenancy reviews, sponsorship packets — and a licensed attorney reviews it before you file.
We charge flat fees that are a fraction of traditional hourly legal billing. The legal advice in any MyCaseworks service comes from a licensed attorney through their own practice; MyCaseworks connects you with that attorney and handles the workflow, secure document portal, and payment.
MyCaseworks is a sister site of YouSafe Consultancy , which has placed 500+ international students across 30+ countries.
How the service works
Every matter begins with a structured intake. You answer questions about your situation — country, visa type, deadlines, and concerns. Our system turns your answers into a completed document set, organized and formatted for the relevant government office or court. A licensed attorney then reviews the packet, flags risks, and returns it with comments. You can ask follow-up questions through the secure portal before you file.
We do not guarantee outcomes. Immigration and tenancy outcomes depend on government discretion, facts we do not control, and changes in law. What we do guarantee is thorough preparation, attorney review, and clear communication about what we found.
Who reviews the documents
For US student-status and work-authorisation guides, MyCaseworks works with Denise Platter Cabrera, Esq. (CA Bar #298948; Law Office of Denise P. Cabrera). She independently reviews F-1, CPT, OPT, and STEM OPT procedure articles for legal accuracy. Review is paid for time, not for outcomes or for steering readers toward paid services. See her firm site .
Reviewer programs for UK matters (SRA-regulated solicitors) and Canadian matters (provincial law-society lawyers) are under development. Until those programs launch, UK and Canada articles are clearly labelled "Editorial-only" at the byline. We do not present unlicensed staff as counsel of record.
Document preparation is handled by trained staff; legal review and advice on a client matter come only from the licensed attorney assigned through the platform when you book a review tier that includes attorney work.
Our editorial standards
Guides are written by subject-matter researchers from primary sources (statute, regulation, and government guidance). US student-visa cluster articles carry a named attorney reviewer where the program is live; other jurisdictions use an Editorial-only label until attorney review is assigned. In 60 seconds
The 485 PTE requirement for most Temporary Graduate (subclass 485) applications lodged on or after 23 March 2024 is PTE Academic overall 57 , with at least 43 in each of listening, reading, writing, and speaking.
Your test must usually be taken in the 12 months immediately before the day you lodge the 485 application (not the older three-year window).
Home Affairs accepts PTE Academic for this pathway; confirm the exact test product name on your score report before you book or upload evidence.
Passport holders from the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, New Zealand, or the Republic of Ireland are generally not required to sit an English test for English ability on this visa.
English is only one 485 criterion. You still need the correct stream, Australian study requirement, skills or qualification settings where relevant, health, character, and other lodgement rules.
The 485 PTE requirement for most Temporary Graduate (subclass 485) applications lodged on or after 23 March 2024 is PTE Academic overall 57 , with at least 43 in each of listening, reading, writing, and speaking.
Your test must usually be taken in the 12 months immediately before the day you lodge the 485 application (not the older three-year window).
Home Affairs accepts PTE Academic for this pathway; confirm the exact test product name on your score report before you book or upload evidence.
Passport holders from the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, New Zealand, or the Republic of Ireland are generally not required to sit an English test for English ability on this visa.
English is only one 485 criterion. You still need the correct stream, Australian study requirement, skills or qualification settings where relevant, health, character, and other lodgement rules.
The 485 PTE requirement is the minimum Pearson Test of English Academic score Home Affairs currently uses for Temporary Graduate visa English ability when you are not passport-exempt. Read the score, validity window, and evidence rules before you lodge.
Subclass 485 is Australia’s Temporary Graduate visa. It lets certain international graduates stay temporarily after eligible Australian study. English ability sits beside the Australian study requirement, stream-specific rules, identity, health, and character. Getting the English piece wrong can stall a valid lodgement or lead to a refusal on the papers, so treat the test like any other mandatory criterion: correct product, correct scores, correct date, correct upload.
This guide explains how the 485 PTE requirement works in practice, how it compares with IELTS and other accepted tests, what documents to keep, and where applicants commonly misread the rules. It is educational only. Always check the live Department of Home Affairs pages and the instrument in force on your lodgement day, because legislative instruments and policy wording can change.
What the 485 PTE requirement means under Home Affairs rules
English ability for subclass 485 is set by the Migration Regulations and related legislative instruments administered by the Department of Home Affairs. For applications made on or after 23 March 2024, the department raised the English standard that applies to Temporary Graduate visas. The practical effect is a higher overall score and higher minimum component floors than many students planned for under the previous settings.
When you use PTE Academic to meet that standard, you need:
An overall score at or above the published threshold; and
A minimum score in each of the four communicative skills (listening, reading, writing, speaking) at or above the published floor.
Meeting the overall score alone is not enough if one skill sits under the floor. The reverse is also true: strong skill scores do not replace a short overall result. Case officers assess the score report against the instrument and policy in force for your application date.
Home Affairs publishes the accepted tests and score tables on its English language and Temporary Graduate visa pages. Primary references include:
Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485): https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-listing/temporary-graduate-485 
English language requirements overview: https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/help-support/meeting-our-requirements/english-language 
Policy manuals and legislative instruments can refine definitions of competent English and visa-specific thresholds. Your lodgement date controls which table applies. If you sat PTE under an older plan (for example, overall 50 with lower skill floors that once aligned to a different competent-English setting), do not assume that report still works for a 485 lodged after the March 2024 uplift.
Streams still share the English gate
Subclass 485 has more than one stream. Names and settings have been reformed over time, including Post-Higher Education Work and Post-Vocational Education Work pathways, plus related second or subsequent settings where available. English ability is a common gate across the Temporary Graduate framework unless a specific exemption applies to you (most often passport-based).
Stream choice still matters for:
The qualification level and field you rely on
Whether a skills assessment or occupation list logic applies to your pathway
Age limits and application timing after course completion
How long a grant may run if the application succeeds
English does not replace those rules. It sits beside them. A strong PTE score does not fix an incomplete Australian study requirement or a stream mismatch.

A 485 visa document checklist is the set of identity, English, study, health, and character files you attach when applying for Australia’s Temporary Graduate (subclass 485) visa.
Gathering papers before you open ImmiAccount reduces incomplete lodgements. The Department of Home Affairs assesses Temporary Graduate applications against the Migration Regulations and the instrument in force on your lodgement date. Your job is to match every answer on the form with a clear, consistent document. Outcomes and processing times vary by stream, country of passport, and case complexity.
This guide walks through what to prepare, why each item matters, and how to keep names, dates, and scores aligned across the file. It is educational only. It is not legal advice and does not predict any result.
What the 485 visa document checklist covers
Subclass 485 lets certain international graduates stay in Australia temporarily after study. Two main streams sit under the current framework: Post-Higher Education Work and Post-Vocational Education Work. Stream names and criteria have changed over recent years, so always read the live page for Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485) on the Home Affairs site before you finalise your pack: https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-listing/temporary-graduate-485 .
Your checklist is not a single government PDF with one fixed list for every person. Evidence depends on your stream, age, study history, family members, and whether you already hold another Australian visa. Core categories still repeat across most primary applications:
Identity and travel documents
English language evidence
Australian study requirement evidence
Skills or qualification evidence where the stream requires it
Health insurance (adequate cover in Australia)
Character documents (police certificates and disclosures)
Relationship and dependent documents if family members apply
Forms, declarations, and fee payment records inside ImmiAccount
Secondary applicants (subsequent entrants or family included in the same application) need their own identity and character files plus proof of the relationship to the primary graduate.
Start with the official stream pages and the document checklist prompts inside ImmiAccount. Those prompts change when policy instruments change. Treat this article as a preparation map, then confirm against the live system on the day you lodge.
Identity documents for your 485 application
Passport biographic pages sit at the centre of the file. Scan the page that shows your photo, full name, date of birth, nationality, and passport number. If you hold more than one passport, disclose that fact and upload the relevant pages. Name order must match your ImmiAccount profile, your English test registration, and your academic transcripts.
Birth certificates help when the passport alone does not show parent details needed for family applications. If your birth certificate is not in English, include a professional translation. Translators should state their credentials on the translation. Keep the original-language scan and the English version together in one clearly labelled PDF where possible.
National identity cards, where your country issues them, can support identity when requested. They do not replace a valid passport for travel or for most visa identity checks.
Change-of-name documents matter if any study, English, or police record uses a former name. Marriage certificates, deed poll documents, or official name-change extracts should appear in the upload set with a short cover note listing every name variant used across your evidence.
Photograph requirements follow the ImmiAccount upload rules at lodgement. Use a recent colour photo that meets the size and background guidance shown in the system. Do not crop a passport scan and call it a photo unless the portal accepts that format for your case type.
Expiry dates deserve a hard look. A passport that expires soon can create travel and bridging complications even when the visa application itself is still under assessment. Renew early if your passport life is short, then update ImmiAccount with the new biographic page.
English evidence on the 485 visa document checklist
English is one of the highest-scrutiny parts of many 485 files. You must meet the English requirement that applies to your stream and lodgement date. Thresholds are set in legislative instruments and can differ from student visa scores you used years earlier.
Accepted tests commonly include IELTS, PTE Academic, TOEFL iBT, Cambridge English, and OET, subject to the instrument in force. Confirm the current list and minimum scores on the Home Affairs English language page: https://immi.homea

Australia student visa restrictions are the conditions attached to your subclass 500 grant.
They cover work hours, study load, attendance, and health cover. You must meet them to keep your visa valid.

What the restrictions cover
What is the australia student visa restrictions set? It is the list of conditions printed on your visa grant letter.
Home Affairs attaches these to every subclass 500 grant. You must follow them for as long as you hold the visa.
The australia student visa restrictions for international students fall into three main areas.
Work limits: You can work up to 48 hours per fortnight while your course is in session.
During scheduled course breaks, you can work unlimited hours. A fortnight counts from Monday to Sunday.
The limit applies to all paid work, including casual jobs.
Study load: You must stay enrolled in a full-time course. Your education provider reports your enrolment to the department.
If you drop below a full-time load without approval, your visa can be cancelled. Changing providers also requires a new Confirmation of Enrolment.
Attendance and progress: You must attend classes and make satisfactory progress. Your provider monitors this and can report you if you fall behind.
Cancellation becomes possible after a provider report.
Address changes: You must tell your education provider your address within 7 days of changing it. In this case, Your provider passes this to the department.
Note: Your visa grant letter lists your exact conditions. Read it carefully. Conditions vary by course and provider.
Eligibility requirements
Do you need a compliance plan before you apply? Yes, because eligibility starts with understanding the conditions you will accept.
In this case, The australia student eligibility rules come from the Department of Home Affairs.
These are the australia student requirements you must meet:
Enrolment: You need a Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE) from an approved education provider. It issues this after you accept an offer and pay any required deposit.
Genuine student requirement: You must show you intend to study genuinely in Australia. Officers assess your circumstances, ties to your home country, and reasons for choosing your course.
Financial capacity: You must prove you can pay for your course, travel, and living costs. The current figure is about AUD 29,710 per year for a single student.
English language: You must meet the English requirement for your course. Most providers accept IELTS, TOEFL, or PTE results. Check your provider's specific score.
Health insurance: You need Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) for your entire stay. Your provider may arrange this for you.
Health and character: You must pass health examinations and character checks. These checks happen during processing.
Is it possible to australia student visa restrictions be waived? In limited cases, yes.
For example, you can apply to work more hours if you are in certain sectors. But most conditions stay fixed.
You cannot change your study load without provider approval.
Note: Eligibility rules change. Check the current guidance on the official student visa page at https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-listing/student-500 before you apply.
Documents you need
The requirements for a compliance plan start with your documents.
As a result, The australia student documents list is shorter than many applicants expect. Gather everything before you lodge.
Passport: Your passport must be valid for the duration of your planned stay. Border officers check this on arrival.
Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE): Your provider issues this after you accept your offer. You need the CoE code for your application.
Financial evidence: Bank statements, loan approval letters, or sponsor letters showing you can cover tuition, travel, and living costs. The amount depends on your course length and location.
English test results: IELTS, TOEFL, or PTE scores that meet your provider's requirement. Keep the original test report.
OSHC policy: Proof of Overseas Student Health Cover for your whole stay. Your provider may include this in your offer.
Health examination records: A medical exam may be requested during processing. You book this with an approved panel physician.
Character documents: Police clearance certificates from countries where you have lived for 12 months or more in the last 10 years.
Genuine student evidence: A statement explaining your study plans, career goals, and reasons for choosing Australia. Include ties to your home country.
Note: Use a certified translator for documents not in English. NAATI provides a list of certified translators at https://naati.com.au/.

title: From Student to PR: Australia Skilled Migration Pathways
body:
Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com
Source URL: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com/au/blog/student-to-pr-pathways/

From Student to PR: Australia Skilled Migration Pathways 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
In 60 seconds
01 Sequence: Subclass 500 → Subclass 485 → Skilled migration (189/190/491) → PR. Each step has its own eligibility requirements and time frames. 
02 The 485 visa gives you 2-4 years (depending on qualification and location) to gain Australian skilled work experience — which adds points under the points test. 
03 A two-year Australian degree gives 5 points for the Australian study requirement. Regional study adds 5 more points. PhD adds 30 total points. 
04 Graduates with health, education, or engineering qualifications are prioritised under Ministerial Direction 111, which may result in faster invitations at lower points scores. 
05 The regional 491 pathway offers 15 bonus points — making it accessible to graduates with base scores as low as 50 before nomination. 
The standard graduate-to-PR sequence
The most common pathway from student to PR follows a predictable sequence. You arrive on a subclass 500 student visa, complete your course (minimum two academic years to satisfy the Australian study requirement), then apply for a Temporary Graduate subclass 485 visa. The 485 gives you permission to work full-time in Australia for two to four years depending on your qualification level. During this period, you gain Australian skilled work experience, improve your English test scores, and potentially obtain a skills assessment if your occupation requires one. With one to two years of Australian work experience and a competitive English score, you can lodge an Expression of Interest for skilled migration through SkillSelect.
For a detailed breakdown of how points are calculated for each visa subclass, see the skilled migration points test guide . For the regional pathway, see the subclass 491 regional visa guide . Both guides explain the specific occupation lists, evidence requirements, and invitation dynamics that apply to each subclass. Understanding which visa subclass matches your profile at each stage is essential for a smooth transition from study to permanent residence.
Which PR pathway fits your profile
Your choice of PR pathway depends on three factors: your occupation, your points score, and your willingness to live in a regional area. If your occupation is on the Medium and Long-term Strategic Skills List (MLTSSL) and you have 85+ points, subclass 189 gives you the most flexibility (no residence restrictions). If your occupation is on the MLTSSL or STSOL and you have 75-85 points, subclass 190 with state nomination (5 bonus points) is your strongest option. If your score is below 75 or your occupation is in demand regionally, subclass 491 with 15 bonus points provides the fastest invitation path.
Employer-sponsored PR through subclass 186 is an alternative path if you secure a job with an approved sponsor. This route does not use the points test — it is based on the employer's nomination and your skills. The 186 visa requires at least three years of full-time work experience (unless you qualify for the graduate stream, which has different criteria). The Temporary Skill Shortage (subclass 482) visa is a common precursor to the 186, allowing you to work for an approved sponsor for two to four years before transitioning to PR.
Understanding the points test for skilled migration
The points test is the backbone of Australia's skilled migration system for independent (subclass 189) and nominated (subclass 190 and 491) visas. You need a minimum of 65 points to lodge an EOI, but in practice most successful invitations require 75–95 points depending on the occupation and visa subclass. Points are awarded across seven categories: age (25–32 years gives the maximum 30 points), English ability (proficient — IELTS 7.0 or equivalent — gives 10 points; superior — IELTS 8.0 — gives 20 points), skilled employment experience (both overseas and in Australia), educational qualifications (PhD: 20 points, bachelor's: 15 points, diploma or trade qualification: 10 points), Australian study requirement (5 points), regional study (5 points), professional year (5 points), and state or territory nomination (5 or 15 points for subclass 190 or 491).
For international graduates, the most achievable points gains come from English proficiency and the Australian study requirement. A 25–32 year old with a bachelor's degree from an Australian institution, competent English (IELTS 6.0), and less than one year of work experience would score approximately 50 points — below the current invitation threshold. The same candidate with superior English (IELTS 8.0) and one year of Australian skilled work experience would score 75 points — competitive for many occupations. This illustrates why English improvement is the single highest-impact action for most graduates.
See the skilled migration points test guide for a full calculator and occupation-specific cutoff analysis.
Common graduate mistakes on the PR pathway
Letting the 485 visa expire without a PR strategy. The 485 has a limited validity period. Use it actively: gain skilled employment, improve your English, and lodge an EOI early. If the 485 expires and you have no pathway, your options narrow significantly.
Ignoring regional migration options. Many graduates dismiss the 491 because they want to stay in Sydney or Melbourne. The 491 offers a faster, more accessible path to PR. After three years in a regional area, you can move anywhere — the 191 does not restrict where you live post-PR.
Not obtaining a skills assessment early. A skills assessment takes months. Start the process while still on your student visa so you can lodge an EOI immediately after graduating.
Underestimating the English test improvement. Moving from IELTS 7.0 to 8.0 gives 10 additional points. For many graduates, this single step moves their score from non-competitive to competitive. B

title: Changing course or provider on a subclass 500 student visa
body:
Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com
Source URL: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com/au/changing-course-or-provider-student-visa/

Changing course or provider on a subclass 500 student visa 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
In 60 seconds
01 Current public rule: Home Affairs states that condition 8516 requires the visa holder to continue to satisfy the criteria for the grant of the visa, including enrolment in a registered course at the appropriate level. 
02 Controlling source: Department of Home Affairs (conditions 8516 and 8202), ESOS National Code 2018 (provider-transfer and release-letter rules). 
03 Main risk: Transferring to a lower-level course (lower AQF) or changing providers without a release letter within the 6-month restricted period can breach visa conditions and require a new visa application. 
The rule in plain English
Condition 8516 on the subclass 500 visa requires you to continue to satisfy the criteria for the grant of the visa. This means that if your visa was granted because you were enrolled in a specific course at a specific level, changing to a different course or provider must not cause you to stop meeting the visa criteria. The most common scenario where condition 8516 becomes an issue is when a student changes from a higher AQF level course (e.g., a Master's degree, AQF level 9) to a lower level (e.g., a Diploma, AQF level 5). In that case, the student may no longer meet the genuine temporary entrant criteria that were assessed when the visa was granted, and a new visa application may be required.
The provider transfer process is governed by the ESOS National Code 2018. Standard 7 of the National Code sets out the rules for releasing international students to transfer to another provider. If you have been enrolled in your principal course for less than six months (the "restricted period"), you need a letter of release from your current provider before the new provider can issue a CoE. If the current provider refuses release, you cannot transfer unless you meet one of the exceptions (compassionate or compelling circumstances, the provider cannot deliver the course, or the provider agrees the transfer is in your best interest).
After six months in your principal course, you do not need a release letter. You can enrol with a new provider directly, and the new provider can issue a CoE. However, condition 8516 still applies — if the new course is at a lower AQF level, you may still need a new visa. The six-month period runs from the start date of the principal course (not any preparatory or foundation course that preceded it).
Who this guide is for
Subclass 500 visa holders who are considering changing their course or education provider and want to understand the visa implications before making the change. Students who have already changed providers and want to confirm they have not breached visa conditions. Education agents and student advisers who help students navigate provider transfers within the ESOS framework.
If you are considering transferring within the first six months of your principal course, the release letter requirement is your first hurdle. Contact your current provider's international student office before enrolling with a new provider. If you transfer without a release letter, the new provider cannot issue a CoE through PRISMS, and you may be enrolled in a course that is not registered in your name — which is a breach of condition 8202 (maintaining enrolment in a registered course).
Documents and evidence to prepare
If you are requesting a release letter from your current provider, prepare: a written request explaining why you want to transfer, evidence supporting your reason (acceptable grounds under the National Code include compassionate circumstances, the provider's inability to deliver the course, or the provider's agreement that the transfer is in your best interest), a letter of offer from the new provider, and any supporting documents for compassionate claims (medical, financial, or personal).
If you are enrolling with a new provider after the restricted period, prepare: evidence of completion of six months in the principal course (attendance records, academic transcripts), the new provider's letter of offer, and a new CoE from the new provider (the new provider can issue this directly after confirming you are not in the restricted period).
If the new course is at a lower AQF level, prepare a new visa application. This requires: a valid CoE from the new provider, a new GS statement explaining why you are changing to a lower level and how it fits your career plan, updated financial capacity evidence, and a new health examination if the previous one has expired.
Deadline and risk triggers
The critical date is the six-month anniversary of your principal course start date. Before that date, you need a release letter. After that date, you do not. Check your CoE or enrolment letter for the official start date of your principal course — not including any ELICOS, foundation studies, or other preparatory courses.
The main risk is enrolling with a new provider before the release letter is issued. If the new provider issues a CoE while you are still enrolled at the old provider (within the restricted period), the PRISMS system will flag a double enrolment. This may trigger a compliance check by Home Affairs. The correct sequence is: obtain the release letter first, the old provider cancels the CoE in PRISMS, then the new provider issues a new CoE.
A second risk is assuming the visa can be transferred to a new course like a ticket. The visa remains the same — it is not "transferred" to the new provider. If the new course is at a lower AQF level or a significantly different field of study, you may need a new visa application. Check with Home Affairs or a registered migration agent before making the change.

English is one part of a wider application that also needs completion evidence, health insurance, and character checks.
A refusal is final, and the application fee is not refunded, so a pre-submission check matters.
The 485 visa is a temporary graduate visa that allows international students to live and work in Australia after completing their studies. You must meet the English language proficiency standards to be eligible for this visa. In this guide, we will walk you through the 485 visa English requirements, accepted tests, and scores.
The 485 visa requires you to demonstrate English language proficiency
Accepted tests include IELTS, TOEFL, PTE, and OET
Minimum scores vary depending on the test and the stream of the visa
You must meet the English language requirement within the specified timeframe
The English language requirement is a critical component of the 485 visa application
The 485 visa English requirement is a crucial aspect of the application process. The Australian Government requires you to demonstrate a certain level of English language proficiency to ensure you can integrate into Australian society and participate in the workforce.
Who this is for / Who it is not for
The 485 visa English requirement is for international students who have completed their studies in Australia and wish to live and work in the country. It is not for students who have not completed their studies or for those who are not eligible for the 485 visa. Additionally, applicants who are citizens of certain countries, such as the United Kingdom, Canada, or the United States, may be exempt from the English language requirement.
English Language Proficiency Tests
The Australian Government accepts several English language proficiency tests for the 485 visa, including:
IELTS (International English Language Testing System)
TOEFL (Test of English as a Foreign Language)
PTE (Pearson Test of English)
OET (Occupational English Test)
Each test has its own scoring system and requirements. You must achieve the minimum score required for your chosen test to meet the English language requirement.
Minimum Scores for 485 Visa English Requirement
The minimum scores for each test are as follows:
IELTS: overall score of 6, with no band less than 5
TOEFL: overall score of 64, with no band less than 4
PTE: overall score of 50, with no band less than 36
OET: overall score of B, with no band less than B
You must meet the minimum score requirement for your chosen test to be eligible for the 485 visa.
Eligibility / Requirements
To be eligible for the 485 visa, you must meet the following requirements:
Meet the English language requirement
Have completed an eligible qualification in Australia
Have a valid passport
Meet the health and character requirements

02 Core question: Is study the primary purpose for entering and staying in Australia? 
03 Main risk: Generic or template answers. GS statements that could apply to any student applying to any course are automatically weaker than specific, personalised answers. If your GS statement does not mention the exact course name, the provider’s location, and the specific skills you will gain, rewrite it before lodging. 
Answer the actual GS questions
Explain current circumstances, why the course and provider make sense, how the study fits the applicant’s background, and what practical outcome the qualification supports.
Use facts instead of slogans
Course units, accreditation, location, employment progression, sponsor relationship, and prior study records are stronger than generic statements about Australia being a high-quality education destination.
Check the contradictions before filing
Look for unexplained course downgrades, sudden field changes, missing sponsor logic, weak ties, old refusals, or documents that conflict with the GS narrative.
Related guides
If your application was refused on GS grounds, read the refusal and reapply guide . For how Ministerial Direction 111 affects processing priority and interacts with your GS assessment, read the MD111 guide .
What the GS requirement asks you to prove
The Genuine Student (GS) requirement replaced the Genuine Temporary Entrant (GTE) requirement for student visa applications lodged on or after 23 March 2024. Home Affairs states that the GS requirement focuses on whether study is the primary purpose for entering and staying in Australia, while recognising that a genuine student may later develop skills Australia needs and may choose to apply for permanent residence. The shift from GTE to GS was part of the Migration Strategy reforms announced in December 2023.
The GS requirement is assessed through a structured set of questions in the visa application form. You are asked to explain: your current circumstances, including ties to your home country, your reasons for choosing the specific course and education provider, how the course fits your academic background and career plan, and the value of the course to your future. The case officer assesses whether your answers are consistent with the supporting documents in your file, including financial evidence, academic records, and prior visa history.
The GS requirement does not ask you to prove you will leave Australia. Unlike the GTE, it explicitly acknowledges that a genuine student may later explore work or migration options. However, if your file makes it look like study is incidental to a primary work or migration goal, the GS requirement will not be met. The key question is: is the study plausible as the main reason for this visa application?
Document preparation for GS evidence
When gathering evidence for your GS statement, pay attention to validating educational credentials from your home country. Degree certificates, transcripts, and professional qualifications may need academic document verification through a recognised assessment service before the Home Affairs case officer can rely on them. If you hold a qualification from a non-English-speaking institution, arrange a certified translation and consider having it assessed against the Australian Qualifications Framework. Document attestation from the issuing authority adds credibility to your evidence packet. Each document in the GS evidence folder should directly support a specific claim in your statement — a course brochure for the industry connections claim, family registration for the ties claim, or property records for the family commitments claim — so the case officer can match every statement to its proof without cross-referencing.

If you have already received a request for further information (RFI) about your GS answers, this guide helps you identify the specific weaknesses in your response and prepare a stronger submission. If your application was refused on GS grounds, you should read the refusal and reapply guide instead, as the approach for reapplying is different from preparing an initial application.

GS statement. A written statement (up to 2 pages) addressing each of the GS questions: your current circumstances and ties to your home country, your reasons for choosing Australia as a study destination, why you chose the specific provider and course, how the course fits your academic background and career plan, and what value the qualification will bring to your future. The statement should be specific to your situation — do not use a template.

This can include: employment records (payslips, employer letters, contracts), property ownership documents, family records (marriage certificates, birth certificates of children staying behind), business registration documents, or evidence of ongoing financial commitments. Ministerial Direction 111: student visa priority & CoE 2026

01 Current public rule: Home Affairs processes student visa applications according to Ministerial Direction No. 111, which assigns priority tiers based on the education provider and the applicant’s enrolment. 
02 Controlling source: Department of Home Affairs Ministerial Direction No. 111 (in force from December 2024, replacing MD107). 
03 Main risk: Choosing a high-risk or over-allocation provider can slow processing, but the visa criteria themselves are not affected by MD111. 
What Ministerial Direction 111 does
Ministerial Direction No. 111 is a direction issued by the Minister for Immigration under section 67 of the Migration Act 1958. It tells Home Affairs how to prioritise the processing of student visa applications. It does not change the legal criteria for the visa — the Genuine Student test, financial capacity, English language, health, and character requirements remain the same. What MD111 changes is the order in which applications are processed when the department faces resource constraints or high application volumes.
MD111 replaced the previous Ministerial Direction No. 107 in December 2024. The key change was a shift to a more granular, tiered priority system based on the education provider’s risk profile and the percentage of Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE) allocations the provider has used. Applications from lower-risk providers with available CoE capacity are processed first. The Direction reflects the government’s policy of directing student visa processing toward providers with strong compliance records and genuine student outcomes.
MD111 does not give you a right to faster processing. If your application is complete and meets all criteria, it will eventually be processed regardless of the priority tier. But processing times for applications in lower priority tiers can be significantly longer — in some cases, months longer than the published median processing time. If you are planning your study start date, factor in potential processing delays based on your provider profile.
Who this guide is for
Prospective international students who have applied or are about to apply for a subclass 500 student visa and want to understand how processing priority works. Current student visa holders who are applying for a subsequent visa (e.g., extending their stay for a second course) and want to anticipate processing time. Education agents and advisers who help students choose providers and plan visa timelines.
If you are applying to a well-established Australian university with a strong compliance record, MD111 likely works in your favour — your application will be processed at a higher priority. If you are applying to a private college or a newer provider, you may face slower processing. Ask the provider about their recent visa processing times for students from your country before committing to enrolment.
Documents and evidence to prepare
MD111 does not add any new document requirements beyond what the subclass 500 visa already requires. Your CoE confirms your provider and course — this is the key document that determines your processing priority under MD111. A valid CoE from a registered CRICOS provider is required for the application regardless of MD111.
However, because MD111 may lengthen processing times, you should ensure all other documents are valid for a longer period. English language test results are typically valid for 2 years. Health examination results (HAP ID) are valid for 12 months. If your documents expire while processing is pending, Home Affairs may request fresh evidence, further delaying the decision. Submit documents with maximum remaining validity when possible.
Your GS statement should explain why you chose the specific provider and course. Under MD111, consistency between your GS answers and your provider choice is relevant to the genuineness assessment. If you chose a high-risk provider without a credible academic or career reason, the GS assessment may be affected. Explain your provider choice in the GS statement as part of the broader study and career plan.
Deadline and risk triggers
MD111 does not create new deadlines, but it affects your planning timeline. If your provider is in a lower processing priority tier, you may need to apply earlier to ensure a decision before your course start date. Home Affairs recommends applying at least 6-8 weeks before the course start date, but for applicants through higher-risk providers, 12-16 weeks may be more realistic.
The main risk under MD111 is starting your course before the visa is granted. If you begin studying while holding a bridging visa or a visitor visa (which does not permit study), you may breach visa conditions. Wait for the visa grant before enrolling in classes or attending lectures. If the visa decision is delayed and the course start date passes, contact your provider to defer your start date.
A second risk is relying on the published median processing time for your provider category. The median masks significant variation — some applications are processed in days, while others take months. Check the actual processing times published monthly by Home Affairs for your specific provider and application type (onshore vs offshore).

01 Combined application: You lodge a single application for both the 820 (temporary) and 801 (permanent) visas. The 820 is assessed first; the 801 is assessed two years after lodgement. 
02 The four relationship pillars: Financial aspects, nature of the household, social aspects, and nature of the commitment. Evidence must cover all four pillars and span the entire relationship — from the start of the relationship to the date of application. 
03 Onshore requirement: The applicant must be in Australia at the time of lodgement and at the time of grant for both stages (with some COVID-era exceptions now phased out). 
04 Sponsor obligations: The Australian sponsor must provide police checks, evidence of citizenship or permanent residence, and a signed sponsorship undertaking. Sponsorship is limited to two people in a lifetime, with a five-year gap between sponsorships. 
05 Processing time: Home Affairs publishes current processing times — the 820 stage typically takes 12-24 months. A Bridging visa A is granted automatically on lodgement for applicants who hold a substantive visa, allowing them to remain lawfully in Australia until a decision. Applicants who are unlawful at lodgement receive a Bridging Visa C or E instead, which may not include work rights. 
The two-stage structure: 820 then 801
The onshore partner visa is a combined application. You submit one application and pay one fee. Home Affairs assesses the subclass 820 (temporary) stage first. If satisfied the relationship is genuine and continuing, and all other criteria are met, the 820 is granted. Two years after the date of the original application (not the date of 820 grant), Home Affairs assesses the 801 (permanent) stage. At that point, you provide updated evidence that the relationship is still genuine and ongoing.
The two-stage structure means the evidence you submit at lodgement must be strong enough for the 820, and you must maintain records throughout the two-year waiting period for the 801 assessment. Many applicants submit strong 820 evidence but fail to continue documenting the relationship after lodgement — and then struggle to produce updated evidence for the 801 stage. Keep collecting joint bills, updated photographs, joint travel records, and statements from friends throughout the waiting period.
Who this guide is for
People already in Australia who are in a genuine relationship with an Australian citizen, permanent resident, or eligible New Zealand citizen and want to apply for permanent residence through the partner visa pathway. Couples who are engaged or newly married and want to understand the evidence standard before applying. Applicants whose circumstances are more complex — recent relationship, age difference, the applicant has overstayed or holds no substantive visa — and who need to assess whether their evidence is sufficient or whether a Schedule 3 waiver is required.
If you are outside Australia, you apply for the offshore subclass 309/100 partner visa instead. This guide covers the onshore 820/801 pathway. If you are in a same-sex relationship, the same rules apply — Australia recognises same-sex marriages and de facto relationships for partner visa purposes. If you are applying as a de facto couple, you must demonstrate at least 12 months of cohabitation before lodgement, unless an exception applies (registration of the relationship under a state or territory law, or compelling and compassionate circumstances).
The four relationship pillars: what evidence proves each one
Home Affairs uses a four-pillar framework to assess whether a relationship is genuine and continuing. Each pillar needs distinct types of evidence. A common mistake is submitting strong evidence for one pillar (e.g. a joint bank account with transactions) and weak or no evidence for another (e.g. no statements from friends and family about the social aspects of the relationship).
Financial aspects. Joint bank account statements showing regular transactions, joint bills (utilities, rent) in both names, joint insurance policies, evidence of shared financial commitments (loan documents, lease agreements), and knowledge of each other's financial circumstances. A joint account that was opened one month before lodgement with minimal transactions is weak evidence — Home Affairs looks for a pattern of financial pooling over time.
Nature of the household. Evidence you live together: correspondence addressed to both partners at the same address, a lease or mortgage in joint names, household bills, and statements describing your living arrangements and division of household responsibilities. Photographs of your home and living space, with both partners present and identifiable, at different times.
Social aspects. How others perceive the relationship: statutory declarations from Australian citizen friends and family (Form 888), photographs with friends and family across different events and time periods, joint travel records, invitations addressed to both partners, and memberships in clubs or organisations that reflect the relationship. Photographs should be dated and include context — a series of selfies with no visible background or date is weaker than photographs at identifiable locations and events.
Nature of the commitment. The depth and duration of the relationship: a written relationship statement from each partner describing how you met, how the relationship developed, your future plans together, and what you know about each other's background, family, and personal circumstances. Evidence of the length of the relationship (date of first meeting, date of commitment), the degree of companionship and emotional support, and whether you see the relationship as long-term.

Australia Skilled Work Regional Visa: Subclass 491 Path

01 15 bonus points for state/territory nomination — significantly more than 190 (5 points). Base pass mark: 65 points, but applicants with scores as low as 50 can reach 65 with nomination. 
02 Designated Regional Areas cover all of Australia except Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Gold Coast, and Perth metro. Adelaide, Hobart, Canberra, and Darwin are classified as regional. 
03 Pathway to PR: subclass 191 permanent residence after three years, requiring regional residence compliance and minimum taxable income (currently AUD 70,000/year — confirm on Home Affairs website). 
04 491 visa valid for five years. You have the full five-year validity to meet the 191 eligibility requirements. Cannot be extended — plan accordingly. 
05 Family members included in the application have work and study rights. Partner skills points (up to 10) can be claimed if the partner meets the relevant requirements. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for skilled workers whose occupation is on the relevant skilled occupation list and who are considering the regional migration pathway as a faster or more accessible route to Australian permanent residence. It covers how the 491 nomination process works, the regional residence obligations, and the steps from provisional visa to permanent residence through subclass 191. It is also useful for applicants who have a points score below the 189/190 invitation cut-off and need the additional 15 nomination points to become competitive.
This guide is not for applicants who have already decided to pursue subclass 189 or 190 and have competitive points scores for those subclasses — those applicants should focus on the points test guide for EOI strategy. It is also not for applicants seeking employer-sponsored regional visas (subclass 494 Skilled Employer Sponsored Regional) or the DAMA (Designated Area Migration Agreement) pathways, which have separate employer-nomination requirements. If you are an international graduate, read the student-to-PR pathways guide first to understand how your Australian study feeds into the different migration streams.
How the 491 visa works: nomination, points, and residence obligation
The subclass 491 visa has three eligibility pathways: state or territory government nomination, family sponsorship by an eligible relative in a designated regional area, or (in limited circumstances) a subsequent entry into the scheme through a legislative amendment. The most common pathway is state or territory nomination, which requires you to apply through the state's own nomination system and receive an invitation to apply for the 491 visa.
The 491 nomination process varies by state. Each state and territory publishes its own occupation list, nomination criteria, and application process. Some states require you to have a current EOI for the 491 subclass before applying for nomination; others require you to apply directly through the state's online portal. Key factors that states consider include: whether your occupation is in demand in the state, whether you have genuine employment prospects in the state (job offer or evidence of job searching), and your willingness to live and work in the state's regional areas (not just the capital city, even if the capital is classified as regional).
Once you hold the 491 visa, your primary obligation is to live and work in a designated regional area. Home Affairs expects genuine settlement — regular presence in the regional area, local employment or business activity, and integration into the regional community. Occasional travel outside the regional area for holidays, work trips, or personal reasons is permitted, but your primary residence and employment should be in the DRA. After three years on the 491 visa, you can apply for subclass 191 permanent residence if you meet the income and residence requirements.
Documents and evidence to prepare
Skills assessment. A positive skills assessment in an occupation on the relevant occupation list for the state you are applying to. Some states require a skills assessment at a higher level than the minimum — check the state's nomination criteria.
English test results. Test results meeting at least Competent English (IELTS 6.0 each band) — though many states require Proficient English (IELTS 7.0) for nomination. If you are claiming points for Proficient or Superior English, verify that the test scores match the claimed level.
State nomination application. Each state has its own application form and supporting documents. Common requirements include: a declaration of your intention to live and work in the state, evidence of employment prospects (job applications, industry research, employer letters), and a financial capacity declaration.
Family sponsorship evidence (if applicable). If claiming family-sponsored 491, evidence that your eligible relative (parent, sibling, child, aunt, uncle, grandparent, or cousin) lives in a designated regional area and is an Australian citizen, permanent resident, or eligible New Zealand citizen.
Resettlement evidence. After the visa is granted, you should keep: lease agreements or property ownership documents showing your address in the DRA, employment contracts and payslips from regional employers, bank statements showing local transactions, and records of community involvement (membership in local organisations, volunteer work, children's school enrolment). These documents are not required at the visa application stage but will be essential for the 191 permanent residence application.
State nomination strategy: choosing the right state
Not every state nominates every occupation. Each state publishes a skilled occupation list that specifies which occupations are eligible for nomination and under which stream (491, 190
