body:
Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com
Source URL: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com/au/renting-nsw-international-students/

Renting in NSW as an international student 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
In 60 seconds
01 Primary authority: NSW Fair Trading renting and Rental Bonds Online guidance. 
02 Core documents: Lease, condition report, bond record, rent receipts, dated photos, repair requests, and agent or landlord messages. 
03 Main risk: Informal shared housing where the student pays a head-tenant but has no clear record of bond, rent, or repair obligations. 
Confirm who you are renting from
Before paying money, identify whether you are dealing with the landlord, agent, provider, head-tenant, or a roommate. The evidence you need changes depending on that relationship.
Treat the condition report as a bond document
Take dated photos and videos before moving furniture in. Match them to the condition report and keep a copy of everything sent to the agent or landlord.
Put repairs and promises in writing
For repairs, furniture, cleaning, keys, utilities, or rent reductions, keep written messages. A verbal promise is hard to use later if the bond or repair dispute becomes formal.
The NSW renting framework for students
Renting in New South Wales is governed by the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) and the Residential Tenancies Regulation 2019. These laws apply to most residential tenancies, including students renting apartments, houses, or rooms. The key protections include: bond lodgement with NSW Fair Trading, minimum notice periods for rent increases and lease terminations, the landlord’s obligation to maintain the property in a reasonable state of repair, and the tenant’s right to a fair condition report at the start and end of the tenancy.
For international students, the most common set-up is a fixed-term lease of 6 or 12 months, followed by a periodic (month-to-month) agreement if you stay beyond the fixed term. Students living in purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) may have different rights under a licence agreement rather than a residential tenancy agreement. Check which type of agreement you have signed — the protections differ.
If you are sharing a rental property with other students, you have two possible arrangements: you may be joint tenants on the same lease (each tenant is jointly and severally liable for the full rent), or you may be a subtenant renting from a head-tenant who holds the lease. Your rights are different in each arrangement, so confirm which applies before signing anything.
Who this guide is for
International students who are renting or about to rent accommodation in New South Wales. Students living in shared housing who need to understand their rights as a tenant or subtenant. Students who are in a rental dispute and need to know what evidence to gather and where to get help.
This guide covers NSW-specific rules. If you are renting in Victoria, Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia, or the Australian Capital Territory, the rules are different — check the relevant state or territory tenancy authority for guidance.
Bond, condition reports, and rent
Rental bonds. In NSW, your rental bond must be lodged with NSW Fair Trading’s Rental Bonds Online service within 10 business days of receiving the bond payment. The bond is typically 4 weeks’ rent. Check that your bond has been lodged by searching the Rental Bonds Online database. If the agent or landlord does not lodge the bond, they are in breach of the Residential Tenancies Act.
Condition reports. The landlord or agent must provide a condition report at the start of the tenancy. You have 7 days to note any changes or damage and return the report. Take dated photos and videos of the property before moving furniture in. These photos are your most important evidence if there is a bond dispute at the end of the tenancy. Focus on areas that are commonly disputed: carpet condition, wall marks, window coverings, appliance function, and garden condition.
Rent increases. In NSW, the landlord can increase the rent once every 12 months for a periodic agreement. They must give you at least 60 days’ written notice. For a fixed-term agreement, the rent cannot be increased during the fixed term unless the agreement includes a rent increase clause. If the increase is excessive, you can apply to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT) to have the increase reviewed.
Repairs and maintenance
If a repair is needed, notify the landlord or agent in writing immediately. For urgent repairs (such as burst pipes, gas leaks, broken toilets, or electrical faults), the landlord must arrange repair within 24 hours. If they do not respond, you can authorise the repair yourself up to a value of A$1,000 and the landlord must reimburse you (check the current limit with NSW Fair Trading). For non-urgent repairs, give the landlord 14 days’ written notice. If they do not respond, you can apply to NCAT for a repair order.
Keep all records of repair requests: written messages, emails, photos of the damage, receipts for any emergency repairs, and correspondence with the landlord or agent. If the landlord fails to maintain the property and it affects your health or safety, you may be entitled to a rent reduction or lease termination.
Worked example: bond dispute prevention
Mei, a 24-year-old student from China, rented a studio apartment in Sydney for 12 months. Before moving in, she took 50 photos and three videos covering every room, including close-ups of existing marks and scratches, the condition of the carpet, and the function of appliances. She completed the condition report within 7 days and returned it to the agent with her photos attached. She paid the bond and received a confirmation from NSW Fair Trading Rental Bonds Online within 2 weeks, confirming the bond was properly lodged.
When Mei moved out, the agent claimed A$800 for carpet cleaning and wall marks. Mei provided the original condition report and her move-in photos, which showed the wall

body:

Australia Skilled Migration Points Test: 189 & 190 Visas 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
In 60 seconds
01 Minimum pass mark: 65 points. However, invitation cut-offs vary by occupation and typically range from 75 to 95 points for competitive occupations. 
02 Points categories: age (0-30), English ability (0-20), skilled employment (0-20), qualifications (0-20), specialist qualifications (0-10), Australian study (5), regional study (5), community language (5), partner skills (0-10), state nomination (5 for 190, 15 for 491). 
03 Subclass 189 requires no nomination — you can live and work anywhere in Australia. Subclass 190 requires state/territory nomination (5 bonus points) and a two-year residence obligation. 
04 EOIs remain valid for two years. Update your EOI if your circumstances change (new English test, more work experience, new qualification) — Home Affairs will use the highest valid score at the time of each round. 
05 Occupation ceilings apply: each occupation has a maximum number of invitations per program year. Check the current occupation ceiling list before deciding which occupation to nominate in your skills assessment. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for skilled workers who have a valid skills assessment in an occupation on the relevant skilled occupation list (MLTSSL for 189; MLTSSL or STSOL for 190) and are preparing to lodge an Expression of Interest through SkillSelect. It covers how points are calculated, how the EOI system prioritises applicants, and how state nomination affects your score and obligations.
This guide is not for applicants who have not yet obtained a skills assessment — you must have a positive skills assessment from a relevant assessing authority before you can lodge an EOI. It is also not for applicants seeking employer-sponsored visas (subclass 482 or 186) or the Global Talent visa (subclass 858), which have separate eligibility frameworks outside the points test. If you are an international graduate exploring student-to-PR pathways, start with the student-to-PR pathways guide for the broader migration map before focusing on the points test.
How the points test works in practice
The points test is a self-assessment system. You claim points across seven categories when you lodge your EOI through SkillSelect. Home Affairs does not verify your claimed points at the EOI stage — verification happens after you receive an invitation to apply for the visa. If your claimed points are not supported by the evidence you submit with the visa application, the visa will be refused. Overclaiming points (inadvertently or otherwise) is one of the most common refusal reasons at the visa application stage.
Your points score at the time of invitation is locked in. If you turn 33 between the EOI and the visa application, your age points do not change — the score used is the score at the date of invitation. The same rule applies to English test expiry: if the test expires between invitation and visa application, the score at invitation date is used as long as the test was valid at that date.
Invitations are issued in descending points order within each occupation group. If two applicants have the same score, the applicant with the earlier EOI lodgement date (date of effect) receives the invitation first. This means lodging a complete EOI as early as possible — even at 65 points — establishes your place in the queue. If the invitation cut-off drops later in the program year, you may receive an invitation even if your initial score was below the cut-off in earlier rounds.
Points categories in detail
Age (0-30 points): 18-24 years: 25 points. 25-32 years: 30 points (maximum). 33-39 years: 25 points. 40-44 years: 15 points. 45 years and over: 0 points (not eligible). The age calculation is based on the applicant's age at the date of invitation, not the date of EOI lodgement.
English ability (0-20 points): Competent English (IELTS 6.0 each band): 0 points. Proficient English (IELTS 7.0 each band): 10 points. Superior English (IELTS 8.0 each band): 20 points. The test must be taken within three years of the visa application date. Only approved tests (IELTS, PTE Academic, Cambridge C1, OET, TOEFL iBT) are accepted.
Skilled employment (0-20 points): Overseas employment: 3-4 years (5 points), 5-7 years (10 points), 8+ years (15 points). Australian employment: 1-2 years (5 points), 3-4 years (10 points), 5+ years (15 points). Employment must be in the nominated occupation or a closely related skilled occupation. The experience must be post-qualification and paid at market rate.
Qualifications (0-20 points): Diploma or trade qualification: 10 points. Bachelor's degree (including honours): 15 points. Doctorate: 20 points. The qualification must be from an Australian institution or assessed as comparable to the Australian level by the relevant assessing authority.
Specialist qualifications (0-10 points): 10 points for a Doctorate from an Australian institution or a qualification assessed as comparable to an Australian Doctorate. These points are in addition to the standard qualification points — a PhD holder receives both the Doctorate points (20) and the specialist qualification points (10) for a possible total of 30 points from education alone.
Other factors (0-20 points): Australian study requirement (5 points) — at least two academic years (92 weeks) of study in Australia resulting in a degree, diploma, or trade qualification. Regional study (5 points) — study at a campus in a designated regional area that also satisfies the Australian study requirement. Community language (5 points) — accredited NAATI credential at the paraprofessional level or above. Partner skills (0-10 points) — partner must meet age, English, and skills assessment requirements. State nomination (5 or 15 points) — 5 points for 190 nomination, 15 points for 491 nomination.

Australia Skills Assessment: Engineers, ACS & VETASSESS

01 A positive skills assessment with a valid reference number is mandatory before submitting any GSM Expression of Interest through SkillSelect. 
02 Six major assessing authorities cover most skilled occupations: Engineers Australia, ACS (ICT), VETASSESS (professional and managerial), ANMAC (nursing), AITSL (teaching), TRA (trades). 
03 The 'deemed skilled date' on your outcome letter determines which years of employment count toward the points test. ACS and VETASSESS deduct years for pre-qualification or below-skill-level employment. 
04 Most skills assessments are valid for 3 years. If the assessment expires while your EOI is in the pool, you must obtain a new one — an invitation issued on an expired assessment is invalid. 
05 The ANZSCO occupation code on your skills assessment, EOI, and visa application must match exactly. You cannot nominate a different occupation than the one assessed. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for skilled professionals planning to apply for a General Skilled Migration visa (subclass 189, 190, or 491) who need to understand the skills assessment process. It covers the six major assessing authorities, what each evaluates, how deduction rules work, common evidence requirements, and what to do if an assessment is negative or expires while in the SkillSelect pool. It is also relevant for anyone whose EOI has not been invited and who suspects their points calculation may be incorrect because of an employment deduction they did not account for.
This guide is not for employer-sponsored visa applicants (subclass 482, 186, 494) — employer-sponsored visas have different skills assessment requirements that are occupation- and stream-specific. It is not a substitute for the assessment guidelines published by each assessing authority on their own website — those guidelines are the controlling documents for the evidence requirements specific to your occupation. Always read your authority's current guidelines before preparing your evidence package, as requirements change periodically.
The skills assessment landscape: who assesses what
Each ANZSCO occupation is assigned to one designated assessing authority. You cannot choose which authority to use — the Department of Home Affairs assigns each occupation to a specific authority, and that authority alone can issue a valid skills assessment for that occupation code. The six major authorities cover the vast majority of skilled migration applicants:
Engineers Australia: All professional engineering occupations (civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical, structural, software — when classified as an engineering occupation rather than ICT). Also covers engineering technologists and engineering associates. Australia is a signatory to the Washington Accord, Sydney Accord, and Dublin Accord — if your engineering degree is from an accredited programme in a signatory country, the assessment pathway is streamlined.
Australian Computer Society (ACS): All ICT occupations — software engineer (when classified as ICT), developer programmer, ICT business analyst, systems analyst, network administrator, security specialist, and related roles. ACS applies the most significant employment deduction rules of any assessing authority.
VETASSESS: The largest assessing authority by occupational coverage. Assesses most managerial, professional, and associate professional occupations not covered by a specialist authority — including marketing specialists, accountants, HR managers, architects, librarians, social workers, and hundreds of others. VETASSESS also assesses trade occupations in certain categories.
ANMAC (Australian Nursing and Midwifery Accreditation Council): All nursing and midwifery occupations. Requires registration with the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) or an equivalent registration pathway.
AITSL (Australian Institute for Teaching and School Leadership): All teaching occupations — early childhood, primary, and secondary. Requires a teaching qualification that includes a supervised teaching practice component.
TRA (Trades Recognition Australia): Trade occupations — electricians, plumbers, carpenters, chefs, motor mechanics, and other skilled trades. Assessment pathways include the Job Ready Program (for onshore applicants) and the Migration Skills Assessment (for offshore applicants).
Other specialist assessing authorities exist for specific occupations — for example, the Australian Psychological Society (APS) for psychologists, the Australian Institute of Medical Scientists (AIMS) for medical laboratory scientists, and the Australasian Veterinary Boards Council (AVBC) for veterinarians. If your occupation is not covered by one of the six major authorities, check the Home Affairs skilled occupation list, which identifies the assessing authority for each ANZSCO code.
Engineers Australia: CDR, accredited qualifications, and the Accords
Engineers Australia assesses professional engineers, engineering technologists, and engineering associates. The assessment pathway depends on whether your qualification is from an accredited programme:
Accredited qualifications (Accord pathway): If your engineering degree is from a programme accredited under the Washington Accord (professional engineer), Sydney Accord (engineering technologist), or Dublin Accord (engineering associate) in a signatory country, the assessment is streamlined. You submit your degree certificate, transcript, and proof of accreditation. No Competency Demonstration Report (CDR) is required.
Non-accredited qualifications (CDR pathway): If your degree is not from an Accord-accredited programme — or if the accreditation status is unclear — you must submit a Competency Demonstration Report. The CDR consists of three career episodes, each d

Student PR in Australia: 485 to 189/190/491 & SID 482

01 Current public rule: Home Affairs offers several skilled migration pathways from a student visa: Temporary Graduate (485), Skilled Independent (189), Skilled Nominated (190), Skilled Work Regional (491), and the Skills in Demand visa (482). 
02 Controlling source: Department of Home Affairs skilled migration pages, points test, Skills in Demand (482) visa page, and skilled occupation lists. 
03 Main risk: Assuming a study course leads to PR when the occupation is not on the relevant skilled list or the points score falls short of the invitation threshold. 
The PR pathway map in plain English
The standard student-to-PR pathway in Australia has four steps: complete an Australian qualification (minimum 2 academic years for most pathways), apply for the Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485) to gain work experience and prepare for skilled migration, meet the points test threshold or secure employer sponsorship, and lodge a skilled migration visa application (subclass 189, 190, 491) or an employer-sponsored visa (subclass 482 transitioning to ENS 186). Each step depends on having your occupation on the relevant skilled occupation list at that time.
The subclass 485 Temporary Graduate visa is the bridge between study and skilled migration. It gives you 2-4 years (depending on your qualification level and passport) to work in Australia, gain skilled experience, complete a skills assessment, and improve your points score. During the 485 period, you should: complete a skills assessment with the relevant assessing authority for your occupation, achieve competent or proficient English (higher than the 485 minimum), gain skilled employment experience that counts toward points, and research state nomination opportunities (for 190/491) if your occupation is on the state's list.
The skilled migration pathways form a hierarchy. The subclass 189 (Skilled Independent) is the most flexible — no employer or state ties — but requires the highest points score. The subclass 190 (Skilled Nominated) adds 5 points and has lower invitation thresholds but requires you to live and work in the nominating state. The subclass 491 (Skilled Work Regional) has the lowest invitation thresholds but requires 3 years in a regional area before you can transition to permanent residence. The new Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482) replaces the TSS and offers a direct employer sponsorship route if you find an approved sponsor.
Who this guide is for
Current subclass 500 student visa holders who are planning their post-study work and PR strategy. Prospective students who are deciding which course to study based on PR outcomes and want to understand which occupations and pathways are realistic. Temporary Graduate 485 visa holders who are in the work-rights period and need to plan their next steps toward PR.
This is a map and orientation page — it covers the structure of the pathways and how they connect. For the detailed 485 eligibility and documents, use the 485 checklist . For English language thresholds for each pathway, read the English requirements guide .
Documents and evidence to prepare
The documents you need depend on the specific pathway, but common requirements across skilled migration visas include: skills assessment from the relevant assessing authority for your nominated occupation, English language test results at the level required for your pathway (competent, proficient, or superior), evidence of skilled employment (employment references, payslips, tax returns), educational qualification certificates and academic transcripts (Australian and any overseas), and a valid passport.
For state-nominated pathways (190, 491), also prepare: evidence of your connection to the state (study, work, or family ties), state nomination application documents (varies by state — check the state's migration website), and a commitment to live and work in the nominating state. For the Skills in Demand 482 and the employer-sponsored pathway (186), prepare: employer sponsorship documents, a Labour Market Testing report (if required), and a skills assessment for the nominated occupation.
If you are seeking points for a partner, prepare: your partner's skills assessment and English test results (for extra points), evidence of your de facto or married relationship (shared finances, joint tenancy, correspondence), and your partner's passport and birth certificate.
Deadline and risk triggers
Each visa subclass has its own deadlines and processing times. The subclass 485 must be applied for within 6 months of completing your Australian qualification (or within 12 months for some post-COVID concessions — check current rules). Invitation rounds for the subclass 189 and 190 are held periodically — you need to submit an Expression of Interest (EOI) through SkillSelect and wait for an invitation. The points score at which you receive an invitation changes based on the occupation and round.
The main risk is relying on the skilled occupation list staying stable. Occupation lists are reviewed and updated by Home Affairs periodically. An occupation that is on the list today may be removed or capped when you are ready to apply. Mitigate this risk by monitoring the occupation lists regularly, choosing occupations that have been consistently in demand, and having a backup pathway if your primary occupation is removed.
A second risk is the age points cliff. Points for age decline significantly after 33 (from 30 points at age 25-32 to 25 points at age 33-39, and 15 points at age 40-44). If you are over 45, you cannot apply for most skilled migration visas at all. Plan your study-to-PR timeline with your age in mind — if you are an older student, consider faster pathways like employer sponsorship or regional migration.

01 Condition 8105 (work): Up to 48 hours per fortnight when your course is in session. Unlimited hours during scheduled course breaks. Work that is a formal registered part of your course (e.g. work placement, internship required for completion) does not count toward the limit. 
02 Condition 8202 (study): Remain enrolled in a registered course (8202(1)), maintain satisfactory academic progress (8202(2)), and do not change to a course at a lower AQF level than the course for which the visa was granted unless an exception applies. 
03 Condition 8501 (health): Maintain adequate health insurance (OSHC) for the entire period of your stay, with no gaps in cover. Your dependants must also be covered. 
04 Condition 8533 (notification): Notify your education provider of your residential address within 7 days of arriving in Australia, and notify them of any change of address within 7 days of moving. Also keep your contact details current in ImmiAccount. 
05 Breach consequences: Condition breaches can result in visa cancellation, a three-year exclusion period, and adverse impact on future Australian visa applications. Minor or inadvertent breaches may result in a warning; systematic breaches lead to cancellation. 
Why visa conditions matter
Your subclass 500 visa grant letter lists the conditions that apply to your visa. These are legal obligations under the Migration Act 1958 — they are not suggestions or guidelines. Breaching a visa condition can lead to visa cancellation, detention, and removal from Australia. Even if you are not immediately detected, a condition breach discovered during a subsequent visa application (e.g. a 485 or skilled migration visa) can result in refusal on character or compliance grounds.
The four conditions that most commonly affect international students are: 8105 (work limitations), 8202 (enrolment and academic progress), 8501 (health insurance), and 8533 (address notification). Each condition is monitored differently — some through data-matching with the ATO and your education provider, others through Home Affairs compliance operations and tip-offs. Understanding the specific requirements of each condition and how compliance is monitored helps you avoid inadvertent breaches.
Condition 8105: work limits and what counts as work
Condition 8105 limits you to 48 hours of work per fortnight when your course is in session. A fortnight is a 14-day period starting on a Monday. The 48-hour limit applies to all paid work, including casual employment, part-time employment, gig economy work (Uber, Deliveroo, Airtasker), and self-employment where you receive payment for services. Unpaid work, such as volunteering for a charity or participating in an unpaid internship that is not part of your course, may still count as "work" if it displaces an Australian worker or creates an employment relationship.
During scheduled course breaks, there is no limit on work hours. A scheduled break means a period published in your education provider's academic calendar as a vacation period — winter break, summer break, or mid-semester break. A week without classes that the academic calendar describes as a study or exam period is not a break. Always use the official academic calendar, not your personal class schedule, to determine when the break applies.
Work that is a formal, registered part of your course — such as a work placement, internship, or clinical placement that is required for course completion and is listed on your CoE — does not count toward the 48-hour limit. However, the placement must be a mandatory component of the course, not an optional or extra-curricular arrangement. Your provider can confirm whether a specific placement is a course requirement.
Condition 8202: enrolment, progress, and course changes
Condition 8202 has three parts. The first part — 8202(1) — requires you to remain enrolled in a registered course. If you withdraw from your course, are excluded by your provider, or let your enrolment lapse without a valid deferral or leave of absence, you breach this condition. You must be enrolled in a course at the same AQF level or higher than the course for which your visa was granted.
The second part — 8202(2) — requires you to maintain satisfactory academic progress. Your provider sets the standard for satisfactory progress and publishes it in their academic progress policy. Typically, failing more than 50% of enrolled units in a semester triggers an academic progress intervention. The provider must give you an opportunity to improve before reporting you to Home Affairs — usually through a formal intervention plan or show-cause process. If you are placed on an intervention plan, take it seriously: failing to meet the plan's requirements leads to a report to Home Affairs, which can trigger visa cancellation proceedings.
The third part — 8202(3) — prohibits you from changing to a course at a lower AQF level than the course for which the visa was granted. If you were granted a visa to study a master's degree, you generally cannot transfer to a diploma course. There are limited exceptions — for example, if the provider has assessed your academic performance and determined that a lower-level course is appropriate, or if your original course was cancelled by the provider and the only available alternative is at a lower level. Before changing courses, check the AQF levels of both courses and confirm with your provider's international student office that the change is permitted.
Condition 8501: Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC)
Condition 8501 requires you to maintain adequate health insurance for the entire period of your stay in Australia. For most international students, this means Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) from an approved provider (Bupa, Medibank

01 Primary authority: Home Affairs subclass 500 financial capacity guidance and the current legislative instrument. 
02 Evidence set: Bank statements, sponsor letters, income proof, tuition receipts, scholarships, loan letters, and translations where needed. 
03 Main risk: Money appears briefly, belongs to someone unexplained, or conflicts with the student’s declared plan. 
Expenses management and budget planning
A proper budget planning approach goes beyond meeting the minimum Home Affairs financial capacity threshold. Create a spreadsheet that accounts for all your living expenses in your chosen Australian city: rent, utilities, groceries, transport, phone plan, OSHC, textbooks, and a contingency fund. The cost of living varies significantly between Australian cities — a budget that works in Adelaide may not cover expenses in Sydney or Melbourne.
Good expenses management in your first semester sets the foundation for the rest of your studies. Track your spending weekly against your budget to identify areas where you are overspending. Build a contingency fund of at least one month of living expenses before you arrive — unexpected costs in the first week (bond payment, transport pass, phone plan, initial groceries) can quickly consume a budget that looked adequate on paper. Many Australian universities offer financial literacy workshops and budget planning tools through their international student support services — take advantage of these resources early. Keeping track of expenses using a money management app helps you stay within your fortnightly budget while also ensuring you do not accidentally breach the 48-hour work limit by working more than permitted.
Show control, source, and purpose
The officer should be able to see whose money it is, where it came from, how long it has been available, and why it is genuinely available for the student’s costs.
Match the funding file to the study file
The sponsor story should align with the course length, tuition, living arrangements, dependants, travel costs, and the applicant’s GS explanation.
Prepare a clean evidence index
Group evidence by student funds, sponsor funds, income, course costs, living costs, scholarships or loans, and translations. Do not make the reviewer reconstruct the story from scattered statements.
Related guides
For OSHC costs that need to be factored into your budget, read the health and OSHC guide . For the overall subclass 500 document timeline, use the subclass 500 checklist .
What the financial capacity requirement asks you to prove
Home Affairs requires subclass 500 applicants to demonstrate they have enough funds to cover the costs of their stay in Australia. The financial capacity requirement is set out in the Migration Regulations and the current legislative instrument. You must show you can cover: course fees for the first year of study, living costs (currently published at A$29,710 per year for the main applicant as of 2026), travel costs (return airfare to your home country), and dependant costs if applicable (education costs for school-aged children and living costs for each dependant). Check the current Home Affairs fee schedule for the exact thresholds in force at the time of your application.
The financial capacity evidence must show that the funds are genuinely available to you. This means the money must be in your account or in your sponsor’s account, and it must be accessible for your education costs. Evidence of a loan approval from a recognised financial institution is acceptable. Lump-sum deposits that appear shortly before the application are scrutinised closely — the case officer will want to know where the money came from and whether it is genuinely available or borrowed temporarily.
If you are relying on a sponsor, the sponsor must provide: a letter confirming their willingness to support you, evidence of their relationship to you, evidence of their financial capacity (bank statements, income records, tax returns, or asset documents), and evidence that the funds can be transferred to Australia. A sponsor letter without supporting financial evidence is not sufficient.
Who this guide is for
Prospective subclass 500 applicants who need to prepare financial capacity evidence that meets the Home Affairs requirements. Self-funded students who need to show their own savings or income. Students relying on family sponsors who need to organise their sponsor’s financial documents. Students with scholarships or education loans who need to confirm their funding meets the requirements.
If you have a complex financial situation — such as funds in multiple accounts, business income, assets held in a different currency, or sponsors who are not immediate family members — you should check whether additional evidence is needed before lodging your application.
Documents and evidence to prepare
Bank statements. The most common financial evidence is bank statements showing consistent deposits over at least three months. Statements should be from a recognised financial institution and show the account holder’s name, account number, transaction history, and current balance. Statements that show a sudden large deposit followed by a withdrawal pattern may raise questions about the genuineness of the funds.
Loan approval letter. If you are using an education loan, provide the loan approval letter from the financial institution showing the loan amount, approval date, and that the funds are available for your education costs. The loan amount should cover your total estimated costs for at least the first year. A loan that only covers a small portion of the costs will not be sufficient for the full financial capacity assessment.

Health requirement & OSHC for Australia student visa (2026)

01 Current public rule: Home Affairs states that condition 8501 requires the visa holder to maintain adequate health insurance (OSHC) for the duration of their stay in Australia. Health examinations are required for stays over 6 months. 
02 Controlling source: Department of Home Affairs (health requirement, OSHC, condition 8501), privatehealth.gov.au for OSHC provider information. 
03 Main risk: OSHC start or end dates not matching the visa period, dependants not covered, or health examination results expiring before the visa decision. 
The health requirement for the subclass 500 visa
Home Affairs requires all subclass 500 student visa applicants to meet the health requirement. This has two components. First, you must have adequate health insurance (Overseas Student Health Cover, or OSHC) for the entire period of your intended stay in Australia, as required by condition 8501. Second, you must undergo a health examination if you plan to stay in Australia for more than 6 months, if you are applying for a visa that specifically requires health assessment, or if you have a medical condition that may require significant treatment or care during your stay.
The health examination is arranged through Home Affairs' panel physician system. You first receive a HAP ID (Health Assessment Pointer) reference number from Home Affairs, which you use to book an appointment with an approved panel physician in your country. The physician conducts a medical examination (including a physical check, chest x-ray, and blood tests) and submits the results electronically to Home Affairs. The results are typically valid for 12 months from the date of the examination.
If you do not meet the health requirement — for example, if you have a condition that would impose significant cost on the Australian healthcare system — Home Affairs may refuse the visa. However, some health conditions can be managed with a health waiver if you have strong compelling circumstances and the cost is below the threshold set by Home Affairs. The waiver is not automatic and requires a specific application.
Who this guide is for
Prospective subclass 500 visa applicants who need to understand the health examination and OSHC requirements before applying. Current student visa holders who need to renew their OSHC or update their health examination before applying for a subsequent visa. Dependants of student visa holders who need their own health examinations and OSHC cover.
This guide covers the health requirement specifically. It does not restate the full document checklist for the subclass 500 — for the complete checklist including CoE, GS statement, financial capacity, and English evidence, use the subclass 500 document checklist .
Documents and evidence to prepare
OSHC policy documentation. The policy certificate from an approved OSHC provider showing coverage dates that span your entire intended stay. The policy must cover the main applicant and all dependants included in the visa application. Check the policy start date — it should be the date you expect to arrive in Australia (or your current visa expiry date if applying onshore). The policy end date must be after the expected visa end date.
HAP ID and health examination receipt. The HAP ID letter from Home Affairs and the appointment confirmation with the panel physician. After the examination, the panel physician provides a receipt or referral letter — keep this as evidence that the examination was completed. The results are sent directly to Home Affairs electronically.
Medical evidence if you have a pre-existing condition. If you have a pre-existing medical condition, provide specialist reports, treatment plans, and evidence that the condition is stable and manageable. This helps Home Affairs assess whether the condition would impose significant cost on the Australian healthcare system. A well-documented condition with a positive prognosis is less likely to trigger a health refusal.
Deadline and risk triggers
The health examination results are valid for 12 months. If your visa application takes longer than 12 months to process, or if you defer your studies and reapply after 12 months, you may need a new health examination. Plan your examination timing so that it will still be valid when the visa decision is expected. The OSHC policy must be purchased before the visa is granted — you cannot promise to buy it later.
The main risk is a gap in OSHC cover. Condition 8501 requires continuous cover for the entire visa period. A gap of even one day is a breach. If you change OSHC providers, ensure the new policy starts on the day the old policy ends. If you are in Australia and your OSHC lapses, Home Affairs can cancel your visa for breach of condition 8501.
A second risk is not covering dependants. If your OSHC policy only covers the main applicant but your visa application includes dependants, the application may be refused. Purchase a family OSHC policy that covers all family members included in the application. If dependants join you later, they need their own OSHC from the date they arrive.
Worked example: OSHC gap prevention
Elena, a 23-year-old student from Brazil, was granted a subclass 500 visa valid from March 2024 to March 2027. She purchased a 3-year OSHC policy from an approved provider. In September 2025, she extended her studies to a second course, which required a visa extension. When applying for the subsequent visa, Elena realised that her OSHC policy expired in March 2027 but the new visa would extend to March 2028.
Elena contacted her OSHC provider and purchased a one-year extension to cover the additional visa period before submitting the new visa application. She submitted the new OSHC certificate with the application, demonstrating continuous cover from March 2024 to

body:

Australia student visa refusal: reapply or ART review 2026 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile

Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates

In 60 seconds
01 Current public rule: Home Affairs states a refused student visa applicant can either lodge a fresh application or apply to the ART for review of the decision, subject to time limits and jurisdiction. 
02 Controlling source: Department of Home Affairs (subclass 500 refusal and review rights), Administrative Review Tribunal (which replaced the AAT in October 2024). 
03 Main risk: Reapplying without fixing the refusal reason. The most common mistake after a refusal is lodging a near-identical application and expecting a different result. Home Affairs case officers can see your application history. If the new application does not address the specific reason for the first refusal, it will likely be refused again. Take the time to understand and fix the weakness before reapplying. 
Subclass 500 refusal: what the decision record tells you
When Home Affairs refuses a subclass 500 student visa application, the decision record states the legal reasons. The most common refusal grounds are: the applicant did not meet the Genuine Student (GS) criterion, the financial capacity evidence was insufficient, the enrolment (CoE) was not valid or was cancelled, the English language requirement was not met, or the health or character requirements were not satisfied. The decision record also states whether you have review rights and the time limit for applying to the ART.
Read the decision record carefully before deciding what to do next. The refusal reason determines whether a fresh application or ART review is the better path. If the case officer found that your GS answers did not demonstrate a genuine intention to stay temporarily in Australia, a fresh application with a stronger GS statement is usually the right response. If the case officer misapplied the criteria or failed to consider evidence you submitted, ART review may be appropriate.
Home Affairs states that a fresh application is assessed independently, but applying without addressing the refusal reason is unlikely to produce a different outcome. If you reapply and the same GS officer reviews your file, they will see the previous refusal. Address the weaknesses head-on in the new application.
Who this guide is for
Onshore student visa holders whose subclass 500 application was refused and who need to decide between reapplying and seeking ART review within the time limits. Offshore applicants whose student visa was refused and who need to understand whether they have review rights and how to prepare a stronger fresh application.
If you are on a bridging visa after your student visa expired and a subsequent visa application was refused, the timing is urgent — your bridging visa may cease 28 days after the refusal decision, and you may become unlawful. This guide helps you understand the two paths available so you can act before the deadlines pass.
The decision you make next
You have two options after a subclass 500 refusal: reapply or seek ART review. The choice depends on the refusal reason, your location (onshore or offshore), and the strength of your evidence.
Option 1: Reapply. Lodge a fresh subclass 500 application with corrected evidence. This is the right choice when the refusal reason is fixable — a missing document, an incomplete GS statement, or insufficient funds evidence. A fresh application costs the same visa application fee as the first one (check the current fee on the Home Affairs fee schedule). There is no limit on how many times you can apply, but each application must be complete and meet all criteria at the time of lodgement.
Option 2: Seek ART review. Apply to the Administrative Review Tribunal for a merits review of the refusal decision. The ART (which replaced the AAT in October 2024) reviews the decision and can affirm, vary, or set it aside. If the ART sets aside the refusal, the application is remitted to Home Affairs for a fresh decision. ART review is appropriate when the case officer made a legal error, applied the wrong criteria, or failed to consider evidence you submitted.
You can do both — reapply and seek ART review — but the strategies serve different purposes. The ART reviews the decision on the first application, not the new application. The fresh application is a separate process with a separate outcome.
Documents and evidence to prepare
Whether you reapply or seek ART review, you need the following documents ready:
The decision record. The full refusal letter from Home Affairs stating the reasons for refusal. This is the most important document — it tells you exactly what needs to be fixed. If you reapplied without reading the decision record, you are guessing.
New or strengthened evidence addressing the refusal reason. If the refusal was based on the GS criterion, prepare a revised GS statement with specific, document-supported answers about your ties to your home country, your study and career plan, and your intention to comply with visa conditions. If the refusal was based on financial capacity, provide updated bank statements, loan approval letters, or sponsor evidence that meets the current financial capacity requirements published by Home Affairs.

Build the file around the decision Home Affairs has to make
The application should show that the course is real, the student understands the program and Australia as the study destination, and the evidence supports the declared plan.
Documents to gather before drafting
Prepare the CoE, passport, academic records, English evidence if required, financial capacity documents, OSHC details, prior visa history, employment or family ties evidence, and any documents requested for health or character checks.
Where students usually lose coherence
The file becomes weak when the GS answers say one thing, the course choice says another, and the bank or sponsor evidence does not clearly explain who is paying and why the funds are available.
Related guides
For detailed health examination and OSHC requirements, read the health and OSHC guide . For English language score thresholds accepted for the subclass 500, read the English requirements guide .
Core documents for the subclass 500 application
A complete subclass 500 student visa application requires several categories of evidence: identity and enrolment documents, genuine student (GS) answers and supporting evidence, financial capacity evidence, health insurance (OSHC), English language evidence, health examination results, and character evidence (police certificates). The key is not just having each document, but ensuring they tell one consistent story about your study purpose and capacity.
A valid Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE) is the foundation document for the subclass 500. Without a CoE issued by a CRICOS-registered provider, the application cannot proceed. The CoE must show your name, course details, course start and end dates, and the provider’s CRICOS code. Check the CoE against your passport name and course details before lodging. A mismatch will delay processing.
Your passport must be valid for the entire period of intended stay in Australia. If your passport is close to expiry, renew it before applying. Home Affairs does not generally require a minimum passport validity period for student visas, but a short-validity passport may result in a shorter visa grant period, requiring you to apply for a subsequent visa or passport renewal sooner.
Who this guide is for
First-time subclass 500 applicants who need a complete checklist of all required documents before lodging through ImmiAccount. Current student visa holders who are applying for a subsequent visa and need to check whether their existing documents are still valid. Education agents who prepare applications for multiple students and need a consistent filing standard.
This checklist covers the standard document requirements for a subclass 500 application. If you have a complex immigration history, a previous visa refusal, or specific health or character issues, you may need additional documents not listed here. This guide does not replace individual migration advice for complex cases.
Financial capacity evidence
Home Affairs requires evidence that you have sufficient funds to cover your course fees, living costs, travel costs, and dependant costs (if applicable) for the first year of your stay. The current cost-of-living threshold is published on the Home Affairs website and updated periodically. Your financial evidence must show that the funds are genuinely available to you and are not borrowed temporarily for the application.
Acceptable evidence includes: bank statements showing consistent deposits over at least three months, a loan approval letter from a recognised financial institution, scholarship or sponsorship letters, and evidence of income from employment or business. If a sponsor is providing the funds, include a sponsor letter, evidence of the sponsor’s identity and relationship to you, and evidence of the sponsor’s financial capacity (bank statements, income records, or asset documents).
Health and character evidence
OSHC (Overseas Student Health Cover) is required for the entire period of your intended stay in Australia. Purchase an OSHC policy from an approved provider before lodging the visa application. The policy must cover the main applicant and all dependants included in the application. Upload the OSHC certificate to ImmiAccount with your application. A health examination is also required if you plan to stay in Australia for more than six months. You will receive a Health Assessment Pointer (HAP ID) after lodging the application or requesting it through ImmiAccount.
Character evidence typically includes an Australian police check (AFP check) if you have spent 12 months or more in Australia in the last 10 years, and overseas police certificates for any country where you have spent 12 months or more cumulatively in the last 10 years. English language test results must be from an approved test provider (IELTS, PTE Academic, TOEFL iBT, or Cambridge C1 Advanced) and meet the minimum score for your course level.

Australia student visa work rights: 48 hours per fortnight

01 Current public rule: Study Australia states 48 hours per fortnight during study terms and semesters. 
02 Break periods: Study Australia states students can work unlimited hours during study breaks. 
03 Main risk: Casual shifts, overlapping payroll periods, or unclear semester dates make hour-counting harder than students expect. 
Count by fortnight, not by pay period
Rosters, payroll cycles, and visa fortnights may not line up neatly. Keep a separate hour log for study periods and another for official breaks.
Know the employment type
Full-time, part-time, and casual work have different practical records. Casual work can change week by week, so payslips and roster screenshots matter.
Separate visa compliance from workplace rights
A student can have workplace protections and still need to comply with visa work conditions. Keep evidence for both: pay, hours, contract terms, and course calendar dates.
The 48-hour fortnight rule in practice
Home Affairs states that international students on a subclass 500 student visa can work up to 48 hours per fortnight while their course is in session. A fortnight is calculated as a 14-day period starting on a Monday. The 48-hour limit applies to all paid work combined — if you work for two different employers, the hours from both count toward the same 48-hour limit.
During scheduled study breaks (semester breaks, trimester breaks, or official holidays), the 48-hour limit does not apply. Study Australia states that students can work unlimited hours during these periods. However, the definition of a study break depends on your provider’s academic calendar. Check with your education provider for the exact dates of each study period and break period.
If you are enrolled in a course that is not in session (such as during the period after completing all course requirements but before graduation), you may be considered to be on a study break and can work unlimited hours. However, if you are enrolled in a course that has continuous assessment with no scheduled breaks, the 48-hour limit applies year-round.
Who this guide is for
Current subclass 500 student visa holders who work while studying and need to stay within the 48-hour fortnight limit. Students who are considering taking on casual or part-time work and want to understand the rules before starting. Students who have received warnings from their employer or DSO about potential work-hour breaches and need to correct their record.
If you are working more than 48 hours per fortnight, you may be breaching your visa condition 8105 (or 8104 for some visa subclasses). A breach of work conditions can lead to visa cancellation under section 116 of the Migration Act. If you are concerned about your work hours, reduce them immediately and keep records of the reduction.
Documents and records to keep
Rosters and work schedules. Keep copies of your work rosters showing the days and hours you are scheduled to work. If your employer uses an online rostering system, take screenshots at regular intervals. Roster evidence helps you plan your hours in advance and avoid exceeding the 48-hour limit.
Payslips. Keep every payslip from every employer. Payslips show the actual hours worked (as distinct from rostered hours) and the payment received. If there is a discrepancy between rostered hours and payslip hours, use the payslip as the official record of hours worked.
Employment contracts. Your employment contract should state the terms of your employment, including whether you are casual, part-time, or full-time. Casual work has variable hours, so tracking your hours is especially important.
Course calendar. Keep a copy of your provider’s academic calendar showing term dates, break periods, and public holidays. This is essential for determining when the 48-hour limit applies and when it does not. If you change providers, update your calendar records.
Deadlines and risk triggers
Work rights compliance is continuous — there is no single deadline. The 48-hour limit applies every fortnight while your course is in session. If you exceed the limit in one fortnight, you must reduce your hours in the next fortnight to stay within the overall pattern. A single breach may trigger a warning from your provider’s DSO, but repeated or significant breaches can lead to visa cancellation.
The main risk is not tracking hours accurately across multiple employers. If you have two casual jobs and a side gig (such as tutoring or freelance work), all paid hours count toward the 48-hour limit. Create a simple spreadsheet or use a time-tracking app to log hours for all paid work.
A second risk is assuming that work during the COVID-era relaxation (which allowed unlimited hours in certain sectors) is still permitted. That relaxation ended. Only the standard 48-hour fortnight limit applies now unless you have a specific work limitation in your visa conditions.
A third risk is volunteer work that includes payment or benefits in kind. If you receive any payment, accommodation, or significant benefits for work, it is likely counted as employment — even if you call it volunteering. Check with Home Affairs or a registered migration agent if you are unsure whether an activity counts toward the 48-hour limit.
Worked example: tracking hours across two jobs
Liam, a 22-year-old student from Malaysia, worked as a casual waiter at a restaurant (12-20 hours per week) and as a delivery driver for a food delivery platform (8-15 hours per week). His course was in session from March to November with a four-week break in July. During term time, Liam tracked his hours using a simple notes app, logging each shift immediately after it ended. In the first week of April, he worked 28 hours at the restaurant and 18 hours for the delivery platform — a total of 46 hours for that f

What it is: A permanent residency visa for skilled workers without employer, state, or family sponsorship.
Key eligibility: Under 45 years old, occupation on the MLTSSL, positive skills assessment, Competent English, and at least 65 points.
How to apply: Submit an EOI in SkillSelect, receive an invitation, then lodge your application within 60 days.
Cost: AUD 4,640 for the main applicant (plus additional fees for family members). For the official fee schedule, refer to the Department of Home Affairs visa pricing table.
Processing time: 4-12 months for most applications. Check the latest processing times on the Department of Home Affairs processing time tool.
Document checklist deep dive
Assembling your evidence pack is where most delays occur. Treat each document as a separate verification step rather than a formality.
Your skills assessment must come from the authority listed for your occupation on the MLTSSL. A mismatch between the assessing body and the ANZSCO code is a common reason for invitations to lapse.
Check the validity window for that assessment; most remain valid for two to three years, but some authorities issue shorter periods. An expired assessment cannot be used at the lodgement stage.
According to the Department of Home Affairs skills assessment guidance , the assessment must be valid at the time of invitation.
English test results from IELTS, PTE Academic, or TOEFL iBT are typically valid for three years from the test date. If you claimed points for Superior or Proficient English, the test result must still be current on the day you lodge your application, not merely on the day you received your invitation.
The official English language requirements page lists accepted tests and validity periods.
Police clearance certificates from every country where you lived for 12 months or more in the last 10 years must be issued no earlier than 12 months before lodgement. Older certificates will be rejected outright.
Identity documents should include a certified copy of your passport bio page, a recent passport photo, and a full birth certificate.
If your name differs across documents, attach a statutory declaration explaining the change.
All copies must be certified by an authorised person, such as a justice of the peace or a notary public, to be accepted.
For partner points, you need evidence of the relationship, joint bank statements, shared lease or mortgage documents, and correspondence addressed to both of you at the same address.
Health examinations are arranged through a panel physician after you lodge, so you do not need those upfront. However, you should book the appointment promptly to avoid processing pauses.
For official health requirements, see the Department of Home Affairs health requirement page .
Step-by-step filing process
Filing for subclass 189 follows a fixed sequence, and skipping a step can reset your timeline entirely.
First, confirm your occupation sits on the MLTSSL and that your skills assessment is valid for that specific ANZSCO code. Second, sit an approved English test and gather your points evidence, including age, English, skilled employment, and any partner or study credits, before you touch SkillSelect.
Third, submit your Expression of Interest through SkillSelect.
Your EOI is a points declaration, not an application; you must be honest about every claim because the department verifies them at lodgement.
Invitations are issued in rounds, typically monthly, and are ranked by points score and then by the date your EOI was submitted. If you receive an invitation, you have 60 calendar days to lodge your full application online through ImmiAccount.
Fourth, pay the visa application charge and upload all supporting documents. You can lodge before every document is finalised, but missing items will slow the assessment.
Fifth, complete your health examinations and await the outcome. The department may request further information, so check your ImmiAccount regularly rather than waiting for email alerts.
Once a decision is made, you will receive a grant notification; if you are onshore, your permanent residency begins on that date.
Common refusals and how to avoid them
Refusals rarely happen without warning signs, but most stem from preventable errors. The leading cause is incorrect points claims.
For example, claiming skilled employment experience that overlaps with your skills assessment date, or counting part-time work without the required 20 hours per week.
Each point claim must be supported by a document that names your occupation and dates of employment; a generic reference letter will not suffice.
A second frequent refusal involves the skills assessment not matching the nominated occupation.
If your assessment names a slightly different ANZSCO code than the one on your invitation, the department may treat the application as invalid.

01 Most common refusal: Genuine Student criterion — weak or generic GS statements that do not demonstrate study as the primary purpose of entering Australia. 
02 Second most common: Financial capacity — funds that do not meet the current cost-of-living thresholds, unexplained large deposits, or insufficient sponsor documentation. 
03 Third most common: Enrolment issues — expired, cancelled, or invalid Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE) at the time of assessment. 
04 Other grounds: English language (expired test, wrong test type, score below minimum), health (missed examination, incomplete HAP ID), and character (undisclosed convictions, previous immigration breaches). 
05 Key principle: Each refusal ground has a specific fix. A fresh application that does not address the stated refusal reason will almost certainly be refused again. 
Why subclass 500 applications get refused: the common grounds
Home Affairs refuses subclass 500 applications on specific legal grounds set out in the Migration Regulations 1994. The most common are: the Genuine Student (GS) criterion under clause 500.212, financial capacity under clause 500.214, enrolment requirements under clause 500.211, English language under clause 500.213, and health or character under clauses 500.216 and 500.217. Each refusal ground requires a different type of evidence to fix — the first step is identifying which ground applies to your case.
When you receive a refusal letter, it will state the specific regulation or clause the case officer relied on. Do not skim this section. The legal reference tells you exactly what evidence was missing or insufficient. A refusal under clause 500.212 (GS) requires a completely different approach than a refusal under clause 500.214 (financial capacity). Treating all refusals the same way is the most common mistake applicants make when reapplying.
Who this guide is for
International students whose subclass 500 application was refused and who want to understand the specific reason before reapplying. Education agents and advisers helping students prepare a stronger fresh application. Students who have not yet applied and want to understand the most common refusal grounds so they can avoid them in their initial application.
If you have already received a refusal and are deciding between reapplying and seeking ART review, this guide helps you assess whether your case is fixable through a fresh application. For the procedural steps after a refusal — time limits, ART jurisdiction, and the reapplication process — read the refusal and reapply guide .
Refusal ground 1: Genuine Student criterion (clause 500.212)
The GS criterion is the most common refusal ground. Note: the Genuine Student test replaced the earlier Genuine Temporary Entrant (GTE) test on 23 March 2024. If your refusal letter references "GTE," the underlying assessment is similar — the case officer was not satisfied that study was your primary purpose in Australia. Post-March 2024 refusals cite the GS criterion. In both cases the fix is the same: demonstrate that study is genuinely the main reason for your entry.
The case officer must be satisfied that the applicant genuinely intends to stay in Australia temporarily for the purpose of study. The assessment considers: the applicant's circumstances in their home country, the applicant's potential circumstances in Australia, the value of the course to the applicant's future, the applicant's immigration history, and any other relevant matter.
Why GS statements fail: Generic answers that could apply to any student at any institution. A GS statement that says "Australia has a world-class education system" without mentioning the specific course, provider, or career plan is a red flag. Other common failures: unexplained study gaps of more than six months, downward course progression (bachelor's to diploma) without a credible reason, inconsistent career plans (e.g. a nursing course when the applicant's background is in accounting), and weak ties to the home country (no property, family, or employment evidence).
How to fix a GS refusal: Rewrite the GS statement to address each of the case officer's concerns point by point. Reference the specific course name, provider location, and unit descriptions. Explain every study or employment gap with documentary evidence. Show a logical progression from your previous study to the Australian course to your planned career. Provide concrete home-country tie evidence: property deeds, family registration documents, employment letters confirming a position waiting for you, or business registration showing ongoing commitments.
Refusal ground 2: Financial capacity (clause 500.214)
The financial capacity requirement means you must have enough funds to cover travel, course fees, and living costs for yourself and any accompanying family members for the first 12 months of your stay. Home Affairs publishes the current cost-of-living thresholds annually — check the current figure before applying.
Why financial evidence fails: The most common issue is funds that do not meet the current threshold. Even if the bank balance is sufficient, the case officer may refuse if: the funds are not genuinely available (e.g. a loan that requires collateral not yet pledged), the source of funds is unexplained (a large deposit shortly before the application with no paper trail), the sponsor's income is insufficient to support the declared amount, or the evidence is outdated (bank statements older than 3 months).
How to fix a financial refusal: Obtain updated bank statements showing funds held for at least 3-6 months before the application. If a sponsor is providing funds, include the sponsor's employment letter, 6 months of payslips, bank statements, and a s

body:

Subclass 485 Stream Selection: PHEW vs PVEW Guide (2026) 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
In 60 seconds
01 PHEW stream: For bachelor's, bachelor honours, master's (coursework, research, extended), and doctoral degrees. Duration: 2 years (bachelor), 3 years (master's), 4 years (doctoral). 
02 PVEW stream: For diploma, advanced diploma, associate degree, and trade qualifications at Certificate III level or above. Duration: typically 18 months. 
03 Shared requirements: Both streams require the Australian study requirement (92+ weeks CRICOS-registered study, 16+ calendar months in Australia), English at IELTS 6.0 or equivalent, AFP check, and adequate health insurance. 
04 Critical check: Confirm your qualification's AQF level on your completion letter and cross-reference with the current Home Affairs stream eligibility table before lodging. Lodging under the wrong stream results in refusal with no fee refund. 
The two streams: what each one requires
The Temporary Graduate visa subclass 485 has two streams, and the choice depends entirely on your qualification level. The Post-Higher Education Work (PHEW) stream — formerly called the Post-Study Work stream before the July 2024 rebrand — covers degree-level qualifications: bachelor's degrees (including honours), master's degrees (coursework, research, and extended), and doctoral degrees (PhD). The Post-Vocational Education Work (PVEW) stream — formerly called the Graduate Work stream — covers sub-degree qualifications: diplomas, advanced diplomas, associate degrees, and trade qualifications at Certificate III level or above.
The distinction matters because the visa duration, cost, and career-plan implications differ between streams. A PHEW visa typically grants 2-4 years depending on your qualification level, giving you a substantial window to gain skilled work experience and explore permanent residence pathways. A PVEW visa is generally shorter, so your post-study planning timeline is more compressed.
Home Affairs has changed the qualification-level eligibility several times since 2023, particularly around graduate diplomas and packaged programs. Always check the current rules on the Home Affairs website at the time of application — rules that applied to a friend's successful application last year may no longer apply to yours.
Who this guide is for
International students who have completed or are about to complete an Australian qualification and are deciding which 485 stream to apply under. Students with packaged programs or combined qualifications who are unsure which stream their qualification falls under. Education agents helping graduates choose the correct stream before lodgement.
If you have not yet completed your course, this guide helps you plan which stream to target so you can gather the right evidence well before your completion date. If you already hold a qualification but are unsure of its AQF level, check your completion letter or academic transcript — the qualification level determines the stream.
PHEW stream: eligibility and duration
The PHEW stream requires a degree-level qualification from a CRICOS-registered course at an Australian education provider. The qualification must be a bachelor's degree (including honours), a master's degree (coursework, research, or extended), or a doctoral degree. The course must meet the Australian study requirement: at least 92 weeks of CRICOS-registered study duration, completed over at least 16 calendar months of physical presence in Australia, with all instruction in English.
Visa duration under PHEW depends on the qualification level. A bachelor's degree (including honours) generally grants 2 years. A master's by coursework grants 3 years. A master's by research grants 3 years. A doctoral degree grants 4 years. There may be additional time granted for study in regional areas — check the current regional classification on the Home Affairs website.
If you hold a master's by coursework but completed it through a packaged program that included a graduate certificate and graduate diploma, the master's is the controlling qualification for PHEW eligibility — the lower-level qualifications do not disqualify you, but the visa duration is based on the highest completed qualification.
PVEW stream: eligibility and duration
The PVEW stream covers qualifications below degree level. Eligible qualifications include: diplomas, advanced diplomas, associate degrees, and trade qualifications at Certificate III level or above. The qualification must be closely related to an occupation on the Medium and Long-term Strategic Skills List (MLTSSL) — this is a key difference from PHEW, which does not require occupational alignment.
The PVEW stream typically grants 18 months. The occupation connection means you must have completed a qualification that directly prepares you for a specific skilled occupation on the MLTSSL. Your completion letter and transcript should clearly state the qualification title and the occupation it relates to. If the occupation is not on the MLTSSL, or your qualification does not clearly relate to it, the PVEW application will be refused.
The occupation alignment requirement makes PVEW more restrictive than PHEW. If you completed a diploma of business but the MLTSSL occupation you nominate is accountant, the connection may be too weak unless your course specifically covered accounting units and your transcript supports the link. Check the current MLTSSL on the Home Affairs website and confirm your qualification matches before lodging under PVEW.
How to confirm your stream before lodging
Before lodging your 485 application, complete these checks in order. First, obtain your official completion letter from your education provider. The letter must state your qualification title, the AQF level, the CRICOS course code, the course sta

Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com

Visa condition 8202: enrolment & attendance for student visa 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats

Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates

In 60 seconds
01 Current public rule: Home Affairs states condition 8202 requires the holder of a subclass 500 visa to remain enrolled in a registered course and meet the education provider’s attendance and course progress requirements. 
02 Controlling source: Department of Home Affairs (condition 8202), ESOS Act / National Code 2018 provider obligations. 
03 Main risk: Provider reports non-compliance to Home Affairs via PRISMS, issuing a s.20 notice that can lead to visa cancellation and a three-year re-entry bar. 
What condition 8202 requires
Condition 8202 is a mandatory condition on every subclass 500 student visa. Home Affairs states that condition 8202 requires you to: remain enrolled in a registered course of study that is a CRICOS-registered course (a course listed on the Commonwealth Register of Institutions and Courses for Overseas Students), meet the attendance requirements of your education provider, and meet the course-progress requirements of your education provider. If you hold more than one CoE (for a package enrolment), condition 8202 applies to each component of the package.
The condition does not set a specific minimum attendance percentage or course-progress benchmark in the Migration Regulations themselves. Instead, it requires you to meet those requirements as set by your education provider under the ESOS National Code 2018. The National Code requires providers to have documented policies for monitoring attendance and course progress, and to intervene when a student falls below the expected standard. These interventions are called "at-risk" processes and give you a chance to improve or explain before the provider reports the breach to Home Affairs.
If you transfer to a different provider or course, you must maintain enrolment in a CRICOS-registered course at all times. A gap in enrolment, even a short one, means you are not meeting condition 8202. If you change to a course that is not CRICOS-registered (such as a purely online course from a non-registered provider), you breach the condition regardless of whether you are still studying.
Who this guide is for
Subclass 500 student visa holders who want to understand their ongoing obligations while in Australia. Students who have received attendance warnings or "at risk" notices from their provider and need to know what happens next. Students who have received a section 20 notice (cancellation warning) and need to respond within 28 days.
If you have not received any warnings, this guide helps you stay compliant and avoid the escalation path from informal intervention to formal reporting. If you have already received a section 20 notice, the timing is urgent — you have 28 days to respond before the CoE is cancelled and visa cancellation begins.
The decision you make next
If your provider has identified that you are at risk of breaching condition 8202, you should respond promptly. The first step is to understand what the provider is concerned about: low attendance, poor course progress, or both. Request a meeting with your provider's international student support officer to discuss the issue. Provide evidence of any compassionate or compelling circumstances that affected your attendance or progress.
If you have received a section 20 notice under the ESOS Act, you have 28 days to respond. Your response should include: an explanation of why you did not meet the condition, evidence of any compassionate circumstances, and your plan to return to compliance (such as a revised study schedule, reduced work hours, or academic support). If the provider accepts your response, the CoE is maintained and the breach is not reported to Home Affairs as a cancellation. If the provider does not accept your response, the CoE is cancelled, and Home Affairs can cancel your visa under section 116 of the Migration Act.
Documents and evidence to prepare
If you are responding to an attendance or progress concern, gather: your current enrolment record (CoE details, course start and end dates), attendance records from your provider's system, course-progress reports (grades, assignment feedback), any correspondence with your provider about the issue, and evidence of compassionate or compelling circumstances (medical certificates, death certificates, police reports, letters from counsellors).
If you have received a section 20 notice, also prepare: the section 20 notice itself, a written response letter addressed to your provider explaining why you breached, your plan to return to compliance, and supporting documents for any compassionate claim. Keep a copy of everything you submit. If the provider rejects your response and cancels the CoE, you may need this evidence for a subsequent visa application or ART review.
Deadline and risk triggers
The timing of condition 8202 compliance is continuous — the condition applies for the entire duration of your visa. A breach can be identified at any point when your provider reports non-compliance through PRISMS. The most critical deadline is the 28-day response period after receiving a section 20 notice. If you do not respond within 28 days, the CoE is automatically cancelled, and Home Affairs is notified.
The main risk is visa cancellation under section 116 of the Migration Act. If Home Affairs cancels your visa for breaching condition 8202, you may face a three-year exclusion period under Public Interest Criterion 4013. This means you cannot be granted certain other visas for three years from the date of cancellation. A visa cancellation is also a significant adverse history for any future visa application to any country.
The secondary risk is the impact on the GS criterion in a future application. If you apply for a new visa after a cancellation history, the case officer will assess whether you are likely to compl

body:

Proving Funds for a Canadian Study Permit · Short Overview 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile

Following 
Discover
