For sponsors and applicants who want a deeper treatment of each topic, the linked articles at the bottom of this page provide full depth with step-by-step instructions and document templates. If you need a structured review of your relationship evidence and sponsorship forms before submitting, our flat-rate checklist service can help.
How to use this FAQ
Choose inland vs outland (and Quebec CSQ steps) before assembling a relationship package — see the inland/outland deep dive linked below.
Confirm processing tools and undertaking rules on canada.ca; do not rely on historical timelines.
Editorial-only until a named lawyer/RCIC review program is live; complex inadmissibility facts need licensed advice.
Last updated 2026-07-14 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
Reviewer programs for Canada matters are under development; until those programs launch, Canada content is editorial-only.
Do I need to be married to sponsor my partner to Canada?
No. Canadian immigration law recognises three types of spousal and partner relationships for sponsorship: legally married spouses, common-law partners who have cohabited for at least 12 consecutive months, and conjugal partners who have been in a committed relationship for at least one year but are unable to marry or cohabit due to exceptional circumstances. Each category requires different evidence. Married sponsors must provide a marriage certificate and evidence that the marriage is genuine. Common-law partners must provide 12 months of cohabitation proof such as joint leases, utility bills, or bank statements. Conjugal partners face the highest evidentiary burden and must explain why marriage or cohabitation was not possible.
What is the difference between inland and outland spousal sponsorship?
Inland sponsorship is for applicants who are already inside Canada with valid temporary status. The main advantage is eligibility for an open work permit while the application is processed, allowing the applicant to work for any employer. The main risk is that leaving Canada while the application is pending can complicate re-entry and may be seen as abandonment of the inland process. Outland sponsorship is processed by the visa office responsible for the applicant's country of residence or citizenship. The applicant can usually travel during processing, and outland applications have a right of appeal to the Immigration Appeal Division if refused. Inland refusals generally do not have the same appeal right. The processing time is roughly similar for both routes, currently around 12 months for most countries.
Can I travel while my spousal sponsorship application is pending?
If you applied through the outland route, you can usually travel during processing, provided you maintain valid temporary status and can demonstrate ties to Canada at re-entry. If you applied through the inland route, leaving Canada is risky. A CBP officer at the border may question your intent to remain in Canada temporarily when you have a permanent residence application in progress. While a valid visitor visa or eTA may allow physical re-entry, the officer is not required to admit you, and some applicants have been refused re-entry. If you must travel on an inland application, carry evidence of your pending application, your sponsor's status, and your intent to return. Consult an immigration practitioner before booking travel.
Does inland sponsorship include an open work permit?
Yes, in most cases. Inland spousal sponsorship applicants can apply for an open work permit at the same time as the sponsorship application or shortly after submission. The open work permit allows the applicant to work for any employer in Canada while waiting for permanent residence. The permit is typically issued for a period that covers the expected processing time. To be eligible, the applicant must have valid temporary status in Canada at the time of the open work permit application. If the applicant's status has expired, they may need to restore status before applying for the work permit. The open work permit is not available for outland applicants who are living outside Canada.
What documents best prove a genuine relationship for spousal sponsorship?
IRCC looks for evidence of a shared life over time, not just a marriage certificate. Strong evidence includes joint ba

01 The LMIA is issued by ESDC/Service Canada, not IRCC. A positive LMIA is submitted to IRCC as part of the worker's work permit application. 
02 Two main streams: high-wage (at or above provincial median hourly wage) and low-wage (below median). Each has different requirements for recruitment, caps, transition plans, and duration. 
03 Minimum recruitment: employers must advertise the position on the Job Bank and at least two additional methods for at least 4 consecutive weeks within the 3 months before applying. 
04 Compliance inspections can occur at any time within 6 years of LMIA issuance. Non-compliance can result in fines up to $100,000 per violation, a ban from the TFWP, and publication on the non-compliant employer list. 
05 An LMIA for PR support (arranged employment) adds 50 or 200 CRS points in Express Entry. The position must be permanent and the employer must indicate PR support on the application. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for Canadian employers who need to hire a foreign worker and must obtain an LMIA through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program. It covers the high-wage and low-wage streams, recruitment requirements, the transition plan obligation, compliance inspections and penalties, and how to use an LMIA to support a permanent residence application. It is also relevant for foreign workers who want to understand what their employer must do before they can apply for a work permit.
This guide is not for employers hiring through the International Mobility Program (LMIA-exempt), the Global Talent Stream (which uses a simplified LMIA process under the Global Skills Strategy), or the Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program (SAWP, which has a separate LMIA process). If the position is in Quebec, the employer must also obtain a Certificat d'acceptation du Québec (CAQ) from the MIFI — an additional step not covered here. Employers with a history of TFWP non-compliance or who have been subject to a ban should consult an immigration lawyer before applying.
High-wage vs low-wage: which stream applies
The dividing line between the two LMIA streams is the provincial or territorial median hourly wage for the occupation. ESDC publishes the median wage table by province and occupation on its website and updates it periodically. The wage used for the determination is the wage the employer is offering, not the prevailing wage for the occupation. If the offered wage is at or above the provincial median, the application is processed under the high-wage stream. If below, the low-wage stream applies.
The high-wage stream imposes two additional requirements that the low-wage stream does not: a transition plan and (in most cases) no cap on the number or proportion of TFWs. The low-wage stream caps the proportion of low-wage TFWs in the workforce — typically 10% for employers who first hired TFWs after June 2014, with higher caps (up to 20-30%) for certain sectors such as agriculture, caregiving, and seasonal industries. Low-wage LMIAs also limit the maximum employment duration to 1 or 2 years depending on the occupation and sector. An employer who misclassifies the stream — for example, offering a wage just below the median to avoid the transition plan obligation — risks having the application returned or refused if Service Canada determines the wage does not match the NOC skill level and regional norms.
Recruitment: what you must do before applying
Before applying for an LMIA, the employer must demonstrate genuine efforts to hire a Canadian citizen or permanent resident. The minimum recruitment requirements are:
Job Bank posting: The position must be advertised on the Government of Canada Job Bank for at least 4 consecutive weeks within the 3 months before the LMIA application is submitted. The posting must include the wage range, work location, duties, and skill requirements. A Job Match service must be used to invite matched candidates to apply.
Two additional recruitment methods: At least two of the following, targeted to the occupation and region: general employment websites (Indeed, Workopolis, Monster), online classifieds (Kijiji), professional association job boards, local community organisations, union halls, university and college career centres, participation in job fairs, or print advertising in local newspapers. The employer must keep records of each method — screenshots, invoices, and copies of advertisements — and submit them with the LMIA application.
Targeted recruitment for high-wage occupations: High-wage employers must conduct at least one additional recruitment method that targets underrepresented groups, such as advertising through Indigenous skills and employment organisations, organisations serving newcomers, or organisations serving persons with disabilities.
Recruitment records must show the number of applicants, the number interviewed, and the specific reasons (with evidence) why each Canadian applicant was not hired. Generic reasons such as "lacked qualifications" without specifying which qualifications were missing are not accepted. Service Canada is most likely to refuse an LMIA on recruitment grounds when the employer cannot demonstrate that a reasonable effort was made to find a suitable Canadian worker.
The transition plan (high-wage only)
A transition plan is a written plan — submitted with the LMIA application — that describes how the employer will reduce reliance on temporary foreign workers during the period of the work permit. Service Canada provides a template, but the content must be specific to the employer and the occupation. A plan that copies generic phrases from the template without describing concrete activities will be rejected. The plan must include at least three distinct recruitment or training activities and o

Canada open work permit for spouses: the rule in plain English
Spouses and common-law partners of eligible foreign workers, international students, and certain other categories may qualify for an open work permit (OWP), allowing them to work for any employer in Canada. However, eligibility narrowed in January 2025 when IRCC restricted which categories of workers' spouses qualify. As of 2026, spouses of workers in TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 occupations generally qualify, while spouses of workers in TEER 4 or 5 or certain lower-wage positions may not.
Key categories that still qualify: Spouses of international students in master's, doctoral, or certain professional programs, spouses of foreign workers in high-skilled occupations (TEER 0-3), spouses of inland spousal sponsorship applicants, and spouses of certain PR applicants under specific pilot programs.
Who this guide is for
Spouses of eligible foreign workers (TEER 0-3), international students in eligible programs, inland sponsorship applicants, and PR applicants where IRCC lists an open-work-permit route for accompanying family members.
Who this guide is not for
Spouses of workers in TEER 4 or 5 occupations or certain lower-wage LMIA positions — these were restricted in January 2025.
Spouses of international students in undergraduate or college diploma programs — only certain post-graduate and professional programs qualify.
Common-law partners who cannot demonstrate 12 months of continuous cohabitation with strong evidence.
Spouses applying from outside Canada without a valid principal applicant status in Canada.
Relationship evidence requirements
IRCC evaluates whether the relationship is genuine and not entered into primarily for immigration purposes. Strong evidence includes: marriage certificate or proof of 12 months cohabitation for common-law, joint bank accounts or credit cards, joint utility bills or lease agreements, photographs spanning the relationship timeline, communication records (calls, messages, emails), statutory declarations from family and friends (IMM 5409 for common-law), and evidence of shared financial responsibilities.
The most common refusal reason in spousal OWP applications is insufficient relationship evidence. A marriage certificate alone is not enough — IRCC expects to see evidence that the relationship is ongoing and genuine.
Timing and documents
Check the exact spouse category before applying because not every worker or student spouse qualifies. Documents to prepare: marriage certificate or common-law proof, principal applicant's work permit or study permit, proof of the principal applicant's qualifying occupation or program (job offer, employment letter, enrolment letter), passport and status documents for both parties, relationship photographs and communication history, and statutory declarations if applicable.
Processing times vary by category. Inland sponsorship-linked OWPs are processed alongside the sponsorship application. Worker-spouse OWPs typically process faster but timelines should be verified on IRCC's current processing times page.
What gets refused / common pitfalls
Relying on pre-2025 rules. Eligibility narrowed in January 2025. Spouses who qualified before may not qualify now.
Weak common-law evidence. Cohabitation must be demonstrated with joint documents, not just sworn statements.
Principal applicant's job not in an eligible category. Workers in TEER 4 or 5 or certain low-wage LMIA positions no longer qualify their spouses.
Missing status proof. Both parties must have valid status in Canada at the time of application.

Canada Parents and Grandparents Program: the rule in plain English
The PGP lets eligible Canadian citizens and permanent residents sponsor parents and grandparents only after receiving an invitation to apply.
Who this guide is for
Canadian citizens and permanent residents hoping to sponsor parents or grandparents, including households comparing PGP with Super Visa.
Documents and evidence to prepare
Invitation to apply, sponsor status proof, proof of income, notices of assessment, family size calculation, relationship proof, civil documents, police certificates, medical instructions, and Quebec undertaking documents if applicable.
Timing, deadlines, and sequencing
Do not prepare a full application unless invited; IRCC help-centre guidance says invitations are not transferable and deadlines have no exceptions.
How to make the file easier to approve
Model family size and income before hoping for an invitation, then prepare documents fast if selected.
Decision checklist before you act
The Canada parents and grandparents program checklist should include the status, contract, form edition, fee, deadline, address, school record, work authorization, tax residence, account term, insurance scope, or local procedure that controls the next step.
What gets refused / common pitfalls
Pitfalls include trying to sponsor in-laws with the wrong invitation, missing the deadline, undercounting family size, weak income proof, and assuming interest-to-sponsor guarantees selection.
PGP starts with the invitation
The Parents and Grandparents Program is not an always-open sponsorship route. The first document question is whether the sponsor has an invitation to apply for the current intake. Without an invitation, the file is planning work, not a ready PGP submission. Preparing forms as if an invitation exists can waste time and lead families to miss better interim options.
When an invitation exists, preserve the invitation, deadline, sponsor identity records, family-size calculation, income proof, parent or grandparent identity documents, and relationship proof. The invitation controls the timeline, so the file should be built around that deadline from the start.
Family size and income proof
The income test is one of the most important parts of a PGP file. Family size can include the sponsor, spouse or co-signer where relevant, dependent children, people previously sponsored under active undertakings, and the parents or grandparents being sponsored. A wrong family-size calculation can make the income proof look sufficient when it is not.
Income documents should match the years and format IRCC asks for. If a co-signer is used, the co-signer's eligibility and income records need the same care as the sponsor's. Do not rely on current salary alone when the program asks for tax-year evidence. The PGP file is retrospective as well as current.
Quebec and undertaking differences
Quebec sponsors have an additional undertaking process after the federal sponsorship stage. A PGP checklist should flag Quebec residence early because the sponsor may need provincial forms, provincial income review, and separate instructions. Treating Quebec like every other province can create sequencing problems.
Even outside Quebec, the undertaking is serious. Sponsoring parents or grandparents creates support obligations after permanent residence is granted. The sponsor should understand the length and effect of the undertaking before filing, especially if family income is close to the required level or household composition may change.
Parent and grandparent documents
The applicant side of the file needs passports, civil status records, parent-child relationship proof, police certificate planning, medical instructions, photos, and any documents needed for accompanying dependants. Name changes, old civil records, and missing birth certificates can take time to solve, so they should be reviewed as soon as an invitation arrives.

PGWP document checklist (Canada, 2026)
Quick answer

Every document IRCC expects for a PGWP, in the order an officer reads them. Includes completion letter, transcript, and study-permit timing evidence.
One-sentence answer: a PGWP file is mostly about timing and completion — the completion letter is the single most important document, and most refusals trace back to a mismatch between completion date, study permit validity, and the application date. Who this is for
You have confirmed PGWP eligibility (see PGWP eligibility ) and you are now assembling the application package.
Who this is not for
Applicants still inside their program who have not yet finished — wait until you have completion evidence.
Applicants whose eligibility is uncertain — go back to the eligibility filters first; assembling documents for a file that will fail Filter 3 is wasted work.
The decision this page helps you make
Does each document in the package prove a specific eligibility element, and is anything missing, duplicated, or internally inconsistent?
The controlling source
IRCC's PGWP document checklist (use the current edition of IMM 5583 from IRCC), the PGWP eligibility page, and IRCC's guidance on completion evidence.
Documents that prove the case
Document preparation and credential validation
A PGWP file is built around three critical dates that must align: your program completion date (from the DLI completion letter), your study permit expiry date (from your current permit), and your application submission date (from the IRCC portal confirmation). If any two of these dates conflict — for example, the completion letter says June 15 but the transcript shows a grade posted June 22 — the officer cannot determine which date anchors the application window. Before assembling documents, confirm that the completion letter and transcript agree on the completion date; if they differ by more than a few days, request a clarifying letter from the DLI registrar. The most common preventable refusal in PGWP applications is not a missing document but a date mismatch between documents that should say the same thing. Align the three dates first, then assemble everything else around them.
In reviewer order:
Identity and current status. 
Passport with sufficient remaining validity.
Current study permit (or most recent study permit if it has expired and you are within an allowed transition).
Most recent visa, eTA, or other status documents.
Proof of program completion. 
Completion letter from the DLI confirming all program requirements have been met, and naming the date on which you met them.
Final official transcript showing all courses, grades, and credits.
For programs requiring a thesis or capstone: confirmation that the final deliverable has been accepted.
If the transcript and completion letter disagree on the end date, attach a short explanation letter from the DLI.
Evidence of full-time, in-person study (with documented exceptions). 
Enrolment records across the full program.
Any communication from the DLI authorizing online study, hybrid delivery, or leave of absence — particularly if you relied on flexibility provisions.
Language results if required. 
Test result confirming the threshold for your program type, where IRCC requires one (confirm the requirement on IRCC's PGWP eligibility page).
Forms and fees. 
Current PGWP application form (use the latest edition published by IRCC).
Open work permit holder fee + work permit fee (check the current amounts on IRCC's fee list).
IMM 5583 document checklist (current edition) signed where required.
Biometrics evidence. 
If biometrics on file are within validity, you typically do not give them again. Otherwise, biometrics evidence per the BIL.

Use this table to confirm every document proves a specific rule. If two documents prove the same thing and nothing proves rule X, you have a gap.

Timeline and deadlines
Completion-letter date is the anchor. All subsequent timing flows from this date.
Window-end date. The latest date you can apply is calculated from completion; confirm the current window rule on IRCC's PGWP eligibility page.
Study permit validity. If your study permit will still be valid at the date of application, work-authorization rules during processing differ from the rules if your study permit has already expired. Both pathways exist; the documents you attach differ.
Transition employment. If you intend to start working immediately after applying, confirm your specific permission to do so under the current rules before accepting a job offer.

Date on completion letter.
Date of application against the post-completion window.
Consistency between completion letter and transcript.

One-sentence answer: a Post-Graduation Work Permit is not automatic — it depends on which DLI you attended, the type and length of your program, the field of study (for many college programs), your study mode during the program, and whether you apply within the post-completion window. Who this is for
You are a current Canadian study permit holder, or recently finished a Canadian program at a DLI, and you want to know whether a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) is realistic for your case before you spend time assembling documents.
Who this is not for
Spouses or dependants looking at open work permits — that is a different pathway and out of scope here.
Applicants who have already applied and received a refusal — restoration and reconsideration require licensed legal review.
Applicants who attended programs outside Canada or in partnership programs delivered abroad — the rules around foreign-delivered components have changed and are tightly fact-specific.
The decision this page helps you make
Are your specific program, DLI, study pattern, and timing inside the PGWP envelope — or does one of them disqualify you? This page walks the five filters IRCC applies, in the order it applies them.
The controlling source
The controlling source is IRCC's PGWP program delivery instructions, including:
The eligibility page (DLI status, program length, study mode).
The eligible-programs / field-of-study page (which has changed in recent years for public college diploma graduates in particular).
The language requirement page where applicable.
Confirm every figure and list on this page against IRCC's current published guidance before you act — IRCC has revised these rules more than once between 2023 and 2026.
The five PGWP filters, in order
Filter 1 — Did you attend a PGWP-eligible DLI?
Not every DLI on the study permit list is also PGWP-eligible. IRCC maintains a separate eligibility marker. Confirm your DLI is on the PGWP-eligible list as of your program's start date, using IRCC's official PGWP-eligible DLI list.
Filter 2 — Was your program at a PGWP-eligible level and length?
Two sub-rules typically apply:
The program must be at an eligible level (certificate, diploma, bachelor's, master's, doctoral, professional degree — the specifics depend on the institution type); confirm the current eligible levels on IRCC's PGWP eligibility page.
The program must meet a minimum length, and the PGWP length is generally tied to the length of the program completed in Canada; check IRCC's current rules on program length and PGWP duration.
Filter 3 — For college diploma graduates: is your field on the approved list?
This is the filter that has surprised the most applicants in recent intakes.
For graduates of public college diploma programs , IRCC applies a field-of-study filter tied to CIP codes (Classification of Instructional Programs). If your program's CIP code is not on the approved list at the time you apply, the PGWP is refused regardless of your other evidence.
University degree programs are treated differently. Some graduate programs are treated differently again. Confirm the current rule for your program type on IRCC's PGWP eligibility page.
Filter 4 — Did your study mode meet IRCC's requirements?
The general rule: full-time study throughout the program, in-person delivery, except where IRCC has explicitly permitted online or hybrid study (typically tied to the program length).
Common red flags:
The program shifted to online or hybrid during a term outside the permitted flexibility.
A "final semester" was completed part-time, which is generally permitted, but the previous semesters were also part-time.
A leave of absence that exceeded a permitted threshold.
Filter 5 — Did you apply within the post-completion window?
There is a fixed window between the date you officially completed all program requirements (typically the date on the completion letter) and the latest date you can apply for the PGWP. The window length and what counts as "completion" have changed, so confirm the current window and completion definition on IRCC's official guidance.
Apply after the window and the application is refused on timing alone.
PGWP eligibility decision tree (diagnostic tool)
Work through the questions in order. The first "No" tells you the filter that disqualifies you.
```
Is the DLI on the PGWP-eligible list as of your program start?
│ YES → 2; NO → not eligible │
Was the program at an eligible level and length?
│ YES → 3; NO → not eligible │
Public college diploma? If yes, is the field on the approved list?
│ YES (or not a college diploma) → 4; NO → not eligible │
Did you study full-time, in-person, within IRCC's flexibility allowance?
│ YES → 5; NO → eligibility depends on the specific deviation — get advice │
Will you apply within the post-completion window?
│ YES → eligibility looks intact; assemble documents NO → not eligible ```

Once you confirm PGWP eligibility, start planning how you will use the open work permit to build your Canadian career. Many universities offer job placement services that remain accessible to alumni for up to a year after graduation, including resume reviews, mock interviews, and employer networking events. PNP comparison: Ontario vs BC vs Alberta: the rule in plain English
Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta each operate their own Provincial Nominee Programs (PNPs) under the federal IRCC framework. Each province targets different occupations, rewards different qualifications, and has different application processes. Choosing the right provincial nomination strategy can significantly improve your chances of Canadian permanent residence.
Ontario Immigrant Nominee Program (OINP): Ontario is Canada’s largest province by population and receives the most immigration. OINP offers multiple streams including Human Capital Priorities (Express Entry-aligned, no job offer required for certain occupations), Employer Job Offer streams (requires a job offer from an Ontario employer), PhD Graduate stream (for Ontario PhD graduates), and Entrepreneur stream. BC is primarily employer-driven — most streams require a valid job offer from a BC employer. The Skills Immigration stream processes applications within 2 to 3 months. BC also offers an Express Entry BC stream that aligns with federal Express Entry processing.
Alberta Advantage Immigration Program (AAIP): Alberta focuses on candidates who can fill labour gaps in healthcare, technology, agriculture, and skilled trades. AAIP offers Express Entry streams that do not require a job offer if the candidate has a family connection in Alberta or works in a targeted occupation. Alberta also issues NOIs directly from the Express Entry pool. Processing times are typically 4 to 6 months but can vary by stream.
Who this guide is for
Candidates choosing where to study, work, or pursue a provincial nomination strategy as part of their Canadian permanent residence plan. This includes Express Entry candidates looking for CRS boosts through PNP, international graduates planning their provincial strategy, and skilled workers evaluating job offers across multiple provinces.
Who this guide is not for
Candidates who are not yet eligible for any PNP or Express Entry program — review basic eligibility first.
Candidates targeting Quebec (which operates its own selection system) or Atlantic provinces (covered under AIP).
Candidates who already have a high CRS score (480+) and expect a direct ITA through general Express Entry rounds — PNP may be unnecessary.
Candidates who cannot commit to residing in the nominating province — PNP requires demonstrated intent to settle.
Comparing Ontario, BC, and Alberta PNP streams

Ontario is best for candidates with strong CRS scores in targeted occupations (tech, healthcare, trades) who can benefit from the Human Capital Priorities stream without a job offer. BC is best for candidates with a tech or healthcare job offer from a BC employer, with the BC PNP Tech stream offering the fastest processing for tech workers. Alberta is best for candidates with a family connection in Alberta or qualifications in targeted occupations (healthcare, agriculture, tech) who can receive an NOI without a job offer.

Quebec immigration PEQ and PRTQ: the rule in plain English
Quebec operates its own immigration system separate from the rest of Canada. While the federal government makes the final permanent residence decision, Quebec selects its own immigrants through the MIFI (Ministère de l’Immigration, de la Francisation et de l’Intégration). There are two main pathways for skilled worker immigration: the PEQ (Quebec Experience Program) for candidates already in Quebec, and the PRTQ (Regular Skilled Worker Program) for candidates applying from outside Quebec.
The Quebec selection process: First, the candidate applies to MIFI for a Certificat de sélection du Québec (CSQ). MIFI assesses the candidate based on Quebec’s criteria, including French language ability, education, work experience, age, and ties to Quebec. If MIFI issues a CSQ, the candidate then applies to IRCC for Canadian permanent residence. IRCC assesses only federal admissibility — it cannot refuse based on Quebec’s selection criteria.
Why consider Quebec: Quebec offers a distinct immigration pathway that can be faster for French-speaking candidates, particularly through the PEQ. The province has strong demand for skilled workers in healthcare, technology, education, and engineering. Quebec also offers lower tuition for international students at Quebec institutions and a unique cultural environment. International students who graduate from a Quebec institution and achieve NCLC 7 in French can apply through the PEQ Graduate stream, which has no points grid, no job offer requirement, and processing times of approximately 20 to 30 business days for the CSQ. This makes the PEQ Graduate stream one of the fastest routes to Canadian permanent residence for French-speaking international graduates who have studied in Quebec and wish to remain in the province after completing their program. The key advantage of PEQ over the PRTQ is speed — while PEQ can process the CSQ in as little as one month, the PRTQ points-based process typically takes 6 to 12 months for the Quebec selection stage alone. Candidates who meet the PEQ criteria should choose that route over PRTQ whenever possible to reduce overall processing time from application to permanent residence landing.
Who this guide is for
Quebec graduates, Quebec workers, and French-speaking candidates with a genuine plan to live and work in Quebec. This includes international students who have completed a program at a Quebec educational institution, temporary foreign workers in Quebec, and candidates applying from outside Quebec who meet the PRTQ points threshold.
Who this guide is not for
Candidates who do not plan to live in Quebec — Quebec immigration requires intent to reside in the province.
Candidates who do not speak French at a functional level — Quebec strongly prioritizes French-speaking candidates.
Candidates who qualify for a faster federal Express Entry route — compare total processing times before choosing Quebec.
Candidates whose education or work experience is not recognized by MIFI — Quebec has specific equivalency rules.
PEQ: the Quebec Experience Program explained
The PEQ is designed for candidates who have already studied or worked in Quebec. There are two streams: the PEQ Graduate stream (for students who have completed a Quebec diploma) and the PEQ Foreign Worker stream (for workers with at least 24 months of skilled work experience in Quebec). PEQ offers faster processing and no points grid — candidates either meet the criteria or they do not. PEQ is a binary assessment, not a competitive ranking.

Spousal sponsorship inland vs outland: the rule in plain English
Inland and outland sponsorship are not quality labels — they are procedural routes with different legal consequences. The inland route (Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada Class) requires the sponsored spouse to be living in Canada with the sponsor for the duration of the application. The outland route (Family Class) processes the sponsored spouse through the visa office responsible for their country of residence, regardless of where the sponsor lives.
The choice between them affects three things that matter more than processing speed: whether the sponsored spouse can work in Canada during processing, whether they can travel outside Canada during processing, and what appeal route exists if the application is refused.
Who this guide is for
Married spouses, common-law partners, and conjugal partners comparing where to file and what risk to accept. This guide is for couples where the sponsor is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident living in Canada, or plans to return to Canada when the sponsored spouse immigrates.
This guide does not cover Quebec-specific sponsorship (which requires a CSQ through MIFI in addition to the federal process), same-sex marriage recognition in countries where the marriage occurred, or applications involving a sponsored spouse who is already inadmissible to Canada. Those situations need jurisdiction-specific legal advice.
Inland vs outland: side-by-side comparison
The table below summarises the practical differences. Each factor should be weighted differently depending on the couple's specific circumstances.
Factor Inland Outland Applicant residence during processing Must live in Canada with sponsor Can live anywhere; processed at local visa office Open work permit Eligible after AOR Not available through the application itself Travel during processing Generally not permitted — leaving Canada abandons the class Permitted; applicant can visit Canada on a visa or eTA as allowed Appeal rights on refusal Limited — judicial review to Federal Court (requires leave) Appeal to Immigration Appeal Division (IAD) Processing location Case Processing Centre — Mississauga Visa office responsible for applicant's country Sponsorship undertaking Standard 3-year undertaking (Quebec: different duration) Same undertaking period, regardless of route 
When to choose inland
The inland route is the better choice when: the sponsored spouse is already living in Canada with valid temporary status (visitor record, study permit, or work permit), the couple needs the sponsored spouse to work in Canada during processing, and the sponsored spouse does not need to travel internationally while the application is pending. The inland open work permit is a practical advantage that the outland route cannot match — it allows the couple to pool incomes and reduces financial pressure during what can be a multi-month processing period.
The inland route also suits couples where the sponsored spouse does not have strong ties to their home country and would not need to return for family, employment, or property reasons during the application period.
When to choose outland
The outland route is the better choice when: the sponsored spouse lives outside Canada and cannot or does not want to remain in Canada during processing, the couple needs the stronger appeal rights (appeal to IAD rather than judicial review), or the sponsored spouse must travel internationally for family or work reasons while the application is in process.
The outland route also works better when the applicant's country of residence has a visa office with predictable processing times, or when the applicant can visit Canada on a visa or eTA during processing without disrupting their permanent residence application. Outland applicants who visit Canada for short periods do not jeopardise their application, unlike inland applicants who leave Canada.

Start-up Visa pathway: the rule in plain English
As of January 1, 2026, IRCC is no longer accepting new applications under the Start-up Visa program. This pause applies to all applicants who do not already hold a commitment certificate or support letter from a designated organisation issued before the pause date. Transition provisions exist for founders who obtained a commitment document in 2025 and are within the window to file a complete application.
Before the pause, the Start-up Visa allowed founders with an innovative business idea to apply for permanent residence if they secured support from a designated angel investor group, venture capital fund, or business incubator. The program required a minimum language level, sufficient settlement funds, and a commitment to incorporate and actively manage the business in Canada.
Who this guide is for
Founders who already hold a commitment certificate or support letter from a designated organisation and need to understand whether their transition case qualifies, and founders who were considering the Start-up Visa and now need to compare alternatives after the pause.
This guide does not cover founders who have already been refused under the Start-up Visa program — that requires case-specific legal assessment. It also does not cover applicants who require a CSQ through Quebec's business immigration programs, which operate under separate rules through MIFI.
Transition eligibility for pre-2026 commitment holders
If you hold a commitment certificate or support letter from a designated organisation that was issued before January 1, 2026, you may still be eligible to apply under the transition provisions. IRCC's public policy on this transition sets out the criteria: the commitment document must be valid at the time of application, the designated organisation must still be on IRCC's current list of designated organisations, and you must meet all other program requirements (language, funds, admissibility).
If your designated organisation has been removed from the list since your commitment document was issued, or your commitment document has an expiry date that has passed, the transition provisions may not apply. IRCC recommends confirming both the organisation's current designation status and the document's validity before assembling a full application package.
Documents and evidence to prepare
Commitment document: The original commitment certificate or support letter from the designated organisation, confirming the investment amount or incubator acceptance, the date of issue, and the business name.
Business evidence: Business ownership records showing the applicant holds at least 10% of voting equity, incorporation documents if the business is already registered in Canada, and a business plan or pitch deck that matches the summary submitted to the designated organisation.
Language test: Approved language test results (IELTS, CELPIP, TEF, or TCF) showing at least CLB/NCLC 5 in all four skills, taken within the two years before the application date.
Settlement funds: Proof of unencumbered, transferable settlement funds at IRCC's current published minimum for the applicant and family members. These funds must be available separately from the business investment — the designated organisation's investment is not considered settlement funds.
Personal documents: Passport, birth certificate, police certificates from every country where the applicant has lived for six or more consecutive months since turning 18, medical exam instructions (IMM 1017B) where applicable, and digital photographs meeting IRCC specifications.
Forms: IMM 0008 (Generic Application Form for Permanent Residence), IMM 5669 (Schedule A: Background/Declaration), IMM 5406 (Additional Family Information), and IMM 5476 (Use of a Representative, if applicable). All forms must be the current editions downloaded directly from IRCC.

The first question is whether the student has a fixed-term tenancy, periodic tenancy, room rental, shared accommodation arrangement, or campus housing arrangement. The answer changes notice, deposit, repair, and dispute options.
The file should keep the lease, move-in inspection report, deposit receipt, rent receipts, roommate agreement if any, landlord messages, repair photos, and notices. Students often lose leverage because they communicate only by text and never save a complete record. A Calgary tenancy packet should be built as a timeline from application to move-out.
Security deposits and inspection reports
Security deposit disputes often turn on the inspection record. The move-in and move-out condition reports should be dated, signed where required, and supported by photos or video. If the landlord claims damage, compare the claim to the move-in condition and ordinary wear. A student should not assume a deduction is valid just because the landlord sends an invoice.
Keep proof of payment and any statement showing where the deposit went. If the landlord did not complete the required inspection process, that fact can matter in a dispute. The student should write down dates, who attended, what was said, and when the deposit statement arrived.

Repair issues should be reported in writing with dates, photos, and a clear description of the problem. Written notice creates a record that can be used if the landlord does not respond.

What is the canada study permit in 2026 explained
A study permit is an official document from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC).
It lets you study at a designated learning institution (DLI) for the length of your program. It's not a visa.
You may still need a visitor visa or an electronic travel authorization (eTA) to enter Canada.
Most international students need this permit before they arrive. A refusal means IRCC reviewed your application and found at least one concern.
The refusal letter names that concern in plain language.
IRCC decides every application on its own facts. Each application is assessed individually, and a previous refusal does not block a new one.
Many students reapply after addressing the specific issue.
The canada study process starts with a letter of acceptance from a DLI. Without that letter, an application cannot move forward.
With it, you build the rest of the file around your funds, your ties to home, and your study plan.
Your canada study plan should show a clear link between your past education and your chosen program. Officers look for a logical story.
If your program does not connect to your background, the refusal letter often says so.
Canada study permit requirements, explained
Before you reapply, confirm you meet the canada study eligibility rules. IRCC publishes these requirements, and an officer weighs them together rather than one at a time.
Letter of acceptance: you need an acceptance letter from a DLI. Check the DLI number on the official list.
A college or university that is not a DLI cannot support a study permit.
Proof of funds: you must show you can pay your tuition, your living costs, and your return travel. For a detailed breakdown, see our Canada study permit financial proof guide.
For 2026, the living cost requirement is CAD 20,635 per year, on top of first-year tuition. That figure comes from IRCC and changes over time.
See the IRCC study permit page for the latest amounts.
Ties to your home country: officers look for reasons you will leave Canada after your studies.
A job offer, property, family, or a clear career path back home all count as ties. Weak ties are a common refusal reason.
Intent to leave: you must convince the officer you'll depart when your permit expires. Your study plan and your ties together support this point.
Medical exam and police certificate: some applicants need a medical exam, and some need a police clearance. The refusal letter tells you if either was the problem.
Meet the canada study requirements before you pay the fee. A second refusal costs the same money and adds months to your timeline.
A qualified professional can review your facts and tell you which gaps to close.
How to apply for canada study permit after a refusal
The canada study application process after a refusal follows a clear order. Don't rush. Each step builds on the one before it.
Read the refusal letter twice. The letter lists the reasons in a section called "refusal grounds." Write each reason down. Your new application must answer every single one.
Gather the documents that fix each reason. If the letter says funds were insufficient, add bank statements with a longer history. If it says ties were weak, add proof of property or a job offer at home. For insufficient funds, provide a detailed explanation of your financial situation and include a sponsor letter if applicable.

Explain why you chose this program, how it connects to your past, and what you'll do in your home country after graduation. Keep it under two pages. Ensure your study plan directly addresses the officer's concerns from the refusal letter.

Quick answer
How IRCC reads your funds evidence: the rule, the documents, the deposits that look borrowed, and the sponsor-letter language that survives review.
How IRCC reads your funds evidence: the rule, the documents, the deposits that look borrowed, and the sponsor-letter language that survives review.
One-sentence answer: IRCC is not asking how much money is in the account today . IRCC is asking whether the money is genuinely available to you for the duration of your studies and whether you can prove where it came from . Who this is for
You are preparing a Canadian study permit application (study destination outside Quebec). Your funds will come from one or more of these:
Personal savings in your own name.
A sponsor — usually a parent or guardian — funding tuition and living costs.
A Guaranteed Investment Certificate (GIC) at a participating Canadian financial institution.
An education loan, often from a bank or government agency.
A scholarship, fellowship, or assistantship from the DLI or a third party.
You want to know how IRCC reads each of those, and what evidence converts a bank balance into "proof."
Who this is not for
Applicants whose destination is Quebec . Quebec's CAQ has its own financial requirements.
Applicants who are already inside Canada and renewing — proof of funds at renewal is judged on the remaining period, not the full program.
Sponsorship-based PR applications (Family Class). Different evidence framework.
The decision this page helps you make
Will an IRCC officer reading your funds documents conclude that:
The minimum required amount is shown.
The money is genuinely available (not borrowed for the application).
The source is plausible given the sponsor's life and work.
If any of those three is shaky, you are in refusal territory.
The controlling source
The controlling source is IRCC's guidance on proof of financial support for study permit applicants. IRCC publishes a per-year minimum for living expenses outside Quebec, plus first-year tuition, plus return travel. That minimum is updated periodically, so confirm the current figure directly on IRCC's official proof-of-financial-support page before you rely on it. 
GIC-based proof under the framework formerly known as the Student Direct Stream is a defined sub-route with its own rules. The participating-institution list and the eligible GIC amount are also published by IRCC and have changed over time — check both against IRCC's current published guidance before relying on this route.
Documents that prove the case
In reviewer order:
The minimum threshold check. 
First-year tuition (from the LOA).
Living expenses for the applicant for one year, at the per-year minimum IRCC currently publishes.
Plus living expenses for each accompanying family member, at IRCC's current published per-person amount.
Plus return travel for each person.
The "where the money is" evidence. 
Bank statements for the last 4–6 months (longer is better) for every account you intend to rely on. The statements must show name, account number, currency, running balance, and dated transactions.
GIC confirmation letter if applicable, naming the holder, the amount, and the institution.
Education loan sanction letter from a recognized lender, naming the disbursement schedule.
The "where the money came from" evidence. 
Salary slips, employer letters, or pension statements supporting the sponsor's regular income.
Tax records — for the sponsor in many cases this is the strongest single document.
Property documents and rental income records, if rental income contributes.
Business registration, partnership returns, and revenue records, if a family business contributes.
Sale-of-asset documents (land, vehicles, gold) if a one-time inflow funds part of the package.
The "is the money for you" evidence. 
A sponsor letter naming the applicant, the relationship, the amount committed, the duration committed (full program, not just year one), and signed.
Relationship evidence (birth certificate, family register) if the sponsor is a parent or relative.
If multiple sponsors, separate letters from each.
Tuition already paid. 
Receipt of tuition deposit or partial payment if any.
Receipt of GIC purchase if applicable.

Canada Study Permit Refused? Reapply Strategy & GCMS Notes

01 Step 1 — read the refusal letter: It will cite the specific legal provision (e.g. R216(1)(b) for purpose of visit, R220 for funds). This tells you which category of evidence was insufficient. 
02 Step 2 — order GCMS notes: The refusal letter is a summary. The GCMS notes reveal the officer's actual reasoning, what specific evidence was missing, and which documents were given weight. 
03 Step 3 — assess the gap: Once you know the real reason, determine whether you can fix it with new evidence. A funds refusal that you can fix with better documentation is a reapplication case. A refusal based on a legal error may warrant judicial review. 
04 Step 4 — reapply with new evidence: Every new application must address the specific refusal grounds and include evidence that was not in the refused file. Reusing the same documents is a waste of a filing fee. 
05 Alternate path — judicial review: If the officer made a legal error (misapplied the test, ignored material evidence, made an unreasonable finding), a lawyer can seek leave for judicial review at the Federal Court. This is slow and expensive — reserve it for cases where the decision was genuinely wrong, not just disappointing. 
What a refusal means — and what it does not mean
A study permit refusal is a decision by an IRCC officer that your application did not satisfy the requirements of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and Regulations. The officer must state the legal ground for refusal, but the level of detail varies. Most refusals cite section 216(1) of the Regulations (purpose of visit — the officer was not satisfied you will leave Canada at the end of your authorised stay) or the financial requirements in section 220.
A refusal is not a ban. It does not prevent you from reapplying, and it does not create a permanent record of inadmissibility. What it does is put you on notice that your next application must be materially stronger. IRCC officers can see the previous refusal in the system and will check whether you have addressed the stated concerns. A second application with the same evidence as the first is almost always refused for the same reason — the officer is looking for what changed.
Who this guide is for
International students whose Canadian study permit application was refused and who want to understand the specific refusal reason before deciding their next step. Students who received a Procedural Fairness Letter and need to prepare a response before the deadline. Education agents helping students assess whether to reapply or seek legal review.
If you have not yet applied, this guide helps you understand the common refusal grounds so you can avoid them in your initial application. For the full document checklist, read the study permit document checklist . For financial proof requirements, read the proof of funds guide .
Step 1: Read the refusal letter and identify the legal ground
The refusal letter will cite one or more provisions of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act or Regulations. The most common are: paragraph 216(1)(b) IRPR (purpose of visit — officer not satisfied you will leave Canada), section 220 IRPR (financial sufficiency — you did not demonstrate adequate funds), and section 219 IRPR (acceptance letter — issues with your PAL/TAL or letter of acceptance).
The refusal letter may use standardised language. Phrases like "I am not satisfied that you will leave Canada at the end of your stay as a temporary resident" appear in many refusal letters and do not tell you the specific reason the officer was unsatisfied. The real detail — what specific evidence was missing, which documents the officer gave weight to or dismissed — is in the GCMS notes. Do not make assumptions about what went wrong based on the refusal letter alone.
Step 2: Order and analyse the GCMS notes
GCMS notes are obtained through an ATIP request to IRCC. The request is free and typically takes 30 days. The notes contain: the officer's case notes (a narrative analysis of your application), the specific documents reviewed, the officer's findings on each requirement, and any internal flags or alerts. The case notes section is the most valuable — it will say something like "PA has not demonstrated sufficient ties to country of residence. Bank statements show a single large deposit on [date] with no source explanation."
When you receive the GCMS notes, look for: (a) which document or claim the officer found insufficient, (b) whether the officer mentions a document that you believe you submitted (if a document is not listed as reviewed, it may not have been received — this can be a ground for reconsideration), and (c) whether the officer applied the wrong legal test (e.g. demanding proof of return travel when this is not a legal requirement). If the officer made a clear factual or legal error, you may have grounds for judicial review rather than reapplication.
Step 3: Fix the specific weaknesses before reapplying
Each refusal ground requires a different type of fix. A purpose-of-visit refusal under R216(1)(b) typically requires: a revised study plan explaining why the specific Canadian programme is the logical next step in your education and career, evidence of ties to your home country (property, family, employment to return to), and an explanation of any study gaps or course changes. A funds refusal under R220 typically requires: bank statements showing funds held for a longer period (6+ months is stronger than 28 days), a documented source for any large deposits, sponsor evidence if applicable, and proof that the funds are genuinely available for your studies.
A PAL/TAL refusal is the simplest to fix — if the province issues a new attestation letter covering your intended programme, include it in the new application and confir

01 Apply before your study permit expires. Maintained status (formerly implied status) lets you continue studying while the renewal is processed — but only if the application is filed before expiry. 
02 If the permit expires without a renewal, you have 90 calendar days to apply for restoration of status and a new study permit. You cannot study during the restoration period. 
03 GCMS notes (free, ~30 days through ATIP) reveal the case officer's specific refusal reasons. Without them, reapplying is guesswork. 
04 Key renewal documents: updated letter of enrolment, proof of funds covering tuition plus living expenses at the level confirmed on the IRCC website, passport, and transcripts showing academic progression. 
05 A renewal refusal while you are inside Canada leaves you without status from the date of the decision. A restoration application or departure must follow within 90 days. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for international students in Canada whose study permit is approaching its expiry date and who need to extend their authorisation to complete their program. It covers the renewal process, maintained status, restoration of status after an expiry, GCMS notes for understanding a refusal, and the documents you need for a renewal application. It also applies to students who changed programs or institutions and need a new permit to reflect the change.
This guide is not for students applying for a study permit from outside Canada for the first time — that is an initial application with different documentary requirements. It is not for students applying for a post-graduation work permit (PGWP) — a PGWP is a separate application with its own eligibility rules and is not a study permit renewal. It is not for students whose DLI has permanently lost its designation — you need a new study permit tied to a new DLI, not a renewal of the existing permit.
Maintained status: the rule that keeps you studying
Under section R183(5) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, if you apply to renew your study permit before it expires, your existing authorisation to study continues under the same conditions until a decision is made on the renewal application. This is called maintained status. It applies automatically upon filing — you do not receive a separate document confirming it. You continue to hold the same study rights, work authorisations (if applicable), and conditions that were on your expiring permit. Maintained status ends when IRCC issues a decision. If the renewal is approved, your new study permit takes effect. If refused, you are out of status from the date of the decision and must either apply for restoration within 90 days or leave Canada.
Maintained status has limits: it does not authorise international travel. If you leave Canada while on maintained status, you lose it. Upon return, you must present a valid study permit or a Port of Entry letter of introduction. If your renewal is still pending when you return, CBSA may admit you as a visitor, which does not authorise study. Wait for the renewal decision before booking international travel unless it is unavoidable. If the original permit had a condition prohibiting work, maintained status does not remove that condition — the work authorisation is determined by the original permit's terms, not the renewal application.
Restoration of status: the 90-day safety net
If your study permit expires without a renewal application being filed, section R182 of the Regulations allows a 90-calendar-day restoration window. Within those 90 days, you may apply to restore your status as a student and for a new study permit — they are a combined application. You must pay the restoration fee (in addition to the study permit processing fee), provide an explanation of the circumstances that led to the expiry, and demonstrate that you continue to meet all the requirements for a study permit. The key documents are the same as for a renewal, plus the explanation letter.
The explanation letter is not a formality. IRCC evaluates whether the failure to apply on time was beyond your control (medical emergency, institutional error, natural disaster) or resulted from neglect. A letter that says "I forgot the expiry date" almost always results in refusal. A letter that includes: the specific date the permit expired, the reason the renewal was not filed (with supporting evidence — a doctor's note, a letter from the DLI confirming an administrative error, proof of hospitalisation), what you did as soon as you became aware, and how you will ensure compliance going forward — is treated with more weight. During the restoration period, you cannot study or work. The 90-day period is strict — day 91 is too late. If restoration is refused, you must leave Canada immediately; there is no further restoration or appeal from within Canada.
Documents you need for a renewal or restoration
IRCC assesses a renewal against the same criteria as an initial study permit application: enrolment, financial capacity, and compliance. The specific documents:
Letter of enrolment: From your DLI, on institutional letterhead, confirming full-time enrolment in a designated program, the program's expected completion date, and your academic standing. The letter must be current — dated within the last 30 days at the time of filing. If you have completed your program, you are ineligible for a study permit renewal — you need a PGWP or a new study permit for a new program at a DLI.
Proof of funds: Bank statements or a Guaranteed Investment Certificate (GIC) showing tuition fees for the remaining program period plus living expenses. IRCC publishes the minimum living expense requirement — check the current figure on the IRCC website. The funds must be i

Canada Study Permit FAQ
Clear answers about Provincial Attestation Letters, financial proof, DLI changes, maintained status, and PGWP eligibility. This FAQ aggregates the most common questions from our Canadian study permit and PGWP articles.
This FAQ is for international students who are planning to apply for a Canadian study permit, renewing an existing permit, or transitioning to a Post-Graduation Work Permit. The questions here reflect the most frequently asked issues we see in IRCC-related forums and from our own document review clients. Each answer is sourced from the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, IRCC operational instructions, and the current IRCC web guidance as of mid-2026.
The Canadian study permit system changed substantively in 2024 with the introduction of the Provincial Attestation Letter and Territorial Attestation Letter requirements, followed by ongoing adjustments to the PGWP field-of-study criteria and the cap on international student intake. These changes mean that rules you read on older forums or from third-party blogs may no longer apply. All answers below reference the current rules in effect as of July 2026.
The table of contents below lets you jump to any question directly. If your specific situation is not covered, the related articles at the bottom of this page provide deeper treatment of each topic. For applicants who need a structured review of their document package before submitting, our flat-fee checklist review can verify your evidence and forms.
How to use this FAQ
Confirm PAL/TAL, funds, and PGWP field rules on canada.ca the week you file — intake caps change.
Complementary: DLI journey pages live on ca.yousafeconsultancy.com/universities ; IRCC procedure stays on this legal host. Both are indexable and cross-linked.
Editorial-only until a named Canadian lawyer/RCIC program is live; refusal or complex status facts need licensed advice.
Last updated 2026-07-14 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
Reviewer programs for Canada matters are under development; until those programs launch, Canada content is editorial-only.
Do I need a Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL) or Territorial Attestation Letter (TAL) for my study permit?
Most post-secondary study permit applicants outside Quebec now need a Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL) or Territorial Attestation Letter (TAL) from the province or territory where they plan to study. The letter confirms that the province has allocated a spot within its international student cap. There are exemptions for primary and secondary school students, master's and doctoral degree students, and certain exchange students. If you are applying to a college diploma program or a bachelor's degree, you should request the PAL from your designated learning institution (DLI) or the provincial ministry of education before submitting your study permit application. A study permit application submitted without a required PAL will be refused. Verify current exemptions on the IRCC website before applying, as the rules and cap allocations change annually.
How much money do I need to show for a Canadian study permit?
You must demonstrate that you have enough funds to cover your first year of tuition, living expenses for yourself and any accompanying family members, and return transportation. The minimum living cost amount is set by IRCC and varies by province; verify the current figure before applying. In addition to the minimum, officers look at whether the funds are genuinely available and traceable. A Guaranteed Investment Certificate (GIC) from a participating Canadian financial institution is required for most Student Direct Stream applicants and is strongly recommended for all applicants. Bank statements should cover at least 4-6 months, and any large deposits must be explained. If a parent or sponsor is providing funds, the sponsor letter must name you, state the relationship, specify the amount committed, and be signed.
Can I change my Designated Learning Institution (DLI) when renewing my study permit?
Yes, you can change your DLI when you renew or extend your study permit, provided the new institution is on the current IRCC list of designated learning institutions and you have a valid letter of acceptance from the new DLI. You must include the new acceptance letter in your renewal application and explain why you are changing institutions. If your current permit is still valid, you must notify IRCC of the DLI change through your online account within a specified period after beginning study at the new institution. Changing DLIs does not automatically extend your permit; you must still apply for a new study permit if your current one will expire before you complete the new program.
What is "maintained status" and can I travel while my study permit renewal is pending?
Maintained status means that if you apply to extend your study permit before it expires, you can continue studying under the same conditions while IRCC processes your application. However, maintained status protects your study rights inside Canada only. If you leave Canada while a renewal is pending, you are not guaranteed re-entry, and your application may be treated differently if you attempt to return. For this reason, most immigration practitioners advise against international travel while a study permit renewal is pending. If you must travel, carry proof of your pending application, your current permit, and evidence that you still meet the requirements. Restoration is a separate, stricter process that applies only if your permit has already expired.
Does every Canadian college diploma qualify for a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP)?
No. PGWP eligibility depends on five sequential filters. First, your DLI must have been on the PGWP-eligible list as of your program start date

01 Up to 5 years per entry at the CBSA officer's discretion — not automatic; limited by passport validity and insurance coverage period. 
02 The child or grandchild must meet LICO (Low Income Cut-Off) for the most recent tax year. LICO depends on family size including the visiting parent(s). 
03 The parent must purchase Canadian medical insurance from a Canadian provider (not travel insurance from a home-country insurer) with at least $100,000 coverage, valid for at least 1 year from entry. 
04 The Super Visa is a temporary resident visa (V-1) — it does not authorize work, grant access to provincial health coverage, or create a path to permanent residence independently. 
05 An Immigration Medical Examination (IME) is required as part of the application. The parent must be admissible on health grounds. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for Canadian citizens and permanent residents who want to bring their parents or grandparents to Canada for extended stays of up to 5 years per entry. It is also for parents and grandparents who have been invited to apply and need to understand the documentary requirements from their side: medical insurance, medical exam, and proof of ties to the home country.
This guide is not for parents who want to work in Canada (the Super Visa does not authorize employment), parents who need immediate permanent residence (use PGP sponsorship or explore Humanitarian and Compassionate grounds), or parents who are inadmissible on criminality or health grounds. If the parent has a prior visa refusal or removal order from Canada, consult an immigration lawyer before applying — the Super Visa does not override existing inadmissibility findings.
Super Visa vs PGP sponsorship: which one fits now
The choice between Super Visa and PGP sponsorship is usually about timing. PGP grants permanent residence, but the annual intake is capped, selection is not guaranteed, and processing takes 12-24 months. The sponsor must demonstrate MNI (Minimum Necessary Income) for three consecutive taxation years — not just one. Super Visa only requires LICO for the most recent tax year and is generally processed within a few months.
Most families use the Super Visa as a bridge: the parent visits for extended periods under Super Visa while the PGP application is in progress. The two processes can run in parallel. A Super Visa application does not prejudice a PGP application, and vice versa. The key distinction is that Super Visa is a visitor status — the parent must maintain genuine temporary intent even while a PR application is pending. At the port of entry, the CBSA officer may ask about the PR application and assess whether the parent genuinely intends to leave at the end of the authorized stay. A pending PR application is not, by itself, grounds to refuse entry, but it is a factor the officer weighs in the overall temporary intent assessment.
LICO: the income threshold your child or grandchild must meet
The Low Income Cut-Off (LICO) is the minimum income the Canadian host must demonstrate to sponsor a parent or grandparent under the Super Visa. LICO is published annually by Statistics Canada and incorporated into IRCC's operational guidance. The host must provide their most recent Notice of Assessment (NOA) from the Canada Revenue Agency showing total income at or above LICO for the applicable family size. Family size includes the host, their spouse or common-law partner, dependent children, any previously sponsored persons still within the undertaking period, and the visiting parent(s).
If the host's income is below LICO, the Super Visa application will be refused. There is no discretionary override. A co-signer (the host's spouse or common-law partner) can combine income by providing their NOA as well. The combined household income on line 15000 of both NOAs must meet LICO. The income must be from Canadian sources reported on a Canadian tax return. Foreign income not reported to the CRA or income earned by the parent cannot be substituted. For hosts on maternity or parental leave, EI benefits reported on the NOA count toward LICO — but note that LICO is based on the most recent completed tax year, and the NOA may reflect reduced income during a leave year.
Medical insurance: the non-negotiable requirement
The parent must purchase private medical insurance from a Canadian insurance company before applying. The policy must meet all of the following requirements:
Canadian provider: The insurance must be issued by a company licensed to operate in Canada. Travel insurance purchased from a home-country insurer, even if it covers treatment in Canada, does not satisfy the requirement. The IRCC officer may verify the insurer's licensing status.
Minimum coverage: At least $100,000 in emergency medical coverage. Higher coverage ($200,000 or more) is advisable given Canadian hospital costs for uninsured patients, particularly for older parents with pre-existing conditions.
Minimum term: Valid for at least one year from the date of entry. The officer at the port of entry may request proof of the policy. If the policy start date is after the entry date, the officer may limit the authorized stay to less than the requested period.
Pre-existing conditions: Most Canadian Super Visa policies cover stable pre-existing conditions — meaning conditions that have not changed in treatment, medication, or symptoms for a defined period (typically 90-180 days, depending on the insurer). An unstable pre-existing condition may result in a coverage exclusion. Read the policy wording carefully. A claim denied for a pre-existing condition exclusion can leave the parent with a significant hospital bill.
Deductible and co-pay: Most policies carry a deductible (commonly $1,000-$5,000

Canadian tax basics for international students: the rule in plain English
International students may need to file Canadian taxes depending on income and tax residency; CRA says tax status depends on residential ties to Canada.
Who this guide is for
International students with Canadian wages, scholarships, tuition credits, benefits, refunds, or uncertainty about residency status.
Documents and evidence to prepare
SIN or ITN, T4, T4A, T2202, rent receipts where relevant, scholarship records, bank details, passport, study permit, address history, and CRA account access.
Timing, deadlines, and sequencing
Use the filing deadline for the relevant tax year and separate federal, provincial, and Quebec filing rules where needed.
How to make the file easier to approve
Teach residence first, then income slips, credits, benefits, filing method, and records.
Decision checklist before you act
The Canadian tax basics for international students checklist should include the status, contract, form edition, fee, deadline, address, school record, work authorization, tax residence, account term, insurance scope, or local procedure that controls the next step.
What gets refused / common pitfalls
Pitfalls include assuming students never file, ignoring residency ties, missing T2202, not reporting scholarships correctly, and using software that does not handle the facts.
Tax status starts with residence facts
Canadian tax for international students starts with residency for tax purposes, not with citizenship or the study permit label. CRA looks at residential ties and income facts. A student may be a resident, non-resident, deemed resident, or deemed non-resident depending on the facts and treaty position. The filing answer changes with that status.
The file should list arrival date, departure date if any, Canadian address history, school location, work history, bank accounts, provincial health coverage, spouse or dependant ties, and ties outside Canada. Those facts help decide whether the student should file a return and how income and credits should be treated.
Income slips and tuition records
Most student tax files begin with slips: T4 for employment income, T4A for scholarships or other amounts, and T2202 for eligible tuition. The student should download the slips from the school, employer, or CRA account and check that the name, SIN or ITN, year, and amounts are correct. A missing slip does not always mean income can be ignored.
Scholarships, bursaries, assistantships, co-op income, and part-time work can be treated differently. The file should separate employment wages from school-issued amounts and keep the school calendar or program records if the tax treatment depends on enrolment. That prevents a software interview from flattening all student money into one category.
SIN, ITN, and CRA account access
A student who worked in Canada may already have a SIN. A student without a SIN may need an Individual Tax Number for filing. The identity number question should be solved before the filing deadline, not during the last hour of a tax-software session. Keep the study permit, passport, school letter, and prior CRA correspondence together.
CRA account access is useful but not always available immediately to first-time filers. If the student cannot access CRA online services yet, they still need a filing plan. Keep copies of anything mailed, uploaded, or submitted through software, plus the notice of assessment once it arrives.
Credits, benefits, and province issues
Tuition credits, GST/HST credit eligibility, provincial credits, rent-related records, and moving between provinces can all affect the return. Students should not claim credits by guessing. They should keep T2202 records, rent receipts where relevant, province of residence on December 31, and any documents supporting dependants or spouse information.
Quebec can require separate attention because provincial filing may differ. A student who studied in one province and moved to another should check the year-end residence position carefully. The tax return should match the student's real residential facts, not just the address on a school account.
Immigration records can still matter
Tax filing is not an immigration application, but immigration records can help reconstruct dates, status, and residence facts. Passports, study permits, work permits, entry stamps, schoo
