International Student Tax Treaties: Tax Treaty Guide

§ Key takeaways
01 The US has 60+ income-tax treaties; many include student/trainee articles that exempt income from US tax. 
02 Common student exemptions: wages up to a dollar cap, scholarships, fellowships, training compensation. 
03 You must affirmatively claim the treaty — submit Form 8233 (wages) or W-8BEN (passive income) to the payer. 
04 India is special: Article 21(2) lets F-1 students claim the US standard deduction on Form 1040-NR. 
05 Treaty benefits often have a "look-back" clause — they can be revoked if you stay too long or change purpose. 
The process at a glance
01 Check Eligibility Determine if your country has a tax treaty with the US
The US has tax treaties with over 60 countries that reduce or eliminate withholding on certain types of income for residents of those countries. Check IRS Publication 901 for the full list. Common treaty benefits include tuition waivers and research grants being tax-exempt.
02 Claim the Benefit File Form 8233 with your employer or payer
To claim a tax treaty benefit, file Form 8233 (Exemption From Withholding) with your employer or the payer of your scholarship. You must have a valid SSN or ITIN. Submit the form before the payment is made — retroactive claims require amended returns.
03 File Correctly Report treaty benefits on your tax return
Even if income is exempt under a treaty, you must still report it on your tax return (Form 1040-NR). Attach Form 8833 (Treaty-Based Return Position Disclosure) to explain the exemption. Failure to file correctly can result in IRS notices and lost benefits.
04 Renew Annually Update your treaty claim each year
Tax treaty benefits must be claimed each year. Some treaties limit benefits to a specific number of years (e.g., 5 years for student exemptions). Track your treaty years carefully. When your treaty benefit expires, the income becomes taxable.
Overview
Work authorization is one of the most important topics for F-1 students planning to gain professional experience in the US. This guide walks through international-student-tax-treaties step by step, from eligibility to maintaining compliance after approval.
For students from India
Two big wins for Indian-cohort F-1s: (1) standard deduction via Article 21(2); (2) no separate $5,000 wage cap because the standard deduction structure is more generous overall. Use Sprintax or a non-resident-aware preparer — most US tax-prep tools miss this.

A Form W-2 
B Form 8233

Start with each schools financial aid page. Look for: merit scholarships (based on GMAT/GPA), diversity scholarships (for underrepresented nationalities), program-specific scholarships (consulting, tech, social impact), and need-based aid (rare for international students).

A 720+ GMAT score dramatically improves scholarship chances at top-25 programs. Each 10-point increase can unlock additional scholarship money. Schools use GMAT to rank candidates for merit-based awards.

Round 1 (September-October) has the largest scholarship budget. Round 2 sees reduced availability. Round 3 rarely offers scholarships. Early applications also signal strong interest and commitment to the program.

External awards (government scholarships, employer sponsorship, foundation grants) require early applications — often a year before matriculation. Build a matrix of schools, typical award ranges, deposit deadlines, and conditions (GPA, internship participation, or work-back clauses). 01 90 Days Before Request OPT recommendation from your DSO

Log into the SEVP Portal and enter your employer name, address, supervisor, and start date. Report any change of employer, address, or name within 10 days. Track unemployment days — the 90-day clock never stops.

This guide provides comprehensive information about optional-practical-training-opt-application for F-1 international students in the United States. Understanding these rules is essential for maintaining your immigration status and making informed decisions about your academic and professional future.
For students from India

03 Allow 2–6 weeks for the card. You can start work without the card if employer accepts Form I-9 alternatives. 
04 An SSN is not a work permit — it is just a number. The work permit is your I-20 (on-campus) or EAD (off-campus). 
05 Your SSN is permanent and lifetime — same number even if your status changes to H-1B, green card, or citizen. 
The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Secure a job offer or CPT/OPT authorisation
You cannot apply for an SSN without one. On-campus jobs need only an offer letter; off-campus needs CPT on the I-20 or an OPT EAD card.
02 Step 2 Get a DSO support letter
Your DSO writes a letter confirming F-1 status, full-time enrolment, and employment authorisation. Many offices have a standard template.
03 Step 3 Wait 10+ days after US arrival
SEVIS records sync to the Social Security Administration roughly 10 days after your last port-of-entry. Apply before that and you will be told to come back.
04 Step 4 Visit a Social Security office
Bring Form SS-5 (printed), passport, I-94 printout, I-20, EAD or employer letter, and the DSO letter. SSA staff do not mail forms — bring originals.
05 Step 5 Receive your card by mail
Cards arrive at the US address listed on Form SS-5 in 2–6 weeks. Store the card securely; carrying it daily is discouraged.
Overview
International students on F-1 visas must follow specific rules when seeking employment. This guide provides detailed information about social-security-number-f1-students, including eligibility criteria, application timelines, and compliance requirements.
For students from India
Your US SSN is not equivalent to an Indian Aadhaar or PAN — it ties only to US tax and employment records. Do not share the 9-digit number on social media or with anyone calling about your "student account" — there is no such thing.

A It authorises any kind of work in the US 
B It is a tax identifier — the work authorisation comes from your I-20 or EAD 
C It is required to enrol in classes 
D It replaces your I-94 
Eligibility and Key Requirements
Meeting eligibility starts with maintaining student status. You must be enrolled full-time with satisfactory academic progress and a clean SEVIS record. Different work options have additional criteria, so review specific requirements before applying.
For students from Nigeria
An SSN does NOT grant you the right to work — that comes from your I-20/EAD. Some Nigerian-cohort agents claim "I’ll get you an SSN so you can work" and quote fees. Walk away; the SSN application is free and you can only get it once you already have authorised work.

Application Process and Timelines
Timing is critical for work authorization. USCIS processing currently takes 2-5 months for Form I-765. Premium processing is available for some types. If denied, review the notice, consult with your DSO, and explore refiling or alternatives before your status is affected.

Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
Common pitfalls stem from misunderstanding rules or missing deadlines. Research your authorization type thoroughly, start early, and maintain communication with your DSO. If something is unclear, ask for clarification before proceeding rather than assuming.
“ The SSN is not your right to work — it is the tax record of the work you are already authorised to do. 
When F-1 students can apply for an SSN and what documents are needed
F-1 students may apply for a Social Security Number only after securing authorized employment — either an on-campus job offer, CPT authorization, or OPT authorization. You cannot apply for an SSN before you have a job offer or work authorization, because the SSN is primarily a tax reporting number tied to employment. The application requires: (1) a completed Form SS-5; (2) a passport valid for at least six months; (3) your I-94 admission record; (4) your most recent I-20 with DSO-endorsed employment page showing the job or CPT/OPT authorization; (5) a letter from your employer confirming the job, start date, hours, and supervisor contact information (for on-campus jobs) or the EAD card (for OPT). The Social Security Administration typically processes applications within two weeks and mails the SSN card to your US address. You need a US mailing address — P.O. boxes are not accepted — so confirm your residential address before applying.
SSN versus ITIN: understanding the difference
An SSN is issued to individuals authorized to work in the US. An Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) is issued to individuals who have a US tax filing obligation but are not eligible for an SSN — for example, F-2 dependents who have taxable US income (e.g., scholarship income, investment income) but no work authorization. If you are an F-1 student without work authorization but need to file a US tax return because of a taxable scholarship or other non-wage income, you would apply for an ITIN (Form W-7) rather than an SSN. Do not apply for both; the IRS will reject a duplicate application. Once you obtain an SSN, use it for all tax and financial purposes and abandon the ITIN. “ STEM OPT is not just "more OPT" — it is a regulated training programme. The I-983 is the contract, not paperwork. 
Initial OPT vs STEM OPT extension: eligibility and timing
Initial post-completion OPT grants 12 months of work authorization for any F-1 student who has been enrolled full-time for at least one academic year and has not used more than 12 months of full-time CPT. The STEM OPT extension adds 24 months for students who earned a degree in a STEM field from a SEVP-certified school and whose employer is enrolled in E-Verify. The extension must be applied for before the initial OPT expires, and USCIS must receive the I-765 within 60 days of the DSO entering the STEM OPT recommendation into SEVIS. If USCIS has not adjudicated the extension before initial OPT expires, you receive a 180-day automatic extension of work authorization while the application is pending, provided you applied on time. The total allowable unemployment during initial OPT is 90 days; during the STEM extension, an additional 60 days — if you exceed these limits, you accrue unlawful presence.
Form I-983 training plan: what the employer must commit to
The STEM OPT extension requires a completed Form I-983 Training Plan for STEM OPT Students, signed by both the student and the employer. The plan must describe the learning objectives, how they will be achieved, the methods of evaluation, and how the employment relates to the STEM degree. 04 Never send money before viewing a property or verifying the landlord's identity — rental scams targeting international students are common in every city. Use your university's off-campus housing portal or verified platforms. 
The process at a glance
01 Research Neighbourhoods Identify student-friendly areas near your campus
Research neighbourhoods within walking distance or along public transit routes to campus. Consider safety ratings, grocery store access, cost of living, and nightlife/ social options. University housing offices and student forums are excellent resources for honest neighbourhood reviews from current international students.
02 Set Budget Calculate your monthly housing budget
A general rule is to spend no more than 30% of your monthly income (or total budget if not working) on rent. Include utilities, internet, renters insurance, and commuting costs in your total housing budget. Using the university's off-campus housing portal can help you compare rents in different neighbourhoods.
03 Search & View Search for rentals and verify listings
Use the university housing portal, established rental platforms, and local real estate agents. Never pay a deposit before viewing or having someone verify the property. Verify the landlord's identity — legitimate landlords will have a rental license or property registration number if required locally. Ask about the lease renewal terms, increase caps, and whether early termination is allowed.

Read every clause in the lease — check the rent amount, due date, late fee, term length, subletting policy, maintenance procedures, and termination notice period. Liverpool Student Housing Guide (UK)

§ Key takeaways
01 Renting in a new city as an international student requires understanding neighbourhoods, public transit, rental costs, and your tenant rights. 
02 Start your housing search 2-3 months before arrival — popular student neighbourhoods near universities fill quickly, and early searches give you more options and better rates. 
03 Budget for rent plus utilities ($100-$300/month), transportation ($50-$200/month), groceries ($300-$500/month), and other living costs — the total monthly student budget in most cities ranges from $1,500-$3,500 depending on location. 
04 Never send money before viewing a property or verifying the landlord's identity — rental scams targeting international students are common in every city. Use your university's off-campus housing portal or verified platforms. 
The process at a glance
01 Research Neighbourhoods Identify student-friendly areas near your campus
Research neighbourhoods within walking distance or along public transit routes to campus. Consider safety ratings, grocery store access, cost of living, and nightlife/ social options. University housing offices and student forums are excellent resources for honest neighbourhood reviews from current international students.
02 Set Budget Calculate your monthly housing budget
A general rule is to spend no more than 30% of your monthly income (or total budget if not working) on rent. Include utilities, internet, renters insurance, and commuting costs in your total housing budget. Using the university's off-campus housing portal can help you compare rents in different neighbourhoods.
03 Search & View Search for rentals and verify listings
Use the university housing portal, established rental platforms, and local real estate agents. Never pay a deposit before viewing or having someone verify the property. Verify the landlord's identity — legitimate landlords will have a rental license or property registration number if required locally. Ask about the lease renewal terms, increase caps, and whether early termination is allowed.
04 Sign & Move In Review the lease and document condition
Read every clause in the lease — check the rent amount, due date, late fee, term length, subletting policy, maintenance procedures, and termination notice period. Take timestamped photos or video of every room before moving in to support your security deposit return. Keep a copy of the signed lease, rent receipts, and all correspondence with the landlord.
Overview of Student Housing in Liverpool
The student housing landscape in Liverpool offers something for every budget. From modern apartment complexes near campus to charming older homes in residential areas, the variety means you can find housing that fits your lifestyle. International students typically spend £700–£1,800 per month on rent.
For students from India
Indian students should begin the credential evaluation process early — many US universities require WES evaluation of Indian transcripts. Connect with the Indian Students Association at your university for academic support, cultural events, and professional networking. For funding, explore education loans from SBI, HDFC, and ICICI that offer collateral-free options for students admitted to US universities. The US consulates in India (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Kolkata) have varying F-1 visa interview wait times — apply early, especially during the summer peak.
Languages: English · Hindi · Tamil · Telugu
Best Neighborhoods for Students in Liverpool
Liverpool has several neighborhoods popular with students. The areas closest to university campuses are most sought after with the shortest commutes. Some students prefer quieter residential neighborhoods slightly farther from campus where rents are lower and housing is more spacious.
For students from China
Chinese students often face a significant adjustment to Western teaching styles — US and UK classrooms prioritise class participation, critical thinking, and independent research over exam-based assessment. Connect with the Chinese Students and Scholars Association (CSSA) at your university for practical support with housing, banking, and cultural adjustment. Prepare documentation in advance: Chinese academic transcripts often need notarised translations, and some universities require additional credential evaluation.
Languages: Mandarin (Simplified Chinese) · Cantonese
Housing Costs and Budgeting in Liverpool
Housing costs in Liverpool vary widely. The most affordable option is typically a shared apartment with roommates slightly farther from campus. Private studios near the university command the highest rents but offer maximum privacy.
For students from Nigeria
Nigerian students should obtain their academic transcripts and degree certificates from their institution well in advance — the NUC verification process can take several weeks. Most US and UK universities require WES evaluation for Nigerian credentials. The Nigerian Students Association at your university can provide peer support, networking opportunities, and guidance on cultural adjustment. Budget for the full cost of tuition plus living expenses, as government scholarships for undergraduate study abroad are extremely limited. Many students fund their education through family support and on-campus employment.
Languages: English (official) · Yoruba · Igbo · Hausa
Tips for International Students Finding Housing in Liverpool
Take advantage of university resources when looking for housing in Liverpool. Most universities maintain lists of verified rentals and can review lease agreements. The best options near campus tend to rent within days of being listed, so act quickly when you find a promising apartment.

The process at a glance
01 Research Neighbourhoods Identify student-friendly areas near your campus
Research neighbourhoods within walking distance or along public transit routes to campus. Consider safety ratings, grocery store access, cost of living, and nightlife/ social options. University housing offices and student forums are excellent resources for honest neighbourhood reviews from current international students.
02 Set Budget Calculate your monthly housing budget
A general rule is to spend no more than 30% of your monthly income (or total budget if not working) on rent. Include utilities, internet, renters insurance, and commuting costs in your total housing budget. Using the university's off-campus housing portal can help you compare rents in different neighbourhoods.
03 Search & View Search for rentals and verify listings
Use the university housing portal, established rental platforms, and local real estate agents. Never pay a deposit before viewing or having someone verify the property. Verify the landlord's identity — legitimate landlords will have a rental license or property registration number if required locally. Ask about the lease renewal terms, increase caps, and whether early termination is allowed.
04 Sign & Move In Review the lease and document condition
Read every clause in the lease — check the rent amount, due date, late fee, term length, subletting policy, maintenance procedures, and termination notice period. Take timestamped photos or video of every room before moving in to support your security deposit return. Keep a copy of the signed lease, rent receipts, and all correspondence with the landlord.
Overview of Student Housing in Vancouver
Vancouver is home to several universities and colleges, making it a popular destination for international students. The student housing market in Vancouver offers a range of options from traditional dormitories to shared apartments and homestays. Monthly rent for a one-bedroom apartment near campus typically ranges from C$1,200–C$2,800, while sharing a multi-bedroom apartment can bring costs down significantly.
For students from India
Indian students should begin the credential evaluation process early — many US universities require WES evaluation of Indian transcripts. Connect with the Indian Students Association at your university for academic support, cultural events, and professional networking. For funding, explore education loans from SBI, HDFC, and ICICI that offer collateral-free options for students admitted to US universities. The US consulates in India (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Kolkata) have varying F-1 visa interview wait times — apply early, especially during the summer peak.

Best Neighborhoods for Students in Vancouver
Students in Vancouver tend to concentrate in neighborhoods near university campuses. These areas offer affordable housing, easy access to campus, and a vibrant student community. Popular student neighborhoods feature coffee shops, bookstores, affordable restaurants, and public transit connections. Many students find that living within walking distance or a short bus ride from campus enhances their academic experience.
For students from China
Chinese students often face a significant adjustment to Western teaching styles — US and UK classrooms prioritise class participation, critical thinking, and independent research over exam-based assessment. Connect with the Chinese Students and Scholars Association (CSSA) at your university for practical support with housing, banking, and cultural adjustment. Prepare documentation in advance: Chinese academic transcripts often need notarised translations, and some universities require additional credential evaluation.
Languages: Mandarin (Simplified Chinese) · Cantonese
Housing Costs and Budgeting in Vancouver
The cost of student housing in Vancouver varies by location, property type, and amenities. A shared bedroom costs less than a private studio. Budget for utilities (electricity, water, internet) which add approximately C$120–C$250 per month. Groceries cost approximately C$300–C$500 per month. Creating a detailed budget before searching helps narrow down affordable options.
For students from Nigeria
Nigerian students should obtain their academic transcripts and degree certificates from their institution well in advance — the NUC verification process can take several weeks. Most US and UK universities require WES evaluation for Nigerian credentials. The Nigerian Students Association at your university can provide peer support, networking opportunities, and guidance on cultural adjustment. Budget for the full cost of tuition plus living expenses, as government scholarships for undergraduate study abroad are extremely limited. Many students fund their education through family support and on-campus employment.

body:

US Tax Guide: Tax Filing 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home

Get weekly immigration updates

§ Key takeaways
01 Every F-1 student must file Form 8843 every year — even with zero US income. 
02 F-1 students are non-resident aliens for the first 5 calendar years (substantial presence test exemption). 
03 Non-resident aliens file Form 1040-NR — NOT the standard 1040 that resident citizens use. 
04 Tax treaty benefits can wipe out US tax on scholarship or wages — but you must claim them on Form 8233 / W-8BEN. 
05 Filing deadline is 15 April. Form 8843 alone (no income) is due 15 June. 
The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Determine your tax residency
F-1 students are "exempt individuals" for the substantial-presence test for their first 5 calendar years on F-1. Year 6 onward, you may flip to resident alien.
02 Step 2 Gather your tax documents
W-2 (wages), 1042-S (treaty-exempt income, scholarships), 1099 forms (gig income), and 1098-T (tuition — informational only for non-residents).
03 Step 3 Pick the right form
Form 8843 (no-income, mandatory). Add Form 1040-NR if you had US-source income. Free filing tools include Sprintax, Glacier, and IRS Free File for some forms.
04 Step 4 Apply treaty benefits if eligible
India, China, South Korea, and 60+ countries have tax treaties. File Form 8233 with your employer for wage exemptions; W-8BEN for passive income.
05 Step 5 File by the deadline
15 April for returns with income; 15 June for Form 8843-only filers. Sign physical returns in ink and mail to the address on the form (most non-resident returns cannot e-file).
Overview
Work authorization is one of the most important topics for F-1 students planning to gain professional experience in the US. This guide walks through tax-guide-international-students-us step by step, from eligibility to maintaining compliance after approval.
For students from India
India is the ONE country with a treaty article (Article 21(2)) allowing F-1 students to claim the US standard deduction on 1040-NR. This is worth roughly $14,600 in 2026 — do not skip it. Cite the treaty article on your return.
Languages: English · Hindi · Tamil · Telugu
§ Test your knowledge
Your first calendar year on F-1 you earned zero US income. Do you still need to file anything with the IRS?
A No — no income means no filing requirement 
B Yes — Form 8843 is mandatory for every F-1 student 
C Yes — but only if you also have a UK or Canadian income 
D Only if your DSO requests it 
Eligibility and Key Requirements
F-1 work eligibility begins after completing one academic year. Your DSO must confirm your status and recommend you in SEVIS. Each work option has specific requirements: CPT needs a job offer, OPT needs a completed degree, and STEM OPT needs an E-Verified employer.
For students from China
The US-China treaty Article 20(c) exempts up to $5,000/year of personal-services wages from US tax for Chinese F-1 students. File Form 8233 with your employer at the start of the year to stop withholding upfront, rather than chasing a refund.
Languages: Mandarin (Simplified Chinese) · Cantonese
Application Process and Timelines
Each F-1 work authorization type has a different process. OPT: Form I-765 filed 90 days before to 60 days after program end. CPT: authorized by DSO before starting work. On-campus: requires securing a qualifying position. Maintain copies of all documents.
Maintaining Compliance and Reporting
Compliance involves maintaining F-1 status and following specific work rules. Continue full-time enrollment, keep your passport and I-94 valid, and report changes promptly. For CPT and OPT, ensure employment relates to your field and document your hours and responsibilities.
Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
Avoid mistakes by preparing carefully. Common errors include unsigned forms, incorrect fees, missing documents, and filing outside the window. Create a checklist and review with your DSO. After approval, avoid compliance mistakes like unreported address changes and unauthorized work.
“ Form 8843 is the form everyone forgets — and the easiest one to file. Five lines, no money, and it keeps the IRS off your back. 
Form 8843, the substantial presence test, and who must file
Most F-1 and J-1 students file Form 8843 even when they have no US wages. The form documents days of presence and exempt days under the student exemption from the substantial presence test. If you have US-source wages (on-campus work, CPT, or OPT), you generally also file Form 1040-NR or 1040-NR-EZ for the tax year and attach Form 8843. The student exemption usually lasts five calendar years for F-1 students; after that, the substantial presence test may make you a resident alien for tax purposes even if you remain in nonimmigrant status. Track your entry dates carefully. State tax returns are separate — some states follow federal residency rules and some do not. Always use the current IRS form editions and instructions for the tax year you are filing.
Treaty benefits, withholding, and common audit triggers
Many countries have income-tax treaties with the United States that can reduce or eliminate US tax on certain scholarship, fellowship, or wage income for a limited period. Claiming a treaty benefit usually requires Form 8233 or Form W-8BEN filed with the payer, plus the correct treaty article citation. Over-claiming treaty benefits, ignoring scholarship portions that are taxable, or failing to report CPT/OPT wages are frequent problems. Keep your I-20, I-94, passport entry stamps, W-2 or 1042-S forms, and bank records for at least three years. If you leave the United States, you may still need to file for the year of departure. This guide is educational — complex multi-country or dual-status years often need a tax professional who understands nonresident returns.

Full-time students in the UK are exempt from paying council tax on their primary residence. The process at a glance

02 Step 2 Pay during the online visa application
IHS is paid in the same flow as the visa fee, before biometrics. The system generates an IHS reference number — screenshot it; you will need it if you query NHS access later.

IHS gives access, not auto-registration. Walk into a local GP surgery with your passport, visa/BRP, and proof of address (university letter works). Registration is free.
04 Step 4 Keep your IHS reference for any disputes
NHS staff occasionally challenge international students at non-GP services. Show the IHS reference + visa; you should never be charged. Report wrongful invoices to the NHS Trust’s overseas patient team.

The Immigration Health Surcharge (IHS) is paid upfront when you apply for a UK visa. Vet employers via your Student Union before accepting — informal Tower Hamlets / east London cafés sometimes pay below minimum wage or off-the-books, which can breach your visa conditions and trigger curtailment.

How much paid holiday is a part-time worker entitled to?
A None — only full-time staff get holiday 
B 2 weeks per year 
C 5.6 weeks (pro-rata to hours worked) 
D 8 weeks per year 
Working During Your Studies
Student visa holders in the UK can work up to 20 hours per week during term time and full-time during holidays, depending on program level. Degree-level students typically have this allowance. Available positions include retail, hospitality, administration, and on-campus roles through the university careers service.
Important Deadlines and Timelines
Important deadlines include visa application timelines, BRP collection within 10 days of arrival, and police registration if applicable. The Graduate Route visa must be applied for from within the UK before your current visa expires. Start preparing your Graduate Route application 3 months before your program end date.
Additional Resources and Support
Your university's international student support team is your primary resource for visa guidance. Additional support includes UK Council for International Student Affairs (UKCISA), the Home Office website, and student advice centers. Many universities offer workshops on visa compliance, part-time work, and post-study options.
“ The best student job is the one closest to your library — short commute, predictable hours, sympathetic employer. The pay rate matters less than your time saved. 
Finding lawful part-time work as a Student visa holder
Target on-campus roles, retail, hospitality, and research assistant posts that accept term-time hour limits. Be transparent about the 20-hour cap in applications. Prepare a UK-style CV, right-to-work share code, and availability grid that matches your timetable. Remote freelance platforms are high risk if they treat you as self-employed. When a manager asks you to stay late, track hours so you do not accidentally breach conditions during busy weeks.
Pay, holidays, and dispute basics
You are generally entitled to National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage as applicable, itemised payslips, and statutory holiday accrual. Unpaid trial shifts beyond a short skills test can be unlawful. If hours or pay look wrong, raise it in writing with HR and keep copies. Serious exploitation can be reported through official channels

01 Degree-level Student visa holders can work 20 hours/week in term time, full-time in vacations. 
02 Below-degree-level students (foundation, language schools) are capped at 10 hours/week. 
03 A "week" is Monday to Sunday — every minute of paid work counts, even unpaid trial shifts. 
04 You cannot be self-employed, fill a permanent full-time role, or work as a sportsperson/entertainer. 
05 Breaching the 20-hour cap can void your visa, end your degree, and trigger a 10-year ban from re-entry. 
The process at a glance
01 Understand Tier 4 Rules Know the work rules for Student visa holders
Tier 4 (Student) visa holders can work up to 20 hours per week during term time and full-time during official holidays. This limit applies to both paid and unpaid work. Work must stop if you drop below full-time enrollment or your visa conditions change.
02 Check Your Visa Verify your specific work conditions
Your BRP (Biometric Residence Permit) shows your work conditions. Most Student visas allow 20 hrs/week during term time. Some short-term study visas allow only 10 hrs/week. Government-sponsored students may have additional restrictions. Always check the specific conditions on your BRP.
03 Find Permitted Work Know what types of work are allowed
Most work is permitted within the hour limit: retail, hospitality, tutoring, internships, and on-campus positions. Some roles are restricted: professional sportsperson, entertainer, doctor/dentist in training (unless on a recognized foundation program), and self-employment/business.
04 Avoid Violations Stay compliant with work conditions
Exceeding 20 hours/week even by one hour is a visa violation. Keep accurate records of your work hours. If you change programs or extend your visa, verify your work conditions remain the same. Violating work rules can affect future UK immigration applications.

For students from India

Most degree-level Student visa holders may work up to 20 hours per week during term time and full-time during official vacation periods. Below-degree courses often have tighter limits. § Key takeaways
01 The Skilled Worker visa (formerly Tier 2) is the main route from study to long-term UK settlement. 
02 You need a sponsor on the Home Office register and a Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS) before applying. 
03 From April 2024, the general salary threshold is £38,700/year — or the role’s "going rate", whichever is higher. 
04 New entrant rates (within 4 years of graduation) can be ~20% lower — a critical concession for recent graduates. 
05 Five continuous years on Skilled Worker → eligible to apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR). 
The process at a glance
01 Step 1 Find a sponsor-licensed employer
Search the Home Office register of licensed sponsors (updated monthly on gov.uk). Filter by sector and tier. Not every company on the register actively hires graduates — confirm before investing in the application.
02 Step 2 Secure a Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS)
Once hired, the employer assigns you a CoS — a digital reference number, not a paper certificate. The CoS lists job title, SOC code, salary, and start date. It is valid for 3 months.
03 Step 3 Check salary against the going rate
Your salary must beat both the general threshold (£38,700) AND the SOC-code going rate. New entrants get ~20% off both. Software developers (SOC 2136), for example, have specific going rates published.
04 Step 4 Apply online and pay fees + IHS
Application fee ~£719 (in-country, 3+ years) or ~£827 (out-of-country). IHS £1,035/year. English language proof (or CAS exemption) required. Application can be made inside or outside the UK.
05 Step 5 Track the ILR clock from day one
5 continuous years on Skilled Worker counts toward ILR. Absences over 180 days in any rolling 12-month period reset the clock — keep a travel log from the first trip.

body:

Unpaid Internship Rules for F-1 Students: Legal Guidelines 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates

§ Key takeaways
01 Unpaid internships still count as employment for F-1 visa purposes — even with no paycheck, you need authorisation. 
02 Volunteer work is only safe if it is at a charity, not in a role that would normally be paid. 
03 Unpaid roles in your field of study require CPT or OPT authorisation — the same as paid roles. 
04 Department of Labor "primary beneficiary" test determines whether an unpaid intern is legally an employee. 
05 An unpaid internship without authorisation can be cited as unauthorised employment — terminating F-1 status. 
The process at a glance
01 Check Legality Determine if the internship qualifies for F-1 work authorization
Unpaid internships for F-1 students require proper authorization — either CPT (during studies) or OPT (during or after). Volunteering for a genuine non-profit is different from an unpaid internship at a for-profit company. Without authorization, even unpaid work violates F-1 status.
02 Verify Academic Connection Ensure the internship is tied to your curriculum
For CPT-authorized unpaid internships, the work must be an integral part of your academic program. You need a signed CPT recommendation from your DSO, a letter from the employer confirming the role, and enrollment in a CPT-authorized course. Unpaid positions still require the same paperwork as paid ones.
03 Document Everything Maintain proper records of your internship
Keep your CPT authorization form, employer letters, timesheets, and academic records. Without proper documentation, USCIS may rule that you worked without authorization — even if the internship was unpaid. This can trigger F-1 status violations and future immigration complications.
04 Avoid Common Mistakes Know what F-1 students cannot do
You cannot volunteer at a for-profit company without authorization. You cannot work without CPT/OPT even if the position is unpaid. You cannot retroactively authorize past work. If in doubt, consult your DSO before starting any work.
Overview
For F-1 international students, understanding work authorization rules is critical to maintaining lawful status. This comprehensive guide explains unpaid-internship-rules-f1-students in detail, covering eligibility, application procedures, and compliance obligations.
For students from India
Indian-cohort students often accept unpaid "training" arrangements at Indian-owned US start-ups because the framing feels familiar from internships back home. The US rule is different — if the work would normally be paid, it needs CPT/OPT, regardless of community ties.
Languages: English · Hindi · Tamil · Telugu
§ Test your knowledge
You take an unpaid internship in your major. What authorisation, if any, do you need?
A None — unpaid work is exempt for F-1 students 
B CPT or OPT, the same as if it were paid 
C Only a letter from your DSO 
D Only an email confirming it is unpaid 
Eligibility and Key Requirements
To be eligible, F-1 students must maintain valid immigration status throughout the process. This means full-time enrollment, no unauthorized employment history, and SEVIS compliance. Your DSO plays a crucial role in verifying eligibility and initiating work authorization applications.
For students from Nigeria
Volunteering at your church or a Nigerian-community non-profit is genuinely fine. Working unpaid for a tech start-up "to build experience" is not — even if the offer comes through a community contact, get the CPT first.
Languages: English (official) · Yoruba · Igbo · Hausa
Application Process and Timelines
The work authorization process involves steps in the correct order. Your DSO recommends you in SEVIS and issues an endorsed I-20. Then compile your application package and submit within the designated window. Track progress through your USCIS online account.
Maintaining Compliance and Reporting
After approval, ongoing compliance is essential. Report address changes within 10 days, stay within authorized hours, and keep your SEVIS record active. For OPT participants, unemployment days count against your authorized period, so track employment status carefully.
Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
The most costly mistakes include missing filing deadlines, exceeding unemployment limits, and accepting unauthorized employment. These errors jeopardize your application and F-1 status. Understand rules thoroughly, maintain a compliance calendar, and seek professional guidance.
“ There is no such thing as a free internship for F-1 students. If it would normally be paid, USCIS treats it as paid. 
When an unpaid position crosses into unauthorized employment
US immigration law defines employment as any service performed for an employer in the United States, regardless of whether the employer pays wages. This means an unpaid internship can still be unauthorized employment if the intern is performing productive work that the employer would otherwise pay someone to do. The Department of Labor’s primary-beneficiary test weighs seven factors: (1) the extent to which the intern and the employer clearly understand that there is no expectation of compensation; (2) the training benefits the intern receives — hands-on instruction, mentoring, classroom components; (3) the internship is tied to the intern’s formal education; (4) the internship accommodates the intern’s academic commitments; (5) the internship is limited to the period when it provides beneficial learning; (6) the intern’s work complements, rather than displaces, paid employees’ work; (7) the intern and the employer understand the internship confers no entitlement to a paid job. If most factors favor the employer, the intern may be deemed an employee — and for F-1 students, unauthorized employment is a status violation regardless of payment.

Document support for Canada study permit applicants
A Canada study permit application requires a complete file: a Letter of Acceptance, a study plan or Statement of Purpose, financial evidence, and — for most provinces — a Provincial Attestation Letter. Weaknesses in any of these can lead to a refusal under IRPA section 11. MyCaseworks provides flat-fee document review services mapped to the stages of the study-permit journey, so you can address gaps before an officer sees them.
This is not a bundled package with a single price. Each service below is priced independently by tier. You choose the services that match your current stage and budget.
Preparing your study-permit application
The quality of your initial application determines whether you receive a permit or a refusal letter. Officers assess program choice, home-country ties, financial capacity, and travel history. The services below help you strengthen each component before submission.
SOP review — Tracked changes, structure check, and edit flags for your Statement of Purpose or study plan. We verify that it addresses program choice, career goals, and home-country ties.
Document checklist review — Per-document verification against IRCC published requirements. Flag missing items such as the Provincial Attestation Letter, biometrics confirmation, or medical exam.
Financial proof review — Bank-statement, sponsor-letter, and proof-of-funds verification against IRCC study-permit funding requirements, including GIC validation if applicable.
If your study permit is refused

For legal advice on a specific tenancy dispute, retain a solicitor regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority.
Frequently asked questions
Does this service cover Scotland, Wales, or Northern Ireland? No. This review is for England only. The Renters' Rights Act 2025 applies to assured shorthold tenancies in England. Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have their own tenancy regimes with different rules. If you rent in Scotland, Wales, or Northern Ireland, this review will not address the specific statutes that apply to your tenancy. 
What happens if my agreement contains clauses that the Renters' Rights Act 2025 made unenforceable? We flag every clause that is no longer enforceable under the Act — including fixed-term clauses, Section 21 eviction provisions, and unilateral rent-increase clauses. We explain why each clause is unenforceable and what the correct process is (for example, rent increases now require a Section 13 notice with a tribunal challenge period). You can use our summary to negotiate with your landlord or agent before signing. 
Will you check whether my deposit is protected? Yes. We verify that your deposit is protected with a government-approved scheme (TDS, MyDeposits, or DPS) and that you have received the prescribed information document within 30 days of payment. If either is missing, we flag it and explain the compensation route you may be entitled to under the Housing Act 2004 (as amended). 
What is Ground 4A and does it apply to my tenancy? Ground 4A is a new possession ground introduced by the Renters' Rights Act 2025. It allows landlords of student-let HMOs to end a tenancy at the end of an academic year, but only if specific notice and evidence requirements are met. We check whether your tenancy agreement references Ground 4A correctly and whether the notice period and timing comply with the Act. 
Is this legal advice? No. This is editorial review of your tenancy agreement against the Renters' Rights Act 2025, the Housing Act 1988 (as amended), and the Tenant Fees Act 2019. We flag clauses, cite the relevant statute, and explain the risk — but we do not provide legal advice on your specific dispute. An SRA-regulated solicitor review program is under development; until then, for legal advice on a specific dispute, retain a solicitor regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority.

Cap-gap extension employer letter for H-1B
The cap-gap extension allows an F-1 student on OPT to continue working legally between the expiration of OPT and the October 1 start date of an approved H-1B petition. The extension is automatic upon a timely filed H-1B petition, but the student's SEVIS record must be updated by the DSO, and the employer must provide a letter confirming the H-1B filing and the continued employment relationship. This template structures that employer confirmation letter.
Who this template is for
Employers who filed an H-1B petition for a current F-1 OPT employee and need to confirm cap-gap status.
F-1 students whose OPT expires before October 1 and whose employer needs a letter template for the DSO.
HR departments drafting cap-gap documentation for compliance audits.
Students in regular or premium processing H-1B petitions with an October 1 start date.
Annotated template
The employer should print this letter on company letterhead and sign it in ink. Replace bracketed fields.
CAP-GAP EXTENSION EMPLOYER LETTER
[Employer name]
[Employer address]
[Employer E-Verify number]
[Date]
To: [University DSO name]
[University name]
[DSO office address]
Re: Cap-gap extension for [Student full name] — SEVIS ID [NXXXXXXXX]
1. STUDENT EMPLOYMENT DETAILS
Student name: [Full name]
SEVIS ID: [NXXXXXXXX]
Current job title: [Title]
Department: [Department]
Employment start date: [DD MMM YYYY]
OPT expiry date: [DD MMM YYYY]
2. H-1B PETITION FILING
[Employer name] has filed a Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, on behalf of [Student name] in the H-1B cap-subject category.
USCIS receipt number: [XXX-XXX-XXXX]
Date filed: [DD MMM YYYY]
Requested start date: October 1, [YYYY]
Job title under H-1B: [Title]
Prevailing wage level: [Level I / II / III / IV]
3. CAP-GAP CONFIRMATION
Because the H-1B petition was filed before the student's OPT expiry date of [DD MMM YYYY], [Student name] is eligible for the cap-gap extension under 8 CFR §214.2(f)(5)(vi). [Employer name] confirms that:
• The student will continue in the same or a similar job duties until September 30, [YYYY].
• The student's employment remains authorised under the cap-gap provisions.
• The student will transition to H-1B status on October 1, [YYYY], upon approval of the petition.
4. EMPLOYER COMMITMENTS
[Employer name] commits to:
• Notify the DSO within 10 business days if the H-1B petition is denied, withdrawn, or revoked.
• Maintain accurate payroll and employment records for the cap-gap period.
• Comply with all USCIS and DOL requirements for the H-1B petition, including the Labor Condition Application (LCA).
5. CONTACT
For questions about this letter or the H-1B petition, contact:
[HR representative name]
[Title]
[Email]
[Phone]
Sincerely,
[Employer representative signature]
[Printed name]
[Title]
[Date] Annotation — Timely filing: The cap-gap extension is only available if the H-1B petition was filed while the student's OPT was still valid. If the petition was filed after OPT expiry, the student loses work authorization and must leave the US or change status. See USCIS — OPT for F-1 Students .
Annotation — DSO update: The cap-gap extension is not automatic in SEVIS. The DSO must update the student's record after receiving the employer letter and the USCIS receipt notice. The student should request an updated I-20 with the cap-gap notation. See USCIS Policy Manual — Practical Training and Cap-Gap Extension .
Annotation — LCA requirement: The H-1B petition must include an approved Labor Condition Application (LCA) from the Department of Labor. The LCA must be posted at the work site before the H-1B start date. The employer letter does not replace the LCA but confirms that the LCA process is underway.
Worked example
Employer L filed an H-1B petition (receipt EAC-26-123-45678) for Student M, a Software Engineer whose OPT expires June 15, 2026. The employer letter confirms the April 2 filing date and October 1 start date, then goes to the DSO at University O with the I-797C receipt. The DSO updates SEVIS and issues an updated I-20 with cap-gap notation, covering June 15 through September 30, 2026.
Common mistakes
Filing the H-1B petition after the OPT expiry date — this voids cap-gap eligibility.
Not notifying the DSO promptly after the H-1B filing — SEVIS must be updated before the OPT expiry.
Continuing to work after a denied or withdrawn H-1B petition without changing status.
Cited sources
USCIS — Optional Practical Training (OPT) for F-1 Students 
USCIS Policy Manual — Practical Training and Cap-Gap Extension 
8 CFR §214.2(f)(5)(vi) — Cap-gap extension 
US DOL — H-1B program / LCA overview 
Study in the States (SEVP) 
Reviewer

CAS appeal letter for UK Student Route
A Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies (CAS) can be withdrawn by the sponsoring institution if the student's documents are incomplete, if the financial evidence does not meet the 28-day rule, or if the English language requirement is not satisfied. Some sponsors also withdraw a CAS if the student misses a deposit deadline or fails to meet academic conditions. This template structures an internal appeal to the sponsor institution. It does not address UKVI visa refusals — those require a new CAS and a new visa application, not a CAS appeal.
Who this template is for
Students whose CAS was withdrawn by the university for incomplete or non-compliant documents.
Applicants who have since obtained corrected or updated evidence that resolves the original issue.
Students who missed a CAS deadline due to circumstances they can document (e.g., bank delay, test centre closure).
Applicants appealing within the sponsor's stated deadline (typically 10–20 working days).
Annotated template
Submit through the university's admissions appeals portal or by email to the designated appeals contact. Replace bracketed fields.
CAS APPEAL LETTER
[Your full name]
[Your address]
[Email]
[Phone]
[Student ID number]
[Date]
To: Admissions Appeals Office
[Sponsor institution name]
[Address]
Re: Appeal against CAS withdrawal — [Program name] — [Student ID]
1. CAS DETAILS
Original CAS number: [CAS number]
Date of issue: [DD MMM YYYY]
Date of withdrawal notice: [DD MMM YYYY]
Reason for withdrawal stated by the sponsor: [exact reason from the notice]
2. GROUNDS FOR APPEAL
I am appealing the withdrawal of my CAS on the following grounds:
Ground 1: [Corrected document]
The CAS was withdrawn because [specific reason, e.g., "bank statement did not show 28 consecutive days"]. I have since obtained a corrected bank statement from [Bank name] showing a balance of £[amount] held continuously from [date] to [date]. The statement is attached.
Ground 2: [Corrected document]
[Explanation of the second issue and the corrected evidence.]
Ground 3: [Extenuating circumstances, if applicable]
[If the withdrawal was due to a missed deadline caused by a documented external factor, e.g., a bank delay or a test centre closure, state the factor and attach evidence.]
3. CORRECTED EVIDENCE ATTACHED
• [Document 1: description and date]
• [Document 2: description and date]
• [Document 3: description and date]
4. REQUEST
I respectfully request that the sponsor reinstates my CAS so that I may proceed with my Student Route visa application. All corrected documents are genuine and available for verification.
I understand that the final decision rests with the sponsor and that I must comply with all UKVI and sponsor requirements.
Yours sincerely,
[Signature]
[Printed name]
[Student ID] Annotation — Sponsor vs UKVI: This letter is for internal sponsor appeals only. If UKVI refused the visa (not the CAS), the student needs a new CAS from the sponsor and must submit a new visa application. There is no appeal process for a UKVI Student Route refusal — the only route is judicial review, which requires legal representation. See GOV.UK — Student visa .
Annotation — Deadlines: Most UK universities have a strict appeals window, often 10–20 working days from the withdrawal notice. Appeals submitted after the deadline are usually rejected without consideration. Check the sponsor's appeals policy before writing.
Annotation — Evidence: The appeal must be based on corrected facts or documented extenuating circumstances. Emotional appeals ("I really want to study here") are not grounds for reinstatement. The evidence must directly address the reason stated in the withdrawal notice.
Worked example
Student I's CAS for an MSc in Finance at University K was withdrawn because a £12,000 deposit lacked a source explanation. The appeal letter explains the deposit as property sale proceeds, attaches the sale deed and transfer record, and provides a new bank statement showing the required balance held for 35 consecutive days. Submitted within 12 working days, University K reinstates the CAS.
Prerequisites before you start
Confirm the appeal deadline with your sponsor's admissions office — most allow 10–20 working days from the withdrawal notice. Calendar it immediately.
Obtain the corrected documents that directly address each reason stated in the withdrawal notice. Attach originals where possible; certified copies if the original is unavailable.
Contact your international student office for a copy of the sponsor's appeals policy and any institution-specific appeal form requirement.
Common mistakes
Appealing after the sponsor's stated deadline has passed.
Submitting the same documents that caused the withdrawal without correction.
Confusing a CAS withdrawal with a UKVI visa refusal — the appeal routes are different.
Writing an emotional appeal instead of addressing the specific grounds stated in the withdrawal notice — officers only consider corrected facts and documented extenuating circumstances.
Next steps after CAS reinstatement
Once the sponsor reinstates the CAS, you can proceed with the Student Route visa application. The new CAS will have updated details and a new CAS number. Submit the visa application within the CAS validity period (typically 3–6 months) and do not reuse the withdrawn CAS number in any correspondence. If the appeal is denied, ask the sponsor whether a fresh CAS application for a later intake is possible, or consider whether a different sponsor institution with a similar program is a viable alternative. Review the UKVI Student Route financial requirement and English language criteria again before re-applying, as policy changes may affect your evidence requirements.

Deposit dispute letter for UK tenants
Under the Housing Act 2004 and the Renters' Rights Act 2025, most tenancy deposits in England must be protected in a government-approved scheme (TDS, DPS, or MyDeposits) within 30 days of receipt. If the landlord fails to protect the deposit, refuses to return it, or proposes unreasonable deductions, the tenant has specific legal routes: free ADR for protected deposits, and a county court compensation claim of one to three times the deposit for unprotected deposits. This template is for tenants in the protected-but-disputed or protected-but-withheld cases. For the full legal context, see our deposit dispute guide .
Who this template is for
Tenants whose deposit was protected but the landlord has not returned it or has proposed unreasonable deductions.
Tenants who have completed the tenancy, returned the keys, and left the property in the condition required by the tenancy agreement.
International students in England who need a formal letter to escalate a deposit dispute.
Tenants who have already tried informal negotiation and need a written record for ADR or court.
Annotated template
Send by email and recorded delivery. Keep proof of postage. Replace bracketed fields.
DEPOSIT DISPUTE LETTER
[Your full name]
[Your forwarding address]
[Email]
[Phone]
[Landlord / agent full name]
[Address as on tenancy agreement]
[DATE]
Dear [Name],
Tenancy at: [property address]
Tenancy start date: [DD MMM YYYY]
Tenancy end date: [DD MMM YYYY]
Deposit amount: £[amount]
Deposit protection scheme: [TDS / DPS / MyDeposits]
Deposit protection certificate number: [number]
RE: RETURN OF DEPOSIT
1. TENANCY END AND PROPERTY CONDITION
I vacated the property on [date], returned all keys on [date], and left the property in the condition recorded in the move-out check-out report dated [date]. I have attached photographs of the property on departure.
2. DEDUCTIONS DISPUTED
You have proposed deductions of £[amount] for:
• [Deduction 1: e.g., cleaning] — I dispute this because [reason: e.g., the property was professionally cleaned on [date]; invoice attached].
• [Deduction 2: e.g., damage to item] — I dispute this because [reason: e.g., the item was noted as worn in the check-in inventory; see page [X] of the attached inventory].
3. LEGAL POSITION
Under the Housing Act 2004, a deposit protected in an approved scheme must be returned promptly after the tenancy ends, less only reasonable deductions supported by evidence. The Renters' Rights Act 2025 abolished fixed-term tenancies and strengthened tenant rights to challenge deductions.
4. REQUEST FOR ACTION
I request that you:
(a) Release the full deposit of £[amount] to me within 14 days of this letter; or
(b) Provide written evidence and cost estimates for each deduction you maintain.
If I do not receive a satisfactory response within 14 days, I will:
• Open a free ADR case with [scheme name] using the certificate number above; and
• If ADR does not resolve the matter, file a county court claim for the deposit plus costs.
5. EVIDENCE ATTACHED
• Tenancy agreement (signed)
• Deposit protection certificate
• Check-in inventory and photographs
• Check-out report and photographs
• Professional cleaning invoice (if applicable)
• All correspondence about deductions
I look forward to your response within 14 days.
Yours sincerely,
[Signature]
[Printed name] Annotation — ADR first: If the deposit was protected, free alternative dispute resolution through the scheme is usually faster and cheaper than court. The letter should mention ADR as the next step. See GOV.UK — Getting your deposit back .
Annotation — s.214 claim: If the deposit was never protected, the tenant can claim one to three times the deposit amount in compensation under s.214 Housing Act 2004, in addition to the deposit itself. ADR is not available for unprotected deposits. See Housing Act 2004, s.214 .
Annotation — Evidence: The strongest deposit disputes are won on records, not arguments. Photographs with timestamps, inventories signed by both parties, and cleaning invoices are the most persuasive evidence.
Worked example
Tenant G, an international student, paid a £1,200 deposit protected with the DPS. The landlord proposed £450 in deductions for cleaning and redecoration. Tenant G's letter rebuts both: a professional cleaning invoice two days before move-out disproves the cleaning claim, and the check-in inventory noting pre-existing marks disproves redecoration. The DPS adjudicator awards the full deposit.
Common mistakes
Accepting deductions without asking for invoices or cost estimates.
Failing to attach the check-in inventory, which is the baseline for assessing condition.
Sending the letter by email only — recorded delivery creates a legal record.
Cited sources
GOV.UK — Tenancy deposit protection 
GOV.UK — Getting your deposit back 
Housing Act 2004, s.214 
Reviewer
This template was prepared by MyCaseworks Editorial. Reviewer programs for UK matters (SRA-regulated solicitors) are under development; until those programs launch, UK templates are editorial-only. For case-specific legal advice, retain a solicitor regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority.

Financial sponsor letter for Canada study permit
IRCC requires proof that a Canadian study permit applicant has enough money to pay tuition and living expenses for the first year. A sponsor letter is one way to show that a parent, guardian, or spouse will provide those funds. Unlike the US F-1 process, IRCC places heavy emphasis on the source of funds—officers want to see that the money was earned or saved lawfully, not borrowed temporarily for the application. This template structures a sponsor letter around IRCC's published requirements.
Who this template is for
Students whose first-year costs will be covered partly or fully by a family member.
Applicants who have purchased a GIC and need the sponsor letter to explain its source.
Sponsors with documented employment income, business income, or documented savings.
Students applying under the Student Direct Stream or the regular study permit stream.
Annotated template
The sponsor should sign this letter in ink. A notarised signature is recommended if the sponsor is self-employed or if the funds come from a business. Replace bracketed fields.
FINANCIAL SPONSOR LETTER
[Sponsor full name]
[Sponsor address]
[Sponsor phone]
[Sponsor email]
[Date]
To: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada
Re: Financial support for [Student full name] — study permit
1. SPONSOR DETAILS
I, [Sponsor name], am the [relationship: father / mother / legal guardian / spouse] of [Student name]. I am a citizen of [country] and reside at [address]. I am employed as [job title] at [Employer name] / I am the owner of [Business name], a [type of business] registered in [country] since [year].
2. COMMITMENT
I commit to providing CAD $[amount] to cover [Student name]'s first-year costs at [DLI name]:
• Tuition: CAD $[amount]
• Living expenses: CAD $[amount] (based on IRCC minimum of $[1,334 or 1,023]/month for [number] months)
• Total first-year commitment: CAD $[amount]
This support will continue for the duration of the program or until [Student name] completes the credential, whichever comes first.
3. SOURCE OF FUNDS
The funds are sourced as follows:
• Annual income: CAD $[amount] from [salary / business profit / rental income]
• Savings: CAD $[amount] held at [Bank name], account [number]
• GIC (if applicable): CAD $[amount] purchased from [Canadian bank name] on [date], certificate [number]
The funds have been accumulated over [number] years through [employment / business / savings]. Attached are my [employment letter / business registration / tax returns] and bank statements.
4. RELATIONSHIP TO THE STUDENT
[Student name] is my [son / daughter / ward / spouse]. I have supported [his / her] education since [year]. I have attached [birth certificate / marriage certificate / guardianship order] as proof of relationship.
5. DECLARATION
I declare that the information in this letter is true and accurate. I understand that IRCC may verify these documents with the issuing institutions.
Sincerely,
[Sponsor signature]
[Sponsor printed name] Annotation — Source of funds: IRCC officers frequently refuse applications where the bank statement shows a large unexplained deposit shortly before the application. The sponsor letter must explain the origin of every significant sum. See IRCC — Study permit .
Annotation — GIC coordination: If the student has purchased a GIC, the sponsor letter should state who provided the funds for the GIC and attach the purchase certificate. The GIC is mandatory for the Student Direct Stream and strongly recommended for all applicants.
Annotation — Income documentation: Salaried sponsors should attach an employment letter and recent tax returns. Self-employed sponsors should attach business registration, tax filings, and bank statements showing business revenue. Retired sponsors should attach pension statements or investment income records.
Worked example
Sponsor Z is the mother of Student E, accepted to a BBA at DLI X in Ontario. Sponsor Z owns a retail business registered since 2015 with annual profit of CAD $48,000 and savings of CAD $35,000. The letter states the business details and commits CAD $28,000 for first-year costs, accompanied by business registration, tax returns, bank statements, and a GIC of CAD $20,635 purchased from a participating Canadian bank.
Common mistakes
Submitting a letter without explaining the source of large deposits.
Using a sponsor whose income is not documented (e.g., cash-based business with no tax filings).
Committing to an amount that does not cover tuition plus the IRCC living-cost minimum.
Cited sources
IRCC — Study permit 
IRCC — Proof of financial support 
IRCC — Get your study permit documents 
IRCC — Get the correct documents

Template — US — Attorney-reviewed
Financial sponsor letter for US F-1
A financial sponsor letter is a formal declaration that a third party will pay some or all of the costs of a US education. Consular officers read this letter alongside the sponsor's bank statements, tax returns, and employment letter. The letter must be specific about the relationship, the income source, the amount committed, and the duration of support. Generic or overly broad letters are a common reason for F-1 delays and refusals.
Who this template is for
Students whose education will be funded partly or fully by a parent, guardian, or spouse.
Sponsors who are salaried employees with documented tax returns and bank statements.
Students applying to programs where the I-20 cost estimate exceeds their personal savings.
Applicants who need a standardised format that consular officers recognise.
Annotated template
The sponsor should write this letter on official letterhead if employed, or on plain paper with a notarised signature if self-employed. Replace bracketed fields.
FINANCIAL SPONSOR LETTER
[Sponsor full name]
[Sponsor address]
[Sponsor phone]
[Sponsor email]
[Date]
To: US Consulate / USCIS
Re: Financial support for [Student full name] — F-1 student visa
1. SPONSOR DETAILS
I, [Sponsor name], am the [relationship: father / mother / legal guardian / spouse] of [Student name]. I am a citizen of [country] and currently reside at [address]. I am employed as [job title] at [Employer name], where I have worked since [start date]. My gross annual income is [currency and amount], as documented by my employment letter and tax returns.
2. COMMITMENT
I commit to paying the following costs for [Student name]'s education at [University name]:
• Tuition and fees: [currency and amount] per [year / semester / program]
• Living expenses: [currency and amount] per [month / year]
• Health insurance and other required costs: [currency and amount]
• Total commitment: [currency and amount] for the [duration] of the program
This support is unconditional and will continue for the duration of the program or until [Student name] completes the degree, whichever comes first.
3. SOURCE OF FUNDS
The funds will come from:
• My salary at [Employer name]: [currency and amount] per year
• Savings held at [Bank name], account [number], balance [currency and amount] as of [date]
• [Other source, if any: property rental, investment income, etc.]
4. RELATIONSHIP TO THE STUDENT
[Student name] is my [son / daughter / ward / spouse]. I have supported [his / her] education since [year]. Attached are copies of [birth certificate / marriage certificate / guardianship order] proving the relationship.
5. DECLARATION
I declare that the information in this letter is true and accurate. I understand that providing false information may result in visa denial and legal consequences.
Sincerely,
[Sponsor signature]
[Sponsor printed name] Annotation — Relationship: USCIS and consular officers require proof of the sponsor relationship. A birth certificate, marriage certificate, or legal guardianship order is standard. Distant relatives or family friends may be asked for additional evidence of why they are sponsoring the student. See USCIS Policy Manual Vol. 2, Part F, Chapter 2 .
Annotation — Amount: The total commitment must meet or exceed the figure on the student's Form I-20. If multiple sponsors are involved, each letter should state the specific portion they are covering, and the sum must equal the I-20 total.
Annotation — Income verification: Officers cross-check the stated annual income against tax returns and bank deposits. A sponsor who claims $80,000/year but whose bank statements show only $30,000 in annual deposits will raise questions. Attach the employment letter and the most recent tax return.
Worked example
Sponsor Y is the father of Student D, admitted to an MS in Mechanical Engineering. Sponsor Y is a senior engineer earning $65,000/year with 12 years tenure and $45,000 in savings. The letter commits $55,000 over two years from salary and savings, accompanied by employment letter, tax returns, bank statements, and a birth certificate. Total matches the I-20 estimate of $52,000.
Prerequisites before you start
Confirm the I-20 total cost figure for your program — the sum of all sponsor commitments must equal or exceed this amount. International student offices can provide a detailed cost breakdown by semester.
Gather the sponsor's supporting documents before writing the letter: employment letter, recent tax returns (1–3 years), bank statements showing the committed funds, and a relationship document (birth certificate, marriage certificate, or guardianship order).
If multiple sponsors are involved, coordinate each sponsor's stated commitment so the total across all letters covers the full I-20 estimate without gaps or overlaps.
Common mistakes
Vague language like "I will support the student as needed" — officers need a specific amount.
Stated income that does not match tax returns or bank deposits.
Committing to an amount less than the I-20 total cost figure.
Notarising the sponsor's signature in a country where notarisation is not required by the consular post — check local embassy guidance before paying for notary services.
Next steps after preparing the letter
Once the sponsor letter and all supporting documents are assembled, upload the completed package to the visa application portal or bring it to the visa interview. Keep a duplicate set organised by tab (sponsor letter, income proof, relationship proof) so the consular officer can verify documents quickly. If the application is approved, the sponsor letter serves as a reference document for the duration of the program. If the application is refused on financial grounds, review the refusal not

I-983 training plan for STEM OPT
Form I-983 is the training plan required for a 24-month STEM OPT extension. Both the student and the employer must sign it, and the employer must be enrolled in E-Verify. USCIS and SEVP auditors review I-983s for compliance. A deficient training plan is one of the most common reasons for STEM OPT RFEs (Requests for Evidence) and denials. This template structures the I-983 Section 5 training plan with specific, measurable objectives that satisfy 8 CFR §214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C).
Who this template is for
F-1 students applying for a 24-month STEM OPT extension with an E-Verify employer.
Employers who need a compliant training plan format for their HR or legal files.
Students who received an RFE on a prior I-983 and need to resubmit with stronger objectives.
DSOs who want a standardised template to recommend to students and employers.
Annotated template
This template covers Section 5 of Form I-983 (Training Plan for STEM OPT Students). Sections 1–4 are administrative and should be filled directly on the USCIS form. Replace bracketed fields.
FORM I-983 — SECTION 5: TRAINING PLAN FOR STEM OPT STUDENT
Student name: [Full name]
SEVIS ID: [NXXXXXXXX]
Employer name: [Company name]
E-Verify number: [XXXXXXXX]
Site of activity: [Address where student will work]
Training start date: [DD MMM YYYY]
Training end date: [DD MMM YYYY] (24 months later)
5.1 STUDENT ROLE
Title: [Job title]
Department: [Department name]
Full-time status: Yes / No (must be at least 20 hours/week)
5.2 TRAINING PLAN — LEARNING OBJECTIVES
The student will receive practical training in the following areas:
Objective 1: [Specific technical skill]
Description: The student will learn [specific technique, tool, or methodology] by completing [specific project or task].
Measurement: [How success is measured: e.g., completion of module, passing score on internal assessment, delivery of working code].
Supervisor oversight: [Name], [title], will review progress weekly / bi-weekly.
Objective 2: [Specific technical skill]
Description: The student will apply [academic knowledge] to [industry problem] using [specific technology or process].
Measurement: [Specific deliverable or metric].
Supervisor oversight: [Name], [title], will review progress [frequency].
Objective 3: [Specific technical skill]
Description: The student will gain proficiency in [specific competency] through [specific activity].
Measurement: [Specific deliverable or metric].
Supervisor oversight: [Name], [title], will review progress [frequency].
5.3 EMPLOYER COMMITMENTS
The employer commits to:
• Provide structured and guided work-based learning related to the student STEM degree.
• Assign a supervisor with expertise in [field] and the capacity to train and mentor the student.
• Not replace a full-time or part-time US worker with the student.
• Provide compensation and benefits comparable to similarly situated US workers.
• Report material changes to the training plan to the DSO within 5 business days.
5.4 EVALUATION SCHEDULE
First evaluation (midpoint): [Date, approximately 12 months from start]
• Review progress against Objectives 1–3.
• Identify any gaps and adjust the plan if needed.
• Signed by student and employer representative.
Final evaluation (end of training): [Date, approximately 24 months from start]
• Assess achievement of all objectives.
• Determine whether additional training or employment is appropriate.
• Signed by student and employer representative.
5.5 CORRECTIVE ACTION
If the student is not making adequate progress, the employer will:
• Meet with the student within [timeframe] to identify obstacles.
• Revise the training plan with modified objectives or additional resources.
• Document the revision and notify the DSO.
Employer signature: ___________________ Date: ___________
Student signature: ___________________ Date: ___________ Annotation — Specific objectives: USCIS and SEVP reject I-983s with vague objectives like "gain industry experience." Each objective must state a specific skill, the method of learning, and the measurement of success. See ICE — Form I-983 Instructions .
Annotation — E-Verify: The employer must be enrolled in E-Verify and maintain enrollment for the duration of the STEM OPT period. Loss of E-Verify eligibility terminates the student's STEM OPT authorization. See USCIS — E-Verify .
Annotation — Evaluation schedule: Two formal evaluations are mandatory. Both must be signed by the student and employer. Missing evaluations are a common audit failure and can result in revocation of STEM OPT.
Worked example
Student H, an MS in Data Science graduate, is hired as a Junior Data Scientist at E-Verify enrolled Tech Company J. The I-983 includes three measurable objectives: build predictive models validated against A/B tests, deploy models via the MLOps pipeline, and present findings to stakeholders. Each has a specific metric and a named supervisor (PhD in Statistics), with evaluations at Month 12 and 24.
Common mistakes
Vague learning objectives with no measurable outcomes.
Employer not enrolled in E-Verify at the time of filing.
Missing or late formal evaluations — both midpoint and final are mandatory.
Cited sources
ICE — Form I-983 and Instructions 
USCIS — Optional Practical Training (OPT) for F-1 Students 
USCIS — E-Verify 
Reviewer
