Template — Canada — Editorial-only
SOP after Canada study permit refusal
Canadian study permit refusals are typically issued under section 11 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), which gives officers broad discretion to refuse if they are not satisfied the applicant will leave Canada at the end of their stay. The most common sub-grounds are an unclear study plan, insufficient financial proof, weak ties to the home country, and a mismatch between the applicant's academic history and the chosen Canadian program. This template structures a reapplication around those discretionary factors.
Who this template is for
Applicants refused under IRPA s.11 for an unclear or generic study plan.
Students whose financial documents did not show a clear path from income to savings to the GIC or first-year funds.
Applicants with weak ties to their home country who can now demonstrate employment, property, or family obligations.
Students reapplying to the same or a different DLI with a more specific academic and career rationale.
Annotated template
Replace bracketed fields. Each annotation explains what IRCC expects for that section.
STATEMENT OF PURPOSE
[Your full name]
[Passport number]
[Date]
To: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada
Re: Study permit reapplication — [Program name] at [DLI name]
Prior refusal date: [DD MMM YYYY]
UCI: [UCI from prior application]
1. THE REFUSAL GROUND
My previous study permit application was refused on [date] under section 11 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. The refusal letter indicated that the officer was not satisfied that [study plan / financial capacity / ties to home country / purpose of visit] was genuine. I have taken the following steps to address those concerns.
2. THE STUDY PLAN — WHY THIS PROGRAM, WHY CANADA, WHY NOW
I am applying to the [program name] at [DLI name] because [specific course, faculty member, research facility, or industry partnership that is unique to this institution].
This program is not available in [home country] because [specific reason: lack of specialisation, different curriculum, no accredited equivalent]. After completing the [credential], I will return to [home country] to [specific job, professional licence, or family business role].
My prior education in [field] at [institution] prepared me for this program by [specific skills]. The gap between my current knowledge and the requirements of my target role is [specific competency], which this program addresses through [module or project name].
3. FINANCIAL CAPACITY
Total first-year cost: CAD $[tuition + living expenses].
Funds available:
• GIC: CAD $[amount] with [Canadian bank name], certificate number [number], purchased on [date].
• First-year tuition balance: CAD $[amount] held at [bank name] in [country].
• Living expenses: CAD $[amount] from [source].
Source of funds:
• [Sponsor name, relationship, annual income, employer, tax document reference]
• [If self-funded: employment letter, tax returns for [years], bank statements showing salary deposits]
The funds are liquid, documented, and available without restriction. There are no unexplained large deposits.
4. TIES TO [HOME COUNTRY]
I will leave Canada at the end of my studies because:
• [Employment: job title, employer name, expected start date, letter reference]
• [Property: address, ownership document, value]
• [Family: specific obligation, e.g., caregiving, family business succession]
• [Professional licence: licence name, issuing body, requirement that it be obtained in home country]
I have no immediate family members in Canada. I have not previously overstayed a visa in any country.
5. TRAVEL HISTORY
I have travelled to [countries] on [visa types] and returned within the authorised period each time. My passport stamps and previous visas demonstrate compliance with immigration conditions.
6. PURPOSE OF VISIT
My sole purpose in Canada is to complete the [program name] at [DLI name]. I understand that the study permit does not authorise work beyond the limits set by IRCC. I will depart Canada no later than [date — typically 90 days after program end].
Sincerely,
[Signature]
[Printed name] Annotation — Study plan specificity: IRCC officers frequently refuse applicants whose study plan is generic ("I want a better future"). The SOP must name the exact program, explain why it is not available at home, and connect it to a dated, specific post-graduation plan. See IRCC — Study permit .
Annotation — GIC: A Guaranteed Investment Certificate from a participating Canadian bank is required for most applicants under the Student Direct Stream and is strongly recommended for all applicants. The minimum amount is set annually by IRCC and varies by province. See IRCC — Study permit .
Annotation — s.11 discretion: Section 11 of IRPA gives officers wide latitude. The burden is on the applicant to demonstrate that they will leave Canada. The SOP should not promise to "apply for PGWP" or "seek permanent residence"—those statements can support a refusal.
Worked example
Student C was refused for a BSc in Renewable Energy at DLI W under s.11 IRPA (study plan and ties). The revised SOP names DLI W's specific wind-energy lab, cites the absence of any accredited renewable-energy BSc in Country Z, and attaches a letter from Power Utility V confirming the BSc is required for promotion to Project Engineer, with a March 2029 start date. A GIC of CAD $20,635 is attached.
Common mistakes
Writing a generic study plan with no connection to the specific DLI program or faculty.
Mentioning the Post-Graduation Work Permit or permanent residence as a goal.
Choosing a program at a lower level than the applicant's current qualification without a career reason.
Cited sources
IRCC — Get your study permit documents 
IRCC — Proof of financia

Template — UK — Editorial-only
SOP after UK Student Route refusal
UK Student Route refusals fall into four main categories: financial requirement failure, CAS credibility doubts, English language concerns, and genuineness under Appendix V. Unlike US §214(b) refusals, which centre on immigrant intent, UK refusals often focus on whether the funds are genuinely available and whether the course fits the applicant's academic history. This template structures a reapplication SOP around those specific doubts.
Who this template is for
Applicants refused under Appendix V for failing the financial maintenance requirement.
Students whose CAS details conflicted with their financial documents or academic record.
Applicants whose bank statements did not meet the 28-day rule or whose funds were not genuinely accessible.
Students reapplying to the same or a different UK institution with corrected documentation.
Annotated template
Replace bracketed fields. Each annotation explains what UKVI expects for that section.
STATEMENT OF PURPOSE
[Your full name]
[Passport number]
[Date]
To: UK Visas and Immigration
Re: Student Route visa reapplication — [Course name] at [University name]
Prior refusal date: [DD MMM YYYY]
1. THE REFUSAL GROUND
My previous Student Route application was refused on [date]. The refusal notice cited [specific paragraph — e.g., Appendix V para 320(2), financial requirement, CAS mismatch, or English language]. I have reviewed the refusal grounds and taken the following corrective steps.
2. CORRECTIVE STEPS TAKEN
Since the refusal:
• [Financial fix: new bank account with 28-day balance history, corrected sponsor letter, or removed unclear large deposits]
• [CAS fix: obtained corrected CAS from the university with matching course title, fee, and start date]
• [English fix: new SELT result at CEFR B2 or above from an approved provider]
• [Academic fit fix: explained the progression from prior degree to this course with a clear skills gap]
3. FINANCIAL MAINTENANCE
My tuition fees for [course name] are £[amount]. My living costs are calculated at £[1,334 or 1,023]/month for [number] months = £[amount]. Total required: £[amount].
These funds are held in:
• [Bank name, account type, account holder name, currency]
• [Opening balance date: DD MMM YYYY]
• [Closing balance date: DD MMM YYYY — must be within 31 days of application date]
• [Balance on closing date: £amount]
The funds have been held continuously for 28 days. There are no unexplained large deposits. The source of the funds is [salary / savings / property sale / family gift — with supporting document reference].
4. COURSE CHOICE AND ACADEMIC PROGRESSION
I am applying for [course name] at [University name] because [specific module, research group, or career-relevant skill]. This course follows my prior qualification in [subject] from [institution] by addressing the gap in [specific skill or knowledge area].
After completing the [degree], I intend to return to [home country] to [specific job, family business, or professional licence requirement]. My [employer / family] has confirmed this plan in writing [attach letter reference].
5. GENUINE STUDENT CRITERIA
I meet the genuine student criteria because:
• My academic history shows consistent progression in [field].
• The course is at a higher level than my current qualification ([RQF level]).
• I have researched the course content, the faculty, and the career outcomes.
• I can explain why this course, at this university, at this time—not a generic statement.
6. ENGLISH LANGUAGE
I have passed [test name] at CEFR [level] with scores: [reading, writing, listening, speaking]. The test was taken on [date] at [centre name] and is listed on the UKVI approved provider register.
Sincerely,
[Signature]
[Printed name] Annotation — 28-day rule: UKVI requires funds to have been held for 28 consecutive days ending no more than 31 days before the application date. The balance must not dip below the required amount on any day. See UKVI — Student visa money requirements .
Annotation — Genuine student: Appendix V requires officers to assess whether the course is credible given the applicant's academic and employment history. A gap of several years without explanation can trigger refusal. Address gaps directly.
Annotation — CAS consistency: The CAS must match the course title, fee, and start date on the unconditional offer letter. Any discrepancy—even a typo—can result in refusal.
Worked example
Student B was refused a Student Route visa for an MSc in Data Science after a £15,000 deposit three days before the statement date lacked source explanation. The reapplication SOP explains the deposit as property sale proceeds, attaches the sale deed and transfer record, and moves funds into a new account 35 days before the application. A module-by-module explanation replaces the generic "I want to study in the UK."
Common mistakes
Submitting the same bank statement with the unexplained deposit still present.
Writing a generic SOP that does not mention the specific refusal paragraph.
Ignoring the 28-day rule by applying with a statement that ends more than 31 days before the application date.
Cited sources
GOV.UK — Student visa 
UKVI — Student visa money requirements 
UKVI — Student visa: your CAS 
Reviewer

The content is based on published UKVI guidance and the Immigration Rules. For case-specific legal advice, retain a solicitor regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority.

Template — US — Attorney-reviewed
SOP after F-1 visa refusal
Most F-1 refusals are issued under INA §214(b), which presumes every visa applicant intends to immigrate permanently. The consular officer found your ties to your home country insufficient to overcome that presumption. This template helps you write a new Statement of Purpose that directly addresses the doubted elements—ties, finances, and post-study plans—without contradicting your prior application.
Who this template is for
Students refused under INA §214(b) who are reapplying for the same or a different US program.
Applicants whose financial documents or family ties have changed materially since the first interview.
Students who can show a specific, time-bound post-graduation plan that returns them home.
Applicants whose first SOP was generic and did not address the officer's specific doubt.
Annotated template
Copy the text below into your own document. Replace bracketed fields. Each annotation explains why the field matters and what the consular officer is looking for.
STATEMENT OF PURPOSE
[Your full name]
[Passport number]
[Date]
To: US Consulate [City]
Re: F-1 visa reapplication — [Program name] at [University name]
Prior refusal date: [DD MMM YYYY]
1. THE REFUSAL GROUND
My previous F-1 application was refused under INA §214(b) on [date]. I understand that the consular officer was not satisfied that I have strong enough ties to [home country] to ensure my departure from the United States after my studies.
2. WHAT HAS CHANGED SINCE THE FIRST APPLICATION
Since my last interview, the following material facts have changed:
• [New or strengthened tie — e.g., property ownership, employment offer, family business role]
• [Updated financial evidence — e.g., higher sponsor balance, new scholarship, reduced loan burden]
• [Academic clarity — e.g., changed to a more specific program, added a defined research topic]
3. TIES TO [HOME COUNTRY]
I intend to return to [home country] because:
• [Specific post-graduation role: job title, employer name, expected start date]
• [Family obligation: caregiving responsibility, family business continuity]
• [Property or asset: address, ownership document reference]
• [Professional licensing requirement: name of license, issuing body, requirement that it be obtained domestically]
4. FINANCIAL CAPACITY
My education will be funded by:
• [Sponsor name, relationship, annual income, source]
• [Liquid funds available: amount, currency, bank, account type]
• [Scholarship or assistantship: name, amount, duration]
• [Loan: lender, amount, repayment start date]
Total first-year cost: $[amount] — available funds: $[amount]
5. ACADEMIC AND CAREER PLAN
I am applying to [Program name] at [University name] because [specific faculty, research lab, or curriculum element]. After completing the [degree] in [expected month/year], I will return to [home country] to [specific job or venture]. This plan is time-bound: my [employer/family] expects me by [date].
6. NO IMMIGRATION INTENT
I have no relatives in the United States. I have not applied for any other US immigration benefit. I understand that the F-1 visa is non-immigrant and that unauthorized work or overstay would bar me from future US entry.
Sincerely,
[Signature]
[Printed name] Annotation — §214(b): INA §214(b) places the burden on you to prove non-immigrant intent. The officer looks for concrete, dated, home-country-specific ties—not general statements like "I love my country." Cite specific employers, properties, or licenses.
Annotation — Financial capacity: USCIS and consular officers cross-check your I-20 cost estimate against your financial documents. The total available funds should equal or exceed the I-20 figure. Do not inflate amounts; officers verify bank statements. See USCIS Policy Manual Vol. 2, Part F, Chapter 2 .
Annotation — Contradictions: Every date, amount, and institution name must match your DS-160, I-20, and financial documents. A single mismatch can trigger a second refusal under §212(a)(6)(C)(i) for misrepresentation.
Worked example
Student A, refused an F-1 visa for a CS MS under §214(b), now has a residential property deed in their name and a written job offer from Tech Firm Z with a January 2028 start date — six months after expected graduation. The revised SOP states the refusal ground, attaches the property deed and job offer as evidence, and ties every claim to a dated, verifiable record without mentioning OPT or US employment.
Common mistakes
Mentioning OPT, H-1B, or any US work-authorisation plan — this reinforces §214(b).
Using the same SOP as the first application with only the date changed.
Claiming ties that cannot be documented (e.g., "my family needs me" without a medical or business record).
Cited sources
US Department of State — Student Visa (F-1) 
USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 2, Part F, Chapter 2 — Students 
USCIS Policy Manual — Form I-20, Certificate of Eligibility for Nonimmigrant Student Status 
Reviewer

Template — Canada — Editorial-only
Study plan for Canada study permit
IRCC officers use the study plan to assess whether an applicant is a "genuine student" under section 11 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. A strong study plan explains why the specific Canadian program was chosen, how it fits the applicant's academic and career history, and why the applicant will return home after graduation. Generic plans are one of the most common refusal grounds. This template structures the plan around IRCC's published criteria.
Who this template is for
Applicants whose first study permit was refused for an unclear or generic study plan.
Students applying to a program that is not an obvious next step from their prior degree.
Applicants with a gap between their last education and the Canadian program.
Students who can show a direct link between the Canadian credential and a specific home-country job or licence.
Annotated template
The study plan is typically 1–2 pages. Replace bracketed fields. Each annotation explains what IRCC expects.
STUDY PLAN
[Your full name]
[Passport number]
[Date]
To: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada
Re: Study plan for [Program name] at [DLI name]
1. CURRENT EDUCATION AND WORK BACKGROUND
I hold a [prior degree] in [field] from [Institution name] in [country], completed in [year]. Since [year], I have worked as [job title] at [Employer name], where I [brief description of responsibilities].
2. WHY THIS PROGRAM
I am applying to the [Program name] at [DLI name] because:
• The program offers [specific course, module, or research group] that is not available in [home country].
• The faculty includes [Professor name], whose work on [topic] aligns with my career goal of [specific role].
• The program includes a [co-op / internship / capstone project] with [industry partner type], which will provide practical experience in [specific skill].
3. WHY CANADA
Canada is the right place for this study because:
• [Specific reason: regulatory environment, research funding, industry concentration, or academic specialisation that does not exist at home.]
• The credential is recognised by [professional body or employer in home country].
• The program duration and cost are structured to allow completion without unnecessary delay.
4. CAREER GOAL AND RETURN PLAN
After completing the [credential] in [expected month/year], I will return to [home country] to:
• [Specific job title] at [Employer name] — offer letter attached.
• [Professional licence requirement] — the Canadian credential is a prerequisite for [licence name] issued by [issuing body].
• [Family business role] — my [family member] has confirmed that my return is required by [date] to [specific responsibility].
5. FINANCIAL PLAN
The total cost of the program is CAD $[amount]. I will fund this through:
• Personal savings: CAD $[amount]
• Sponsor: [Name, relationship, amount] — letter attached
• GIC: CAD $[amount] — certificate attached
6. TIES TO HOME COUNTRY
I will leave Canada after my studies because:
• [Property: address, ownership document]
• [Employment: job offer or expected promotion]
• [Family obligation: specific responsibility]
• [Professional licence: requirement to practise in home country]
I have no relatives in Canada and no pending immigration applications in any country. Annotation — Program specificity: IRCC officers frequently refuse applicants who write generic statements like "Canada has a world-class education system." The plan must name the exact courses, faculty, or facilities. See IRCC — Study permit .
Annotation — Career coherence: The plan must show a logical progression from prior education to the Canadian program to the post-graduation role. A gap without explanation (e.g., an accountant applying to a culinary program) can trigger refusal.
Annotation — Return intent: The plan should not mention the Post-Graduation Work Permit or permanent residence. Those goals conflict with the requirement to leave Canada at the end of the authorized stay.
Worked example
Student F, a junior structural engineer with a BSc in Civil Engineering, applies for an MSc in Seismic Engineering at DLI V in BC. The study plan explains that no university in Country Z offers a dedicated seismic program, DLI V's earthquake-simulation lab is unique in North America, and Firm W confirms the MSc is required for promotion to "Senior Structural Engineer — Seismic Design," now mandated for high-rise projects.
Common mistakes
Writing a generic "why Canada" section with no reference to the specific DLI or program.
Mentioning the PGWP or express entry as post-graduation goals.
Choosing a program at the same or lower level than the current qualification without explaining the skills gap.
Cited sources
IRCC — Get your study permit documents 
Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, s.11 
IRCC — Study in Canada 
IRCC — Prepare your study permit application

title: UK Graduate Route 2026 Changes: What Students Need to Know
body:
Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com
Source URL: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com/uk/blog/graduate-route-2026-changes/

UK Graduate Route 2026 Changes: What Students Need to Know 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
In 60 seconds
01 Current duration: 2 years for bachelor's/master's, 3 years for PhD. No changes implemented as of July 2026. 
02 MAC recommended retaining the route in May 2026 with tighter compliance checks rather than a duration cut. 
03 Timing: apply before your Student permission expires. Section 3C leave covers pending in-time applications. 
04 No restrictions on job type or salary level during the Graduate Route — you can work in any role, be self-employed, or be unemployed for a reasonable period. 
05 Graduate Route time does not count toward settlement. You must switch to Skilled Worker or another qualifying route for ILR eligibility. 
What the Graduate Route currently offers
The Graduate Route was introduced in July 2021 as the replacement for the former Post-Study Work visa. It allows international students who have successfully completed a UK degree at a Home Office-licensed sponsor to remain in the UK for two years (bachelor's and master's) or three years (PhD) to work or look for work. There are no restrictions on the type of work, no minimum salary requirement, and no employer sponsorship is needed. You can work as an employee, be self-employed, run a business, or take time to find a role that matches your career plan.
The route is uncapped — there is no annual limit on the number of Graduate Route visas granted. You must have valid Student Route permission at the time your university reports your course completion to UKVI. The application is made from inside the UK, and the visa fee and Immigration Health Surcharge must be paid at the time of application. Dependants who were already in the UK as your dependants during your Student Route can also apply to stay.
What the 2026 proposals would have changed
In early 2026, the Home Office consulted on several proposed changes to the Graduate Route, including: reducing the duration from two years to 18 months for non-PhD graduates; requiring a job offer at or above a minimum salary threshold before the visa could be granted; and restricting the route to graduates of specific universities or courses deemed to have high employability outcomes. These proposals generated significant opposition from universities, business groups, and the Migration Advisory Committee.
The MAC published its formal review in May 2026. It recommended retaining the current two-year/three-year duration structure but strengthening compliance checks to ensure universities are monitoring attendance and course completion. The MAC explicitly advised against introducing a salary threshold or restricting the route by institution type, finding that the route had not been associated with significant abuse and that its economic benefits to the UK outweighed the risks. As of July 2026, the government has not announced whether it will accept or reject the MAC recommendations in full.
What this means for current and prospective students
For students currently on the Student Route or applying for 2026 entry: the Graduate Route remains available under the current rules. Apply before your Student permission expires, ensure your university confirms your course completion promptly, and keep digital copies of your CAS, completion letter, and BRP for the application.
For students planning to switch from the Graduate Route to a Skilled Worker visa: start the job search early. While the Graduate Route gives you two years to find sponsored employment, the Skilled Worker application itself can take eight to twelve weeks, and the employer must hold a valid sponsor licence. Major UK employers who hire international graduates regularly — consulting firms, technology companies, banks, and engineering firms — are familiar with the Graduate-to-Skilled-Worker transition and can advise on the timeline. For a detailed breakdown of salary thresholds and the two-test system, see the Skilled Worker salary threshold guide .
If your ultimate goal is settlement (Indefinite Leave to Remain), the Graduate Route does not count toward the five-year residence qualifying period. Each year spent on the Graduate Route is a neutral year for ILR purposes — it extends your lawful stay but does not advance the settlement clock. This makes it essential to switch to a qualifying route (Skilled Worker, Global Talent, Innovator Founder) as early as feasible to begin accumulating settlement-qualifying time. If you switch within the first year of your Graduate Route, you still have the remaining Graduate Route permission as a fallback should the new application be refused or delayed.
How to prepare your Graduate Route application
The application itself is straightforward but timing-sensitive. You must apply before your Student Route permission expires, and your university (the sponsor) must have reported your successful course completion to UKVI before you submit. UKVI typically processes Graduate Route applications within eight weeks, although some take longer during peak periods (July to October, when most students complete their courses). Processing times are published on GOV.UK and updated regularly.
Required documents include: your current passport or travel document, your Biometric Residence Permit (BRP) or UKVI account details, your Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies (CAS) number, and proof that you were granted Student Route permission for the course. If you have dependants who are already in the UK as your Student Route dependants, they can apply to stay through the Graduate Route as well, but each dependant must submit a separate application and pay the visa fee and Immigration Health Surcharge. Applications for all Graduate Route dependants were restricted from 2024 onward — check the current dependant eligibility rules before including family members in your plan.

02 Core rule: A Biometric Residence Permit (BRP) is the physical proof of your UK immigration status. If it is lost, stolen, or damaged, you are legally required to report it to UKVI within three months. The BRP itself is not your visa — it is evidence of your leave — but without it, proving your right to work, rent, or access services becomes significantly harder. 
03 Documents: For a standard BRP replacement application, prepare: 
04 Timing: Report lost or stolen documents promptly and verify whether the issue is card expiry or actual permission expiry. 
05 Main risk: Late reporting. The most common error is waiting weeks or months before reporting. UKVI checks the reporting date against the date you state you discovered the loss. A gap of months with no explanation raises credibility concerns. 
06 Review status: Editorial review only. 
§ Key takeaways
01 In 2026, many BRP issues are really eVisa or UKVI account issues because physical BRPs were phased into digital status. 
02 The guide covers people with lost, stolen, expired, or incorrect BRPs and people unable to access or prove their eVisa status. 
03 Evidence includes passport, UKVI account details, share code, old BRP copy, police report if stolen, travel itinerary, grant letter, and screenshots of account errors. 
04 Report lost or stolen documents promptly and verify whether the issue is card expiry or actual permission expiry before requesting a replacement. 
05 Teach readers to distinguish card expiry from leave expiry before requesting a replacement. 
06 Pitfalls include traveling without checking eVisa access, confusing expired BRP with expired leave, and waiting until the airport to fix account errors. 
BRP replacement process: the rule in plain English
A Biometric Residence Permit (BRP) is the physical proof of your UK immigration status. If it is lost, stolen, or damaged, you are legally required to report it to UKVI within three months. The BRP itself is not your visa — it is evidence of your leave — but without it, proving your right to work, rent, or access services becomes significantly harder.
The Home Office transitioned to a digital eVisa system in 2026, which replaced physical BRPs. During this transition, replacing a lost or damaged BRP follows a specific process that includes online reporting, biometrics, and a replacement fee. The rules differ depending on whether the BRP was lost in the UK or abroad, whether a police report was obtained, and whether the card is still within its validity period.
This guide covers the step-by-step process for replacing a UK BRP, the documents you need, the timelines UKVI works to, and how the eVisa transition affects your obligations.
Who this guide is for
Non-EEA nationals who hold or have held a BRP as evidence of their UK immigration status and need to replace a lost, stolen, or damaged card. This includes:
Students on a Student Route visa whose BRP has been lost or stolen
Workers on Skilled Worker, Global Talent, or other work routes
Family members with leave under Appendix FM who hold a BRP
Settled persons with indefinite leave to remain evidenced by a BRP
Applicants whose BRP was never delivered or contains incorrect details
If you are outside the UK and need to return but have lost your BRP, the process differs — see the travel section below for the replacement BRP visa route.
Documents and evidence to prepare
For a standard BRP replacement application, prepare:
Valid passport or travel document — must be current and contain your personal details
Police crime reference number — required for stolen BRPs, recommended for lost cards
Digital photograph — taken at a UK Post Office or uploaded during the online application
BRP reference number — if you have it, found on the decision letter or old correspondence
Proof of address — the BRP will be delivered by courier to your UK address
Written statement — explaining the circumstances of the loss or theft
For a replacement due to incorrect details (UKVI error), include the original decision letter showing the correct information and a covering note explaining the discrepancy.
Timing, deadlines, and sequencing
The three-month reporting window is the most important deadline. From the date you discovered the loss or theft, you have three calendar months to report it to UKVI using the online service. Reporting after this window does not automatically invalidate your leave, but it creates a compliance concern.
After reporting, you submit the online replacement application and book a biometric appointment at a UK Post Office or UKVCAS centre. Standard processing takes up to eight weeks from the biometric appointment. If you need the replacement urgently, no priority service is available for BRP replacements — plan for the full eight-week window.
If you need to travel internationally while waiting, apply for a replacement BRP visa (GBP 154) which allows a single entry to the UK. This should be obtained before departure.
How to make the file easier to approve
UKVI needs three things to issue a replacement: proof of identity, proof of the loss or theft, and confirmation that you remain eligible for the underlying leave. Prepare a clear timeline of events — when you last had the BRP, when you realised it was missing, and what steps you took to search or report it.
If the BRP was stolen, the police crime reference number speeds up the process and reduces the risk of UKVI questioning the genuineness of the claim. If the BRP was lost, a dated written statement describing your search efforts serves the same purpose.

One-sentence answer
A household of full-time students is exempt from council tax — but exemption is not automatic, the council needs the right certificate from your university, and one non-student housemate flips the household from "exempt" to "liable", which is why most international student bills happen by accident.
Who qualifies as a full-time student for council tax purposes
The legal definition of a full-time student for council tax purposes is set out in the Council Tax (Discount Disregards) Order 1992. To qualify, you must be enrolled in a course of education that requires at least 21 hours per week of study, attendance, or work experience for at least 24 weeks per year. Most undergraduate and postgraduate degrees meet this threshold, but some intensive master's programmes with condensed teaching periods may not if the weekly study hours fall below the statutory minimum during dissertation-only terms.
PhD students in the writing-up phase are assessed based on their registration status with the university. If you are registered as a full-time student on the university's records, most councils accept the standard certificate of full-time student status. Some councils, however, require a specific letter from the department confirming that writing-up constitutes full-time study under the 1992 Order. Get the certificate from your student records portal before assuming exemption, and if the certificate does not explicitly state full-time status, request a corrected version from the university registry before submitting it to the council.
For international students, the interplay between visa conditions and council tax rules matters. A Student Route visa holder who is enrolled in a full-time course that meets the 21-hour threshold is a full-time student for council tax purposes regardless of nationality. A Student Dependant visa holder living with a full-time student is not automatically a student themselves — they are disregarded for the count only if they are also enrolled in a qualifying course. If they are not studying, their presence in the household means the household is no longer fully exempt, though a 25% single-person discount will apply.
The three cases (exempt, disregarded, liable)
Case 1 — Exempt household. Every adult occupier is a full-time student (or other disregarded category). The property is exempt from council tax. The bill should not arrive at all once the certificate is filed.
Case 2 — You are disregarded, household is not. You are a full-time student living with adults who are not. Council tax is charged on the household, but you are disregarded for the count and the household may get a 25% discount if only one adult is "counted".
Case 3 — Liable. No exemption applies. The bill stands.
Which case you are in is decided by who else lives in the property , not by whether you are an international student. Citizenship is not the test; student status of every adult occupier is.
The evidence councils actually want
Almost every English council wants the same three things:
Your university's certificate of full-time student status ("council tax letter" or "student certificate"). Available from your university's student-records portal.
Your tenancy agreement showing you occupy the property as your main residence.
Your council tax account number (if you've been billed) or just the property address.
What happens when a housemate stops being a student
If you live in a student household where everyone was exempt at the start of the tenancy, and one housemate finishes their course mid-year, the household's exemption ends on the date that housemate ceases to be a full-time student. This is a common source of retrospective council tax bills that surprise students who believed their exemption covered the full tenancy period regardless of changes in the household.
When a housemate completes their degree or withdraws from their course, notify the council in writing within 14 days. The council will recalculate the household's position: the remaining students are disregarded for the count, and the non-student housemate becomes the liable person. The household will receive a bill from the date the housemate's student status ended, typically with a 25% single-person discount if only one non-student adult is now in the household. If the household had already submitted certificates for all students, the council may process this change automatically, but it is safer to notify them proactively to avoid accumulated arrears.

Before you write anything
Work out which of three deposit cases you are in. The right route depends on it.
Case A — protected, deductions disputed: open free ADR with the scheme first.
Case B — protected, no return at all: send the formal letter below, then go to ADR.
Case C — never protected: file a county court claim under s.214 Housing Act 2004. The court can award one to three times the deposit on top of its return.
Scheme ADR deadlines run from the end of the tenancy, but the exact window differs between TDS, DPS, and MyDeposits. Pull your protection certificate or call the scheme with your reference number before relying on a date.
One-sentence answer
Before you write any letter, work out which of the three deposit cases you are in — protected and disputed, protected but the deductions are wrong, or never protected at all — because each one has a different best route (free ADR, formal pre-action letter, or s.214 compensation claim).
Three deposit cases (which one are you?)
Case A — Protected, deductions disputed. Deposit was registered with TDS, DPS, or MyDeposits within 30 days; the landlord has now proposed deductions you think are wrong. Best route: free scheme ADR.
Case B — Protected, no return at all. Registered as above, but the landlord is silent or refusing to release anything. Best route: the formal letter below, then scheme ADR.
Case C — Never protected. No certificate within 30 days, no prescribed information given, or registered late or in the wrong scheme. Best route: county court claim under s.214 Housing Act 2004 — you may be entitled to one to three times the deposit in compensation in addition to its return. ADR is not available where the deposit was never protected. The s.214 claim is issued using Form N1 in the county court with a court fee added to the total claim amount. Most s.214 claims settle before the hearing because the multiplier risk — one to three times the deposit amount on top of its return — makes early settlement more attractive to landlords than defending the claim. The court considers whether the failure was deliberate or careless, whether the landlord cured the breach before the claim was issued, the length of the breach, and any prejudice caused to the tenant. A tenant whose deposit was never protected and who receives a settlement offer of the deposit plus one times the deposit may need to weigh the certain settlement against the uncertain but potentially higher court award of up to three times the deposit. Getting the file reviewed by a solicitor specialising in tenancy deposit disputes before issuing a s.214 claim is strongly recommended because the claim process involves court procedures that differ significantly from the simpler ADR process used for protected deposits. The pre-action protocol for deposit claims requires the tenant to send a formal letter before claim giving the landlord 14 days to respond, and failure to follow this protocol can result in the court reducing the compensation award. Most tenants who win s.214 claims recover their deposit in full plus between one and three times the deposit as compensation, but the outcome depends heavily on whether the tenant has documented the protection failure with clear evidence of when the tenancy started, whether the deposit was ever protected, and whether the prescribed information was provided within the statutory timeframe.

UK EU Settlement Scheme: 2026 Guide for Applicants 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library

In 60 seconds
01 Settled status requires five continuous years of qualifying UK residence. Pre-settled status is granted to those with less than five years. 
02 Late applications are still accepted where reasonable grounds for the delay exist — each case is assessed individually with no fixed cut-off date. 
03 Irish citizens are not required to apply under EUSS — their rights are protected by the Common Travel Area, but they may apply for documentation if they wish. 
04 Applications are digital: use the GOV.UK portal and the UK Immigration: ID Check app. No biometric appointment is needed for most applicants. 
05 Pre-settled status does not automatically expire after five years — the Home Office has a duty to remind holders to convert, and the status continues until a decision on a conversion application. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for EU, EEA, and Swiss nationals who are resident in the UK and need to regularise their immigration status under the EU Settlement Scheme. It is also for family members of those nationals — spouses, partners, children, and dependent relatives — who need to apply in their own right. If you are an Irish citizen, you do not need to apply, but this guide explains your optional application route if you want formal documentation of your UK residence rights.
This guide is not for non-EEA nationals who have no family connection to an EU/EEA/Swiss citizen — those applicants should use the relevant points-based or family visa route (Skilled Worker, Student Route, or Appendix FM partner visa). It is also not for EU nationals who arrived in the UK after 31 December 2020 and do not have a family connection to a qualifying EU citizen — those applicants will need a visa under the new points-based system rather than the EUSS.
How the EU Settlement Scheme works in practice
The EU Settlement Scheme was established by Appendix EU of the Immigration Rules, implementing the UK's obligations under the Withdrawal Agreement with the European Union. The scheme grants two forms of immigration status: settled status (indefinite leave to enter or remain) and pre-settled status (limited leave to remain for five years). Both statuses confer the right to live, work, study, and access public funds and healthcare in the UK on the same basis as a British citizen. The key distinction between them is the duration of UK residence the applicant can demonstrate at the time of application.
To qualify for settled status, an applicant must show five continuous years of qualifying residence in the UK, where each 12-month period contains no more than six months of absence from the UK (subject to specific exceptions for childbirth, serious illness, study, or overseas posting). An applicant who can show less than five years receives pre-settled status, which is valid for five years from the date of grant. Before the pre-settled status expires, the holder must apply to convert to settled status — this requires showing that the five-year qualifying period has now been completed.
A 2023 High Court ruling in IMA v Secretary of State for the Home Department confirmed that pre-settled status does not automatically lapse after the five-year validity period if the holder has not yet applied for settled status. The Home Office is required to send reminders and must process any late conversion application before the pre-settled status can be considered expired. This ruling provides important protection for pre-settled status holders who may not have realised they needed to apply for conversion. However, the safest course is to apply for settled status as soon as you have completed five years of continuous qualifying residence — do not wait for a reminder that may arrive after your pre-settled status has technically expired, even if the courts have confirmed you retain the right to convert.
Who qualifies as a family member under the EUSS
The EUSS defines family members broadly to include: spouses and civil partners (the marriage or civil partnership must have existed by 31 December 2020 if the EU citizen is a qualifying person); durable (unmarried) partners in a committed relationship akin to marriage or civil partnership; children and grandchildren under 21 (or over 21 if dependent); parents and grandparents of the EU citizen or their spouse, if dependent; and other dependent relatives who were part of the household before the UK left the EU.
A critically important category is the "Zambrano carer" — a person who is the primary carer of a British citizen child and would be unable to remain in the UK if refused status. The Court of Justice of the European Union established this protection, and it has been incorporated into the EUSS framework. If you are an EU national who is the primary carer of a British citizen child, you may have a right to reside even without meeting the standard qualifying criteria. This is a complex area of law, and applicants in this situation should seek specialist advice before filing an application.
Documents you'll need
Identity document: A valid passport or national identity card from your EU/EEA/Swiss country. If your passport has expired, you can still apply using an expired document if it has not been cancelled — but a valid document speeds processing. The identity document is verified through the UK Immigration: ID Check app on a smartphone with NFC capability.
Digital photograph: A recent passport-style photograph taken on your phone through the ID Check app. The app provides guidance on positioning and lighting.
Proof of UK residence: For each year of the qualifying period, you need evidence of continuous UK residence. Acceptable documents include: bank statements showing UK transactions, tenancy agreements or mortgage statements, P60 or payslips from UK employers, le

body:

UK EU Settlement Scheme: Settled & Pre-Settled Status 2026 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home

In 60 seconds
01 The EUSS deadline for most applicants was 30 June 2021. Late applications are accepted if you have reasonable grounds for missing the deadline — the Home Office has confirmed this policy remains in force. 
02 Settled status is indefinite leave to remain. Pre-settled status is limited leave for 5 years. Both allow you to work, study, use the NHS, and travel. Only settled status provides a permanent right to remain. 
03 To upgrade from pre-settled to settled status, you need 5 years of continuous residence — meaning no absence exceeding 6 months in any 12-month period, with limited exceptions for one absence of up to 12 months for an important reason. 
04 Evidence of residence can be automated (HMRC and DWP data for recent tax years) or manual (P60s, council tax bills, bank statements, university letters, tenancy agreements for earlier years). 
05 Pre-settled status holders who have been resident in the UK for 3 years may qualify for home fees and student finance. The rules vary by UK nation — check your Student Awards Agency's guidance. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for EU, EEA, and Swiss nationals and their family members who are in the UK and need to apply to the EUSS for the first time (including late applications) or who hold pre-settled status and need to upgrade to settled status. It covers the evidence needed for continuous residence, what counts as a permitted absence, how student years count toward the 5-year qualifying period, and the practical implications of each status — including access to home fees and student finance. It also covers family members who are not themselves EU nationals but who are the spouse, civil partner, child, or dependent relative of an EU national with EUSS status.
This guide is not for people who arrived in the UK for the first time after 31 December 2020 and have no prior UK residence — the EUSS is not available to them, and they must apply under the Immigration Rules that apply to their nationality (usually the Student Route, Skilled Worker, or family visa categories). It is not for Irish citizens, who do not need to apply to the EUSS (though they may choose to) because the Common Travel Area preserves their rights independently of the EUSS. It is not for people applying for British citizenship — settled status is a prerequisite for naturalisation for most applicants, but the EUSS application and the citizenship application are separate processes.
Settled vs pre-settled: which status you get and why it matters
The EUSS grants one of two statuses depending on how long you have been continuously resident in the UK. Settled status is granted if you can evidence at least 5 years of continuous residence in the UK, the Islands (Channel Islands and Isle of Man), or a combination of both. Pre-settled status is granted if you have been resident for less than 5 years. The length of residence is measured from the date you started your continuous qualifying period — usually the date you moved to the UK — to the date of the Home Office decision on your application. Pre-settled status holders can apply to upgrade to settled status as soon as they reach the 5-year threshold — they do not need to wait for the pre-settled expiry date.
The practical differences are significant. Settled status holders can apply for British citizenship after 12 months (if married to a British citizen, no waiting period applies after settled status is granted under certain circumstances), access public funds without restriction, and sponsor family members for EUSS family permits. Pre-settled status holders can work, study, and use the NHS but may face restrictions on student finance and home fee classification depending on their length of residence. Both statuses are digital — there is no physical document. Your status is held electronically and accessed through the UKVI online "View and Prove Your Immigration Status" service using the identity document you applied with. Employers, landlords, and universities verify your status through the Home Office online checking service using a share code you generate.
Late applications: reasonable grounds for missing the deadline
The EUSS application deadline for most people was 30 June 2021. However, the Home Office has confirmed that late applications continue to be accepted where the applicant has reasonable grounds for missing the deadline. The Home Office caseworker guidance identifies several categories of reasonable grounds, and the list is not exhaustive. The most common categories relevant to students are:
Lack of awareness: You were a child or young adult at the time the scheme was introduced, and no parent or guardian applied on your behalf. Many people who arrived in the UK as children with EU parents assumed they had status because their parents applied, but children must have their own individual application — a parent's grant does not automatically cover a child.
Study-related reasons: You left the UK temporarily for study abroad during the application window and did not receive the Home Office communications sent to your UK address. If you can demonstrate that you were enrolled in a course of study overseas during the relevant period and returned to the UK, this is a recognised reasonable ground.
Medical or vulnerability grounds: A serious illness, mental health condition, or caregiving responsibility prevented you from applying. Supporting medical evidence is required.
Compelling practical reasons: Homelessness, domestic abuse, lack of digital access or English language skills, or reliance on incorrect advice from a person you reasonably trusted (such as an employer or university adviser who told you the scheme did not apply to you).
The late application itself must include a detailed explanation

body:

UK Family Visa Parent Route: Appendix FM Guide (2026) 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home

In 60 seconds
01 Primary authority: Appendix FM, paragraphs E-ECPT.2.1–2.4 (eligibility for entry clearance as a parent), Appendix FM-SE (specified evidence), and the Immigration Rules Part 8 transitional provisions where applicable. 
02 Core rule: The parent route requires a qualifying child (British, settled, or pre-settled, under 18, living in the UK) AND either (a) sole parental responsibility for the child, or (b) the child has lived in the UK for 7 continuous years and it would be unreasonable for them to leave. There is no fixed minimum income threshold — the test is adequate maintenance. 
03 Documents: Child's birth certificate, child's British passport or status proof, school letters and medical records showing the parent's role, court orders or written agreements about custody, evidence the other parent is not involved (if claiming sole responsibility), accommodation evidence, 6 months of bank statements, budget spreadsheet, English test certificate at CEFR A1, TB certificate if applicable. 
04 Timing: Applications are made from outside the UK (entry clearance). Standard processing: 12–24 weeks. Priority service may be available. Initial leave is for 33 months (or 30 months for in-country applications), extendable for another 30 months, leading to settlement (ILR) after 5 years. 
05 Main risk: The most common refusal reason is insufficient evidence of sole parental responsibility — the Home Office defaults to assuming shared responsibility unless the applicant proves otherwise. Other pitfalls: confusing the partner route with the parent route, weak financial evidence, missing child status proof, and unsupported exceptional-circumstances claims. 
06 Review status: Editorial review — researched from primary Home Office sources. Attorney review available for complex cases (sole-responsibility disputes, prior refusals, Article 8 arguments). 
Family visa parent route: the rule in plain English
Appendix FM is the part of the Immigration Rules that covers family visas. Within it, the parent route (paragraphs E-ECPT.2.1–2.4) allows a parent outside the UK to join a child who is living in the UK, where that child is British, settled, or has pre-settled status.
The route has two possible grounds for eligibility — you need to meet one of them:
Sole parental responsibility. You alone make all major decisions about the child. The other parent has no role — by choice, death, or court order. This must be proven with contemporaneous records, not just a statement.
Seven-year child residence. The child has lived in the UK continuously for at least 7 years, and it would not be reasonable to expect the child to leave the UK if the application were refused.
Additionally, the applicant must show adequate maintenance (enough income to support the family without public funds), suitable accommodation, and English at CEFR level A1.
Who this guide is for
Parents applying to join a child in the UK where the child is British, has indefinite leave to remain, or pre-settled status. This includes parents who have sole day-to-day care, parents where the other parent has died or is absent, and parents whose child has spent 7 years in the UK.
Who this guide is not for
Partner route applicants. If you are the spouse, civil partner, or unmarried partner of a British or settled person, you need the partner route (Appendix FM, section E-ECP), not the parent route — even if you have children together.
Adult dependant relatives. The parent route is for joining a minor child. If you are an elderly parent needing care from an adult child in the UK, that is the Adult Dependant Relative route (different, very restrictive rules).
Visitor visa applications. If you only want to visit your child temporarily, apply as a Standard Visitor — do not use the parent route.
Parents with shared responsibility. If you share parental responsibility with the other parent (who lives with or near the child), you do not qualify under the sole-responsibility ground. The seven-year child residence ground may still apply.
Sole parental responsibility: what the Home Office looks for
Sole parental responsibility means that one parent has the exclusive right to make decisions about the child's upbringing, and exercises that right in practice. The Home Office starts from the presumption that both parents share responsibility unless the applicant proves otherwise.
Strong evidence includes: 
Court orders granting sole custody or residence to you.
A court order or formal agreement limiting the other parent's contact — or confirming no contact.
Letters from the child's school addressed only to you, discussing progress, attendance, or disciplinary matters.
GP or hospital letters showing you as the sole contact for the child's healthcare.
A detailed witness statement explaining: what happened to the other parent (death, abandonment, domestic abuse leading to separation), how long you have been the sole decision-maker, and who helps with childcare when you work.
Evidence from a social worker, health visitor, or children's services confirming your role.

Who qualifies as a dependant
A dependant is a close family member who applies to join or stay with a main visa holder (the "sponsor") in the UK. The sponsor's visa route decides who counts as a dependant and what evidence you must supply.
Partner or spouse: You can apply as a partner if you are married or in a civil partnership, or if you have lived together in a relationship akin to marriage for at least two years. Unmarried partners must show cohabitation evidence.

The letter must be dated within 3 months of the visa application. If applying through an eligible prize, provide evidence of the prize and the applicant's role in winning it. 04 Timing: Endorsement and visa stages are separate; use check the current UKVI fee schedule, Immigration Health Surcharge, endorsement time, and settlement category before publication. 
05 Main risk: Generic, non-specific recommendation letters. A letter that says "X is a talented researcher" without specific evidence is weak. The endorsing body wants to see concrete examples: "X's work on Y was cited Z times and led to A." Generic letters are the most common reason for endorsement refusal. Ensure each recommender writes in detail about specific achievements and their impact on the field.

§ Key takeaways
01 Global Talent does not require a job offer, but it requires endorsement or an eligible prize and evidence of leadership or potential leadership in the field. 
02 Researchers, technologists, artists, designers, architects, and field leaders with external recognition beyond normal employment are the target cohort. 
03 Endorsement and visa stages are separate; check the current UKVI fee schedule, Immigration Health Surcharge, endorsement time, and settlement category before acting. 
04 Common pitfalls include generic letters, internal-only achievements, weak field fit, unsupported innovation claims, and confusion between exceptional promise and exceptional talent. 
The rule in plain English
The UK Global Talent visa does not require a job offer or employer sponsorship. Instead, it requires endorsement from a recognised UK body (such as the Royal Society, Royal Academy of Engineering, British Academy, Arts Council England, Tech Nation legacy routes through UKRI, or the Royal Society of Literature) or an eligible prize (such as a Nobel Prize, Oscar, BAFTA, or Olympic medal). Endorsement proves that the applicant is a recognised leader (exceptional talent) or emerging leader (exceptional promise) in their field. The visa is separate from the endorsement stage: you first apply for endorsement, then apply for the visa using the endorsement letter.
The Global Talent route was designed to attract the brightest minds to the UK. Unlike the Skilled Worker route, it is not tied to one employer. Global Talent holders can change jobs, work for multiple employers, be self-employed, take time off between roles, and work toward settlement (indefinite leave to remain) in 3 years for exceptional talent applicants or 5 years for exceptional promise applicants. The trade-off is a high evidence bar: the endorsement body must be satisfied that the applicant is at the level claimed, and the evidence must go beyond normal employment achievements.
There is no fixed salary or investment requirement. The visa fee and Immigration Health Surcharge are payable at the visa application stage. The Global Talent route also permits dependants to work full-time in any role, including self-employment or study, without the restrictions that apply under the Skilled Worker dependant rules. This flexibility makes the route attractive for families where the partner wants to pursue their own career or education in the UK while the main applicant focuses on their work as a recognised leader or emerging leader in their field. The endorsement stage has no fee for most routes (check the specific endorsing body's guidance). Processing times vary by endorsing body and the complexity of the application. Endorsement can take 3 to 8 weeks; the subsequent visa application takes similar time. Settlement (ILR) is available after 3 years for exceptional talent applicants and 5 years for exceptional promise, provided the continuous residence and other requirements are met.
Who this guide is for
Researchers in STEM, humanities, and social sciences with a track record of publications, citations, and grant funding who can obtain endorsement from the Royal Society, Royal Academy of Engineering, British Academy, or UKRI. Technologists and digital innovators who can demonstrate commercial or open-source impact, patents, or technical leadership. Artists, designers, architects, and performers applying through Arts Council England. Founders and entrepreneurs who have built businesses with significant commercial impact. Applicants who have won an eligible prize and can apply through the accelerated (no endorsement needed) route.
This guide is also for current Skilled Worker or Graduate Route holders who want to switch to the Global Talent route for its flexibility and faster settlement path. 01 A Graduate visa application depends on eligible UK study, current Student or Tier 4 permission, sponsor completion reporting, and in-country filing.

03 Evidence includes passport, BRP or eVisa access, CAS details, Student visa details, completion report confirmation, degree outcome, UKVI account access, and dependant documents if eligible.

The rule in plain English
A Graduate Route visa application depends on four requirements: eligible UK study (a degree-level qualification or equivalent from a recognised UK Higher Education Institution with a track record of compliance), current Student or Tier 4 permission that has not expired, sponsor completion reporting (the education provider must have reported the student's successful completion to UKVI before the application), and in-country filing (the applicant must be in the UK at the time of application). The application is made through the UKVI account system, not the standard visa application form. There is no requirement for a job offer, and there is no minimum salary or employment type restriction — Graduate Route holders can work in any role, including self-employment and freelance work.
The key distinction from the Student Route is that the Graduate Route is not linked to a sponsor in the same way. Your education provider reports completion, but they do not sponsor the Graduate Route visa. You manage your own UKVI account after the grant and are responsible for reporting changes to your circumstances (such as passport renewals, address changes, or contact details). The route is unsponsored, which means you are not tied to one employer and can change jobs, work multiple jobs, be self-employed, or take time off between roles without needing permission.
Duration depends on the application date. Non-doctoral grants: 2 years if applied for by December 31, 2026, reducing to 18 months from January 1, 2027. Doctoral grants: 3 years regardless of application date. The duration is a fixed period and cannot be extended. If you want to stay in the UK after the Graduate Route expires, you must switch to another immigration route (Skilled Worker, Global Talent, Innovator Founder, etc.). The Graduate Route does not lead directly to settlement and is not a path to indefinite leave to remain on its own — you must switch to another route that offers settlement before the Graduate Route expires.

International students in the UK who have completed an eligible UK degree and want to stay for post-study work. 06 Review status: Basic review for UK Graduate Route visa explained available now; attorney-review tiers coming soon. 
§ Key takeaways
01 A Graduate visa lets eligible students stay after completing an eligible UK course. 
02 GOV.UK says non-doctoral grants last 2 years if applying by December 31, 2026 and 18 months from January 1, 2027. 
03 The route is for students on Student or Tier 4 permission whose sponsor has reported successful completion to the Home Office. 
04 Apply inside the UK before Student permission expires and do not travel outside the Common Travel Area while pending. 
05 Explain the route as a bridge to work or Skilled Worker, not a route that can be extended indefinitely. 
06 Pitfalls include applying before completion is reported, applying outside the UK, travelling while pending, assuming every dependant can join, and missing the 2027 duration change. 
The rule in plain English
The Graduate Route lets international students who have successfully completed an eligible UK degree stay in the UK for post-study work. Non-doctoral grants last 2 years if applied for by December 31, 2026, reducing to 18 months from January 1, 2027. Doctoral grants last 3 years regardless of when applied. The route is unsponsored  you do not need a job offer to apply.
Key requirement: Your education provider (sponsor) must have reported your successful completion to the Home Office before you apply. If they have not yet submitted the report, your application will be refused, even if you have physically graduated. The sponsor report is submitted electronically through the Home Office sponsor management system, and your university may have a specific process and timeline for submitting these reports after the results are finalised. Contact your university's international student support team to confirm when the report will be filed, because some institutions submit reports on a scheduled batch basis rather than individually for each student on the day their results are confirmed after the examination board meeting at the end of the academic term.
The Graduate Route offers significant flexibility compared to sponsored routes. There is no minimum salary requirement, no employer sponsorship, and no restriction on the type of work you can do. You can be employed, self-employed, freelance, work multiple jobs, or take time off between roles. The only restriction is that you cannot work as a professional sportsperson or doctor in training. This flexibility makes the Graduate Route a popular bridge to longer-term work visas, giving graduates time to find sponsored employment or build a business before switching to a different route. Graduates who intend to switch to the Skilled Worker route should use the Graduate Route period to secure a job offer from a licensed sponsor, because the Skilled Worker application requires a Certificate of Sponsorship from the new employer and the salary must meet the applicable threshold for the occupation code assigned to the role the graduate will be filling after the Graduate Route permission expires and the new Skilled Worker visa is granted by the Home Office.
Professional development opportunities on the Graduate Route
The Graduate Route offers significant professional development opportunities because it is an unsponsored visa with no restrictions on the type of work you can do. Use this flexibility to build your career through strategic employment choices: internships, contract roles, or self-employed projects that develop your skills portfolio. Many universities offer career services and job placement services that remain accessible to alumni for a period after graduation — leverage these resources to find roles that align with your long-term career plan.
Attend job fairs for students and industry networking events to build connections with employers who may sponsor Skilled Worker visas later. Graduate Route holders who actively use networking opportunities and mentorship programs during their post-study period are better positioned to find sponsored employment before the Graduate Route expires. Consider volunteering opportunities and part-time work in your field to build your UK professional network while you search for a sponsor. Treat the Graduate Route period as a bridge to build the professional experience and employer relationships needed for a successful Skilled Worker or Global Talent application.
Switching from Graduate Route to other visa categories
The Graduate Route is designed as a bridging visa, not a permanent immigration route. Most graduates will eventually switch to a Skilled Worker, Global Talent, Innovator Founder, or family visa. The Graduate Route does not lead directly to settlement

§ Key takeaways
01 Ground 4A is the only mandatory possession ground built specifically for student lets, inserted into Schedule 2 by the Renters' Rights Act 2024. 
02 Four cumulative conditions must all be met: the property is an HMO; all tenants were full-time students at grant; prior written notice was given; and the claim is brought inside the prescribed window. 
03 Any one of the four conditions failing kills the ground entirely. 
04 Prior written notice must be given at or before the tenancy was granted; a clause buried in the agreement is usually insufficient. 
05 The 'all full-time students' test is applied at the time the tenancy was granted, not at the time of the notice. 
06 Examples that kill the ground: one tenant on a placement year, one tenant who intercalated, one graduate-scheme holder, or one non-student partner in the household at grant. 
Last updated 2026-05-14 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
In 60 seconds
Ground 4A is the only mandatory possession ground built specifically for student lets.
Four conditions must all be met: HMO let; all tenants full-time students at grant; prior written notice given; timing inside the prescribed window.
Any one of the four failing kills the ground.
The prior-notice trap is the most common defect: a clause in the agreement is usually not enough.
Notice period and claim window are subject to statutory instrument. Check current Ground 4A service window and notice period on the official government source.
One-sentence answer
Ground 4A is the mandatory Section 8 ground purpose-built so landlords of student houses can recover the property between academic years — but it only applies where the household was all full-time students at grant, the property is an HMO, the landlord gave prior written notice, and the timing falls inside the prescribed window, and any one of those failing kills the ground.
Ground 4A in context: why this ground exists
Ground 4A was inserted into Schedule 2 of the Housing Act 1988 by the Renters' Rights Act 2024 specifically to fill a gap created by the abolition of Section 21 evictions. Before the Renters' Rights Act, landlords of student houses in multiple occupation typically used the no-fault Section 21 procedure to recover possession between academic years. With Section 21 abolished for new tenancies from 2025, the government introduced Ground 4A as the replacement mechanism — a mandatory possession ground available only where the property is genuinely let to a household of full-time students.
Understanding this legislative context matters for tenants because it clarifies why the four conditions are so tightly drawn. Parliament intended Ground 4A to be a narrow, purpose-built ground for the specific scenario of academic-year turnover, not a general-purpose eviction route for student housing. If a landlord's circumstances do not fit squarely within all four conditions, the ground fails — and the landlord must rely on a discretionary ground instead, which gives the tenant significantly more procedural protection and the opportunity to argue that it is not reasonable to make a possession order.
For international students, a Ground 4A claim also has implications beyond the tenancy itself. A possession order on your housing record can complicate future rental references, and losing stable housing mid-year can disrupt your SEVIS-equivalent visa reporting obligations under the Student Route. Understanding your defences early gives you time to plan alternative accommodation without the pressure of a pending court hearing.
When Ground 4A applies (and when it doesn't)
The four cumulative conditions:
HMO let. The property must be let as a house in multiple occupation under the meaning of the Housing Act 2004.
All full-time students at grant. At the time the tenancy was granted, all of the joint tenants must have been pursuing a full-time course at a higher education provider, or about to start one.
Prior written notice. The landlord must have given the tenants prior written notice that possession may be recovered on Ground 4A. Burying it in a clause without separate notice is the usual defect.
Timing. The possession claim must be brought inside the window the landlord can rely on Ground 4A each year. Check the current Ground 4A claim window on the official government source.
If any of (1)–(4) fails, the ground fails.
The prior-notice requirement landlords get wrong
This is where most Ground 4A defences are won. The notice must be:
Prior — given at or before the tenancy was granted, not weeks into the let.
Written — a verbal warning is not a notice.
Specific — referring to Ground 4A or to the possibility of possession being recovered for re-letting between academic years.
Received by all tenants — not just the lead signatory.
If the "notice" is a single clause buried halfway down a 40-page agreement that the tenants didn't have time to read, that is at minimum a serious factual argument and in many cases a successful defence. Ask the landlord to produce the prior notice in disclosure.
The "all full-time students" test in a mixed household
The test is at the time the tenancy was granted , not at the time of the notice.
Examples of households where the test fails:
One tenant on a placement year (not in full-time study).
One tenant who intercalated before signing.
One tenant on a graduate scheme moving in alongside three students.
One tenant who is the partner of a student but not a student themselves.
If the household at grant was not all-students, the landlord can still let to you — they just can't rely on Ground 4A later.
Notice periods and the September-recovery window
The mandatory Ground 4A is structured so a landlord can recover the property at the natural break between academic year
