§ Key takeaways
01 Many UK settlement routes require no more than 180 days outside the UK in any rolling 12-month period, unless an exception applies. 
02 Skilled Worker, Global Talent, Innovator Founder, and other applicants approaching settlement must audit absences carefully. 
03 Start the absence audit months before filing because a broken rolling window can delay the safe application date. 
04 Evidence includes passports, travel history, boarding passes where needed, employer travel letters, remote-work records, absence spreadsheet, visa grant dates, and exception evidence. 
05 Teach rolling-window counting with concrete examples and map every absence before payment. 
06 Pitfalls include counting calendar years only, ignoring old passports, relying on unsupported exceptions, and filing as soon as five years pass. 
ILR continuous residence: the rule in plain English
Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR) requires you to have lived in the UK continuously for a qualifying period without excessive absences. The core rule is that you cannot be outside the UK for more than 180 days in any rolling 12-month period during the qualifying period. This is not a total cap — it is a rolling window test applied to each 12-month period independently.
The rule exists because ILR represents a permanent commitment to the UK. UKVI wants to see that you have made the UK your home throughout the qualifying period, not just been present on paper while living abroad. The absence rules differ by immigration route — work routes have stricter caps, while the partner route evaluates whether the relationship subsisted during absences.
This guide explains how to calculate continuous residence, what counts as an absence, the applicable rules for each route, common mistakes, and how to prepare the absence schedule for the ILR application.
Who this guide is for
Applicants for indefinite leave to remain who need to understand the continuous residence requirement. This includes:
Skilled Worker visa holders approaching the five-year qualifying period
Global Talent visa holders on the three-year route to settlement
Partner route (spouse visa) holders at the five-year mark
Long residence applicants on the 10-year route
Innovator Founder visa holders on the two-year route
The advice applies to applications made in the UK. Those applying from outside the UK for entry clearance have different rules.
Documents and evidence to prepare
An absence schedule and supporting documents are critical for the ILR application:
Passport entry/exit stamps — the primary evidence of each departure and return
Travel records from UKVI — request your travel history through the UKVI subject access request process
Boarding passes and flight itineraries — for trips where passport stamps are unclear
Employer travel records — letters confirming business trips with dates and purpose
Tenancy agreements and utility bills — showing continuous UK residence throughout the period
Bank statements — showing UK transactions during the qualifying period
HMRC tax records — employment and tax history showing UK economic activity
NHS registration records — GP or hospital letters addressed to your UK address
Absence schedule — a spreadsheet or table listing every trip: departure date, return date, total days absent, destination, purpose of travel
Timing, deadlines, and sequencing
The ILR application can be submitted up to 28 days before reaching the end of the qualifying period. The qualifying period is counted from the date of first entry under the relevant visa route. For Skilled Worker, this is the date of the Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS)-based entry clearance or the date leave was granted.
Each 12-month window is counted backwards from the date of the ILR application. For example, if you apply on 1 June 2026, UKVI looks at the period from 1 June 2025 to 1 June 2026, then from 1 June 2024 to 1 June 2025, and so on, for each year of the qualifying period. If any window exceeds 180 days, the application is refused.
Prepare the absence schedule at least three months before applying. This gives time to gather travel records, check for discrepancies, and calculate whether any window is at risk of exceeding the cap.
How to make the file easier to approve
The absence schedule is the most scrutinised document in an ILR application. Format it clearly with columns for departure date, return date, total days absent, destination, and purpose. UK immigration is governed by the Immigration Rules, administered by UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI), with primary authority from the Immigration Act 1971 and the Nationality and Borders Act 2022 .
Most routes follow a points-based or relationship-based framework: Skilled Worker (sponsor + salary + skill), spouse / partner (genuine relationship + finances + accommodation), Student Route (CAS + maintenance), Global Talent (endorsement), and family routes for parents and children.
After five years on a qualifying route — and ten years for some long-residence cases — you can apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR), the UK's settlement status.

Clear answers about UK spouse visas, partner visas, indefinite leave to remain, and the financial requirement. This FAQ aggregates the most common decision points from our family-route articles.
This FAQ is for partners and family members applying for UK spouse or partner visas, extending their stay, or working toward indefinite leave to remain. The questions below reflect the most common uncertainties we see from family-route applicants in UKVI forums and from our own document review clients. Each answer is grounded in the Immigration Rules (Appendix FM and Appendix FM-SE), Home Office caseworker guidance, and current UKVI policy as of mid-2026.
The spouse visa financial requirement has changed significantly in recent years, increasing from £18,600 to £29,000, and further adjustments remain possible. The rules around combining income sources, acceptable evidence periods, and the 5-year versus 10-year route to settlement are frequent sources of confusion and refusal. The answers below reflect the current published rules and thresholds as of July 2026. You should verify the exact figures on GOV.UK before filing, as the minimum income requirement may change again.
The question list below serves as a table of contents for the topics covered here. For a deeper treatment of any subject, the linked articles at the end of this page cover step-by-step guidance, document checklists, and the specific Home Office policy references that apply to each application stage.
How to use this FAQ
Confirm the current spouse/partner minimum income and evidence rules on GOV.UK before you budget — thresholds change.
Deep dives live on the financial-requirement and checklist pages linked below; this FAQ is orientation only.
Campus journey logistics for UK universities live on uk.yousafeconsultancy.com ; procedure stays on this legal host (editorial-only until a named solicitor review program is live).
Last updated 2026-07-14 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
Reviewer programs for UK matters are under development; until those programs launch, UK content is editorial-only.
What is the financial requirement for a UK spouse or partner visa in 2026?
The sponsor must show a gross annual income of at least £29,000, or equivalent cash savings using the formula £16,000 + 2.5 × (shortfall). The threshold is the same for initial applications, extensions, and ILR, though the evidence period differs. Income can come from employment (Category A or B), self-employment, property rental, pensions, or certain disability benefits under the "adequate maintenance" exception. Bank statements must end no more than 28 days before the application date. If the sponsor changed jobs recently, Category B may be required. Verify the exact figure on GOV.UK before filing, as the minimum income requirement has changed in recent years and further changes are possible.
Can I combine income from multiple sources to meet the spouse visa threshold?
Yes, but only within specific combinations permitted by Appendix FM-SE. You can combine employment income with cash savings, or non-employment income (rental, dividends) with cash savings. You generally cannot mix Category A employment with Category B employment in the same application. Self-employment income is assessed over a full financial year and cannot be averaged with salaried income in the same category. If you are close to the threshold, it is usually safer to rely on cash savings held for 6 months rather than trying to combine marginal income streams, because mixed-category calculations are a common reason for refusal.
How long do I need to live in the UK before applying for indefinite leave to remain (ILR)?
Most applicants on the 5-year partner route apply for ILR after completing 5 years on a spouse or partner visa. You must apply within 28 days of completing the 5-year qualifying period; earlier applications are refused. The 10-year route is available for those who do not meet the 5-year requirements or who have spent time on other visas that count toward the longer period. Time on a fiancé(e) visa generally does not count toward the 5 years. Absences from the UK are assessed on a rolling 12-month basis; a single absence of more than 180 days requires explanation, and cumulative absences above 540 days are heavily scrutinised.
What documents best prove a genuine relationship for a spouse visa application?
UKVI looks for evidence of cohabitation, financial interdependence, and communication over time — not just wedding photographs. Strong evidence includes: joint bank statements or utility bills, a tenancy agreement or mortgage in both names, life insurance or wills naming each other, travel bookings together, and dated photographs with locations spanning the relationship. If you have lived apart for periods, explain why (work, study, visa delays) with supporting documents. A common mistake is submitting only wedding photos and love letters; these help but do not replace documentary proof of a shared life.
Can I apply for ILR before completing 5 years on a spouse visa?
No. You must complete the full qualifying period before applying, and you should submit within the 28-day window before your 5-year anniversary. Applying even one day early results in a refused application and loss of the fee. The only exceptions are the bereaved partner concession (if your sponsor died during the qualifying period) and certain cases of domestic abuse or human rights claims. If you are unsure whether your absences or prior visa history affect qualifying time, verify your dates against your passport stamps and biometric residence permits before booking the Life in the UK test or English exam.

§ Key takeaways
01 The Innovator Founder route is for endorsed founders with a business that is innovative, viable, and scalable; it is not a generic self-employment route. 
02 Endorsement comes before the visa application; the three route words must be proven with evidence: innovative, viable, and scalable. 
03 Required evidence includes endorsement letter, business plan, market proof, founder CV, ownership structure, funds evidence, English evidence, maintenance evidence if required, and role evidence. 
04 Pitfalls include ordinary consulting businesses, passive investment, weak endorsement, unclear funds, and claims of innovation without market proof. 
The rule in plain English
The UK Innovator Founder visa is for endorsed founders with a business that meets three statutory criteria: innovative (new or significantly different from existing offerings in the UK market), viable (credible business plan with realistic growth potential and identified market), and scalable (evidence of job creation potential, international expansion, or new market access). The route does not have a minimum investment requirement (unlike the former Tier 1 Entrepreneur visa). Instead, the endorsing body assesses whether the founder has sufficient funds to execute the business plan. The route is not a generic self-employment or freelance visa — it is specifically for business founders with an endorsed, credible, and scalable venture.
Endorsement must come from an approved endorsing body authorised by the Home Office. These include organisations like UK Endorsement Service, Global Entrepreneurs Programme (GEP), and other bodies approved for the Innovator Founder route. The endorsing body assesses the business against the three criteria and, if satisfied, issues an endorsement letter. The endorsement letter is valid for 3 months and must be used to apply for the visa within that window. The visa application itself assesses the standard immigration requirements: age (18+), English (B2 level — higher than Skilled Worker's B1), maintenance funds, and suitability.
The Innovator Founder visa is typically granted for 3 years and can be extended for 3 years at a time. Settlement (indefinite leave to remain) is available after 3 years if the endorsing body confirms the founder has made significant progress against the business plan. This makes it one of the faster routes to settlement — comparable to Global Talent's exceptional talent track. Naturalisation and Life in the UK test: the rule in plain English
British citizenship by naturalisation is the final step for foreign nationals who have lived in the UK and wish to become full citizens. The process requires you to meet residence, language, and good character requirements, pass the Life in the UK test, and pay the application fee. The decision is made at the Home Secretary's discretion, meaning that meeting the minimum requirements does not guarantee approval — character and other factors are weighed independently.
The Life in the UK test is a computer-based exam that assesses your knowledge of British traditions, customs, history, government, and everyday life. It is a mandatory step for all citizenship applications, as well as for those applying for ILR. The test must be passed before submitting the citizenship application.
This guide covers the naturalisation requirements, the Life in the UK test structure and preparation, the English language evidence, the good character assessment, and the step-by-step application process.
Who this guide is for
Foreign nationals who hold indefinite leave to remain (ILR) or settled status and are considering applying for British citizenship. This includes:
Non-EEA nationals who have completed the five-year ILR route and now want citizenship
Spouses of British citizens on the three-year route to citizenship
Commonwealth citizens who hold ILR and meet the residence requirements
Individuals with EUSS settled status who are eligible for naturalisation
Anyone who needs to pass the Life in the UK test as part of their ILR or citizenship application
Children born in the UK to non-British parents have a separate registration process, not the naturalisation route described here.
Documents and evidence to prepare
The naturalisation application (form AN) requires extensive supporting documentation:
Valid passport — current and valid at the date of application
Life in the UK test pass certificate — the original or a certified copy

Proof of ILR — BRP card with ILR endorsement, or eVisa share code showing settled status

Absence schedule — listing all trips outside the UK during the qualifying period with dates and total days absent
Proof of residence — P60s, employment letters, tenancy agreements, utility bills, council tax statements covering the qualifying period
Two passport-size photographs — one endorsed by one of the referees
Timing, deadlines, and sequencing
The naturalisation application can be submitted as soon as you hold ILR and meet the residence requirements. For those married to a British citizen, the residence requirement is three years with no more than 270 days absent (and no more than 90 days absent in the final 12 months). For others, the requirement is five years with no more than 450 days absent (and no more than 90 days in the final year).
The Life in the UK test should be taken well before the citizenship application. Book the test online through the official GOV.UK booking service. Tests are available at over 30 test centres across the UK. Results are emailed within 24 hours and the certificate is posted within seven working days.
Once the application is submitted, processing currently takes two to six months. Plan the application to avoid travel during this period, as you may need to attend an interview or provide additional information.

03 Documents: Course dates, visa length estimate, passport, CAS, dependant details, payment card, IHS reference, visa application, and refund evidence if refused or overpaid.

UK student NHS surcharge: the rule in plain English
The Immigration Health Surcharge (IHS) is a mandatory fee paid by most non-UK nationals applying for a visa lasting longer than 6 months. For Student Route applicants, the IHS must be paid as part of the visa application before a decision can be made. As of 2026, the rate is GBP 776 per year for students and their dependants.
How it is calculated: The IHS is calculated on the full visa duration granted, not the course length. If your course is 3 years but the visa is granted for 3 years and 4 months (common for students with pre-sessional or post-study periods), you pay IHS for the full visa period rounded up to the nearest year. Always calculate IHS based on the expected visa length, not just the academic calendar.
Who this guide is for
Student Route applicants budgeting for visa costs, Graduate Route applicants, dependants of students, and students comparing private insurance options against IHS obligations.
Who this guide is not for
Short-term study visa holders (6 months or less) — IHS is not required.
Visitors to the UK — separate travel insurance is needed.
Applicants for other visa routes (Skilled Worker, Family, etc.) — different IHS rates and rules apply.
What the IHS covers — and does not cover
The IHS entitles you to NHS care on the same basis as a UK resident. This includes GP visits, hospital treatment, A&E services, and mental health support through the NHS. You do not need private medical insurance for these services.
Medical services for students available through the NHS include routine check-ups, vaccinations, sexual health services, and management of long-term conditions. Many universities also have on-campus NHS GP practices that offer appointments designed around the student timetable, with extended hours during term time. Registering with a GP near your accommodation as soon as you have a permanent address gives you access to these services throughout your studies.
Not covered by IHS: Dental treatment (NHS dental charges apply separately), prescription charges (GBP 9.90 per item in England in 2026, free in Scotland/Wales/NI for students), optical services (eye tests and glasses), and some specialised treatments. Students from the EU/EEA with a valid GHIC may have additional coverage for pre-existing conditions.
Timing and payment
The IHS is paid upfront as part of the online visa application. You cannot submit the visa application without paying the surcharge. Payment is by debit or credit card. The IHS reference number is generated after payment and must be saved for your records. If the visa is refused, the IHS is automatically refunded.
Refunds — when and how
Refunds are issued automatically if the visa is refused or if you withdraw before a decision. If you are granted less time than you paid for (e.g., paid for 3 years but granted 2), you can request a partial refund through the GOV.UK IHS refund portal. Refunds are not available if you simply change your mind after the visa is granted. Processing time for refunds ranges from 6 to 12 weeks.
What gets refused / common pitfalls
Assuming private insurance replaces IHS. Having private medical insurance does not exempt you from paying the IHS. Both may be required.
Underbudgeting for dependants. Each dependant pays the full IHS rate. A family of four may face several thousand pounds in surcharge fees alone.
Losing the IHS reference. The reference is needed for refund claims. Save the confirmation email.
Misunderstanding that IHS does not cover dental or prescriptions. Budget separately for these costs.
Calculating IHS on course length instead of visa length. Overlooking the pre-sessional or post-study period means underpaying and risking visa refusal.

body:
Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com

Periodic Tenancies After May 2026: How They Work 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following

§ Key takeaways
01 On 1 May 2026 every assured shorthold tenancy in England converted to an assured periodic tenancy; fixed terms no longer have legal effect. 
02 A tenant can end a periodic tenancy by serving two months' written notice ending on a rent day, at any time. 
03 A landlord can only end the tenancy on a Section 8 ground; there is no 'no-fault' eviction route anymore. 
04 Rent can only rise once per year via a Section 13 notice in the prescribed form; an informal email is not sufficient. 
05 A tenant can challenge a Section 13 rent increase at the First-tier Tribunal within one month of receiving the notice. 
06 Scotland has used the private residential tenancy (PRT) since December 2017; Wales uses the Renting Homes (Wales) Act 2016. 
Last updated 2026-05-14 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
In 60 seconds
On 1 May 2026 every assured shorthold tenancy in England converted to an assured periodic tenancy.
No more fixed terms — old "12-month minimum" clauses have no legal effect.
You can leave on two months' written notice ending on a rent day, at any time.
Your landlord can only end the tenancy on a Section 8 ground — no "two months without a reason" anymore.
Rent can only rise once per year via a Section 13 notice; challengeable at the First-tier Tribunal within one month.
One-sentence answer
On 1 May 2026 every assured shorthold tenancy converted to an assured periodic tenancy — there is no longer a fixed term, you can leave on two months' written notice at any time, your landlord must use a Section 8 ground to end it, and rent can only rise once a year via a Section 13 notice you can challenge.
What "periodic" means now
A periodic tenancy is a rolling tenancy with a period (almost always one month, matching the rent cycle). It continues period by period until one side ends it lawfully.
What this changes in practice:
You are no longer locked in to a 6-month, 12-month, or any other fixed term. Old contracts that said "12-month minimum" have no effect on the new structure.
The landlord cannot make you sign a new fixed term as a condition of continuing.
A "break clause" is meaningless — you don't need one to leave.
The tenancy ends only when a tenant serves notice, both sides agree, or the landlord obtains possession on a Section 8 ground.
Notice you give to leave (two months, in writing)
As a tenant, you can end a periodic tenancy by serving the landlord two months' written notice at any time, ending on a rent day. The notice must be:
In writing. Email is usually fine but check what the contract says about service.
Signed. On a joint tenancy, any one joint tenant's notice ends the whole tenancy for everyone — check all housemates agree before you use it.
Dated. 
Served on the landlord at the contractual address (or at the agent if the contract says so).
If you need to leave faster, you can ask the landlord to accept an earlier surrender — that requires the landlord's written agreement. Don't move out and stop paying rent without the surrender in writing.
Notice your landlord can give (Section 8 only)
Your landlord now has only one route: a Section 8 notice (Form 3) naming at least one ground from Schedule 2 of the Housing Act 1988 — see Section 8 grounds for possession: a tenant's reference . There is no "two months' notice without a reason" anymore. There is no Section 21.
This means:
The landlord has to make a positive case for possession at hearing, even on mandatory grounds.
The landlord must serve the right notice period for the ground used.
A defective notice is a real defence, not a technicality.
Rent rises — once per year, Section 13 form
The Renters' Rights Act 2024 keeps rent rises on a single track: the Section 13 notice in the prescribed form (check the post-2026 form version).
Only once in any twelve-month period. A landlord cannot raise rent six months after the last increase.
Prescribed form. A verbal "I'm putting it up to £X" is not a rent rise. An informal email "the rent is going up" is not a rent rise.
Effective date. The notice must specify the date the new rent applies, with the prescribed minimum notice period before that date.
Right to challenge. You can refer the increase to the First-tier Tribunal (Property Chamber — Residential Property) if you think it exceeds market rent for similar local properties.
If the form is wrong, the cycle is wrong, or the notice period is wrong, the increase is not effective. Pay the existing rent and write to the landlord saying so.
Challenging a rent increase at the First-tier Tribunal
Receive a properly-served Section 13 notice.
Apply to the First-tier Tribunal before the new rent takes effect, using the prescribed form.
Provide evidence: comparable local rents, property condition, any deficiencies that justify a lower rent.
Tribunal decides what is the market rent. The decision binds both sides prospectively.
The tribunal can decide the rent is lower than the landlord proposed; it can also confirm the landlord's figure. The risk is real but rare in clear-cut cases where the landlord has tried to push significantly above market.
Worked example: a 12-month contract that became periodic
Sara signed a 12-month AST in Manchester on 1 November 2025 at £900/month. The fixed term was due to run to 31 October 2026.
On 1 May 2026 her tenancy automatically converted to an assured periodic tenancy. The remaining months of the fixed term ceased to bind her.
In June 2026 her landlord emailed: "Your rent goes up to £1,050 in August." This is not a valid Section 13 notice — wrong form, no rent-day timing. Sara pays £900 and writes back asking for a Section 13 notice in the prescribed form.
In August 2026 Sara decides to move. She serves two months' written notice on 5 Augus

Section 21 Abolished: What Tenants Should Do (2026)

§ Key takeaways
01 Section 21 was abolished for all assured tenancies in England on 1 May 2026. 
02 A Section 21 notice dated on or after 1 May 2026 is invalid on its face. 
03 Pre-1 May 2026 Section 21 notices still work in a transitional window, but the landlord must start a court possession claim within the prescribed window from service. 
04 Existing assured shorthold tenancies converted to assured periodic tenancies on the cut-off date; landlords now need a Section 8 ground to end the tenancy. 
05 Rent rises must use a Section 13 notice in the prescribed form, no more than once per year, and are challengeable at the First-tier Tribunal within one month. 
06 A landlord who changes locks, removes belongings, or cuts off utilities commits an unlawful eviction — a criminal offence and a civil claim. 
Last updated 2026-05-18 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
In 60 seconds
Section 21 "no-fault" eviction was abolished for all assured tenancies in England on 1 May 2026.
A Section 21 notice dated on or after 1 May 2026 is invalid on its face.
Pre-1 May 2026 notices still work in a transitional window — but that window has a court-timing expiry.
Any valid possession claim now requires a Section 8 notice naming a specific ground.
Do not move out on a notice you have not had reviewed.
One-sentence answer
Section 21 stopped being available for new and existing assured shorthold tenancies on 1 May 2026 in England, but pre-1 May 2026 notices live in a transitional window — so the first thing you do with any "Section 21" or "two months' notice" letter in 2026 is check the date and the court timing, not pack a box.
What "Section 21 abolished" actually means
Until 1 May 2026, a landlord on an assured shorthold tenancy in England could end the tenancy without fault on two months' notice in the prescribed form (Form 6A), provided certain pre-conditions were met — deposit protected, prescribed information given, gas safety certificate, How to Rent guide. That was Section 21 of the Housing Act 1988.
From 1 May 2026 the Renters' Rights Act 2024 took that away:
No new Section 21 notices can be served. The form is dead.
Existing ASTs converted to assured periodic tenancies on the cut-off date. The landlord now needs a Section 8 ground to end the tenancy.
Pre-1 May 2026 notices still work, but only under transitional rules. (Source: GOV.UK — Possession notices before 1 May 2026 .)
The transitional question: when was the notice served?
This is the single test that decides which rules apply.
Critical date on the notice: the date the notice was served on you — not the date the landlord typed it, not the date the envelope is post-marked. "Served" usually means the date you actually received it (or the deemed date in the agreement's service clause).
Served on or before 30 April 2026: transitional Section 21. Go to the next section.
Served on or after 1 May 2026: cannot be a Section 21. If it is presented as one, it is invalid .
If the date on the notice is missing or has been altered, treat the notice as suspect and ask the landlord in writing for the original service date.
Notices served before 1 May 2026
A Section 21 served in the transitional window still works, but it has a use-by date. Under the GOV.UK pre-1 May 2026 possession guidance, the landlord must start a court possession claim within the prescribed window measured from service. After that window, the notice expires and the landlord must start again — under the new regime, which means a Section 8 with a real ground.
What to check on a transitional Section 21:
Was the deposit protected within 30 days of receipt? If not, the Section 21 is invalid regardless of date.
Was the prescribed information given? If not, ditto.
Was the gas safety certificate given before move-in? If not, the Section 21 can be challenged.
Was the most recent How to Rent guide given? If not, defective.
Has the court window expired? Compare service date to the pre-1 May guidance. Expired notices are dead.
Notices dated on or after 1 May 2026
There is no such thing as a valid Section 21 dated on or after 1 May 2026. If your landlord has handed you a "two months' notice" dated 1 May 2026 or later, it is one of two things:
a mis-described Section 8 notice — possible if the substance (a Section 8 ground, the right Form 3, the right notice period) is actually there; or
a legally meaningless letter — far more common, especially from smaller landlords or agents working off old templates.
Run the notice through the validity test on the pillar ( Renters' Rights Act 2026: tenant's guide to your new rights ). If no Section 8 ground is named, no notice period is specified, and no Form 3 is used, the letter is meaningless and you are not under any duty to leave. Reply in writing acknowledging receipt and asking the landlord to confirm which Section 8 ground they intend to rely on. That reply is your paper trail.
What landlords sometimes do instead
Three workarounds, and how they fail:
"Mutual surrender." Landlord asks you to sign a one-line agreement that the tenancy is ending. Surrendering ends the tenancy by mutual consent — but you give up your right to stay, your defences, and your bargaining position on the deposit. Don't sign without a tenancy review.
New "fixed term" you have to sign or leave. Fixed terms ended on 1 May 2026. Your landlord can offer one; you do not have to accept it; refusing it does not end your tenancy.
Rent increase you can't afford as a constructive way to push you out. Rent rises must use a Section 13 notice in the prescribed form, no more than once a year, and you can challenge the increase at the First-tier Tribunal (see Periodic tenancies after May 2026: how the new rolling regime works ).

body:
Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com

Section 8 Grounds Explained: a Tenant's Reference (2026) 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library

Your stats 
Following

Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
§ Key takeaways
01 A Section 8 notice must use Form 3, cite one or more specific grounds from Schedule 2 of the Housing Act 1988, and give the correct notice period for those grounds. 
02 Mandatory grounds: if the landlord proves the facts, the court must order possession (Grounds 1, 1A, 2, 4A, 6, 7A, 7B, 8). 
03 Discretionary grounds: the court can refuse possession even if the facts are true, if it would be unreasonable (Grounds 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 14A, 15, 17). 
04 Ground 8 requires at least 8 weeks' rent arrears both at the notice date and at the hearing date; clearing arrears before the hearing kills the ground. 
05 Deposit non-compliance (unprotected deposit or prescribed information not given) is a defence to several grounds, notably Ground 8. 
06 A letter that does not use Form 3 or fails to name a ground is usually a defective notice. 
Last updated 2026-05-14 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
In 60 seconds
A Section 8 notice ends an assured periodic tenancy only when it names a specific ground from Schedule 2 of the Housing Act 1988.
Mandatory grounds: the court must grant possession if the ground is proved.
Discretionary grounds: the court weighs reasonableness and can refuse possession even if the facts are true.
Notice periods differ by ground — a wrong period is a defective notice.
Deposit non-compliance (unprotected, prescribed information not given) is a defence to several grounds.
One-sentence answer
A Section 8 notice ends an assured periodic tenancy only when it names a specific ground from Schedule 2 of the Housing Act 1988, uses the right notice period for that ground, and the landlord can prove at hearing what the ground requires — and your job, on receiving one, is to read it for which ground rather than whether it scares you.
How Section 8 actually works
A landlord ending a tenancy under Section 8 must:
Serve a notice in Form 3 (the "Notice seeking possession of a property let on an assured tenancy"), citing one or more specific grounds from Schedule 2.
Wait out the notice period for those grounds before issuing a court claim.
Issue a possession claim in the county court and prove the ground(s) at hearing.
For mandatory grounds the court has no choice once the ground is proved; for discretionary grounds it can still refuse possession if it considers it unreasonable. Section 21 is gone (see Section 21 abolished: a tenant's action page ) — Section 8 is the entire route now.
Mandatory grounds (court must grant possession if proved)
Confirm current notice periods per ground under the Renters' Rights Act 2024 on the official government source, as these can change.
Ground What it covers Min. notice Evidence the landlord must show 1 Landlord's own / family principal home Check current notice period Prior written notice given at grant; honest intention to occupy 1A Landlord wants to sell Check current notice period Genuine plan to sell; supporting paperwork 2 Mortgagee in possession Check current notice period Mortgage default; lender's right to possess 4A Student HMO recovery for next cohort Check current notice period Prior written notice at grant; all tenants full-time students at grant; HMO let to a household of students 6 Demolition / substantial works Check current notice period Works are genuine and cannot be done with tenant in situ 7A Serious anti-social behaviour Check current notice period Conviction, IPNA, or other specified trigger 7B Right to rent / immigration Check current notice period Home Office notification 8 At least 8 weeks' rent arrears at notice and at hearing 4 weeks Rent statement; arrears persist to hearing Ground 8 is the most common mandatory ground — and the most defendable, because the at hearing test means clearing the arrears before the hearing kills the ground.
Discretionary grounds (court may grant possession)
Ground What it covers What the court weighs 9 Suitable alternative accommodation available Suitability genuine? 10 Some rent owed at notice and at issue Amount, history, reason 11 Persistent late payment, even if zero arrears at notice Pattern over time 12 Breach of any other obligation in the tenancy Materiality 13 Deterioration of the property by the tenant Causation 14 Nuisance / annoyance / illegal use Severity, ongoing risk 14A Domestic violence by a member of a couple Specific to cohabiting context 15 Deterioration of furniture by the tenant Causation 17 False statement to obtain tenancy Materiality of the statement For discretionary grounds, you can win even if the facts are true, by showing it would not be reasonable to grant possession.
Reading the notice: the four things to check first
Is it Form 3? A letter that doesn't use the form is usually defective.
Which grounds are named? No ground = no notice.
Is the notice period correct for those grounds? A 4-week period attached to a 2-month ground is a defective notice.
Has the deposit been protected and prescribed information given? Several grounds (notably Ground 8) require the landlord to be compliant with deposit rules at the time the notice is served. Non-compliance is a defence.
What evidence a court actually wants
Ground 1 / 1A: Original prior written notice at grant; signed statement of intention; for 1A, evidence of marketing.
Ground 4A: Prior written notice at grant; evidence that all tenants were full-time students at grant; HMO licence.
Ground 8: Bank statements showing the arrears at notice date and at hearing date.
Ground 14: Police reports, complaint logs, witness statements.
If the bundle is thin, the ground is thin.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between a mandatory and a discretionary ground?
On a mandatory ground, if the landlord proves the facts, the court must order possession — there is no discretion.

03 Documents: Relationship evidence for partners. Marriage or civil partnership certificate (with certified translation if not in English or Welsh). For unmarried partners: evidence of at least 2 years of cohabitation (joint tenancy agreements, joint bank statements, utility bills in both names, council tax statements). Photographs together, correspondence addressed to both partners, and witness statements from friends or family who can attest to the genuine relationship. 04 Timing: Use check the current dependant maintenance requirement, filing fee, and Immigration Health Surcharge and check care-sector dependant restrictions on publication day. 
05 Main risk: Weak relationship evidence. A marriage certificate alone is not sufficient for partners who have not built a shared life. UKVI expects evidence of ongoing commitment: shared finances, joint living arrangements, communication history, and plans for the future in the UK. For newly married couples who have lived apart, provide evidence of regular communication, visits, and future plans. 
06 Review status: Editorial review only. 
§ Key takeaways
01 Dependants can often join a Skilled Worker, but each dependant must independently prove relationship, age or dependency, funds where required, and suitability. 
02 Eligible dependants include partners, spouses, civil partners, unmarried partners, and children. 
03 Evidence includes passports, marriage or partnership evidence, cohabitation evidence, birth certificates, consent letters, proof of funds, main applicant CoS, and residence plan. 
04 The dependant file should stand alone rather than assuming the main worker approval proves the family case. 
05 Pitfalls include weak relationship evidence, missing consent for children, sponsor certificates that do not cover dependants, and current care-route restrictions. 
The rule in plain English
Dependants of Skilled Worker visa holders can join the main applicant in the UK, but each dependant must independently prove their eligibility. The main applicant's visa approval does not automatically extend to family members. Each dependant — whether a partner (spouse, civil partner, unmarried partner), child under 18, or adult dependent child — must submit a separate visa application, provide their own evidence of relationship, meet the maintenance funds requirement, and satisfy the suitability requirements (no criminal record, no previous immigration breaches).
The key distinction is between dependants who apply at the same time as the main applicant and those who join later. Dependants who apply at the same time can be included in the same application process. Dependants who join later must apply separately, but still need to prove relationship, funds, and suitability. The maintenance requirement is additional to the main applicant's funds: GBP 285 for a dependant partner and GBP 315 per child (check live rates). The funds must be held for 28 consecutive days ending within 31 days of the application date, unless the employer certifies maintenance on the CoS. This timing consideration matters when planning whether to apply together or separately, because applying together means the dependant's visa runs from the same start date as the main applicant's, maximizing the total time the family can remain together in the UK before each member needs to apply for further leave or settlement individually. Dependants who apply separately after the main applicant has already received their visa will have their visa duration aligned to the remaining time on the main applicant's visa, which means a shorter overall grant period and potentially a sooner need to apply for an extension. Planning the dependant application timing carefully can significantly affect the family's overall immigration timeline in the UK.
Care-sector dependant restrictions apply to Skilled Worker visa holders sponsored in care roles (SOC code 6145 — care workers and home carers). Dependants of care workers sponsored under the Health and Care Worker route or the Skilled Worker route in a care occupation face additional restrictions. As of 2026, dependants of care workers may not be permitted to work or may have restricted work rights. Check the current policy on care-sector dependant restrictions before filing, as this policy has changed multiple times in recent years.
Who this guide is for
Partners (spouses, civil partners, unmarried partners) of Skilled Worker visa holders or applicants who want to join the main applicant in the UK. Children under 18 of Skilled Worker holders who need their own visa to accompany the parent. Parents of Skilled Worker holders who are applying for dependant children and need to understand consent requirements, maintenance funds, and timing. Care workers applying under the Health and Care Worker route who need to understand the current dependant restrictions and whether their family members can work when they arrive.
This guide is also for current Skilled Worker visa holders in the UK whose dependants want to join them later. Dependants who join later follow a different application process (separate application, but still within the UK or from overseas). The key requirement is proving the relationship and maintenance funds at the time of the dependant's application, not the main applicant's application date.

§ Key takeaways
01 A Skilled Worker job must meet both the route salary threshold and the occupation going rate unless a valid tradeable-points discount or route-specific rule applies. 
02 The salary analysis starts with the Certificate of Sponsorship and occupation code. 
03 Evidence includes CoS, job description, SOC code, salary amount, weekly hours, sponsor licence details, contract, payscale evidence if applicable, English proof, maintenance evidence, and dependant documents. 
04 Check current salary tables, going rate, new-entrant status, healthcare route rules, fee, and IHS before assigning or accepting a CoS. 
05 Audit the job by SOC code, duties, hours, salary, tradeable points, sponsor genuineness, and start date. 
06 Pitfalls include using the wrong occupation code, counting allowances that do not qualify, salary below the going rate, incorrect new-entrant assumptions, and sponsors assigning inconsistent CoS data. 
The rule in plain English
Skilled Worker salary is a two-test problem. The first test is the general threshold: in 2026, this is typically GBP 38,700 per year for most applicants. The second test is the occupation-specific going rate: the minimum salary for the specific SOC 2020 occupation code assigned on the Certificate of Sponsorship. You must meet whichever figure is higher. If the general threshold is GBP 38,700 and the going rate for a software developer (SOC 2134) is GBP 52,000, you need GBP 52,000. If the going rate for a laboratory technician (SOC 3111) is GBP 25,000, you still need at least the general threshold of GBP 38,700 — unless a tradeable-points discount or route-specific exemption applies.
The two-test system exists to prevent wage undercutting. The going rate ensures that sponsored workers are paid no less than the market rate for their occupation, protecting both the worker and the resident labour market. Tradeable points allow applicants to meet the requirement through other attributes: a PhD relevant to the job (10 points), a job in a shortage occupation (20 points), or new entrant status (reduced salary threshold). These points are added to the mandatory salary points (20 for meeting 70% of the going rate, 30 for 80%, 40 for 90%, 50 for 100% or more).
The salary analysis starts with the Certificate of Sponsorship and the occupation code assigned on it. Before the employer assigns the CoS, both parties should verify that the salary figure on the CoS meets both thresholds. A CoS with a salary below the requirement cannot be corrected after assignment — a new CoS must be generated. Check the live Home Office salary tables (updated periodically) rather than relying on cached or third-party data.

Workers with a UK job offer who want to confirm whether the proposed salary meets the Skilled Worker threshold before the employer assigns the CoS or before the applicant files the visa application. Healthcare workers who may benefit from the lower going rate applied through the Health and Care Worker route. Applicants changing sponsors who need to check whether the new salary meets the threshold independently of their previous grant.

If you are applying in a shortage occupation, verify that the occupation code is on the current shortage occupation list before assuming the discount applies.

§ Key takeaways
01 Skilled Workers usually must update their visa before starting a new sponsored job with a different employer or a job in a different occupation code. 
02 You can apply up to 3 months before the new job start date and should not start the new job until permission is confirmed. 
03 The application requires a new Certificate of Sponsorship, job description, occupation code, salary evidence, sponsor licence details, current visa details, passport, UKVI account, dependants details, and funds evidence if required.

The rule in plain English
Skilled Workers must update their visa before starting a new sponsored job with a different employer or a job in a different occupation code. The application is made online through the UKVI account system, using the new Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS) issued by the new employer. You cannot start the new role until the Home Office confirms the updated permission.
When an update is not required: Promotions or internal role changes within the same employer and same occupation code do not require a visa update, as long as the salary still meets the threshold. Changes to a different occupation code within the same employer generally do require an update.
The key timing rule: you can apply up to 3 months before the new job start date. If you apply from inside the UK, you remain on your current Skilled Worker conditions while the application is pending (section 3C protection). This means you can continue working for your current employer until the new visa is granted. Do not resign from your current role until the new application is submitted or ideally until it is approved, as a gap in sponsored employment could create complications.
Who this guide is for
Skilled Worker visa holders changing employer, changing occupation code, adding substantial second employment, or moving from Student or Graduate Route to Skilled Worker sponsorship.
This guide is also for HR teams managing sponsorship changes for existing employees who are moving to a new role within the same organisation or moving to a different employer. If you are managing a pipeline of sponsorship changes, track the key dates: when the previous employment ends, when the new CoS is assigned, when the visa application is submitted, and when the new role can lawfully begin.
Who this guide is not for
Health and Care Worker visa holders — different rules and reduced application fees apply.
Global Talent or Innovator Founder visa holders — switching to Skilled Worker is a separate route change, not a same-route update.
Workers whose new role is with the same employer in the same occupation code — no update needed as long as the salary threshold is still met.
The new CoS and occupation code
The new employer must assign a Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS) through the sponsor management system before you can apply. The CoS confirms the job title, occupation code (SOC 2020), salary, and that the employer holds a valid sponsor licence. Check that the occupation code is correct — a wrong code is a common refusal reason. The role must be at RQF level 3 or above (most graduate roles are RQF 6).

The new role must meet both the general salary threshold and the going rate for the specific occupation code. As of 2026, the general threshold is typically GBP 38,700 per year (check current rates). If the going rate for the occupation code is higher than the general threshold, the going rate applies. Some transitional rules allow lower rates for new entrants or workers switching from the Graduate Route. Always check both figures against the live Home Office salary tables before accepting a job offer. A role called "Data Scientist" needs to be assigned one of the existing SOC codes such as 2135 (IT business analysts, architects and systems designers), 2136 (programmers and software development professionals), or 2139 (information technology and communications professionals not elsewhere classified). The mapping determines the salary going rate and directly affects whether the application succeeds.
UKVI does not use custom or employer-specific occupation titles. The CoS must reference a standard SOC 2020 code. The code determines the going rate, the skill level requirement (RQF 3 minimum for Skilled Worker, but most tech roles are RQF 6), and whether the role qualifies for any tradeable points or shortage-occupation discounts. A software developer (SOC 2136) has a different going rate from an IT project manager (SOC 2135), and mapping the wrong code can lead to a salary shortfall or a refusal based on occupation mismatch. Tech employers and applicants should review the SOC 2020 occupation descriptions before the CoS is assigned.

At the higher end, software developers and IT project managers typically have going rates above GBP 52,000 in London and GBP 46,000 outside London. At the lower end, web design and development professionals (SOC 2137) may have lower going rates. Verify the live going rate for the specific SOC code on the date of application — rates change periodically and relying on cached data is a common mistake.

01 The standard ILR qualifying period for Skilled Workers is 5 years of continuous lawful residence. Time on Tier 2 General, Skilled Worker, Global Talent, and some other work visas counts toward the 5 years. 
02 You must not exceed 180 days outside the UK in any rolling 12-month period. All absences count — business travel, holidays, family visits. The 12-month window rolls backward from the ILR application date. 
03 Salary requirement: at or above the going rate for your SOC occupation code, or the general threshold — whichever is higher. Check current thresholds on the GOV.UK Skilled Worker page at the date of application. 
04 Life in the UK test (£50, 24 questions, 75% pass mark) and English language at B1 level are required. The test result never expires — take it early to avoid delays. 
05 Your employer must provide a sponsor letter confirming your job title, SOC code, salary, ongoing need, and dates of employment. The letter must be dated within one month of the ILR application. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for Skilled Worker visa holders (and former Tier 2 General visa holders) approaching the 5-year mark and preparing to apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain. It covers the continuous residence requirement, the 180-day absence rule, the salary threshold at the date of application, the Life in the UK test and English language requirement, and the employer letter that your sponsor must provide. It also covers applicants who changed employers during the 5-year period and need to confirm their residence was continuous across multiple sponsors.
This guide is not for ILR applicants on the 10-year long residence route, the family route (spouse/partner of a British citizen or settled person), the Global Talent route (which has a 3-year accelerated path), or the Innovator Founder route. It is also not for applicants who have exceeded 180 days of absence in a rolling 12-month period — if your continuous residence is broken, the 5-year clock resets and this guide's timeline does not apply to you. If your absence record is marginal (175-185 days in any 12-month window), consult an immigration adviser before applying — a refusal on absence grounds resets your qualifying period.
The 180-day absence rule: how it works and how to calculate it
The continuous residence requirement for ILR is broken if you have been outside the UK for more than 180 days in any rolling 12-month period during the 5-year qualifying period. Every full day outside the UK counts. The day of departure and the day of arrival in the UK are not counted as absences — only full days spent entirely outside the UK count. The 12-month period is rolling: start from the date of your ILR application and count backward in 12-month blocks, checking each block for a total that exceeds 180 days. Repeat the exercise for each overlapping 12-month period throughout the 5 years.
All types of absence count: annual leave, family visits, business travel, overseas assignments, and unpaid leave. There is no separate allowance for business travel or compassionate leave. The Home Office may exercise discretion for absences caused by serious illness, natural disaster, or travel disruption beyond your control, but this is not guaranteed — it must be raised with supporting evidence in a cover letter, not assumed. Absences for maternity, paternity, or adoption leave are counted but may be considered under the 'serious or compelling reasons' discretion if the total absence period is reasonable relative to the leave taken. If you travelled frequently for work, pull your travel history from your passport stamps, flight bookings, and employer records — then count each absence to confirm you did not breach the 180-day limit in any 12-month window. The Home Office cross-references its own entry and exit records, so an estimate based on memory will not match their data if your count is wrong.
Documents you need to evidence continuous residence
The ILR application requires evidence that you have been continuously resident and lawfully employed in the UK for the 5-year qualifying period. The core documents:
Passport(s): All passports covering the 5-year period, showing entry and exit stamps. If you renewed your passport during the period, include the old and new passport. If a passport does not show every entry (some countries do not stamp on departure), supplement with flight booking confirmations or employer travel records.
Absence spreadsheet: Not a mandatory Home Office document, but highly recommended. List every absence: departure date, return date, number of full days outside the UK, purpose, and a running total for each rolling 12-month period. Attach this as a cover letter table — it demonstrates that you have done the calculation and makes the caseworker's review easier.
Employer letter: On company letterhead, confirming your job title, SOC code, current salary, that you are still required for the role for the foreseeable future, and the dates of your employment. The letter must be dated within one calendar month of the ILR application date. If the letter is older than one month, the Home Office may request a new one.
Payslips and bank statements: Typically the most recent 3 months of payslips and corresponding bank statements, to evidence the current salary. If your salary is variable (overtime, commission), you may need 6-12 months of payslips to demonstrate the average meets the threshold. The bank statements must show the salary being deposited — the name on the bank account must match the applicant.
Life in the UK test pass notification: The unique reference number from the test result. You do not need the physical certificate — the reference number is checked against the Home Office database.

UK Skilled Worker visa guide
The UK Skilled Worker visa is the main route for non-UK nationals who have a job offer from a licensed sponsor at or above the salary threshold. It replaced the Tier 2 (General) route in December 2020 and now covers a broad range of occupations, from software engineers and healthcare workers to construction managers and academics. This guide orients you to the cluster: how the two-test salary system works, what a Certificate of Sponsorship is, how to switch employers without breaking your visa, how to bring dependants, and what employers must do to obtain a sponsor licence. If you are a software engineer, healthcare worker, or tech professional, start here and follow the path that matches your situation. Every article in this cluster links back to this guide, so you can navigate depth-first without losing context.
Last updated 2026-05-19 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
Reviewer programs for UK matters are under development; until those programs launch, UK content is editorial-only.
How the Skilled Worker route works
The Skilled Worker visa is a points-based immigration route. Applicants must score a minimum of 70 points under the Home Office tradeable points system. All applicants must score 20 points for a job at the appropriate skill level (RQF 3 or above), 20 points for English language proficiency at B1 level, and 20 points for salary meeting the minimum threshold (currently GBP 38,700 per year for most applicants). The remaining 10 points can be earned through tradeable attributes: a PhD relevant to the job (10 points), a job in a shortage occupation (10 points), or new entrant status (10 points, which also reduces the salary threshold to approximately 70% of the going rate). Understanding the points system is essential before preparing an application — the tradeable points can make the difference between a qualifying and non-qualifying salary offer.
The application process begins with the employer. Before a worker can apply, the employer must assign a Certificate of Sponsorship through the Sponsor Management System. The CoS confirms the job title, occupation code (SOC 2020), salary, and that the employer holds a valid A-rated sponsor licence. Once the CoS is assigned (it is valid for 3 months), the worker can submit the visa application online, pay the fee and Immigration Health Surcharge, attend a biometric appointment (or use the UK Immigration: ID Check app), and submit supporting documents. The processing time from inside the UK is approximately 8 weeks; from outside the UK, approximately 3 weeks after biometrics.
The Skilled Worker visa is typically granted for up to 5 years, with extensions available. Settlement (indefinite leave to remain) is available after 5 years of continuous residence, provided the applicant meets the continuous residence requirement (no more than 180 days absences from the UK in any rolling 12-month period) and passes the Life in the UK test. Time spent on other visa categories (Student, Graduate Route, Tier 2) may count toward the 5-year settlement period, depending on the specific combination of routes. Workers should track their absences from the UK carefully throughout the Skilled Worker period, because absences over 180 days in any 12-month rolling period can break the continuous residence requirement and reset the settlement clock, adding months or years to the time needed before the worker becomes eligible to apply for indefinite leave to remain under the long residence provisions of the Immigration Rules.
The application fee depends on the length of the visa, the worker's circumstances, and whether the role is in a shortage occupation or healthcare. Standard fees range from GBP 719 to GBP 1,500 for entry clearance or leave to remain, with lower fees for roles on the Immigration Salary List or Health and Care Worker visas. The Immigration Health Surcharge is payable at the full rate of GBP 1,035 per year for most Skilled Workers, though healthcare workers benefit from a reduced surcharge as part of the Health and Care Worker visa pathway. Dependants pay the same IHS rate as the main applicant, and the surcharge must be paid in full for the entire duration of the visa at the time of application. Understanding the total cost of the application before submitting is essential because the IHS surcharge is not refundable if the visa is refused, and the applicant will need to pay the full fee and surcharge again if they reapply after a refusal or if they need to extend their Skilled Worker permission beyond the initial grant period of up to 5 years.
Dependants of Skilled Workers enjoy broad work and study rights in the UK. Partners can work full time in any role, including self-employment and company directorship, without the occupation-code restrictions that apply to the main Skilled Worker applicant. Children can attend state schools without needing a separate student visa. Each dependent must submit a separate visa application linked to the main applicant's Skilled Worker application, and the relationship must be evidenced with marriage or civil partnership certificates for partners and birth certificates for children. Maintenance funds must also be demonstrated for each dependant, typically GBP 285 for a partner and GBP 315 for the first child, unless the main applicant has been in the UK with valid permission for at least 12 months at the time of application. Care-sector dependant restrictions may apply for workers sponsored under the Health and Care Worker visa in certain roles, so workers considering bringing family should verify the current dependant rules for their specific occupation code before submitting the visa application to the Home Office.

UK Skilled Worker Visa FAQ
Clear answers about salary thresholds, the Certificate of Sponsorship, switching employers, dependants, and the Immigration Skills Charge. This FAQ aggregates the most common questions from our Skilled Worker and sponsor licence articles.
This FAQ is for skilled workers who are applying for a UK Skilled Worker visa, switching employers while on the route, or bringing dependants to the UK. The questions reflect the most common situations we see from applicants in UKVI forums and from our own document review clients. Each answer draws on the Immigration Rules (Appendix Skilled Worker, Appendix Dependant, and Appendix English Language), Home Office caseworker guidance, and current UKVI policy as of mid-2026.
The Skilled Worker route saw significant changes in 2024 and 2025, including the increase of the general salary threshold to £38,700, adjustments to shortage occupation lists, and stricter going-rate requirements for specific SOC codes. The Health and Care Worker route continues to operate with separate, lower thresholds, but has faced increased scrutiny around dependent arrangements. The answers below reflect the current rules and salary bands in effect as of July 2026. Before accepting a job offer, confirm both the general threshold and the occupation-specific going rate for your SOC code on GOV.UK.
The question list below covers the most frequently asked Skilled Worker topics. For deeper guidance on any subject, the articles linked below include step-by-step instructions, document checklists, and the specific Home Office policy references that apply to each stage of the visa process.
How to use this FAQ
Match salary thresholds and SOC codes to the live GOV.UK Skilled Worker tables before accepting an offer.

What is the minimum salary for a UK Skilled Worker visa in 2026?
The Skilled Worker visa uses a two-test system: you must meet both the general threshold and the occupation-specific "going rate" for your SOC code. As of 2026, the general threshold is typically £38,700 per year, but lower thresholds apply for new entrants, healthcare roles, and jobs on the shortage occupation list. The going rate varies by SOC code and is published on GOV.UK. You must meet whichever figure is higher. If you are paid hourly, the annual equivalent is calculated using a 39-hour week. A common mistake is assuming the general threshold is the only test and discovering at application stage that the going rate for the specific occupation is higher. Verify both figures against the live GOV.UK tables before accepting a job offer.
Can I switch employers while on a Skilled Worker visa?
Yes, but your new employer must hold a valid sponsor licence and issue a new Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS) before you start work. You must apply to update your visa before beginning the new role. In most cases, you can start working for the new employer as soon as UKVI confirms receipt of a valid application, provided the new job meets the skill and salary requirements. You cannot start work for a new employer using your old CoS. If your new role has a different SOC code, the salary threshold may change. If you leave your current employer before filing the update application, you risk a gap in lawful employment. Plan the timing so that the new CoS is issued and the update application is submitted before your last day with the previous employer.
What is the Immigration Skills Charge and who pays it?
The Immigration Skills Charge is a fee paid by the sponsoring employer, not the worker. It is designed to encourage employers to train UK resident workers. The amount depends on the size of the organisation and the length of the CoS: typically £1,000 per year for medium or large sponsors and £364 per year for small or charitable sponsors. The employer pays this when assigning the CoS. If you are negotiating a job offer, confirm in writing whether the employer will cover this cost and whether it is included in any relocation package they have described. The charge is not refundable if you leave the job early, though the employer may be able to claim a partial refund in specific circumstances.
Can my dependants work in the UK on a Skilled Worker visa?
Yes. Dependants of Skilled Worker visa holders can work full time in any role, including self-employment, with very few restrictions. They can also study. Each dependant must have their own visa application approved, proving the relationship (marriage certificate, birth certificate, or evidence of cohabitation for unmarried partners) and that there is sufficient maintenance funds. The maintenance requirement for dependants is additional to the main applicant's funds. Dependants can apply at the same time as the main applicant or join later. Children born in the UK while the parents hold Skilled Worker visas do not automatically become British citizens; they acquire the same immigration status as the parents.
How long does it take to get a Skilled Worker visa?
Standard processing from outside the UK is typically 3 weeks after the biometric appointment, though times vary by country and season. From inside the UK, standard processing is usually 8 weeks. § Key takeaways
01 A sponsor licence is permission plus a compliance system: the employer must prove it is genuine, lawfully operating, and able to carry out sponsor duties. 
02 Required evidence includes Companies House records, PAYE or VAT proof, employer liability insurance, premises proof, HR policies, right-to-work process, key personnel details, and route-specific documents.

The rule in plain English
A sponsor licence is permission from the Home Office to hire workers from outside the UK's resident labour market. It is not simply a registration — it is a compliance relationship with UKVI. Employers that hold a sponsor licence must comply with a detailed set of sponsor duties: record-keeping (Appendix D), reporting (changes to worker circumstances, absences, or non-compliance), a genuine vacancy requirement, and a robust right-to-work checking process. Failure to meet these duties results in licence downgrade (to B-rating), suspension, or revocation.
The application requires the employer to prove it is genuine (a real, operating business with a UK presence), lawfully operating (registered with Companies House, HMRC, and other relevant bodies), and capable of carrying out sponsor duties (HR systems, key personnel in place, reporting processes). The application is made online through the Sponsor Management System (SMS), with supporting documents uploaded to evidence the business's genuine operation and HR capability. Processing time is typically 8 weeks from submission of all required documents.
Once licensed, the employer can assign Certificates of Sponsorship to workers. The number of CoS an employer can assign depends on the licence type and the employer's allocation. New licence holders typically receive a limited allocation for the first year. CoS allocation can be requested through the SMS. Each CoS must be linked to a genuine vacancy at the appropriate skill level (RQF 3 or above for Skilled Worker, RQF 6 for most graduate roles) with a salary meeting the relevant thresholds.
Who this guide is for
UK employers who are considering applying for a sponsor licence for the first time and need to understand the application process, required documents, and ongoing compliance obligations. HR and legal teams who manage sponsor licence compliance within their organisation and need to stay current with Appendix D requirements, reporting duties, and compliance visit preparation. Small businesses and startups that are new to sponsorship and need practical guidance on setting up HR systems, appointing key personnel, and managing the SMS.
This guide is also for organisations that already hold a sponsor licence but want to audit their compliance before a UKVI compliance visit. If your organisation has not had a compliance visit recently, review your record-keeping processes against the current Appendix D guidance. A proactive audit is significantly less stressful than a reactive one triggered by a UKVI notification.

Companies House records. Certificate of incorporation, list of directors, registered address, and proof of active status. If the business is a sole trader or partnership, provide equivalent evidence of lawful business registration. The business must be actively trading — a shell company with no operations will not qualify.
PAYE and VAT registration evidence. Proof that the business is registered with HMRC for PAYE and VAT. This demonstrates that the business is a genuine employer with a UK payroll and is collecting and reporting taxes. If the business is newly established and not yet VAT-registered (below the GBP 90,000 threshold), provide evidence of PAYE registration and a letter explaining why VAT registration is not yet required.

UK spouse visa refusal reasons: the rule in plain English
Most UK spouse visa refusals are not about whether the couple loves each other — they are about whether the documents satisfy a strict rule. The Immigration Rules (Appendix FM and Appendix FM-SE) set out exactly what documents UKVI expects and what form those documents must take. A document that is present but in the wrong format is treated as missing.
The five most common refusal categories are: (1) the financial requirement is not met, (2) the relationship is not proven to be genuine and subsisting, (3) the English language requirement is not met, (4) the accommodation requirement is not met, and (5) the applicant does not meet the suitability requirements (previous immigration breaches, criminality, or deception).
This guide covers each category in detail, explains why UKVI refuses on each ground, and provides practical steps to avoid or respond to a refusal.
Who this guide is for
Spouses, civil partners, and unmarried partners preparing a fresh application or responding to a refusal. This includes:
Applicants whose spouse visa was recently refused and need to understand why
Couples preparing a new application and want to avoid the most common refusal grounds
Sponsors in the UK whose partner's visa was refused and are considering administrative review or a fresh application
Solicitors and immigration advisers preparing representations in spouse visa cases
Documents and evidence to prepare
The bundle for a spouse visa application or response to a refusal should include:
Financial evidence: Six months of payslips (signed/stamped), corresponding bank statements, employer letter confirming salary and length of employment, P60 for the last full tax year, and the employment contract. For self-employed: SA302, tax year overview, business bank statements, and accounts.
Relationship evidence: Marriage certificate with apostille if foreign, cohabitation evidence (joint tenancy, joint utility bills, joint bank statements), dated photographs, communication records, travel evidence of time spent together, and supporting statements from family and friends.
English evidence: SELT certificate at A1 (entry clearance) or A2 (extension) from an approved provider, or a degree taught in English with an NARIC/ENIC equivalence statement.
Accommodation evidence: Tenancy agreement or property deeds, council tax bill, utility bill, and a property inspection report confirming the property is not overcrowded.
Immigration history: Previous visas, refusal notices, immigration applications, and biometrics confirmation.
Timing, deadlines, and sequencing
If the application has been refused, the first deadline is the administrative review window: 28 calendar days from the date of the refusal decision if applied from outside the UK, or 14 days if applied from inside the UK. The date on the refusal notice is day zero. Do not wait for the refusal letter to arrive by post — UKVI sends decisions by email as well.
If you are submitting a fresh application, the timing depends on gathering the correct evidence. Bank statements must end no more than 28 days before the new application date. Payslips must cover the six-month period ending no more than 28 days before the application. A fresh application cannot rely on evidence from the refused application if that evidence is now out of date.
The financial requirement threshold should be verified before the application. The current threshold (GBP 29,000) may be subject to change, as may the fee and the Immigration Health Surcharge rate.

UK Student Route checklist: the rule in plain English
The UKVI decision-maker reviewing a Student Route application works through a structured checklist: the CAS confirms the course and sponsor, financial evidence proves maintenance funds, English language evidence satisfies the B2 requirement, and suitability documents (ATAS, TB test, parental consent for under-18s) address statutory gateways. Every item on that list must be present and compliant — a gap in any one can derail the entire application regardless of how strong the other evidence is.
Who this guide is for
International students applying for UK study visas, including under-18 applicants and students with dependants where allowed.
Documents and evidence to prepare
CAS, passport, financial evidence, tuition payment proof, English proof, academic documents listed on CAS, ATAS if required, TB certificate where required, parental consent for 16-17 applicants, and IHS reference.
Timing, deadlines, and sequencing
Apply no earlier than the allowed window and verify current funds, fee, IHS, and evidence-date rules before submission.
How to make the file easier to approve
Map the checklist to UKVI's requirements rather than the school's admissions checklist.
Document preparation: what to do before you apply
Before submitting your application, ensure all your official documents required are properly prepared. Some documents from non-English-speaking countries require document attestation by the issuing authority before UKVI will accept them. For financial evidence from outside the UK, check whether your bank statements need notarization of documents or a letter from the bank on official letterhead confirming the account holder's name, account number, and balance — UKVI may question documents that lack institutional backing. If you hold academic credentials from an institution outside the UK, consider validating educational credentials through UK ENIC to confirm the equivalency against UK education standards.
If you have academic credentials from your home country that are not listed on your CAS, consider having them professionally attested before submission. Keeping documents safe in both physical and digital form ensures you can reprint lost originals quickly. Make scanned copies of every document — passport, CAS, financial evidence, academic transcripts, ATAS certificate if required, and TB test certificate — and store them in encrypted cloud storage accessible from anywhere.
If you are applying from a country where TB testing is required, book your tuberculosis test with an approved clinic well before your application date. The TB certificate is valid for six months from the date of the chest x-ray — timing it so it covers your visa application window and planned travel date avoids the need for a repeat test. Some countries also require proof of necessary vaccinations as part of the health screening for a Student Route visa; check the latest UKVI health screening requirements for your nationality before submitting your application. If you have a medical condition that requires regular treatment, obtain a letter from your consultant confirming the condition, treatment plan, and any medications you will need in the UK, as this supports your IHS payment and helps your new GP provide continuity of care after you register with an NHS practice upon arrival.
After your visa: arrival and settlement
Once your Student Route visa is approved, plan your arrival and settlement. The UK offers post-arrival support through university international student services, which can help with BRP collection (within 10 days of arrival), council tax exemption registration, GP enrolment, and opening a bank account. Many universities offer airport pickup services and temporary accommodation for the first week.
Understanding settlement assistance options before you travel reduces stress. Jo
