Language support and bilingual resources
Once your Student Route visa is approved and you arrive in the UK, language barriers in academic writing and everyday conversation are normal even if you met the English requirement for your CAS. Most UK universities offer free language courses and bilingual support through academic writing centres, English for Academic Purposes workshops, and conversation groups where you can practise speaking in a low-pressure environment.
Improving your communication skills early in your studies helps with seminar participation, tutorial discussions, and building professional networks. If you are studying in a region with a local language variation — for example, in Scotland or Wales — the university's international student office can connect you with resources for understanding local dialects and vocabulary. These services are typically included in your tuition fees and available throughout your entire course.
What gets refused / common pitfalls
Pitfalls include CAS errors, stale bank evidence, wrong English proof, missing ATAS, under-18 consent gaps, and assuming admission alone creates visa eligibility.

Fill out forms accurately, pay applicable fees, and submit through the correct channel. For USCIS filings, include the correct filing fee and submit to the correct lockbox address.
04 Follow Through Track processing and maintain status while waiting
Monitor case status online, keep proof of timely filing, and continue to maintain your underlying status until a decision is made. Respond promptly to any RFEs or requests for additional evidence.

UK Student Route FAQ
Clear answers about CAS, financial evidence, the 28-day rule, the Graduate Route, ATAS clearance, switching visas, and working while studying. This FAQ aggregates the most common questions from our Student Route and Graduate Route articles.
This FAQ is for international students applying for a UK Student Route visa, renewing their permission, planning to transition to the Graduate Route, or considering switching to a Skilled Worker visa mid-course. The questions reflect the most common situations we see from student applicants in UKVI forums and from our own document review clients. Each answer is grounded in the Immigration Rules (Appendix Student, Appendix Graduate, Appendix Skilled Worker), Home Office caseworker guidance, and current UKVI policy as of mid-2026.
The Student Route has undergone several recent changes, including the restriction on dependants for most taught postgraduate courses from September 2023, adjustments to working-hour limits, and the upcoming reduction of the non-doctoral Graduate Route from 2 years to 18 months from 1 January 2027. The financial evidence requirements and the 28-day rule remain common refusal triggers. The answers below reflect the current rules in effect as of July 2026.
The question list below covers the most frequently asked Student Route topics. For a deeper dive into any subject, the articles linked at the bottom of this page provide step-by-step guidance, document checklists, and the specific Home Office policy references that apply to each stage.
How to use this FAQ
Start with CAS + funds evidence (28-day rule) before dependants or Graduate Route timing questions.
Confirm maintenance levels and CAS validity on GOV.UK / your sponsor's CAS letter the week you file.
Dual-graph: campus journey on uk universities ; form-level Student Route procedure on this library (editorial-only).
Last updated 2026-07-14 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
Reviewer programs for UK matters are under development; until those programs launch, UK content is editorial-only.
How much money do I need to show for a UK Student Route visa?
You must show enough money to cover your first year of course fees plus living costs. The living cost amount is £1,529 per month if studying in London, or £1,171 per month outside London, for up to 9 months. If your course is 9 months or longer, you show 9 months of living costs. If your course is shorter, you show the full course length. The funds must have been in the account for the required evidence period ending no more than 31 days before you apply. If you are using a student loan, the loan letter must confirm the amount, that it is available to you, and the disbursement schedule. Verify the exact figures on GOV.UK before applying, as they are updated periodically.
What is the 28-day rule for Student Route financial evidence?
The 28-day rule means the closing balance in your account must not dip below the required amount on any day during a continuous 28-day period. The 28th day must end no more than 31 days before your application date. A common refusal reason is showing a statement where the balance dropped below the threshold on day 15, even if it was back above the threshold by day 28. Another common error is using a statement that ends more than 31 days before the application date. If you are using a parent's account, you must also provide a birth certificate and a financial consent letter that meets UKVI's format requirements.
Can I work while studying on the Student Route?
Yes, but with restrictions that depend on your course level and sponsor type. Most degree-level students can work up to 20 hours per week during term time and full time during official vacation periods. Students at below-degree level (for example, studying at a further education college) are generally limited to 10 hours per week during term time. You cannot fill a permanent full-time vacancy, be self-employed, or work as a professional sportsperson or entertainer. Your employer and the university are both responsible for checking these conditions. Working more than your permitted hours is a breach of immigration conditions and can affect future applications, including the Graduate Route.
What is a CAS and why does it matter?
A Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies (CAS) is a unique reference number issued by your licensed student sponsor. It confirms that the university has made you an unconditional offer, checked that you can meet the course requirements, and assessed that you are genuine about studying. The CAS is the single most important document in your Student Route application because every other piece of evidence — funds, English test, ATAS certificate — must align with the details on the CAS. If your CAS says your course starts on 15 September but your bank statements are dated July, the officer may question whether the funds will still be available. If the CAS fee figure does not match your offer letter, the application can be refused for inconsistency.
How long does the Graduate Route let me stay in the UK?
If you complete an eligible degree-level course at a licensed Higher Education Provider, the Graduate Route grants permission to stay for 2 years (or 3 years for PhD graduates). You must apply from inside the UK before your Student permission expires. You cannot travel outside the Common Travel Area while your Graduate Route application is pending. The route does not require a job offer, but it is not renewable — you can only hold Graduate Route permission once. From 1 January 2027, the non-doctoral Graduate Route is expected to reduce to 18 months for most applicants, so check the current rules before making long-term plans.

Renting as a student in the UK means navigating different legal regimes depending on whether your university is in Scotland or England. From 1 May 2026, the Renters' Rights Act 2025 fundamentally changed the tenancy landscape for students in England, while Scotland has operated under its own Private Residential Tenancy (PRT) framework since December 2017. This guide explains which legal regime applies to you, what protections you have in Glasgow, Edinburgh, Bristol, Leeds, Liverpool, Manchester and Nottingham, and what to check before signing a tenancy agreement in 2026.
If you are an international student also navigating visa requirements, our Student visa document checklist covers the immigration documentation you need alongside your housing arrangements. For broader coverage of how the Renters' Rights Act affects all tenants, see our guide to renters' rights in 2026 .
Which legal regime applies to your city
The UK does not have a single national tenancy law for students. Your rights depend on which side of the border your university sits:
City Legal regime Tenancy type (private rentals) Glasgow Scotland Private Residential Tenancy (PRT) Edinburgh Scotland Private Residential Tenancy (PRT) Bristol England Assured periodic tenancy (from 1 May 2026) Leeds England Assured periodic tenancy (from 1 May 2026) Liverpool England Assured periodic tenancy (from 1 May 2026) Manchester England Assured periodic tenancy (from 1 May 2026) Nottingham England Assured periodic tenancy (from 1 May 2026) If you rent directly from your university (on-campus halls), you will typically hold a licence to occupy rather than a tenancy, and the rules below may not apply. Purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) operated by private providers may fall under separate codes of practice. The guidance here covers private rentals with landlords or letting agents — the sector most international and UK students enter when moving off-campus in their second or third year.
For city-by-city deep dives, MyCaseworks also maintains dedicated pages for Glasgow , Edinburgh , Bristol , Leeds , Liverpool , Manchester and Nottingham .
Part 1: Scotland — Glasgow and Edinburgh
The Private Residential Tenancy (PRT) framework
Since 1 December 2017, all new private tenancies in Scotland have been Private Residential Tenancies (PRTs) under the Private Housing (Tenancies) (Scotland) Act 2016. A PRT has no fixed end date. Your landlord cannot include a minimum term or expected end date in your agreement, and you can give notice to leave at any point after the tenancy begins. This is confirmed by the Scottish Government's private residential tenancy guidance for tenants and the enacted legislation on legislation.gov.uk.
This open-ended structure gives Scottish students considerably more flexibility than the old assured and short-assured tenancy system. However, it also means your landlord cannot simply agree to a fixed-term contract that aligns with the academic year. Understanding how notice works in both directions is essential.
How much notice you must give
As a tenant under a PRT, you must give your landlord 28 days' written notice to end the tenancy. You must state the day you want the tenancy to end, which is normally the day after the notice period expires. You can give notice by email if your tenancy agreement allows it; otherwise use post and keep proof of sending. All joint tenants must agree and sign the notice — one tenant cannot end the tenancy on behalf of everyone.
If you leave without giving proper notice, you remain liable for rent until the notice period expires or until the landlord finds a replacement tenant, whichever comes first.
How much notice your landlord must give
Your landlord can only end a PRT by using one of 18 statutory grounds for eviction. The notice period depends on how long you have lived in the property and which ground the landlord uses:
Tenancy length Notice period Less than 6 months 28 days (4 weeks) regardless of ground More than 6 months — conduct grounds 28 days (4 weeks) More than 6 months — other grounds 84 days (12 weeks) The six "conduct" grounds that attract 28 days' notice even after six months are: not occupying the property as your home; breaching the tenancy agreement; rent arrears for three consecutive months; criminal behaviour; antisocial behaviour; and associating with someone who has a relevant conviction or has engaged in antisocial behaviour. All other grounds — including the landlord wanting to sell, move in, or refurbish — require 84 days' notice if you have lived there more than six months.
Even after the notice period expires, your landlord cannot evict you without obtaining an eviction order from the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Housing and Property Chamber). You have the right to remain in the property until the Tribunal grants that order.
Rent increases in Scotland
Your landlord can only increase your rent once in any 12-month period and must give you at least three months' written notice . As of 2026, there is a 3% cap on rent increases during a tenancy, though landlords may apply for up to 6% if they can evidence increased costs. If you believe a proposed increase exceeds the cap, you can ask Rent Service Scotland to assess whether it is lawful.
Tenancy deposit protection in Scotland
Landlords must protect your deposit in one of three government-approved schemes — SafeDeposits Scotland, my|deposits Scotland, or Letting Protection Service Scotland — and provide you with prescribed information within 30 working days of receiving the deposit. If your landlord fails to comply, you can apply to the First-tier Tribunal for sanctions, which may include an order requiring the landlord t

01 Birmingham follows the national Renters' Rights Act framework, but local HMO licensing has three layers: national mandatory, additional, and Article 4 in Selly Oak and parts of Edgbaston. 
02 Ground 4A prior notice included as a clause in the agreement (rather than a separate signed document) is the most common local defect in Birmingham. 
03 An unlicensed HMO is the strongest single defence available to a tenant in any possession or deposit dispute. 
04 The dominant Selly Oak pattern is a 4-bed terraced house, joint tenancy, agent-managed — watch for cash-collected rent and July-start summer rent traps.

Birmingham at a glance
Same national Renters' Rights Act framework as the rest of England.
Birmingham HMO licensing: national mandatory + additional (defined areas) + Article 4 in Selly Oak and parts of Edgbaston.
Ground 4A prior notice as a clause (not a separate document) is the most common local defect.
Additional licensing designations subject to change. Check current scheme designations on the official government source.
What's the same as the rest of England
Read Renters' Rights Act 2026: tenant's guide to your new rights for the regime and Renters' Rights Act 2026: the international student's working guide for the student-specific framing. The notice rules, deposit cap, two-month tenant notice, Section 8 grounds, and Ground 4A all apply in Birmingham exactly as elsewhere in England.
Birmingham HMO licensing
Three layers apply:
National mandatory HMO licence — required for HMOs with 5+ tenants from two or more households.
Birmingham additional HMO licensing — covers smaller HMOs (3+ tenants) in defined areas. Check current scheme designations on the official government source.
Article 4 directions — restrict conversion of family houses to small HMOs in named wards. Selly Oak and parts of Edgbaston are typical Article 4 areas.
Before paying a holding deposit, check the property address against the council's HMO licensing register. An unlicensed HMO is the strongest single defence available to a tenant in dispute.
Selly Oak / Edgbaston specifics
The dominant pattern: a 4-bed terraced house, joint tenancy for 12 months from September, all four tenants on the same contract, agent-managed. Watch for:
"All-students" Ground 4A prior notice included in the agreement as a clause rather than a separate signed notice. As Ground 4A: student possession explained explains, that is a defect.
Article 4 status. If the landlord converted a C3 house to C4 use without planning consent, the property is operating in breach — that gives you leverage.
Cash-collected rent in some pockets of Selly Oak. Pay by bank transfer to a named payee; cash with no receipt is a documentation crisis waiting to happen.
September 1 vs July 1 starts — many Selly Oak lets start in July to lock students into summer rent. The rent for July/August is part of your bargaining position before signing.
Common landlord patterns and how they fail
"You'll lose the deposit if you don't sign a new contract." No — your tenancy continues without a new fixed term and your deposit follows the property. See Periodic tenancies after May 2026: how the new rolling regime works .
"Cleaning is £500." Only deductible if your contract required it and you didn't do it. See Deposit dispute letter (2026): the template and the steps .
"The owner wants the property back." Not a Section 8 ground on its own. Ask in writing which Section 8 ground.
Documents and evidence to keep
Almost every winnable student-tenancy dispute in Birmingham turns on a document you either kept or wish you had. Build the file from the day you start viewing properties and store it somewhere you control — a personal cloud folder, not just the agent's portal, which you can lose access to the moment the tenancy ends.
The signed tenancy agreement — every page, including any inventory, schedule, or house-rules annex. If all you have is an unsigned draft, ask in writing for the executed copy countersigned by the landlord.
The deposit protection certificate and prescribed information. In England the deposit must be protected in the Deposit Protection Service, MyDeposits, or the Tenancy Deposit Scheme within thirty days of receipt, and the prescribed information served on you. That certificate is the single most valuable document you hold, because its absence or lateness is what powers a deposit-penalty claim.
Dated move-in photographs and the inventory. Photograph every room, including existing marks and damage, on the day you collect the keys, and email the photos to yourself so the timestamp does not depend on your phone.
The HMO or selective-licence reference for the exact property address, captured from the council register on the day you check it.
A complete rent ledger — every payment made by bank transfer to a named payee, with the payment reference you used. Avoid cash entirely; where cash is unavoidable, demand a dated receipt for every single payment.
Every repair request and the landlord's reply , in writing. A dated email or message thread is worth far more in a dispute than a phone call nobody can prove happened.
Any notice the landlord serves — kept together with the envelope, the date, and the method of service, because the validity of a possession notice frequently turns on precisely how and when it reached you.

Bristol at a glance
Same national Renters' Rights Act framework as the rest of England.
Bristol HMO licensing: national mandatory + additional + selective in certain wards.
Additional and selective designations are subject to change. Check current additional and selective designations for Bristol's student-heavy wards on the official government source.
Sub-let chains and agent-as-head-tenant arrangements are more common in Stokes Croft/Montpelier than people realise.
What's the same as the rest of England
The national framework — Section 21 abolished, all tenancies periodic, two-month tenant notice, five-week deposit cap, Section 8 only, Ground 4A on its existing terms — applies in Bristol exactly as elsewhere. Read Renters' Rights Act 2026: tenant's guide to your new rights for the regime and Renters' Rights Act 2026: the international student's working guide for the student-specific framing.
Bristol HMO licensing
Bristol City Council operates:
National mandatory HMO licensing for 5+ tenant HMOs from two or more households.
Additional HMO licensing for smaller HMOs in defined wards. Check current additional and selective designations for Bristol's student-heavy wards on the official government source.
Selective licensing in certain ward designations covering all private rented properties.
Run the property address against the council's licensing register before signing. If the property should be licensed and isn't, you have leverage from day one.
Practical steps for Bristol student tenants
If you are renting in Bristol as a student, start with three checks before you pay anything. First, run the property address through the Bristol City Council HMO licensing register to confirm the property is properly licensed for the number of tenants who will live there. An unlicensed HMO that should be licensed gives you significant leverage — a Rent Repayment Order of up to 12 months' rent is available, and the landlord cannot use Ground 4A to seek possession in many cases. Second, check the property against the Article-4 direction map on the council's planning portal to confirm whether a C3 family home has been converted to a C4 student HMO without the required planning permission. Unauthorised conversions can affect your tenancy's validity and your eligibility for council tax exemption. Third, ask for the legal owner's name and a service address in England under Section 48 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 — an agent who cannot or will not name the landlord is a red flag that points to sub-let chains or unregistered landlords.
If you are already renting and encounter a problem — an unregistered deposit, a landlord who refuses to make repairs, or a Ground 4A notice that seems defective — the University of Bristol Students' Union housing advice service and Bristol City Council's tenant support team are free starting points. Many issues can be resolved with a well-drafted written request before they escalate to formal proceedings. For deposit disputes, the tenancy deposit scheme's free Alternative Dispute Resolution service is faster and cheaper than court and is binding on the landlord if you accept the outcome.
Redland / Clifton / Stokes Croft specifics
Redland and Cotham — classic 4–6-bed student HMOs in tall terraces. Watch for Article-4-style planning issues where C3 family houses have been quietly turned into C4 student HMOs without consent.
Clifton — higher-rent student lets in larger Georgian houses. Five-week deposit cap calculations matter more here because of the larger sums.
Stokes Croft / Montpelier — more mixed-use; sub-let chains and agent-as-head-tenant arrangements are more common. Ask who the legal landlord is, in writing, before paying anything.
Bedminster — newer wave of student rentals; council tax exemption forms have caused some friction with the south-of-river billing flow. Submit early.
Deposit protection: what Bristol students should know
If you paid a deposit to a letting agent in Bristol, the 30-day protection clock starts ticking from the date the agent receives the deposit, not the date you transferred the money. Some agents in Bristol use overseas bank transfers to delay the start of the protection period, claiming they have not received the funds until the transfer clears their offshore account. If your deposit was paid by international bank transfer, ask the agent for a dated receipt confirming the date of receipt and cross-check it against the deposit protection certificate from TDS, DPS, or MyDeposits. If the certificate was issued more than 30 days after the receipt date, the deposit was not protected on time and you may have a claim under section 214 of the Housing Act 2004 for one to three times the deposit amount in compensation.

Cardiff: Welsh regime at a glance

One-sentence answer
Cardiff is not on the English Renters' Rights Act framework — Wales has its own statute, the Renting Homes (Wales) Act 2016, with its own vocabulary (you are a "contract-holder" on an "occupation contract"), its own notice rules, and its own landlord-licensing regime through Rent Smart Wales, and reading the English pillar will mislead you on every one of these points.
Why Cardiff is not on the English regime
The Renters' Rights Act 2024 reforms in England do not apply in Wales. Housing is a devolved matter. An unlicensed agent operating in Wales commits a Rent Smart Wales offence. (Source: Rent Smart Wales .)

Prior notice appears only as a clause in the agreement (insufficient on its own).
At-grant student status is assumed because everyone "looked like" a student — if any one tenant had withdrawn or finished at grant, the ground fails.

body:

Student Tenant Rights in London (2026): Borough Caveats

§ Key takeaways
01 London follows the national framework but has three London-specific layers: borough HMO licensing, the Mayor's Rogue Landlord Checker, and per-borough council tax portals. 
02 Four HMO licensing layers operate: national mandatory, additional, selective, and Article 4. 
03 Higher London rents mean larger deposits and therefore larger s.214 compensation exposure. 
04 Sub-let chains and agent-as-head-tenant arrangements are more common in London than elsewhere. 
05 Use the Mayor's Rogue Landlord and Agent Checker before paying a holding deposit, and screenshot results as evidence. 
06 "Six months' rent up-front" instead of a guarantor is legal, but the five-week deposit cap still applies separately. 
07 "Premium for keys" or "finder's fee" beyond rent and capped deposit is banned under the Tenant Fees Act 2019. 
Last updated 2026-05-18 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
London at a glance
Same national Renters' Rights Act framework as the rest of England.
Three London-specific layers: borough HMO licensing, Mayor's Rogue Landlord Checker, and per-borough council tax portals.
Four HMO licensing layers: national mandatory, additional, selective, and Article 4.
Higher rents → larger deposits → larger s.214 exposure.
Sub-let chains and agent-as-head-tenant arrangements are more common in London than elsewhere.
What's the same as the rest of England
Section 21 abolished, all tenancies periodic, Section 8 only, two months' tenant notice, five-week deposit cap, 30-day deposit registration, Ground 4A unchanged in substance. Read the pillar at Renters' Rights Act 2026: tenant's guide to your new rights and the international student guide at Renters' Rights Act 2026: the international student's working guide for the national rules.
The London-specific layer
Borough HMO licensing. Each of the 33 London local authorities runs its own scheme on top of the national mandatory HMO licence. A landlord can be national-compliant but borough-non-compliant.
Rogue Landlord and Agent Checker. The Mayor of London publishes a checker against which you can run any London landlord or agent before signing.
Higher rents → larger deposits → larger s.214 exposure. The five-week cap on a £36,000-a-year tenancy is a £3,461 deposit; the s.214 multiplier is "one to three times" that. London is where deposit-protection cases bite hardest.
Borough HMO licensing — the four schemes
National mandatory HMO licence. Required for HMOs with 5+ tenants from two or more households. Applies everywhere.
Additional HMO licensing. A borough can require licensing for smaller HMOs (3+ tenants from two or more households). Many inner London boroughs do.
Selective licensing. Some boroughs license all private rented properties in defined wards. Common in areas with historic enforcement issues.
Article 4 directions. Planning, not licensing — restricts converting family houses to HMOs without planning permission. Landlords without permission have been operating illegally and are vulnerable in any dispute.
Before signing, check the borough's licensing register for the specific property address . An unlicensed HMO is one of the strongest defences if the landlord ever tries possession or withholding.
Using the Rogue Landlord and Agent Checker
The Mayor of London maintains a public checker (see sources). Use it twice:
Before paying the holding deposit: search the landlord's name, the agent's name, and the property address.
If a dispute escalates: screenshot the result on the date you check it; it's evidence of due diligence.
Other UK city guides
If you are considering or comparing Manchester, see Student tenant rights in Manchester (2026) for Fallowfield HMO licensing, Curry Mile fire safety, and build-to-rent distinctions.
Common London-specific risks
"Six months' rent up-front" instead of a guarantor. Legal, but it does not extend the five-week deposit cap; the security deposit is still capped on top.
Sub-let chains in HMO conversions. You sign with "agent" who is actually a head-tenant; the legal landlord is two or three layers up. Ask in writing for the identity of the legal owner before paying anything.
"Premium for keys" or "finder's fee" beyond the rent and capped deposit — banned under the Tenant Fees Act 2019; report to the borough trading-standards team.
Renters' Rights Act 2026: what changed for London students
From 1 May 2026, the national abolition of Section 21 and fixed-term tenancies applies in London exactly as it does in the rest of England. For London students, three practical effects stand out.
Higher deposit values mean larger s.214 claims. A typical London student deposit of £2,500 to £3,500, multiplied by one to three times under s.214, creates a compensation claim of £7,500 to £10,500. Landlords in London are more likely to settle pre-ADR because the financial exposure is significant.
Build-to-rent towers often use "lease" language that is now misleading. Many city-centre developments market 12-month or 51-week "leases" to students. If the document is an AST, those fixed terms are unenforceable from 1 May 2026. Read the cover page: if it says "Assured Shorthold Tenancy," the Renters' Rights Act overrides the fixed-term clause regardless of what the marketing material says.
Sub-letting chains are harder to trace. London's high rents create complex sub-letting arrangements where the person you pay is not the legal landlord. The Act does not change the rule in s.48 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985: you are entitled to the landlord's name and a service address in England. Ask in writing before paying any holding deposit.
Council-tax exemption: by-borough notes
Per Council tax for international students: exempt

01 Manchester follows the national framework, with M14 HMO licensing covering national mandatory plus additional licensing in parts of Fallowfield, Withington, and Rusholme. 
02 City-centre build-to-rent "student" developments may be true PBSA (not on the new framework) or ASTs that are on the new framework — check the contract type. 
03 True PBSA rights come from the accommodation agreement and consumer-protection codes, not the Renters' Rights Act. 
04 Article 4 considerations apply in parts of Fallowfield and Withington for C3-to-C4 conversions without consent. 
05 Curry Mile (Rusholme) mixed-use properties have specific fire-safety and HMO considerations the council enforces actively. 
06 Fallowfield letting cycles no longer lock students in for a full academic year because all ASTs became periodic from 1 May 2026. 
Last updated 2026-05-18 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
Manchester at a glance
Same national Renters' Rights Act framework as the rest of England.
M14 HMO licensing: national mandatory plus additional licensing in parts of Fallowfield, Withington, and Rusholme. Check the Manchester City Council current licensing map for the specific property address, as designation boundaries can change.
City-centre build-to-rent tower blocks may be true PBSA (not on new framework) or ASTs that are (on new framework) — check the contract type.
What's the same as the rest of England
National framework as set out in Renters' Rights Act 2026: tenant's guide to your new rights and Renters' Rights Act 2026: the international student's working guide . Section 21 abolished, periodic-only, Section 8 only, two-month tenant notice, five-week deposit cap, Ground 4A on its own terms.
Manchester HMO licensing — what applies to M14
Manchester City Council operates national mandatory HMO licensing plus additional licensing in defined wards including parts of Fallowfield, Withington, and Rusholme. Check the council's current licensing map for the specific property address, as designation boundaries can change.
Before paying a holding deposit:
Confirm the property is on the council's HMO licensing register.
Confirm the licence has not expired.
Confirm the licence holder name matches the landlord on the contract.
Fallowfield / Withington / Rusholme specifics
Standard pattern. 4–6-bed terraces, joint tenancy, all-students household, deposit (in theory) with DPS or TDS. Most disputes are about Ground 4A, deposit deductions, or who has to fix what.
Article 4 considerations apply in parts of Fallowfield and Withington — landlords converting C3 to small HMOs without consent.
Curry Mile (Rusholme) mixed-use properties — student lets above shops have specific fire-safety and HMO considerations the council enforces actively.
City-centre new-build: "PBSA-style" leases vs ASTs
A growing share of Manchester student housing is in city-centre tower-block "PBSA-style" developments. Watch the distinction:
True PBSA (purpose-built student accommodation under a non-assured licence) — not on the Renters' Rights Act framework; your rights come from the accommodation agreement and consumer-protection codes.
Build-to-rent let to students under an AST — this is on the new framework. Periodic, two-month tenant notice, no fixed term.
If you've signed a "lease" with a build-to-rent operator and it talks about a 12-month fixed term — read Periodic tenancies after May 2026: how the new rolling regime works because the regime now overrides those terms.
Renters' Rights Act 2026: Manchester-specific impact
From 1 May 2026, every AST in Manchester became periodic. For Manchester students, two local effects matter most.
Fallowfield letting cycles no longer lock you in for a full academic year. The traditional pattern of signing in November for the following September, locked into a 12-month joint tenancy, is now legally unenforceable as a fixed term. You can give two months' written notice and leave earlier — but in a joint tenancy, all joint tenants must give notice together unless the agreement says otherwise.
Build-to-rent near Oxford Road and the city centre. Developments marketed as "student studios" or "luxury student living" sit on different legal frameworks depending on which agreement they use. ASTs are on the new framework; non-assured licences (true PBSA) are not. The first line of the contract usually tells you which one you have — see the pillar at Renters' Rights Act 2026: tenant's guide to your new rights for how that distinction plays out across the rest of the Act.
Other UK city guides
If you are considering or comparing London, see Student tenant rights in London (2026) for borough HMO licensing, the Rogue Landlord Checker, and higher-deposit s.214 exposure.
Documents and evidence to keep
Almost every winnable student-tenancy dispute in Manchester turns on a document you either kept or wish you had. Build the file from the day you start viewing properties and store it somewhere you control — a personal cloud folder, not just the agent's portal, which you can lose access to the moment the tenancy ends.
The signed tenancy agreement — every page, including any inventory, schedule, or house-rules annex. Read the cover line to confirm whether it is an assured shorthold tenancy or a non-assured PBSA licence, because that decides which rights you have.
The deposit protection certificate and prescribed information. In England the deposit must be protected in the Deposit Protection Service, MyDeposits, or the Tenancy Deposit Scheme within thirty days of receipt, and the prescribed information served on you. That certificate is the single most valuable document you hold, because its absence or lateness is what powers a deposit-penalty claim.

Nottingham at a glance
Same national Renters' Rights Act framework as the rest of England.
NG7 HMO licensing: national mandatory + additional in much of NG7. Check current additional licensing designations and dates on the official government source.
Beeston sits under Broxtowe Borough Council (not Nottingham City) — confirm which register applies.
January–March renewal-pressure cycle: a commercial calendar, not a legal deadline.
What's the same as the rest of England
National framework as set out in Renters' Rights Act 2026: tenant's guide to your new rights and Renters' Rights Act 2026: the international student's working guide . Section 21 abolished, periodic-only, two-month tenant notice, five-week deposit cap, Section 8 only, Ground 4A on its own terms.
Nottingham HMO licensing — what applies to NG7
Nottingham City Council operates national mandatory HMO licensing plus additional HMO licensing in much of NG7. Check current additional licensing designations and dates on the official government source.
Before paying a holding deposit:
Confirm the property is on the council's HMO licensing register at the correct address.
Confirm the licence holder name matches the contract landlord.
Practical steps for Nottingham student tenants
Start with three checks before you commit to a Nottingham tenancy. First, confirm which licensing authority covers the property — Nottingham City Council for properties in Lenton, Dunkirk, Radford, and the city centre; Broxtowe Borough Council for properties in Beeston. The incorrect register may show a property as unlicensed when it is actually licensed under the other authority, or vice versa. Second, ask the landlord or agent for the property's HMO licence number and check it against the correct council's online register. If the property requires an HMO licence and does not have one, you may be entitled to a Rent Repayment Order and the landlord cannot use Ground 4A to seek possession in most circumstances. Third, ask for the legal owner's name and a service address in England under Section 48 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 — if the agent cannot or will not name the landlord, that is a significant red flag.
Nottingham's lettings cycle runs on a commercial calendar that does not match the legal position. January through March is the peak period for agents to pressure tenants into signing renewal agreements for the following academic year, using language like "renew now or lose the house." Under the post-May 2026 periodic tenancy framework, no fixed-term renewal is required — your tenancy continues on a rolling basis without any new document. The "renewal pressure cycle" is a commercial tactic, not a legal process. If you have paid a holding deposit or signed a draft agreement under pressure during this period, you have the right to withdraw from the agreement before the tenancy starts, subject to any holding deposit deduction rules that apply under the Tenant Fees Act 2019. The university's housing advice service can review any documents you were pressured into signing and advise on your options.
Lenton / Dunkirk / Beeston specifics
Lenton and Dunkirk. Classic 3–6-bed student HMOs. Most of the local letting market is on an October-to-October cycle, with signing pressure from January for the September following.
Radford / Forest Fields. Edges of the student belt; more mixed tenures.
Beeston. Sits under Broxtowe Borough Council rather than Nottingham City. Confirm which authority's licensing register applies before relying on the Nottingham City list.
Deposit protection in Nottingham: what to check
Nottingham letting agents frequently handle deposits paid by international bank transfer, which can delay the start of the 30-day protection window. Under the Housing Act 2004, the deposit must be lodged with one of the three approved schemes (TDS, DPS, or MyDeposits) within 30 days of the date the landlord or agent receives the funds, not the date you initiate the transfer. If your deposit was paid from an overseas account, ask the agent for a dated receipt confirming when the funds cleared in their UK account. If the deposit protection certificate shows a registration date more than 30 days after the receipt date, the deposit was not protected on time and you may have a claim for compensation of one to three times the deposit under section 214.
The five-week deposit cap under the Tenant Fees Act 2019 applies to the total rent for the property, not per tenant. If your Nottingham student house has four tenants paying £100 per week each, the maximum deposit is five weeks of the total £400 weekly rent (£2,000). Some agents in Nottingham request deposits on a per-room basis that add up to more than five weeks of the total rent when combined — check the figures carefully before paying. If the total exceeds the cap, the excess is unlawful and the letting agent can be fined by the local authority trading standards team. The University of Nottingham Students' Union housing advice service can review any deposit

UK Student Visa Refused: Admin Review, Reapply & PAP Guide

In 60 seconds
01 Admin review deadline: 14 days from refusal receipt (in-country) or 28 days (out-of-country). The clock starts on the date the refusal notice was issued, not the date you opened it. 
02 Admin review examines caseworking errors only — no new evidence allowed. If the decision was correct based on the evidence submitted, admin review will not overturn it. 
03 A fresh application allows corrected evidence (new bank statements, new CAS, new English test). It resets the clock but requires a new application fee and Immigration Health Surcharge. 
04 A Pre-Action Protocol (PAP) letter is a pre-litigation step alleging unlawful decision-making — procedural unfairness, failure to follow published guidance, or irrationality. 
05 Common Student Route refusal grounds: maintenance shortfall (including the 28-day rule), credibility interview failure, CAS withdrawn or expired, English test not on SELT list, academic progression not demonstrated. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for international students whose Student Route (formerly Tier 4) visa application has been refused by UKVI. It covers the three options available after refusal: admin review, fresh application, and PAP letter. It explains the deadlines, what each process can and cannot achieve, and how to read a refusal notice to identify the correct next step.
This guide is not for refusals of Skilled Worker, Graduate Route, family visas, or visit visas — each has its own refusal and review framework. It is also not a substitute for immigration legal advice when the refusal involves complex grounds such as deception allegations, general grounds for refusal under Part 9, or a previous adverse immigration history. If your refusal notice cites paragraph 9.4.1 (false representations) or 9.7.1 (previous breach of immigration laws), consult a regulated immigration adviser before responding — the consequences of an adverse finding on these grounds extend beyond the current application.
Read the refusal notice first: what the paragraph numbers mean
The UKVI refusal notice is structured around Immigration Rules paragraphs. The key paragraphs for Student Route refusals are:
ST 1.1-ST 1.5 (valid application): The application was not validly made — fee not paid, biometrics not enrolled, form incomplete, or passport not provided. Usually a correctable error in a fresh application rather than an admin review issue.
ST 3.1-ST 3.3 (entry clearance requirements): Eligibility under the Student Route was not demonstrated. This is the most common refusal paragraph and covers the substantive requirements.
ST 12.3-ST 12.4 (financial requirement): Maintenance funds were not demonstrated at the required level, for the required period, or in the required format. Often involves the 28-day rule — the funds must have been held for 28 consecutive days ending no more than 31 days before the application date. A one-day breach results in refusal.
ST 17.1-ST 17.3 (English language): The English language requirement was not met. Common triggers: test not on the SELT list, test expired, score below B2, or test provider not approved for the applicant's country of test location.
ST 22.1-ST 22.6 (credibility interview): The credibility interview raised concerns about genuine student intent, and UKVI was not satisfied. The refusal notice will quote specific answers from the interview record.
ST 27.1-ST 27.3 (academic progression): For applicants who have previously studied in the UK, the new course does not demonstrate academic progression from previous study.
Part 9 (general grounds for refusal): Covers suitability issues — criminality, deception, previous breaches, NHS debt over £500. Refusals under Part 9 are among the most serious and require specialist advice.
Option 1: Admin review — when the decision was wrong on the evidence you sent
Admin review is the correct route when the refusal contains a demonstrable caseworking error. Examples: UKVI states the CAS was not submitted, but the CAS reference number was on the application form and the CAS status was "Assigned" on the date of decision. UKVI states maintenance funds were £500 short, but the bank statement shows a closing balance above the required amount for every day of the 28-day period. UKVI states the English test was not on the SELT list, but the SELT unique reference number resolves to an approved test and provider on the Home Office's online verification tool.
Admin review cannot correct an error in your own evidence. If the bank statement genuinely showed only 27 days of fund maintenance instead of 28, an admin review will not succeed — UKVI correctly applied the rule to the evidence you submitted. In that case, a fresh application with a new bank statement covering the full 28 days is the correct path.
File the admin review online. The application must state which caseworking error was made, referencing the specific paragraph of the refusal notice and the specific document in your application that the caseworker overlooked or misinterpreted. A generic "the decision was wrong" submission will not succeed. Be precise: "The refusal notice at paragraph 3 states that maintenance funds for the period 1-28 June were not demonstrated. The bank statement at page 14 of my application shows a closing balance of £12,006 on each day from 1-28 June, satisfying the £12,006 requirement for inner London study as stated in Appendix ST 12.3."
Option 2: Fresh application — when your evidence needs correction
A fresh application is the appropriate route when your evidence genuinely fell short and can be corrected. You must pay the application fee and Immigration Health Surcharge again. The new application is assessed on its own merits — the prior refusal is not, by itself, a ground for refusing the new ap

body:

UK Renters' Rights Act 2025: Student Guide 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home

§ Key takeaways
01 The Renters' Rights Act 2025 (in force 1 May 2026) is the largest reform to private renting in England since the Housing Act 1988. 
02 Every assured shorthold tenancy in England converted to a periodic tenancy by operation of law on 1 May 2026. 
03 Section 21 "no-fault" eviction is abolished; possession is only available on defined statutory grounds. 
04 Four operative changes: fixed terms abolished, Section 21 abolished, new possession grounds, Section 13 rent regime. 
05 Deposit protection, right-to-rent immigration checks, and HMO licensing rules did not change. 
06 Most pre-2026 contracts still contain unenforceable clauses; acting on a clause that no longer exists weakens your position later. 
Last updated 2026-05-18 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: the Renters' Rights Act 2025 (in force 1 May 2026), with implementation guidance from the Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities.
Core rule: every assured shorthold tenancy in England is now a periodic tenancy. Section 21 "no-fault" eviction is abolished. Possession is only available on a defined statutory ground.
Documents: tenancy agreement, deposit protection certificate, every notice received since 1 May 2026, immigration status documents.
Timing: the change applies to existing tenancies. No re-signing was needed.
Main risk: most pre-2026 contracts still contain unenforceable clauses. Acting on a clause that no longer exists in law weakens your position later.
The rule in plain English
The Renters' Rights Act 2025 abolished Section 21 evictions and ended fixed-term assured shorthold tenancies in England. The controlling source is the Renters' Rights Act 2025 , with implementation guidance issued by the Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities (DLUHC) in April 2026.
From 1 May 2026 every assured shorthold tenancy in England operates as a monthly periodic tenancy. Your landlord cannot end the tenancy without naming a specific statutory ground. Most grounds require two months' written notice and most allow you to defend yourself in the county court before a possession order is granted.
The Act applies to England only. Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have their own legislation that already provided most of these protections in different forms.
Who this guide is for
Likely fit
You rent in England under an assured shorthold tenancy or its post-2026 successor; you are a student, a working tenant, or a family renting privately; your tenancy is with a private landlord or letting agent.
Needs review
You rent under a 'company let', a lodger arrangement where the landlord lives on the premises, or a tenancy created before 15 January 1989. The Act may not apply in full and your contract should be reviewed.
Usually not a fit
You rent in Scotland, Wales, or Northern Ireland; you live in halls of residence or other purpose-built student accommodation; you have already received a Section 8 notice with a hearing date inside the next 14 days.
What the Act actually changed
The Act made four operative changes. Every other change in the legislation flows from these four.
1. Fixed-term tenancies are abolished. Pre-2026 contracts almost always state a fixed term — typically 12 months. That clause is no longer enforceable as a fixed term. By operation of law your tenancy is now monthly periodic. Read Periodic tenancies after May 2026: how the new rolling regime works for the day-to-day consequences: notice periods, rent payment frequency, and how to leave on your terms.
2. Section 21 is abolished. A landlord can no longer end a tenancy without giving a statutory reason. Any Section 21 notice served on or after 1 May 2026 is invalid on its face. Read Section 21 abolished: a tenant's action page for the steps to take if you have received one.
3. New possession grounds replace Section 21. Landlords retain repossession rights in defined circumstances — own-use, sale, persistent rent arrears, antisocial behaviour, and, for student-let HMOs only, ending the tenancy at the end of an academic year under the new Ground 4A. Each ground has specific evidence and notice requirements. Read Ground 4A possession notices: how landlords can still evict students under the Renters' Rights Act before assuming any end-of-year notice is valid.
4. Rent increases are governed by Section 13. Rent can only be raised once every 12 months, only by a market-rate amount, and only via a written Section 13 notice. You have one month to challenge the increase at the First-tier Tribunal (Property Chamber). Read Rent increases under the Renters' Rights Act for the challenge process.

This pillar links to every cluster article in the UK tenancy series, in reading order. Start with the article closest to your situation and follow the inbound links from there.

Ground 4A possession notices: how landlords can still evict students under the Renters' Rights Act — when student-HMO landlords can still evict.

UK Renters' Rights Act 2025 FAQ
Clear answers for tenants and students renting in England. This FAQ covers the Renters' Rights Act 2025, Section 21 abolition, deposit disputes, rent increases, and how to leave a tenancy safely. For deeper guidance, see our cluster articles below.
The Renters' Rights Act 2025, which took full effect on 1 May 2026, represents the most significant reform of English private rented sector law in a generation. It abolished the Section 21 no-fault eviction procedure, converted all existing assured shorthold tenancies to periodic tenancies, introduced new mandatory and discretionary possession grounds under Section 8, and strengthened rent increase protections by requiring landlords to use a prescribed Section 13 form with a one-month tribunal challenge window. The Act also introduced the Decent Homes Standard for the private rented sector, established a new Private Rented Sector Database, and created a new Ombudsman scheme for tenant complaints. These changes apply to all assured shorthold tenancies in England, regardless of when they were signed, and they affect every tenant currently renting from a private landlord in the English jurisdiction.
For international students renting in England, understanding the post-May 2026 framework is particularly important because the abolition of Section 21 and the transition to periodic-only tenancies removes the previous flexibility that some landlords relied on to manage academic-year turnover outside the Ground 4A student-HMO framework. You now have stronger procedural protections against eviction, but you also need to be more careful about how you give notice when you want to leave, how you respond to possession notices, and how you challenge unlawful rent increases or deposit deductions. The answers below address the most common questions we receive from tenants navigating these new rules, with cross-references to the detailed cluster articles where each topic is covered in full.
If you have received a possession notice from your landlord, start by identifying whether it is a valid Section 8 notice. A valid notice must use Form 3 (not the old Form 6A which was used for Section 21), name a specific ground from Schedule 2 of the Housing Act 1988 as amended, state the date after which possession proceedings can begin (which varies by ground), and include the prescribed information about where the tenant can get advice. If the notice does not meet these requirements, it is likely invalid and the landlord must serve a corrected notice before they can proceed to court. If you are unsure whether your notice is valid, the linked articles on Ground 4A, periodic tenancies, and Section 8 grounds provide the specific statutory references and practical steps for checking each element of the notice.
The answers below draw on the Housing Act 1988 (as amended by the Renters' Rights Act 2025), the Tenant Fees Act 2019, the Deregulation Act 2015, and the Protection from Eviction Act 1977, and reflect the law as it stands in July 2026. Where specific financial thresholds, notice periods, or prescribed form editions are referenced, you should verify the current figure against the official government source on the date you read this, as these can be updated by statutory instrument. The linked cluster articles provide step-by-step guidance, document templates, and the statutory references for each topic area.
This FAQ is for tenants and students renting in England who need to understand their rights under the Renters' Rights Act 2025, respond to a possession notice, challenge a deposit deduction, or navigate the transition from a fixed-term assured shorthold tenancy to a periodic tenancy. Each answer draws on the Housing Act 1988 (as amended by the Renters' Rights Act), the Deregulation Act 2015, and current guidance from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government as of mid-2026.
The 1 May 2026 commencement of the Renters' Rights Act abolished Section 21 no-fault evictions, converted all existing assured shorthold tenancies to periodic tenancies, and introduced new mandatory and discretionary possession grounds. These changes affect every AST in England, regardless of when the tenancy was signed. Landlords now must use Section 8 and name a specific statutory ground to seek possession, and tenants cannot be locked into a fixed term beyond the first 12 months under the revised rules. 01 Visa type: Standard Visitor visa (Appendix V of the Immigration Rules). There is no separate family or parent visitor category. Apply online through GOV.UK, attend a biometrics appointment at a visa application centre in the visitor's home country. 
02 Key requirement: The visitor must satisfy UKVI they are a genuine visitor who will leave the UK at the end of their visit, can support themselves without working, and will not live in the UK for extended periods through frequent visits. 
03 What the student provides: Invitation letter stating relationship, visit purpose and dates, plus supporting documents — passport copy, BRP/eVisa, university enrolment confirmation, and accommodation evidence if hosting. 
04 What the visitor provides: Passport, bank statements showing funds for the trip, evidence of ties to home country (employment letter, property deed, family responsibilities), travel itinerary, and any previous UK immigration history. 
05 Processing time: Typically 3 weeks from biometrics for standard service, but varies by country. Priority and super-priority services are available in some locations at additional cost. 
The Standard Visitor route: what it covers
The Standard Visitor visa (Appendix V of the Immigration Rules) is a single route covering tourism, visiting family and friends, attending events, short study, and certain business activities. For family members of international students, the most common purposes are: attending a graduation ceremony, visiting during a holiday period, and helping the student settle in at the start of a course. There is no separate category for parents or family — the same application form and evidence requirements apply regardless of the visit purpose.
The Standard Visitor visa does not permit work (paid or unpaid), access to public funds, marriage or civil partnership registration, or long-term study. A visitor who stays beyond the permitted period becomes an overstayer with consequences for future UK immigration applications. The maximum stay on a Standard Visitor visa is 6 months per visit. Long-term visitor visas (2, 5, or 10 years) allow multiple entries but each individual stay remains limited to 6 months.
Who this guide is for
International students on a UK Student Route visa who want their parents or other family members to visit. Family members preparing a Standard Visitor visa application and needing to understand the evidence requirements. Students who want to time a visit around a specific event (graduation, holiday period, university open day).
If your visitor has a previous UK visa refusal, an adverse immigration history in any country, or complex personal circumstances (unemployment, no fixed address, family members already overstaying in the UK), the application requires more detailed preparation. Visitor visas from certain nationalities face higher scrutiny — if your visitor's home country has a high refusal rate for UK visitor visas, the evidence package must be particularly strong.
The invitation letter: what it must include
The invitation letter from you (the student host) is the centrepiece of the visitor's application. It should be a signed letter on plain paper (university letterhead is not required but adds credibility) and must include: your full name and date of birth, your relationship to the visitor, your UK address, your course and university details including expected completion date, the purpose of the visit (be specific — "to attend my graduation ceremony on 15 July 2026" is stronger than "to visit me"), the planned dates of the visit, whether you are providing accommodation, and whether you are contributing to the visitor's costs.
A weak invitation letter says "I invite my mother to visit me in the UK." A strong invitation letter says "I invite my mother, [full name], to attend my Master of Public Health graduation ceremony at the University of Birmingham on 15 July 2026. She will stay with me at [address] from 10-20 July 2026. I will cover her accommodation; she will cover her flights and personal expenses. I have attached my university enrolment letter confirming my course and completion date." The stronger letter gives the caseworker a clear, falsifiable narrative that can be checked against the supporting documents.
Visitor's evidence: proving they will return home
The most common reason for visitor visa refusal is that the caseworker is not satisfied the visitor will leave the UK. This is a forward-looking assessment — the caseworker considers the visitor's circumstances in their home country, their immigration history, and the credibility of the visit purpose. The evidence of ties to home is the most important part of the visitor's application.
For an employed visitor: a letter from the employer on company letterhead confirming the position, salary, length of employment, that leave has been approved for the specific dates, and the expected return date. Recent payslips (3-6 months) and bank statements showing salary deposits. For a self-employed visitor: business registration documents, tax returns, business bank statements, and evidence of ongoing business commitments during the visit period. For a retired visitor: pension statements, property ownership documents, evidence of other children or dependants in the home country, and a clear explanation of the visit purpose.
A visitor with no employment, no property, no dependants at home, and a child already settled in the UK has a higher refusal risk — regardless of how much money they have in the bank. The caseworker will consider whether the visitor has more reason to stay in the UK than to return home. A UK 0300 number is a non-geographic telephone number reserved for public bodies and not-for-profit organisations.
Your organisation generally needs to provide a public service or operate on a not-for-profit basis.
Ofcom sets the eligibility rules, but you normally obtain the number through a communications provider rather than directly from Ofcom.
You should prepare evidence of your legal status, public-service function, charitable purpose, or other qualifying activity.
A US organisation cannot assume that it qualifies simply because it serves people in the United Kingdom. Your UK activity, legal structure, and provider arrangement matter.
A 0300 number is usually available to a UK public-sector body or not-for-profit organisation that meets Ofcom’s conditions. You apply through a communications provider, which checks your organisation and assigns an available number.
What 0300 number eligibility means
0300 numbers are UK non-geographic numbers. They are not tied to a particular city or area code, so callers can reach an organisation without knowing its physical location. Ofcom, the UK communications regulator, reserves the 0300 range for specific categories of organisations.
The range is associated with public services and organisations that operate without distributing profits to owners or members. Eligible users can include government departments, local authorities, emergency-related services, registered charities, and other qualifying not-for-profit bodies. The precise category depends on the organisation’s legal status and the service it provides.
Ofcom’s numbering rules are the starting point. The relevant rules appear in the National Telephone Numbering Plan and Ofcom’s guidance for 03 numbers:
National Telephone Numbering Plan: https://www.ofcom.org.uk/phones-and-broadband/phone-numbers/numbering 
Ofcom guidance on 03 numbers: https://www.ofcom.org.uk/phones-and-broadband/phone-numbers 
The term “eligibility” has two parts. First, your organisation must fall within an allowed user category. Second, your intended use must comply with the provider’s service terms and Ofcom’s numbering conditions. Meeting one part does not automatically settle the other.
A provider may ask for incorporation records, charity information, details of your public service, and the name of the responsible officer. It may also ask where the organisation operates, how callers will use the number, and whether the service will support a genuine public or not-for-profit function.
Who may qualify?
The following examples can help you identify the relevant category:
Organisation or service Potential position Evidence commonly requested UK central government department Usually within the public-sector category Department identity, official website, responsible contact Local authority or council service Usually within the public-sector category Authority records and service description Registered charity May qualify as a not-for-profit organisation Charity registration and governing documents Community interest organisation Depends on structure and provider review Companies House or regulator records US nonprofit serving UK users Not automatic US nonprofit records plus evidence of UK public-service activity Commercial company Usually not eligible for the reserved 0300 range Alternative 03 or geographic number options Individual or informal group Usually not eligible Formal organisational status would normally be required These are practical categories, not a substitute for the current Ofcom rules. A provider may apply its own customer due diligence requirements, and Ofcom can change the numbering framework.
Step 1: Identify your organisation’s legal status
Start with the entity that would hold the telephone service contract. The contracting entity should match the organisation represented in your eligibility documents.
A UK government department may identify itself through its official department page and government records. A local authority can usually provide its council details and the public service connected to the requested number. A charity should check that its registration information is current and matches the proposed account holder.
US organisations need closer review. A US 501(c)(3) determination letter can show federal tax-exempt status, but it may not by itself establish that the organisation qualifies for a UK 0300 number. Your provider may ask for evidence of UK operations, a UK service address, a UK subsidiary, a UK charity registration, or a defined public-service function for UK callers.
Gather the following information before you contact a provider:
The organisation’s full legal name.
Its registration number and registering authority.
The principal business or service address.
The organisation’s website and public contact page.
The name and role of the authorised representative.
The organisation’s legal or not-for-profit status.
A short description of the service that callers will access.
The countries and communities served.
The expected call volume and operating hours.

International student tax filing: 1040-NR 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks

In 60 seconds
01 Primary authority: IRS 1040-NR instructions and IRS Publication 519 
02 Core rule: F, J, M, Q holders file as nonresident aliens until the substantial presence test makes them residents, typically after 5 calendar years. 
03 Documents: W-2, 1042-S, 1099 if any, passport, visa history, I-20/DS-2019, SSN/ITIN, treaty details, Form 8843, state tax materials. 
04 Timing: Federal deadline April 15 (extended to June 15 by filing Form 4868); state deadlines vary. 
05 Main risk: Using consumer software for nonresident filing, skipping Form 8843, claiming treaty benefits without evidence, ignoring state tax. 
06 Review status: Basic review for 1040-NR available now; attorney-review tiers coming soon. 
§ Key takeaways
01 Many F, J, M, and Q visa students file as nonresident aliens for federal tax until the substantial-presence counting rules make them residents for tax purposes. 
02 Teach tax residence before form selection; the wrong residency status can make the whole return wrong. 
03 Core documents include W-2, 1042-S, 1099 if any, passport, visa history, I-20 or DS-2019, SSN or ITIN, treaty article details, Form 8843, and state tax documents if required. 
04 Sequence the file in the order a reviewer will test it: eligibility first, deadline second, evidence third, and payment or submission last. 
05 Pitfalls include using resident-only software, skipping Form 8843, claiming treaty benefits without evidence, ignoring state tax, and using SSN/ITIN incorrectly. 
How international student tax filing works
International students on F, J, M, or Q visas have specific tax filing obligations. Determine whether you are a resident or nonresident alien using the substantial presence test from IRS Publication 519. Students are generally exempt for the first 5 calendar years. File Form 8843 annually regardless of income.
The substantial presence test counts the number of days you have been present in the United States over a three-year period using a weighted formula. You are considered a resident alien if you were present in the US for at least 31 days during the current calendar year and 183 days during the three-year period that includes the current year and the two preceding years. The 183-day total is calculated by adding all the days you were present in the current year, one-third of the days you were present in the first preceding year, and one-sixth of the days you were present in the second preceding year.
F-1 and J-1 students are classified as exempt individuals for the substantial presence test if they substantially comply with the requirements of their visa status. The exemption applies for a maximum of 5 calendar years. Students who have been in the United States for more than 5 calendar years must apply the substantial presence test to determine their tax residency status. If you had US-source income including wages or scholarships, file Form 1040-NR. Use nonresident-specific software like Sprintax. The IRS provides full guidance in Publication 519 and Form 1040-NR instructions.
The first tax decision
Determine your tax residency status first. If in your first 5 calendar years, you are likely a nonresident. If you exceed 5 years, use the substantial presence test calculation. Then decide whether to file 1040-NR or only Form 8843 based on whether you had reportable income.
Document checklist
Form W-2: From your employer showing wages and withholding.
Form 1042-S: For scholarship income not on W-2.
Form 1099: For interest or investment income.
Passport and visa: I-94 admission record.

AOS vs consular processing: the rule in plain English
Adjustment of status is for eligible applicants physically in the United States; consular processing is for applicants abroad or applicants who cannot adjust in the United States. The choice between Adjustment of Status (AOS) and consular processing is one of the most consequential decisions in the green card application process. The right route depends on where the applicant is physically present, whether they entered the US with inspection, their current immigration status, and whether they can tolerate the risks of international travel during the process.
AOS allows the applicant to file Form I-485 with USCIS while staying in the United States. The applicant can remain in the US during the entire process, obtain employment authorization and advance parole while the I-485 is pending, and attend the green card interview at a local USCIS field office. AOS is available only to applicants who were inspected and admitted or paroled into the US, who are in valid nonimmigrant status (or certain exceptions apply), and who have not violated their status in a way that bars adjustment. Consular processing is for applicants who are outside the US or who are in the US but ineligible for AOS (such as those who entered without inspection or have accrued unlawful presence).
Who this guide is for
Green card applicants who are deciding which processing route to take. This includes family-based applicants (petitioned by a US citizen or permanent resident spouse, parent, or child) and employment-based applicants (petitioned by a US employer through Form I-140). If you are physically present in the US and have a legal entry (I-94 record), AOS may be available. If you are outside the US or do not have a legal entry, consular processing through the National Visa Center and a US consulate abroad is likely the only option.
This guide is also for immigration attorneys and paralegals who need a practical comparison of the two routes to advise clients on the best strategy. The decision between AOS and consular processing affects processing time, cost, travel flexibility, work authorization availability, and risk profile. Each applicant's circumstances are different, and the right choice depends on factors such as visa bulletin priority date backlogs, unlawful presence history, prior immigration violations, and the consulate's interview backlog in the applicant's home country.
Documents and evidence to prepare
For adjustment of status (I-485): The I-485 packet requires Form I-485, the current filing fee as listed on the USCIS fee schedule, two passport-style photos, a copy of the I-94 arrival record printed from the CBP website, a copy of the passport bio page and all nonimmigrant visa stamps, the beneficiary's certified birth certificate with English translation, a copy of the approved or pending immigrant petition (I-130 or I-140), Form I-864 Affidavit of Support from the petitioner with supporting financial documents (three years of tax returns, W-2s, and recent pay stubs), the medical exam (Form I-693) completed by a USCIS civil surgeon, and any prior immigration records or court documents.
For consular processing: The consular processing packet is managed through the National Visa Center's CEAC online portal. Required documents include Form DS-260 (online immigrant visa application), the Affidavit of Support (Form I-864) with supporting financial documents, the applicant's passport valid for at least six months beyond the visa issuance date, certified birth certificate with English translation, marriage certificate (if applicable), divorce decrees from prior marriages (if applicable), police certificates from every country where the applicant has lived for six months or more since age 16, and the medical exam completed by a panel physician designated by the US consulate.
Visa bulletin tracking: Both routes require tracking the Department of State's monthly Visa Bulletin to determine when a visa number is available in the applicant's preference category and country of chargeability. The Visa Bulletin has two charts: Dates for Filing (when the applicant can submit the I-485 or pay the NVC fee) and Final Action Dates (when USCIS or the consulate can approve the application). Check the Visa Bulletin each month to identify which chart applies to your case.

§ Key takeaways
01 An asylum applicant physically present in the United States generally must file Form I-589 within one year of last arrival unless an exception applies. 
02 Identify whether the applicant is in immigration court before filing; the wrong filing location can cause rejection or delay. 
03 Protect the one-year deadline first, then build the facts and corroboration carefully. 
04 Core documents include Form I-589 in English, personal statement, identity documents, entry records, country-condition evidence, witness declarations, translations, family documents, and EOIR case information if in proceedings. 
05 Pitfalls include filing in the wrong place, missing the one-year deadline, unsigned forms, no explanation of harm, duplicate filings, and not tracking annual asylum fee notices. 
Understanding the asylum application process
Form I-589 is used to apply for asylum under INA 208. Asylum allows individuals physically present in the US to remain if they fear persecution based on race, religion, nationality, social group, or political opinion. The process operates through two systems: affirmative through USCIS and defensive through EOIR.
Filing in the correct system is critical. The one-year filing deadline is strict but exceptions exist for changed or extraordinary circumstances. Working with an experienced attorney is strongly recommended.
The first decision before filing
Determine if you are in removal proceedings. If you have a Notice to Appear, file with immigration court, not USCIS. Calculate your one-year deadline from your last arrival. If expired, document the exception carefully.
Evidence checklist
Form I-589: Complete in English with G-28 if represented.
Personal statement: Detailed narrative with dates, locations, and protected ground.
Identity documents: Passport, birth certificate, national ID.
Country condition evidence: State Department, UNHCR, human rights reports.
Witness declarations: Signed under penalty of perjury.
Translations: Certified with translator certificate.
Worked example: Amina's case
Amina, a journalist from Ethiopia, arrives on a B-2 visa. Two of her colleagues are detained for their reporting. She files I-589 within 2 months, including her passport, I-94, copies of her articles, and State Department country reports. Her case is pending with the asylum office.
Related guides
The DACA renewal guide explains Form I-765 after 365 days. The Temporary Protected Status renewals guide covers alternative relief.
Preparing a strong personal statement
The personal statement is the most critical part of the I-589 application. It must describe in detail the past persecution or well-founded fear of future persecution that the applicant experienced or fears. The statement should include specific incidents with dates, locations, the identity of the persecutors, and a description of what happened during each incident. The statement must also explain which of the five protected grounds the persecution is based on: race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion. Vague or general statements that do not connect the harm to a protected ground are insufficient for USCIS to grant asylum.
Country condition evidence from reliable sources is essential to support the personal statement. The USCIS asylum officer evaluates whether the applicant's fear is objectively reasonable based on conditions in the home country. Reports from the U.S. State Department, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and reputable news organizations are the most persuasive types of country condition evidence. The evidence should be as current as possible, ideally published within the last 12 months, and should specifically address the conditions that relate to the applicant's claim.
If the applicant has documents that corroborate their claim, such as detention records, medical reports, photographs, or threatening communications, these should be included with the application. Witness declarations from family members or others who can verify the applicant's account should be signed under penalty of perjury and include the witness's contact information. The applicant should provide a certified English translation of every non-English document. The translation must include a certificate signed by the translator attesting to the accuracy and completeness of the translation. USCIS will not accept uncertified translations.
Understanding the credible fear standard
The credible fear standard is the threshold used in the asylum process to determine whether an applicant has a significant possibility of establishing eligibility for asylum. For affirmative asylum filings with USCIS, the applicant must establish that they meet the refugee definition under INA 101(a)(42)(A) by showing past persecution or a well-founded fear of future persecution on account of a protected ground.
