International student banking: the rule in plain English
U.S. bank-account rules vary by institution, but students should compare identity requirements, fees, digital access, international transfer costs, ATM coverage, and FDIC insurance. The core rule is straightforward: US banks are private businesses that set their own account-opening policies, so the account that works for one international student may not work for another. Banks evaluate identity verification under the Customer Identification Program (CIP) rules, which require a name, date of birth, address, and identification number — but the identification number does not have to be a Social Security Number. A foreign passport with a visa and I-94 record satisfies CIP requirements at most major banks that serve international students.
FDIC insurance covers deposits up to $250,000 per depositor per bank, which means your money is protected even if the bank fails. This insurance applies to checking accounts, savings accounts, money market deposit accounts, and certificates of deposit (CDs). Not all financial products offered by banks are FDIC-insured — investment products, mutual funds, and cryptocurrency accounts are not covered. Always confirm that your account type is FDIC-insured before depositing funds, especially if the bank markets itself as a fintech or neobank that partners with a traditional bank for pass-through insurance.
Student-specific accounts typically waive monthly maintenance fees and require lower minimum opening deposits. These accounts are available to full-time students at accredited US institutions, regardless of citizenship or immigration status. Some banks impose an age limit (under 25 or under 30) for student account eligibility, while others accept any enrolled student. If you do not qualify for a student account, look for a basic checking account with no monthly fee that can be waived through direct deposit or minimum balance.
Who this guide is for
New international students arriving in the US for the first time who need to open a checking account, savings account, or student credit product. This guide is also for continuing students who are dissatisfied with their current bank and want to switch to an account with lower fees, better digital tools, or stronger international transfer options. If you are an exchange student staying for one semester only, focus on banks with no monthly fees and easy account closure procedures — you do not want to leave a dormant account with fees when you return home.
This guide is also for graduate students and researchers who receive stipends or fellowship payments that may be deposited through direct deposit. Some university-affiliated credit unions offer accounts specifically for graduate students with features like higher ATM withdrawal limits and overdraft protection lines. If you are a sponsored student receiving funds through a government or organisational sponsor, check whether your sponsor requires a specific bank or account type for fund disbursement.

01 Cap-gap automatically extends F-1 status and OPT work authorization through September 30 
02 You must have a timely filed H-1B cap-subject petition (change of status requested) 
03 Cap-gap ends immediately if USCIS denies, revokes, or rejects the H-1B petition 
04 No separate application — the extension is automatic once USCIS confirms receipt 
05 Employers should continue I-9 verification with the cap-gap I-20 (recommended) 
What is the cap-gap extension?
The cap-gap extension is an automatic benefit for F-1 students whose OPT or STEM OPT expires between April 1 and September 30 of the H-1B fiscal year. If your employer filed a timely cap-subject H-1B petition requesting change of status, your F-1 status and (if applicable) work authorization extend automatically through September 30.
No separate application to USCIS is required. Your DSO issues an updated I-20 noting the cap-gap extension, and your SEVIS record is updated to reflect the bridge period. The key requirement is that the H-1B petition was timely filed (received by USCIS during the filing window) and requests a change of status — consular processing does not qualify for cap-gap.
The cap-gap extension is not guaranteed. If USCIS selects your registration but the petition is never filed, or if the filing is rejected as improperly filed, cap-gap does not apply. Your DSO will confirm eligibility once they receive proof of filing from your employer.
Eligibility timeline and key dates
Understanding the timeline is critical. Here is how the cap-gap calendar works by scenario:
OPT expires May 30, H-1B filed April 1: Cap-gap starts May 31, runs through September 30. You can continue working for the petitioning employer during this period.
STEM OPT expires August 15, H-1B filed April 1: Cap-gap starts August 16, runs through September 30. STEM OPT benefits (including the 180-day automatic extension) apply until cap-gap takes over.
OPT expires March 15 (before April 1): No cap-gap available because OPT expired before the filing window. You must maintain lawful status through other means (e.g., starting a new degree program or departing).
Your DSO must issue the cap-gap I-20 within 30 days of receiving the H-1B receipt notice. If your OPT expires before the DSO issues the I-20, your work authorization pauses until the I-20 is issued — but your F-1 status remains valid as long as the petition was timely filed.
What your DSO needs from you to issue the cap-gap I-20
Your Designated School Official (DSO) cannot issue the cap-gap I-20 automatically — they need proof that your H-1B petition was actually filed. The most common mistake students make is assuming the DSO will know about the filing through SEVIS or the H-1B registration system. In reality, the DSO relies entirely on evidence that you or your employer provide.
Send your DSO the following as soon as your employer confirms the H-1B was filed: the USCIS receipt notice (Form I-797C, Notice of Action) showing the petition was received, the employer's name and contact information for verification, and a brief note confirming that the petition requests a change of status (not consular processing). If your employer filed the petition with premium processing, include that information as well — it helps the DSO understand the expected timeline.
Once the DSO verifies the filing, they update your SEVIS record and issue a new I-20 with a notation in the "Employer Information" section that reads: "Cap-Gap Extension through September 30, [year]." Keep this I-20 with your employment records and provide a copy to your employer's HR department for I-9 purposes. If you change employers during the cap-gap period (rare but possible if the new employer files a new H-1B petition), you need a new cap-gap I-20 from your DSO reflecting the new employer.
What happens after the cap-gap ends?
Once October 1 arrives and your H-1B petition has been approved, your status automatically changes from F-1 to H-1B. You do not need to leave the US or apply for a new visa stamp (unless you travel internationally and need one to re-enter). Your employer should update your I-9 with the new H-1B approval notice (Form I-797) as evidence of work authorization going forward.
If your H-1B petition is denied after the cap-gap has started, your F-1 status and work authorization end on the date of denial. You enter a 60-day grace period to depart the US, transfer to another school, or change to another non-immigrant status. During the grace period, you cannot work. If your employer plans to appeal the denial or file a motion to reopen, discuss whether they will continue your pay during the gap or place you on unpaid leave while the appeal is pending.
For students whose OPT expires early in the cap-gap period (April or May), the bridge to October 1 can feel long. Use this time to ensure your employer has completed all compliance steps: confirm they are enrolled in E-Verify if required, verify your H-1B receipt notice is correct, and keep your DSO informed of any status changes. If you change jobs during the cap-gap period (rare but possible with a new H-1B filing), your cap-gap I-20 must be updated to reflect the new employer before you can start working for them.
Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
The most common cap-gap pitfall is assuming it applies automatically without any action. In reality, you and your employer must take several steps:
Notify your DSO immediately after your employer confirms the H-1B was filed. Provide the receipt notice as proof.
Employers must update I-9s. Once the cap-gap I-20 is issued, the employer should complete Section 2 of Form I-9 using the new I-20 as a List C document. Many HR departments miss this step and flag employees as out-of-status.

How service center assignment affects your timeline
One of the biggest variables in marriage-based green card processing is which USCIS service center adjudicates your I-130 petition. While applicants can influence their timeline by filing comprehensively the first time, the center itself — its current backlog, staffing, and case complexity mix — often determines whether you wait 8 months or 18 months.
As of mid-2026, USCIS operates five service centers that handle family-based I-130 petitions: Texas (TSC), Nebraska (NSC), California (CSC), Vermont (VSC), and Potomac (PSC). The National Benefits Center (NBC) processes most I-485 adjustment of status applications, but the I-130 timeline is the primary driver of the overall wait.
Service center processing time comparison (2026)
Based on USCIS published processing times, historical case data, and recent applicant reports, here is how each center compares for marriage-based I-130 petitions:
Texas Service Center (TSC): 8–12 months. TSC is the fastest center for straightforward marriage-based petitions. Cases filed by US citizens for spouses living in the US or abroad both benefit from TSC's relatively lighter backlog.
Nebraska Service Center (NSC): 10–14 months. Nebraska handles a mix of family and employment petitions. Its marriage-based I-130 times are moderate, with recent improvements in efficiency.
Vermont Service Center (VSC): 11–15 months. Vermont processes a significant volume of international adoption and humanitarian cases, which can slow family-based I-130 adjudication during peak periods.
Potomac Service Center (PSC): 12–16 months. Potomac handles online filings and complex cases, including those with waivers or prior immigration violations. Initial evidence quality heavily impacts speed here.
California Service Center (CSC): 14–18 months. California has the longest backlog for marriage-based petitions, partly due to its geographic jurisdiction (high-volume west coast districts) and complex caseload mix.
How to prepare for service center delays
Regardless of which service center handles your case, proactive preparation can prevent unnecessary delays. The most common holdup is not the service center itself but incomplete or inconsistent evidence that triggers a Request for Evidence (RFE). An RFE can add 2–4 months to your timeline regardless of which center is adjudicating your petition.
File comprehensively the first time. Submit your joint financial evidence, relationship timeline photos, affidavits from friends and family, joint lease or mortgage documents, and shared utility bills all at once. The more evidence you provide with the initial filing, the less likely the service center will need to request additional documentation. Pay special attention to the I-130 petition instructions — each service center has slightly different formatting preferences for evidence, and following them exactly can speed up initial processing.
Track your case using the USCIS online account. Create a USCIS online account and link your receipt number to receive real-time updates. With an account, you can see when your case is transferred between service centers, when an RFE is issued, and when a decision is made. You can also upload RFE responses electronically through the account, which is faster than mailing them. Set up email and text notifications so you never miss a status change.
Plan for field office variability too. The service center adjudicates the I-130, but the local field office where your adjustment of status interview is scheduled can also affect your total timeline. Field offices in major cities (New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston) typically have longer interview wait times — sometimes 6–12 months after the I-130 is approved — while field offices in less populated areas may schedule interviews within 2–4 months. If you have flexibility to move, adjusting your address before filing the I-485 could change which field office handles your interview, though USCIS may question a recent address change without a genuine reason. Checking your local field office's published processing times on the USCIS website before filing gives you a data point for timeline expectations.
Understand the National Benefits Center role. After the I-130 is approved at a service center, the case is typically transferred to the NBC for I-485 processing before being sent to the local field office for interview scheduling. The NBC processes biometrics, background checks, and initial evidence review, which can take 2–4 months on its own. If your case is transferred between service centers before reaching the NBC, add another 2–4 months. Building these transfer buffers into your timeline expectations will reduce frustration and help you plan around processing delays.

Consider two couples filing at the same time in early 2026:
Case A (Austin, TX — TSC jurisdiction): I-130 approved in 9 months. I-485 filed concurrently, processed at NBC in 4 months. Interview scheduled at Austin FO (typically within 2 months of I-485 approval). Total: ~15 months.
Case B (Los Angeles, CA — CSC jurisdiction): I-130 approved in 16 months. I-485 processed at NBC in 5 months. Los Angeles field office has high interview demand (additional 3-month wait). Total: ~24 months.

Borrower defense: the rule in plain English
Borrower defense asks the Department of Education to discharge federal student loans because the school misled the borrower or engaged in covered misconduct related to the loans or education. The borrower defense to repayment program is a federal remedy for students whose schools violated state law through misrepresentation, deceptive practices, or other misconduct related to the making of federal student loans or the provision of educational services. It applies only to federal Direct Loans — including Direct Subsidised, Unsubsidised, Grad PLUS, and Parent PLUS loans — not to private student loans, institutional loans, or loans from foreign governments.
The legal basis for a borrower defense claim is state law. The borrower must identify a specific state law that the school violated — typically a state consumer protection statute, false advertising law, or unfair trade practices act. Common examples include: the school misrepresented job placement rates, accreditation status, transferability of credits, program costs, or licensure exam pass rates. The application must explain what the school said, when they said it, how the borrower relied on that statement to enroll, and how the statement was false or misleading. Vague claims of "the school was bad" without specific evidence of misrepresentation are not sufficient for a borrower defense claim.
Who this guide is for
Borrowers with federal Direct Loans who believe their school made false claims or engaged in misconduct that induced them to enroll or take out loans. This guide is for students of both for-profit and nonprofit institutions — borrower defense claims are not limited to for-profit schools. If your school exaggerated job placement rates, promised salaries that graduates do not typically earn, misrepresented whether credits would transfer to another institution, or engaged in aggressive or deceptive recruiting practices, you may have a borrower defense claim.
This guide is also for borrowers whose schools have closed and who are considering whether to file a borrower defense claim or a closed school discharge. Closed school discharge is faster and does not require proof of misconduct, but it applies only to loans taken for a program at a school that closed. Borrower defense applies to any federal Direct Loan taken for a program where the school engaged in misconduct, regardless of whether the school is still open. If you qualify for both, closed school discharge is typically the faster option.
Documents and evidence to prepare
Evidence of the school's misrepresentation: This is the most important part of a borrower defense application. Collect every document that shows what the school told you before and during your enrollment. Examples include: the school's website pages advertising job placement rates, salary expectations, or accreditation status at the time you enrolled; emails, text messages, or letters from admissions representatives making specific promises about employment outcomes or program quality; screenshots of social media posts or online ads from the school; the enrollment agreement or program catalog you signed showing the school's representations; and recordings of phone calls or in-person meetings with admissions representatives (if you have them).
Evidence of reliance and harm: You must show that you relied on the school's statements when deciding to enroll and that you suffered harm as a result. 05 Main risk: Moving out without a valid legal ground or written release can result in liability for the remaining rent; unpaid balances may appear on your US credit report and affect future housing. 
06 Review status: Basic review for lease break situations available now; attorney-review tiers coming soon. 
In 60 seconds
Most leases bind you to the full term unless state law or the contract creates an exception.
International students have no special visa-based right to break a lease, but state tenant protections still apply.
Early termination clauses, military orders, and uninhabitable conditions are common legal grounds.
You may be able to sublet or find a replacement tenant if your lease and state law allow it.
Document every notice, repair request, and communication in writing.
Unpaid rent after a broken lease can appear on your credit report and affect future rental history.
Can an international student break a lease early?
No visa category gives you an automatic right to end a residential lease before the contract term finishes. You are subject to the same state landlord-tenant laws as any domestic tenant. Your F-1 or J-1 status does not create a separate legal exception, and US Citizenship and Immigration Services does not regulate private rental contracts.
If you leave without a valid legal ground, the landlord can treat the remaining months as due and may pursue the balance through a collections action or small-claims suit. Some states require the landlord to mitigate damages by trying to re-rent the unit, which can reduce what you owe. The exact duty to mitigate, and any formula for calculating damages, varies by state. Check your state's landlord-tenant statute and any local ordinances before you act.
Legal grounds that may let you terminate early (varies by state)
State laws and local housing codes provide several recognized grounds for early termination, though the exact requirements differ by jurisdiction. Constructive eviction is one example: if the landlord fails to provide heat, running water, pest control, or a secure dwelling, you may have a defense. The threshold for what counts as uninhabitable varies by state, and you generally must give the landlord a reasonable chance to cure the defect before you move out.
Some states allow early termination for victims of domestic violence or harassment, often with specific notice and documentation rules that you must follow precisely. Active-duty military orders can also trigger termination rights under federal law. Review your lease for an early-termination clause as well. These clauses exist in some student-housing contracts and may set conditions like extra notice or a flat fee, but they are governed by state contract law and cannot override stronger tenant protections in your jurisdiction.
How to break a lease with minimum liability — step by step
1. Read your lease for an early-termination clause or subletting provision before you do anything else. Note any notice period, fee, or condition the landlord attached, because those terms will shape your options and your timeline.
2. Review your state's landlord-tenant act to see whether you qualify for a statutory exit ground such as constructive eviction, domestic violence protections, or military orders. Local housing court websites and HUD-approved housing counselors often publish plain-language guides that explain the rules in your city.
3. Document the condition of the unit with dated photos and written repair requests if habitability is your ground. Save all emails, texts, and certified-mail receipts in a single folder so you can produce them quickly if a dispute arises.
4. Notify your landlord in writing using the method your lease requires, such as certified mail or email. State notice periods vary, so confirm the minimum timeline under your state's statute rather than relying on general advice from online forums.
5. Offer to find a replacement tenant or subletter if your lease permits it. Some states bar landlords from unreasonably withholding consent to a qualified replacement, which can shift the remaining rent obligation away from you.
6. Keep copies of every document. If the landlord rejects a lawful request or charges improper fees, you may need to present this record in small-claims court or to a local tenant-rights organization.
What happens to your security deposit and credit record
Your landlord may apply your security deposit toward unpaid rent or repair costs. State law governs how quickly the landlord must return any remaining balance and what documentation they must provide. That timeline varies by state, and some states require an itemized statement within a fixed number of days after you surrender the unit.
If the deposit does not cover the full loss, the landlord may send the balance to collections or obtain a civil judgment. A collection account or judgment can appear on your credit report and may complicate future rental applications. TL;DR — Civics test version explained in one minute
The 2025 naturalization civics test applies to N-400 applications that USCIS received on or after October 20, 2025. If you filed before October 20, 2025, you take the 2008 version regardless of when your interview is scheduled. The 2025 version has a different format: multiple-choice questions delivered on a tablet or through a guided interview process, with 128 potential questions compared to the 2008 version's 100 oral questions. The English reading, writing, and speaking test components are the same regardless of which civics version you take. The single most important thing you can do to prepare is to check your N-400 receipt date and study the correct version. Studying the wrong test version is the most common and most avoidable mistake N-400 applicants make in 2026.
Who this guide is for and who should look elsewhere
This guide is for: N-400 applicants who filed or are preparing to file in 2026 and need to determine which civics test version applies to their case. It is also for applicants who filed before the October 20, 2025 cutoff date but whose naturalisation interview has been scheduled for 2026, because those applicants still take the 2008 test and need to prepare accordingly. The guide is also useful for community organisations, legal aid providers, and immigration attorneys who advise naturalisation applicants on test preparation strategy.
This guide is not for: Applicants who have already passed the naturalisation test or taken the oath of citizenship. It is also not a substitute for the official USCIS study materials. Applicants should use this guide to determine which version applies to them, then study the official USCIS materials for that version rather than relying on third-party summaries alone. Permanent residents who are not yet eligible to apply for naturalisation do not need to prepare for the civics test until they reach the filing window.
The controlling source and how to verify the current rule
The controlling authority for the naturalisation civics test is the USCIS Citizenship Resource Center. The official study materials, test updates, and policy guidance are published at uscis.gov/citizenship . Specific updates about test changes are posted on the USCIS Test Updates page . The USCIS Policy Manual Volume 12, Part E covers the testing requirements in detail, including exemptions, accommodations, and the two-attempt rule.
Key differences between the 2008 and 2025 civics test formats
The 2008 test (100 questions, oral format): The USCIS officer asks ten oral questions from the official list of 100 civics questions. The questions cover US government, US history, and integrated civics topics including geography and national symbols. The applicant must answer six out of ten questions correctly to pass. The officer reads each question aloud and the applicant responds verbally. The questions are predictable and the acceptable answers are published by USCIS. Many applicants prepare by memorising the official 100 questions and practicing with a friend or family member who reads the questions aloud.
The 2025 test (128 questions, multiple-choice format): The officer administers the test using a tablet or computer interface. The question bank contains 128 questions, and the format is multiple-choice with four answer options per question. The passing standard is approximately 75 percent correct, though this may be subject to revision as USCIS evaluates the new format. Questions may be scenario-based, requiring the applicant to apply knowledge of US government and history to a realistic situation rather than simply reciting a memorised fact. For example, instead of asking "What is the supreme law of the land?" the 2025 test might present a scenario involving a constitutional dispute and ask which document controls the outcome. The multiple-choice format may be easier for applicants who struggle with oral recitation but requires careful reading and the ability to distinguish between similar answer choices.
How to determine which test version applies to your case
The filing date is the date USCIS receives and processes your N-400 application, as shown on the I-797 receipt notice. This is the date USCIS uses to determine which civics test version applies. It is not the date you mailed the application, the date it was delivered by courier, or the date of your interview. If the I-797 shows a receipt date before October 20, 2025, you take the 2008 test. 04 Timing: Start with a secured card as soon as you have a stable bank account; first score appears after 6 months.

§ Key takeaways
01 U.S. credit history is built from reported credit activity, payment history, utilization, account age, credit mix, and inquiries; immigration status alone does not create a score. 
02 Start with a low-limit product and autopay after the bank account is stable. 
03 Safe habits include paying in full, keeping utilization low, avoiding unnecessary hard pulls, and monitoring reports. 
04 Core documents include passport, student ID, SSN or ITIN if available, bank account, secured-card deposit, proof of address, rent records, phone bills, and credit-report access. 
05 Pitfalls include carrying balances, applying for many cards, using debit as credit-building, co-signing casually, and ignoring identity theft. 
How building US credit works for students
Building a US credit history is essential for renting an apartment, financing a car, or getting a mobile phone plan. The CFPB provides guidance on building credit from scratch. The US credit system starts from zero for newcomers. International credit history generally does not transfer.
The most important principle is that building credit takes time. Start with a single secured card, maintain on-time payments, and avoid high-interest debt. There are no shortcuts.
The first step
Open a US bank account first. Then apply for a secured credit card with a $200 to $500 deposit. Use it for small purchases and pay the full balance monthly. If you cannot get a secured card, become an authorized user on a trusted person's card with good credit habits.
Document checklist
Valid passport: For identity verification.
Student ID: Many student cards accept it.
SSN or ITIN: Or look for issuers accepting passport numbers.
Proof of address: Lease, utility bill, bank statement.
US bank account: For automatic payments.
Income evidence: Offer letter, pay stubs, or scholarship letter.
Risk factors
Credit is easy to damage and slow to repair. Carrying a balance increases utilization, which signals risk to scoring models. Multiple applications create hard inquiries, lowering the score by 5 to 10 points each. A single 30-day late payment stays on the report for 7 years.
Worked example: Kwame builds credit from zero
Kwame, a Ghanaian F-1 student in Houston, opens a bank account and applies for a $300 secured card. He uses it for gas and groceries, spending about $100 monthly with autopay. After 8 months, his first FICO score is 690. After 12 months, the bank converts to unsecured and returns his deposit. He adds a second student card and reaches a 730 score by year two.
Related guides
The ITIN application guide explains tax IDs for credit applications. The banking guide for international students covers error correction. The SSN application guide page provides card recommendations for new arrivals.
Financial aid options and funding sources
Building a US credit history is easier when you have a stable financial foundation. Before focusing on credit products, exhaust the financial aid options available to you as an international student. Many US universities offer need-based and merit-based scholarships that do not require US credit history. Some schools also offer institutional loans for international students with more favourable terms than private lenders.
If you need additional funding, research funding sources through your home country's education ministry, bilateral agreements with the US, and professional associations in your field. Grants for study abroad from organisations like the Fulbright Program, the American Association of University Women, and country-specific foundations can cover partial tuition without requiring US credit. Using these funding sources before taking on credit products reduces the amount of credit you need and makes it easier to maintain a low credit utilization ratio once you start building your US credit history. If you do need a student loan from a US lender, the loan itself can help build your credit mix — one of the five factors that determine your FICO score — provided you make all payments on time.
Credit score factors explained
Understanding the five factors that determine a FICO credit score helps international students prioritize their credit-building efforts. Payment history is the most important factor at 35% of the total score. This means that making all payments on time every month is the single most effective way to build and maintain good credit. Even one late payment can drop a credit score by 50 to 100 points, and the late payment remains on the credit report for 7 years. Setting up automatic payments for at least the minimum amount due on every credit account prevents accidental late payments.
Credit utilization is the second most important factor at 30% of the score. Utilization measures the amount of available credit being used at any given time. For example, if a student has a credit card with a $1,000 limit and a $300 balance, the utilization is 30%. Credit scoring models prefer utilization below 30%, and the best scores typically come from utilization below 10%. Utilization can be easily managed by payin

DACA renewal: the rule in plain English
USCIS continues to accept and process DACA renewal requests and related employment authorization under current court orders, while initial requests are accepted but not processed. As of 2026, DACA remains in effect under ongoing federal court orders that require USCIS to accept and process renewal applications from current and recently expired DACA recipients. First-time DACA applications are accepted by USCIS but are not being adjudicated while litigation continues. This means that if you have never had DACA before, or if your DACA expired more than one year ago, you can submit the application but USCIS will not process it until the court orders change.
The DACA renewal process requires filing three forms together: Form I-821D (Consideration of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals), Form I-765 (Application for Employment Authorization), and Form I-765WS (Worksheet). The I-821D is the core application for deferred action, while the I-765 requests the employment authorization document (EAD) that allows you to work lawfully in the US. The I-765WS calculates the fee amount and confirms that the applicant is requesting employment authorization based on deferred action. All three forms must be filed together with the correct fee as listed on the USCIS fee schedule.
Who this guide is for
Current DACA recipients who need to renew their deferred action and employment authorization before their current DACA expires. This guide is for recipients who are within the renewal window (120 to 150 days before expiration) and want to ensure their renewal packet is complete and accurate. If you received your first DACA grant in the past two years and are approaching your first renewal, this guide covers the specific documents and evidence you need to prepare.
This guide is also for DACA recipients whose DACA has recently expired (within the past year) and who want to renew. USCIS accepts renewal applications from individuals whose DACA expired within the last 12 months. If your DACA expired more than one year ago, you must file as an initial applicant, which means USCIS will accept your application but will not process it under current court orders. Speak with an immigration attorney or a DACA- accredited representative if you fall into this category, as the legal landscape for DACA can change rapidly.
Documents and evidence to prepare
Form I-821D (Consideration of Deferred Action): The primary application form for DACA renewal. Complete all sections accurately, using the same name, date of birth, and other biographical information as your previous DACA applications. If any information has changed since your last grant (new address, new criminal history, new travel history), disclose the change in the appropriate section. USCIS cross-references your new application against your prior filings, so inconsistencies can trigger an RFE or denial.
Form I-765 (Employment Authorization): Apply for a new EAD that will be valid for two years from the date of approval. Use the same eligibility category code as your previous DACA EAD. The filing fee for DACA renewal is listed on the USCIS fee schedule and must be paid together with the I-821D fee. If you cannot afford the fee, check whether you qualify for a fee exemption based on a means-tested benefit, income below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines, or financial hardship. Fee exemptions require documentation proving eligibility.
Form I-765WS (Worksheet): Complete the worksheet to confirm your household size and income. This form determines whether you qualify for the standard filing fee or a fee exemption. Include accurate information about your current income and household size. If you are a dependent of your parents, include your parents' household information.

DACA Renewal 2026: Costs, Timelines & Common Mistakes

In 60 seconds
What it is: DACA renewal extends your deferred action and work permit for two years by re-filing Form I-821D with USCIS.
When to file: Submit your application 150 to 120 days before your current DACA and Employment Authorization Document (EAD) expire.
What you need: Form I-821D, Form I-765, filing fees, two passport-style photos, and evidence you still meet DACA guidelines.
Who is eligible: Current DACA recipients who have not departed the U.S. without advance parole on or after August 15, 2012, and who have not committed disqualifying crimes.
Next step: Gather your documents and confirm your eligibility against the official USCIS checklist before mailing your packet.
Common mistakes that delay or reject DACA renewals
USCIS rejects Form I-821D packages for reasons that are almost always preventable.
A rejected application does not stop the clock on your expiration date, and you lose weeks while you refile.
Knowing the top rejection triggers helps you avoid them.
Incorrect fee amount. USCIS updates fee schedules periodically. Sending a check for the wrong amount results in an immediate rejection.
Verify the current fee on the official USCIS fee page before you write your check or money order.
Missing signature on Form I-765. The work authorization application requires your signature in the designated field.
An unsigned form gets rejected at the lockbox facility. Check every signature block before you seal the envelope.
Expired passport photos. USCIS requires two identical color photos taken within the last 30 days. Submitting older photos triggers a Request for Evidence (RFE), which adds weeks to your processing time.
Filing outside the 150-day window. Filing too early or too late creates problems. USCIS may reject packages filed more than 150 days before expiration, and filing inside 120 days risks a lapse in work authorization.
Note: A rejection differs from a denial. Rejections happen at the lockbox for procedural errors like missing fees. Denials happen after an officer reviews your case on the merits.
Review every page of your packet against the USCIS filing checklist before you mail your package. A 20-minute self-audit can save you a month of delays.
Preparing your DACA renewal packet before you file
Preparation reduces errors and stress. Gather your documents and review your forms in the weeks before your filing window opens.
A prepared applicant files confidently and avoids last-minute scrambling.
Pre-filing preparation checklist Current EAD copy: make a clear photocopy of both sides of your current work permit
Prior approval notice: locate your most recent DACA approval notice (Form I-797)
Two passport photos: taken within 30 days at a pharmacy or post office
Money order or check: made payable to "U.S. Department of Homeland Security"
Form I-821D: completed in black ink or typed, signed and dated
Form I-765: completed with your current DACA category code (c33)
Form I-765 Worksheet: filled out with your current employment and income information
Mailing envelope: large enough to hold your packet without folding the forms
Tracking number: purchase USPS Priority Mail with delivery confirmation
Personal copy: make a complete copy of everything you send for your own records
Store your personal copy in a labeled folder. If USCIS issues an RFE, you will need to reference exactly what you submitted and when.
Keep the tracking receipt until your new EAD arrives.
What happens after USCIS receives your renewal
The lockbox facility in Chicago or Phoenix processes incoming DACA renewal packets. Within 2 to 4 weeks, you should receive three separate notices in the mail.
Receipt notice (Form I-797C). This confirms USCIS accepted your packet and deposited your fee.
Your receipt number starts with three letters followed by ten digits. Use this number to track your case online.
Biometrics appointment notice. Most DACA renewals do not require new fingerprints if your biometrics are still valid. If USCIS needs them, you will receive an appointment notice with a date, time, and location.
Request for Evidence (RFE). Not every applicant receives an RFE. If you do, respond by the deadline stated in the letter. Late responses result in automatic denial.
Processing times fluctuate based on USCIS workload. Check your case status weekly at the official USCIS portal.
If your current EAD is within 30 days of expiring and your renewal is still pending, contact USCIS through the e-Request tool to inquire about the delay.
Travel and family considerations during your renewal period
Your DACA renewal period affects more than just your work authorization. Family, travel, and state benefits all depend on your continued deferred action status.
Advance parole. Do not travel outside the United States while your renewal is pending unless you have an approved Advance Parole document.
Departing without approval causes your DACA to be considered abandoned. This rule applies even if your current DACA has not yet expired.
Driver licenses. Many states tie license validity to your EAD expiration date.
If your renewal is still processing when your EAD expires, your license may lapse. Some states offer temporary extensions.
Contact your local DMV to ask about their policy on pending DACA renewals.
Family members. DACA does not provide a direct path to permanent residency for your spouse or children.
Your renewal keeps your own work authorization active but does not change your family's immigration standing.
If a family member has a separate immigration case, consult a qualified attorney about how your DACA timeline intersects with theirs.
Note: Always carry copies of your pending renewal receipt notice and your expired EAD. Some employers accept the receipt notice

01 Driver license rules are state-specific, but international students usually need identity, lawful status, residence, and sometimes SSN or SSN-ineligibility evidence.

How state driver's license rules apply to students
Each state's DMV sets its own requirements. The general framework includes four document categories: identity (passport), lawful status (visa, I-94, I-20), residency (lease, utility bill), and SSN or ineligibility. The REAL ID Act adds federal security standards.
USA.gov provides links to each state's DMV. Check your state's requirements before visiting to avoid long waits without proper documents.
The first step
Check your state DMV's international student document checklist. Obtain the SSN Ineligibility Letter from the SSA if you do not have an SSN. Gather two proofs of residency showing the same address. Ensure your SEVIS record is active before the appointment.
Document checklist
Identity: Valid passport from your home country.
Lawful status: Visa, printed I-94, current I-20/DS-2019 with DSO endorsement.
Residency (2 docs): Lease, utility bill, bank statement, or school housing letter.
SSN or ineligibility: SSN card or SSA ineligibility letter.
Foreign license: With certified translation or IDP if applicable.
Worked example: Lila gets her California license
Lila, an F-1 student from Brazil in Los Angeles, checks the CA DMV website and gathers her passport, printed I-94, I-20, lease, utility bill, and SSA ineligibility letter. She passes the vision and written tests. Because she holds a valid Brazilian license, the driving test is waived. Her REAL ID-compliant license arrives by mail in 3 weeks.
Related guides
The SSN application guide page provides state-specific checklists. The banking guide for international students guide explains compliance rules. The building US credit history guide covers insurance and registration.
Understanding the REAL ID requirements
The REAL ID Act established minimum security standards for state-issued driver's licenses and ID cards. As of May 7, 2025, a REAL ID-compliant license or ID card is required for boarding domestic flights and entering certain federal facilities. International students with valid nonimmigrant status are eligible for REAL ID-compliant licenses if they can present the required documentation. The application requires proof of identity, proof of lawful status, proof of Social Security Number or ineligibility, and two proofs of state residency.
Students who cannot meet the REAL ID documentation requirements may still obtain a non-compliant driver's license or ID card in some states. These licenses are marked as not valid for federal identification purposes and cannot be used for boarding domestic flights or entering federal buildings. Students who expect to travel domestically should verify that their state offers REAL ID-compliant licenses for noncitizens and gather the required documents before visiting the DMV.
The DMV verifies immigration status through the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) program. The SAVE system checks the applicant's noncitizen status against DHS databases, including the SEVIS system. This verification process can take anywhere from several minutes to several days. The DMV cannot issue a driver's license or ID card until SAVE confirms the applicant's lawful status. Students whose SEVIS records are not yet active may face delays. Updating the SEVIS record through the DSO before the DMV appointment can prevent these delays.
State-by-state differences in testing requirements
Testing requirements vary significantly by state. Some states, including California and Illinois, waive the driving test for applicants who hold a valid driver's license from a country with which the state has a reciprocal agreement. Countries covered by these agreements typically include Canada, Germany, South Korea, France, and Taiwan, but the specific list varies by state. Students should check their state DMV's website for the complete list of reciprocal countries before assuming the driving test is waived.
Most states require both a written knowledge test and a driving skills test for all new applicants who do not hold a valid license from a reciprocal country. 02 Core rule: E-2 allows nationals of treaty countries who invest substantial capital in a real U.S. business to enter and develop the enterprise. 
03 Documents: Treaty nationality proof, ownership records, source of funds, bank wires, escrow docs, lease, contracts, business plan, payroll, tax records, non-marginality evidence. 
04 Timing: Consular processing vs change of status have different evidence and travel effects; verify treaty eligibility before committing capital. 
05 Main risk: Passive investments, funds not at risk, weak source-of-funds trail, marginal businesses, and assuming any investment qualifies as substantial. 
06 Review status: Basic review for E-2 available now; attorney-review tiers coming soon. 
How the E-2 treaty investor visa works
The E-2 nonimmigrant visa under INA 101(a)(15)(E)(ii) allows treaty-country nationals to enter the US to develop and direct a business enterprise in which they invested substantial capital. Unlike H-1B, E-2 does not require employer sponsorship. The investor controls the enterprise, making it popular for entrepreneurs and business buyers from eligible countries.
E-2 is renewable indefinitely with no annual lottery or prevailing wage requirement. It is one of the most flexible nonimmigrant categories for eligible nationals who want to build or acquire a US business. Status is available through consular processing abroad or change of status within the US.
The E-2 visa is governed by 8 CFR 214.2(e) and the State Department's Foreign Affairs Manual at 9 FAM 402.9. USCIS adjudicates change-of-status applications while the State Department adjudicates visa applications at consular posts. Before committing capital, verify that your country of nationality maintains a qualifying treaty with the United States.
Who qualifies for E-2
This guide is for nationals of E-2 treaty countries who have invested or plan to invest substantial capital in a US business and intend to develop and direct the enterprise. This includes founders, business buyers, franchise investors, and current nonimmigrant holders wanting to change status.
This guide is not for nationals of non-treaty countries (India, China, Brazil, Russia, South Africa), passive investors, or those whose business will only support themselves without creating US jobs. Treaty-country citizens by naturalization or descent may qualify but face additional requirements about the source of investment funds.
Consular processing versus change of status
Decide whether to apply through consular processing abroad or change of status within the US. Consular processing requires a visa interview at a US embassy in the treaty country and results in a visa stamp allowing free travel. Change of status through Form I-129 to USCIS does not produce a visa stamp, so travel requires a separate E-2 visa application before re-entry.
If you travel frequently, consular processing is usually the better option. Change of status is simpler for those who plan to stay in the US and do not need to travel internationally during their E-2 period.
Document checklist for E-2 application
Organize evidence in five categories:
Treaty nationality proof: Valid passport from the treaty country. Include naturalization certificate if naturalized.
Investment documentation: Bank statements, wire receipts, escrow agreements, purchase agreements, loan or gift documentation showing funds are committed and at risk.
Enterprise evidence: Business licenses, articles of incorporation, lease, contracts, and professional licenses.
Non-marginality evidence: Payroll records, tax returns, profit/loss statements, and a business plan showing capacity to generate income beyond supporting the investor.
Investor role evidence: Organization chart, job description, board resolutions showing authority, and required licenses.
Each document should include a brief explanation of what it proves.
Risk triggers for E-2 denial
The most common denial reason is insufficient evidence that the investment is substantial relative to the total cost. Proportionality is the test, not a fixed dollar amount. The second most common reason is marginality. The safest approach is to employ at least 2 to 3 US workers within the first year.
The third risk is insufficient evidence of lawful fund control. Gifts must be documented with gift letters and bank records. Loans must be enforceable with personal liability. Circular transfers are heavily scrutinized.
Worked example: Carlos opens a Miami franchise
Carlos, a Spanish citizen, purchases a restaurant franchise in Miami for $250,000. He wires funds from his Spanish bank account showing 3 years of lawful salary income. He applies for E-2 at the US consulate in Madrid, including the franchise agreement, lease, wire receipts, and a business plan projecting 8 employees within year 1. The officer approves the E-2 visa for 5 years.
Related guides
The O-1A extraordinary ability visa may be an alternative for founders with industry recognition. The adjustment of status vs consular processing covers employment sponsorship. The EB-2 National Interest Waiver guide explains the $800,000 minimum investment path to permanent residence.
Key decisions for E-2 investors
The E-2 visa approval process involves several key decisions that treaty-country nationals must make before and after investing. First, an investor must confirm that they are a national of a country that maintains a qualifying treaty with the United States. This is not always straightforward. For example, citizens of countries that were formerly part of larger treaty entities may have questions about their eligibility, and investors who hold dual citizenship must determine which nationality they will rely on for the application. 02 Core rule: EB-1A requires evidence of sustained national or international acclaim through at least 3 of 10 criteria plus a final merits review. 
03 Documents: Awards, memberships, media, judging, original contributions, scholarly articles, high salary evidence, leading roles, exhibitions, recommendation letters, CV, patents, and a future work plan. 
04 Timing: Check the current Visa Bulletin for EB-1 category availability by country of birth before deciding I-485 concurrent filing.

How the EB-1A self-petition pathway works
The EB-1A immigrant visa category, established under INA 203(b)(1)(A), provides a green card path for individuals with extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics. Unlike other employment-based categories, EB-1A does not require a job offer or labor certification. The applicant may file Form I-140 on their own behalf without employer sponsorship.
To qualify, the applicant must demonstrate sustained national or international acclaim through extensive documentation. USCIS evaluates petitions using a two-part framework: first, whether the applicant meets at least 3 of the 10 regulatory criteria at 8 CFR 204.5(h)(3), and second, whether the totality of the evidence shows that the applicant is among the small percentage at the very top of the field.
The self-petitioning aspect means the applicant controls the filing timeline, evidence selection, and legal argument. This flexibility is valuable for individuals whose work does not fit a traditional employer-employee relationship, such as freelance artists, independent researchers, founders of startups, and consultants with international recognition.
Who this guide serves and who needs a different path
This guide is for individuals who believe their achievements place them at the top tier nationally or internationally and want to understand the EB-1A evidence requirements before investing in the process. It is relevant for researchers with significant citation records and patents, artists and performers with major awards and international exhibitions, business founders with industry-wide recognition, and athletes with national or international competition success.
This guide is not for individuals whose work is primarily local or regional in scope, those who have not received awards beyond their immediate employer, or applicants who cannot document at least 3 of the 10 criteria with objective evidence. If you do not meet the EB-1A threshold, consider the EB-2 NIW category, which has a lower acclaim requirement and also permits self-petitioning.
The first decision to make before filing
Before preparing the I-140 petition, decide which of the 10 criteria you can meet with the strongest evidence. List each criterion you intend to use and gather the documentary evidence before writing the petition narrative. A common mistake is starting with the narrative and then searching for evidence to fit it. The stronger approach is to let the evidence determine the argument.
The second decision is whether to file Form I-485 concurrently with the I-140 or wait for I-140 approval. Concurrent filing is available only when the Visa Bulletin shows EB-1 as current for your country of birth. For applicants from India or China, the EB-1 category has a backlog, and you may need to wait for your priority date to become current.
The controlling authority for EB-1A adjudication
USCIS adjudicates EB-1A petitions under the regulations at 8 CFR 204.5(h)(3) and the USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 6, Part F. The Policy Manual provides detailed guidance on how officers should evaluate each of the 10 criteria and conduct the final merits determination. AAO non-precedent decisions also provide insight into how USCIS applies the law in specific factual scenarios.
USCIS updates its adjudication guidance periodically. The most common reason for RFE in EB-1A cases is insufficient evidence that the acclaim is sustained rather than a single achievement, followed by weak final merits arguments.
Evidence checklist for a complete EB-1A petition
A thorough EB-1A petition requires documentary evidence organized by criterion. Prepare the following categories based on which criteria you intend to meet:
Major awards: Evidence of nationally or internationally recognized prizes including award criteria, selection process, and why the award is significant in your field.
Association memberships: Membership in associations requiring outstanding achievement for entry, as demonstrated by published membership standards.
Published media: Published material about the applicant in professional or major media, including publication name, circulation data, and date.
Judging others' work: Evidence of serving as a peer reviewer, conference program committee member, grant review panelist, or award juror.
Original contributions: Evidence of original contributions of major significance such as patents, publications with citation evidence, or industry-adopted technologies.
Scholarly articles: Authorship of scholarly articles in professional journals with citation counts, impact factors, and independent references.
Leading or critical role: Performance in a leading or critical role for organizations with distinguished reputations, with specific responsibilities described.
High remuneration: Evidence of high salary compared to others in the field using surveys and compensation data.

02 Core rule: An NIW is a petition that asks USCIS to waive the standard job offer and labor certification requirements because the applicant's work benefits the United States in a way that makes the labor certification process unnecessary. The waiver is discretionary — USCIS evaluates each case under the three-prong Dhanasar framework. 
03 Evidence categories: Degrees, evaluations, work letters, publications, citation metrics, patents, grants, contracts, business plan, expert letters, and proof the applicant is well positioned. 
04 Timing: Check visa bulletin movement and whether concurrent I-485 filing is available. Priority date portability may apply if you have an earlier EB-2 or EB-3 filing. 
05 Main risk: Confusing personal career benefit with national importance. An endeavor that benefits only the applicant or their employer is not national importance under Dhanasar. 
06 Review status: Basic review available now; attorney-review tiers coming soon. 
EB-2 NIW: the rule in plain English
An NIW is a petition that asks USCIS to waive the standard job offer and labor certification requirements because the applicant's work benefits the United States in a way that makes the labor certification process unnecessary. The waiver is discretionary — USCIS evaluates each case under the three-prong Dhanasar framework.
Step one: Prove EB-2 eligibility. You must show either that you hold an advanced degree (master's or higher, or a bachelor's plus five years of progressive experience) or exceptional ability in the sciences, arts, or business.
Step two: Prove the waiver is warranted. Under Dhanasar, you must show: (1) the proposed endeavor has substantial merit and national importance, (2) you are well positioned to advance it, and (3) on balance, waiving the labor certification benefits the United States.
Who this guide is for
Professionals with advanced degrees or exceptional ability whose work has a credible U.S. benefit. The NIW is available to self-petitioners and employer-sponsored applicants across virtually every field.
Who this guide is not for
Applicants who do not meet the EB-2 threshold — the NIW does not waive this.
EB-1 applicants — different standards apply under Matter of Kazarian.
Applicants considering priority date portability from an earlier I-140 — consult an attorney.
The Dhanasar framework in detail: evidence per prong
Prong one: Substantial merit and national importance. Substantial merit is broadly defined — USCIS has found substantial merit in fields as varied as biotechnology, education technology, business consulting, and the arts. The harder standard is national importance: the proposed endeavor must affect the field broadly, not merely benefit the petitioner or their employer. USCIS evaluates whether the endeavor has significance for the field as a whole, not whether the petitioner is the most accomplished researcher in their field.
Prong one evidence — tiered by strength: 
Tier 1 (direct adoption): Evidence that the applicant's work has been adopted, implemented, or cited by independent third parties. Examples: government agencies using the applicant's research methodology, federal grant award letters naming the applicant as PI or co-PI, licensed patents generating revenue or being used in commercial products, citation analysis showing independent citing institutions.
Tier 2 (recognition by peers): Conference keynote invitations, journal editorial board memberships, peer review assignments from top-tier publications, national awards or fellowships (NSF CAREER, NIH New Innovator, DARPA Young Faculty), media coverage in national outlets that describes the specific work.
Tier 3 (positional evidence): Affiliations with nationally prominent institutions, leadership roles in professional organisations, patents filed or granted (even if not yet commercialised), publications showing the arc of the applicant's contribution.
Note that Tier 3 evidence alone is rarely sufficient for Prong One. Patents that have never been cited, licensed, or produced revenue do not demonstrate national importance — they demonstrate invention, which is a separate factor. Successful NIW petitions typically combine evidence from at least two tiers.
Prong two: Well positioned to advance the endeavor. This prong evaluates whether the applicant has the skills, experience, and track record to execute the proposed endeavor. USCIS does not require the applicant to be the best in their field — the standard is whether they are well positioned, not whether they are uniquely positioned. Evidence categories include academic record showing relevant training, publication record with citation metrics demonstrating impact, patent assignments showing commercial potential, grant funding confirming that peer reviewers deemed the applicant's research worthy of funding, peer review invitations confirming standing in the field, expert letters from independent US-based researchers who describe specific contributions, and entrepreneurial evidence for startup founders such as incorporation documents, business plan, funding raised, and strategic partnerships.
Entrepreneur-specific evidence for Prong Two: If the applicant is self-petitioning based on a business or startup endeavor, Prong Two evidence should include: a detailed business plan with milestones, evidence of funding or investment (angel investor letters, venture capital term sheets, SBIR/STTR grant awards), customer letters of intent or contracts demonstrating market validation, and evidence the applicant has the relevant industry experience to execute the plan. 01 PERM requires the employer to demonstrate no qualified US worker is available for the position through a structured, DOL-supervised recruitment process. 
02 Average PERM timeline: 6-18 months including PWD (2-4 months), recruitment (2-3 months), and DOL processing (6-10 months). Audited cases add 4-8 months. 
03 About 30% of PERM applications are audited. Audit requires submission of all recruitment documentation within 30 days. 
04 Once certified, PERM is valid for 180 days — the I-140 must be filed before the certification expires. If it expires, a new PERM is required. 
05 EB-3 requires a bachelor's degree, two years of experience, or (for unskilled workers) less than two years. EB-3 visa wait times vary significantly by country of birth. 
Who this is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for US employers who are sponsoring a foreign national employee for an EB-3 green card and need to understand the PERM labor certification requirements, timeline, and documentation. It is also for foreign national employees who want to understand what their employer must do to obtain a labor certification on their behalf and how the process works from start to finish.
This guide is not for applicants who qualify for a PERM exemption such as EB-1A (extraordinary ability), EB-2 NIW (national interest waiver), or EB-5 (investor) — those categories do not require labor certification. It is also not for applicants pursuing EB-2 PERM — while the PERM process is the same, the education and experience requirements differ. EB-3 applicants should also be aware that the annual visa quota for EB-3 is shared across three subcategories (skilled workers, professionals, and unskilled workers), and waiting times depend on the applicant's country of birth and the current Visa Bulletin priority date cut-offs.
Step one: the prevailing wage determination from DOL
The PERM process begins with the employer requesting a prevailing wage determination from the DOL National Prevailing Wage Center. The employer submits ETA Form 9141, which specifies the job title, SOC occupation code, job duties, education and experience requirements, geographic area of intended employment, and proposed wage. The NPWC reviews the submission against the Occupational Employment Statistics wage data and issues a determination that establishes the minimum wage the employer must pay for the position.
Common PWD issues include: selecting the wrong SOC code (which changes the prevailing wage because each occupation has a different wage range), requesting the wrong wage level (Level I is entry level, Level IV is fully competent — the level must match the job requirements), or submitting an incomplete form. The PWD is valid for 90 days (extendable to 180 days with documentation). The employer must begin recruitment before the PWD expires, and the offered wage must be at least 100% of the prevailing wage for the SOC code and level.
Step two: recruitment and labour market test
Once the employer has a valid prevailing wage, they must complete the mandatory recruitment steps. For professional positions (requiring a bachelor's degree or higher), the recruitment must include: two Sunday newspaper advertisements in the general circulation newspaper most likely to reach qualified applicants for the position (or professional journal ads if the position is highly specialised), a job order placed with the state workforce agency for at least 30 days, and three additional recruitment steps from the DOL-approved list. The DOL-approved options include job fairs, employer website postings (which are mandatory and do not count as one of the three optional steps), on-campus recruiting, private employment firms, employee referral programs, trade association and professional organisation job banks, and newspaper ads in additional newspapers or journal formats.
The recruitment must run for at least 30 calendar days and must be completed within the 30-to-180-day window before the PERM application filing date. The employer must maintain a detailed recruitment report that lists each recruitment source, the dates the advertisement ran, the number of applicants received, and the lawful, job-related reasons why each US applicant was rejected. Under DOL regulations, US workers who are rejected because they lack a particular qualification that the foreign worker possesses but that was not included in the advertised minimum requirements may serve as the basis for a finding that the employer tailored the requirements to the foreign worker. The recruitment report is the single most important document in a PERM audit and must be prepared with as much care as the application itself.
Step three: filing Form 9089 and DOL processing
After the recruitment is complete and the 30-day quiet period (post-recruitment) has ended, the employer files ETA Form 9089 electronically through the DOL's PERM system. The form captures the job details, the prevailing wage, the recruitment results, and the employer's attestations. The employer attests that the recruitment was conducted in good faith, that no qualified US worker was available, and that the offered wage meets or exceeds the prevailing wage.
The DOL processes the application in one of three ways: certified (no issues), audited (the application is selected for random or targeted review), or denied (the application fails on the merits). Approximately 30% of applications are audited. If audited, the employer has 30 days to submit the full recruitment file, including copies of all advertisements, the recruitment report, resumes received, and evidence of the Notice of Filing. Complete Guide: Education Verification Service 2026 at a glance
The education verification process is a required step when a U.S. employer relies on a foreign degree.
USCIS doesn't evaluate degrees itself.
Independent evaluators who follow recognized standards issue the opinions USCIS accepts.
The most widely accepted standard comes from the National Association of Credential Evaluation Services (NACES).
You can review the current member list at https://www.naces.org/members.
Each section below covers documents, typical costs, and how to handle problems that arise.
Step 1: Confirm you need a credential evaluation
USCIS requires a credential evaluation when a petitioner relies on a foreign degree for H-1B specialty occupation or EB-2 advanced-degree claims.
The agency doesn't perform the evaluation itself. It accepts opinions from independent evaluators who follow recognized standards.
If your degree comes from a U.S. institution, you don't need this step.
When the degree is from outside the United States, you must obtain a course-by-course report.
That report should state U.S. comparability and, where relevant, the major field of study.
Policy Manual guidance says the evaluator must explain the basis for that conclusion.
The explanation should cover the source of the foreign credential and the U.S. educational framework used for comparison.
See the policy guidance at https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-2-part-h.
How to verify foreign degree starts with checking whether your occupation requires a specific degree level.
H-1B specialty occupations generally require a U.S. bachelor's degree or higher in a specific specialty.
EB-2 advanced-degree positions require a U.S. master's degree or a bachelor's degree plus five years of progressive experience.
If your role fits either category and your degree is foreign, move to the next step.
Step 2: Gather foreign transcripts and degree records
Foreign transcripts are the primary evidence.
You need complete, official transcripts issued by the awarding institution.
Those records should show all courses, grades, and the date the degree was conferred.
If the institution issues a separate degree certificate or diploma, include that as well.
Academic credentials not in English require a certified translation that meets USCIS standards.
The translator must certify competence and that the translation is complete and accurate.
The translation should mirror the original layout, including seals, signatures, and grading scales.
Documents needed for credential evaluation typically include:
Official transcripts in sealed envelopes or electronic delivery directly from the registrar
Degree certificate or diploma (front and back if seals appear on the reverse)
Certified English translations for any non-English documents
Grading scale or key if the transcript does not explain the grading system
Proof of institution recognition such as ministry of education listing or accreditation body confirmation
Some evaluators also request a copy of your passport biographic page to confirm identity.
Keep a complete set for your records. You may need to submit the evaluation with multiple petitions over time.
Step 3: File with a NACES evaluation provider
NACES evaluation providers are members of the National Association of Credential Evaluation Services.
Membership signals adherence to published standards and a code of ethics.
USCIS doesn't endorse a specific company.
Reports from NACES members and from evaluators affiliated with regionally accredited U.S. universities are generally accepted.

03 Documents: Eviction notice, signed lease, rent receipts, dated photos of property condition, landlord correspondence, and housing court response forms. 
04 Timing: Count calendar days from receipt of the notice; the response deadline varies by state (typically 3 to 30 days) — verify yours immediately. 
05 Main risk: Missing the eviction notice response deadline by even one day can result in a default judgment; failing to document the notice and landlord communications weakens any later defence.

In 60 seconds
An eviction notice is a legal warning, not an immediate lockout — you have time to respond.
Your F-1 or J-1 status requires a current residential address, so housing loss can affect your SEVIS record.
Deadlines and defenses vary by state — check your state's landlord-tenant statute and local housing court rules.
Document every notice, payment, and communication in writing from the moment you receive the papers.
Free legal aid, university housing offices, and HUD-certified counselors can help at no cost.
What an eviction notice means
An eviction notice is a landlord's written warning that they intend to start a court case to remove you. It is not a court order, and it does not allow the landlord to lock you out, remove your things, or shut off utilities. In most states, the landlord must serve a formal notice and then file a case in local housing court.
The notice must state a reason, such as unpaid rent or a lease violation. The required form, delivery method, and minimum response time vary by state — check your state's landlord-tenant statute. Some states require specific language; missing details can sometimes invalidate the notice.
Keep the original and make a copy the same day. Write the date and time you received it on your copy. This date starts the clock for your response, so an accurate record protects you if the landlord claims you had more time.
How eviction can affect your F-1 or J-1 status
Your SEVIS record must list a current residential address. If you lose housing and cannot provide a new address to your Designated School Official quickly, your record may show a compliance problem. Email your DSO within a few days of any change, even if the address is temporary.
Eviction itself does not automatically end your visa or OPT. However, an arrest during a dispute, failure to update your address, or an inability to maintain a full course load because you are homeless can trigger a status review. Universities report address changes to SEVIS, so delays matter.
If you are on OPT or STEM OPT, your employer needs your current address for I-9 verification. Losing housing can disrupt this if you cannot receive mail. Tell your employer's human resources contact if your address changes so your records stay current. For students who receive mail at a campus mailbox or a friend's address while searching for new housing, set up USPS Informed Delivery to track incoming mail digitally. This prevents important correspondence from your DSO, school, or employer from being missed during the transition period.
How to respond — step by step
Step 1: Read the notice carefully and write down the date you received it and the deadline to respond. That deadline varies by state — check your state's landlord-tenant statute. Look for the named court and any instructions on how to answer.
Step 2: Contact your university housing office or international student services office the same day. Many schools maintain emergency funds, temporary housing lists, or attorney referrals for students in crisis. They may also contact your DSO on your behalf if you give permission.
Step 3: File a written response with the local housing court if the landlord has already started a case. Missing the deadline can lead to a default judgment, which means the landlord wins without a hearing. Bring your lease and any evidence with you.
Step 4: Gather your lease, rent receipts, emails, text messages, and photos of the property condition. These documents are your evidence if the landlord's claim is inaccurate or if you have counterclaims such as uninhabitable conditions.
Step 5: Speak with a HUD-certified housing counselor or a legal-aid clinic before you sign any settlement or move-out agreement. They can explain your defenses under state law and review whether the timeline gives you enough time to find new housing.
What legal protections you may have
You cannot be removed from your home without a court order in most jurisdictions. Self-help evictions — such as changing the locks, shutting off utilities, or removing your things — are illegal in many states. The specific penalties and remedies vary by state — check your state's landlord-tenant statute.
The notice period, allowable reasons for termination, and protections against retaliation differ from state to state. Some states require landlords to give you a chance to cure a lease violation before filing in court. Others limit how much a landlord can raise rent on short notice. Local housing court rules may add extra procedural requirements.

body:
Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com

F-1 cap-gap explained 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home
