In 60 seconds
01 Primary authority: USCIS H-1B guidance and ICE SEVIS program 
02 Core rule: Cap-gap extends F-1 status through September 30 when a timely filed cap-subject H-1B change-of-status petition requests an October 1 start date. The extension is automatic in the sense that no separate USCIS application is required, but it is not automatic in the practical sense — the student must take specific steps to benefit from it. First, the student must confirm with the employer that the H-1B petition requests change of status rather than consular processing, because only change-of-status petitions qualify for cap-gap protection. Second, the student must obtain an updated I-20 from the DSO showing the cap-gap endorsement after USCIS receipts the H-1B petition. Without that I-20, the employer may not accept proof of continued work authorization, and the student may be placed on unpaid leave until the H-1B start date on October 1. Third, the student must ensure that their OPT EAD was still valid on the date USCIS received the H-1B petition — if the OPT expired before the filing date, the student qualifies for the status extension but cannot work during the cap-gap period. 
03 Documents: H-1B receipt notice (Form I-797), cap-gap I-20 endorsed by DSO, OPT EAD, passport, I-94, SEVIS record, and denial or withdrawal notices if any. 
04 Timing: Request the cap-gap I-20 from your DSO immediately after USCIS receipts the H-1B petition, not after approval. 
05 Main risk: Travel abandons change of status, denial ends cap-gap immediately, and consular-processing petitions do not qualify for cap-gap. 
06 Review status: Basic review for F-1 cap-gap available now; attorney-review tiers coming soon. 
What the cap-gap rule does for F-1 students
The cap-gap rule at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi) addresses the timing problem between the April H-1B filing season and the October 1 H-1B start date. F-1 students on OPT whose OPT expires between April 1 and September 30 face a gap in status and work authorization. The rule bridges that gap automatically for students whose employers file cap-subject H-1B petitions requesting change of status.
Cap-gap extends the F-1 status and, in some cases, the OPT work authorization through September 30 of the fiscal year. The extension is not automatic in the sense that no separate application is required, but it does require the student to obtain an updated I-20 from the Designated School Official showing the cap-gap endorsement. Without that I-20, an employer may not accept proof of continued work authorization.
The rule applies only to cap-subject H-1B petitions that request change of status rather than consular notification. If the employer files for consular processing, cap-gap does not apply, and the student must maintain valid status through other means or depart and activate the H-1B abroad.
Who this guide is for and who should look elsewhere
This guide is for F-1 students whose employers have registered them in the H-1B lottery, received a selection notice, and plan to file a cap-subject H-1B petition requesting change of status to H-1B on October 1. It addresses the period between OPT expiration and October 1, which the cap-gap rule covers.
This guide is not for students whose employers file for consular processing rather than change of status. It is not for students with cap-exempt H-1B petitions, which follow different timing rules. Students on J-1 status with pending H-1B change of status face different bridging options covered elsewhere on this site.
Students whose OPT ends after October 1 do not need cap-gap, because the H-1B start date arrives before OPT expires. Similarly, students whose OPT ended before the H-1B was filed qualify only for the status extension portion of cap-gap, not the work authorization extension.
The next decision you need to make
After your employer files the H-1B petition, your next decision is whether to remain in the United States during the cap-gap period or travel abroad. Staying preserves the change-of-status path. Traveling, even for an emergency, abandons the change-of-status request and requires consular processing of the H-1B visa abroad before you can re-enter and start work on October 1.
If you stay, the next decision is when to request the cap-gap I-20 from your DSO. Wait until USCIS sends the receipt notice, then request the I-20 immediately. Do not wait for H-1B approval, because the receipt alone triggers the cap-gap extension. The I-20 serves as your proof of continued status and, if applicable, work authorization for your employer.
The controlling source and where to verify the rule
The cap-gap rule is codified at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi) , which USCIS administers. USCIS publishes interpretive guidance on the H-1B cap process, including the cap-gap extension, on its website. The SEVIS program at ICE manages the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System through which DSOs endorse cap-gap I-20s.
Each year USCIS publishes a final rule or guidance memo confirming the cap-gap dates for that fiscal year's H-1B season. Students should verify the current fiscal year's cap-gap start and end dates against the latest USCIS guidance, not against prior years' timelines, because filing windows and lottery dates shift.
Document checklist for cap-gap preparation
Organize the following documents before and during the cap-gap period:
H-1B receipt notice (Form I-797) from USCIS confirming the petition was received. This triggers the cap-gap extension.
Cap-gap I-20 issued by your DSO after USCIS receipts the H-1B petition. The I-20 must include the cap-gap endorsement in the employment authorization section.
Current or expired OPT EAD showing the dates of your most recent OPT authorization. If the EAD expiration date is after the H-1B filing date, you qualify for work authorization e

Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home

In 60 seconds
01 Documents in your carry-on: Passport with F-1 visa, Form I-20 signed by DSO, SEVIS I-901 fee receipt, university acceptance letter, financial evidence. Never put these in checked luggage. 
02 Primary inspection: The CBP officer scans your passport, reviews your I-20 and visa, asks questions about your study plans, and decides whether to admit you in F-1 status or refer you to secondary. 
03 Secondary inspection: A more detailed document review in a separate area. Not necessarily a problem — many students are referred for routine verification. Wait patiently, answer questions honestly, do not use your phone. 
04 30-day rule: You can enter up to 30 days before your I-20 programme start date. Earlier arrival risks denial or admission in the wrong status. 
05 I-94 check: After entry, check your I-94 online immediately. Confirm it says F-1 and D/S (Duration of Status). Errors must be corrected within days, not weeks. 
Before you fly: the document packet that must be in your carry-on
CBP inspects your documents before you reach baggage claim. The following must be in your carry-on, not in checked luggage. Passport: valid for at least 6 months beyond your intended period of stay. F-1 visa stamp: unless you are a Canadian citizen exempt from the visa requirement. Form I-20: signed by you and your DSO, with a travel signature within the last 12 months (for returning students; first-time students should have the original signed I-20). SEVIS I-901 fee receipt: printed confirmation showing payment. University acceptance or enrolment letter: confirming your programme and start date. Financial evidence: bank statements, scholarship award letter, assistantship offer letter, or sponsor documentation matching the financial information on your I-20.
Optional but recommended: a printed copy of your class schedule (if already registered), your university's DSO contact information including the 24-hour emergency phone number, and any prior I-20 forms if you have transferred schools or changed programmes. CBP may also request evidence of ties to your home country — family, property, employment to return to — though this is less commonly asked of F-1 students than of visitor visa holders.
Who this guide is for
First-time F-1 students travelling to the United States for initial entry in F-1 status. Returning F-1 students re-entering after a trip abroad. Parents and families of international students who want to understand what their child will experience at the border. University DSOs and international student advisers preparing pre-arrival guidance for incoming students.
If you are entering on a different visa type (J-1, H-1B, B-1/B-2), the inspection process is similar but the document requirements differ. If you have a prior immigration violation, overstay, or removal order, you should consult an immigration attorney before travelling — the CBP systems will flag your record and the officer may have grounds to deny entry regardless of a valid visa.
Primary inspection: the conversation at the booth
After landing, you will proceed to the CBP inspection area. There are usually separate lines for US citizens, permanent residents, and nonimmigrant visitors — follow the signs. At the booth, the CBP officer will scan your passport, review your I-20 and visa, and may ask questions. Common questions include: "What is the purpose of your visit?" (answer: you are entering as an F-1 student to study [programme] at [university]), "Where will you be staying?" (state your university name and city, or your specific address if you have housing arranged), "How are you funding your studies?" (refer to your I-20 financial information and have supporting documents accessible).
Answer questions directly and honestly. Do not make jokes about working illegally, overstaying, or other immigration violations — CBP officers are trained to take statements at face value, and a joke about immigration can have real consequences. If you do not understand a question, ask the officer to repeat or clarify. You are not required to hand over your phone or social media passwords at primary inspection, though CBP has authority to search electronic devices at secondary inspection.
If the primary officer is satisfied, they will stamp your passport, annotate your I-20, and admit you in F-1 status. The admission stamp may be electronic (no physical stamp in your passport) — your I-94 record online confirms your admission. You will then proceed to baggage claim and customs.
Secondary inspection: why it happens and how to handle it
If the primary officer refers you to secondary inspection, you will be escorted to a separate waiting area. This is not necessarily adverse — many referrals are routine. Common reasons for F-1 students include: a mismatch between the visa and I-20 information (different programme, different university), a SEVIS record flag requiring manual clearance, the officer wanting a supervisor to verify your documents, or random selection.
During secondary inspection: wait until your name is called — secondary can take 15 minutes to several hours depending on caseload. Do not use your phone unless instructed by an officer — CBP waiting areas typically prohibit phone use. Answer questions honestly. If asked to unlock your phone or laptop, you may comply or decline — but refusal may prolong the inspection. CBP officers in secondary have access to SEVIS, law enforcement databases, and your full immigration history. If your documents are in order and your answers are consistent, most F-1 students are cleared and admitted. CBP may also call your university's DSO to verify your enrolment — this is why you should have the DSO emergency contact number accessible.

F-1 visa for community college students: the rule in plain English
F-1 study is available at SEVP-certified community colleges when the student has a valid I-20, full-time academic plan, funds, and temporary-student intent. Community colleges — also called junior colleges or two-year colleges — offer associate degrees, certificates, and transfer pathways to four-year universities. For international students, community colleges can be a cost-effective entry point into the US education system, provided the institution holds SEVP certification and the student maintains full-time F-1 status throughout the program.
The legal framework: The F-1 visa is authorised under INA 101(a)(15)(F) and regulated by 8 CFR § 214.2(f). Community college students are subject to the same F-1 regulations as university students: full-time enrolment (12 credits per semester for undergraduates), valid I-20 maintenance, work restrictions, and timely program completion. The key difference is that community college programs are typically two-year associate degree programs or shorter certificate programs, which can affect OPT eligibility (requires at least one academic year of study) and the student's overall academic trajectory.
Why choose a community college: Lower tuition (often $5,000–$15,000 per year vs $20,000–$60,000 at four-year universities), smaller class sizes, English-language support programs, flexible scheduling, and established transfer pathways to four-year universities through articulation agreements. Many community colleges have dedicated international student offices and DSOs who support F-1 students through the transfer process. Community colleges in states with large international student populations — California, Texas, Washington, New York, and Florida — often have the most developed international student infrastructure.
Who this guide is for
International students considering an associate degree or certificate at a US community college as a starting point for their US education. This includes students who plan to transfer to a four-year university after two years (2+2 pathway), students seeking technical or vocational training at SEVP-certified community colleges, students with limited funding who want a lower-cost entry into the US education system, and students who need to improve English-language skills before transferring to a university program.
This guide is also for students who have been refused an F-1 visa for a four-year university and are considering community college as an alternative pathway. A well-documented community college application with a clear transfer plan can succeed where a university application did not, provided the student addresses the underlying reason for the prior refusal (such as insufficient ties to the home country or unclear academic goals).
SEVP certification and community college eligibility
Before applying for an F-1 visa for community college, confirm that the institution holds SEVP certification. SEVP certification means the school is approved by the US Department of Homeland Security to admit F-1 students and issue Form I-20. The school must have a valid Form I-17 on file with USCIS. You can verify certification using the DHS Study in the States School Search tool. If the school is not in the SEVP database, it cannot issue an I-20, and you cannot obtain an F-1 visa to attend that institution regardless of admission or payment.
What SEVP certification means for students: An SEVP-certified community college has a Designated School Official (DSO) who manages SEVIS records, issues I-20s, and provides guidance on F-1 regulations. The DSO is your primary point of contact for status maintenance, program extensions, transfers, and employment authorisation. Before enrolling, meet with the DSO to confirm the school's policies on full-time enrolment, reduced course loads, online courses, and transfer procedures. Some community colleges limit the number of international students they admit or have specific English-language requirements beyond what the DSO manages.
Documents and evidence to prepare
I-20 form: Issued by the community college after admission and SEVIS record creation. Verify that the I-20 lists the correct program, start date, and estimated cost. The I-20 is the most important document for the visa application and for maintaining F-1 status. Keep the I-20 with your passport at all times while in the US.

01 214(b) is the most common F-1 refusal ground — it is not a finding of ineligibility, only that the officer was not persuaded on nonimmigrant intent or funding. 
02 There is no mandatory waiting period to reapply, but you must demonstrate changed circumstances with new evidence. 
03 Each reapplication requires a new DS-160 form and visa fee; the SEVIS I-901 fee remains valid as long as the I-20 is active. 
04 A cover letter explaining what changed — and what new evidence you are submitting — helps the second officer focus their review. 
05 214(b) refusals do not trigger bars or penalties. A pattern of refusals without changed circumstances, however, can raise credibility concerns in future applications. 
What 214(b) actually says — and what it means for your application
Section 214(b) of the Immigration and Nationality Act states that every nonimmigrant visa applicant is presumed to be an intending immigrant unless they convince the consular officer otherwise. For F-1 applicants specifically, this means you must demonstrate: (1) you intend to pursue a full course of study at an accredited US institution, (2) you have sufficient funds to cover your first year of tuition and living expenses (with a credible plan for subsequent years), and (3) you maintain a residence abroad that you have no intention of abandoning.
When a consular officer refuses a visa under 214(b), the refusal notice does not specify which element was not satisfied — it simply states that the officer was not persuaded. The officer may have said something during the interview that hints at the reason (“your ties to Nigeria are not strong enough” or “I am not satisfied your sponsor has sufficient income”), but the written notice will not include this detail. Reconstructing the refusal reason requires analyzing what you presented and what the officer focused on during the interview.
A 214(b) refusal is not a bar. It does not trigger a period of inadmissibility, does not need to be waived, and does not prevent you from travelling to the US on other visa categories (though the new application will also be evaluated under 214(b) for that category). The refusal becomes part of your visa record and must be disclosed on all future visa applications. Multiple 214(b) refusals without changed circumstances can make future applications harder, but a single 214(b) refusal followed by a successful application with stronger evidence is a common and non-prejudicial sequence.
Who this guide is for — and who it isn't
This guide is for international students whose F-1 visa application has been refused under INA 214(b) and who want to reapply with a stronger case. You may have received a verbal refusal at the interview window or a written refusal notice by email or post. Either way, the path forward is the same: identify the weakness, gather new evidence, and submit a fresh application that addresses it. This guide is also for students who have not yet applied but want to understand what leads to refusals and how to avoid them.
This guide is not for applicants refused under INA 212(a) grounds (health, criminal, security, fraud, or previous immigration violations). If your refusal notice cites a paragraph other than 214(b), the remedies are different and may require legal advice. It is also not for applicants who have been removed from the US or who have accrued unlawful presence — those situations involve bars under INA 212(a)(9) that a fresh visa application cannot cure without a waiver.
Step one: diagnose what went wrong
Reconstructing the refusal reason is the most important step. The consular officer's questions during the interview are the best clue. Common lines of questioning and what they signal:
Questions about your school choice: “Why this school?” “Why this program?” “How did you hear about this university?” — The officer may be concerned that the school is not legitimate or that the program does not match your stated career goals. If the school is a lesser-known institution or a community college, bring evidence of accreditation and program quality. Be specific about why this program fits your career plan.
Questions about funding: “Who is paying?” “What does your sponsor do?” “How long have they had this money?” — The officer may be concerned that the funds are not genuine or that the sponsor cannot sustain the cost across multiple years. Large deposits made shortly before the statement date are a red flag. Business-owner sponsors face higher scrutiny because business income can be irregular.
Questions about return plans: “What will you do after graduation?” “Do you have a job offer at home?” “What about your family?” — The officer may be concerned that you lack sufficient ties to your home country. A vague answer like “I will come back and find a job” without a specific industry, company, or career path signals weak ties. Name a specific role, industry, or business you plan to return to.
Questions about US relatives: “Do you have family in the US?” — The officer is assessing immigrant intent. If you have a US citizen or permanent resident relative, disclose it honestly on the DS-160 and be prepared to explain why you still intend to return home. A discrepancy between your DS-160 answers and your oral answers about family is a common 214(b) trigger.
Step two: gather new evidence
Once you have identified the likely refusal reason, gather evidence that directly addresses it. Do not resubmit the same documents you used the first time. New evidence could include:
For ties concerns: Property title documents or land registry certificates, a letter from a home-country employer confirming a reserved position, evidence of ongoing business ownership, family census documents showing dependents, or proof of enrollment in a professional

US family-based visas guide
US family-based immigration covers marriage green cards, K-1 fiancé visas, conditional permanent residence (I-751), and DACA renewal. The right path depends on where you are — inside the US or abroad, married or engaged, and whether your spouse is a US citizen or permanent resident. This guide orients you to the cluster, explains the key decision points — including the choice between adjustment of status and consular processing — and routes you to the article that matches your situation. The cluster also covers F-2 dependent status for spouses and children of F-1 students. Every guide in this cluster is attorney-reviewed.

Last updated 2026-05-19 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
The 5 most important things to know
Adjustment of status (Form I-485) is for eligible applicants already inside the US; consular processing is for applicants abroad or those who cannot adjust. The wrong choice can trigger a 3-year or 10-year bar if unlawful presence or entry-history issues exist. See USCIS policy guidance.
A K-1 visa holder must marry the US citizen petitioner within 90 days of entry. After marriage, file I-485 to adjust status. The K-1 does not permit employment until the EAD or green card is issued, and the beneficiary cannot adjust through a different petitioner without leaving.
Form I-751 to remove conditions must be filed during the 90-day window before the 2-year conditional green card expires. Filing within this window extends conditional residence under the receipt rule. Late filings require a written explanation and USCIS discretion.
The most common financial sponsorship mistake is using the wrong household size on Form I-864. The household size includes the sponsor, spouse, dependents, other sponsored persons, and the intending immigrant. Using too small a household size makes the income requirement appear met when it is not.
DACA renewals are accepted and processed in 2026; initial requests are accepted but not processed due to ongoing litigation. File Forms I-821D, I-765, and I-765WS between 150 and 120 days before expiration to avoid a gap in work authorization.
Choose your path
Family-based immigration has several distinct routes. Pick the guide that matches your current situation. If you are already married to a US citizen or permanent resident, start with the marriage green card checklist. If you are engaged, the K-1 guide explains the 90-day rule and the AOS process. If you already hold a conditional green card, the I-751 guide covers the removal-of-conditions window and waiver categories.

US Family Visa FAQ
Attorney-reviewed answers about marriage green cards, K-1 fiancé visas, I-751 removal of conditions, DACA renewal, and I-485 work authorization. This FAQ aggregates the most common decision points from our US family immigration articles.
This FAQ is for spouses, fiancés, and family members of US citizens or lawful permanent residents who are navigating the marriage green card process, the K-1 fiancé visa route, or the removal of conditions on a two-year green card. The questions below reflect the most common uncertainties we see from family-based immigration applicants in USCIS forums and from our own document review clients. Each answer has been reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera, a licensed California attorney (CA Bar #298948), and draws on the Immigration and Nationality Act, USCIS policy guidance, and current processing rules in effect as of mid-2026.
Family-based immigration involves several interacting USCIS forms and processes that change frequently. Filing fees, form editions, and processing times are updated periodically, and the policies around DACA renewals continue to evolve with ongoing litigation. The answers below reflect the current published guidance as of July 2026. You should verify the latest form editions and fees on uscis.gov before filing.
The question list below serves as a table of contents for the topics covered here. For deeper treatment of each subject, the linked articles at the bottom of this page provide step-by-step guidance, document checklists, and the specific USCIS policy references that apply to each process.
How to use this FAQ
Choose the path that matches your facts first (AOS vs consular, K-1 vs IR-1/CR-1, I-751 joint vs waiver) — see the family visas pillar .
Confirm current fees, form editions, and DACA posture on uscis.gov the day you file — FAQ text is orientation, not a live fee schedule.
Complex unlawful-presence, criminal, or prior-refusal facts need licensed counsel before you pick a filing path.
Last updated 2026-07-14 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
Should I choose adjustment of status or consular processing for my marriage green card?
Adjustment of status (Form I-485) is available if you are already in the United States in a status that permits adjustment, such as a valid nonimmigrant visa or parole. It allows you to remain in the US while the case is pending and typically includes work authorization and advance parole for travel. Consular processing is for applicants outside the US or those who cannot adjust status, such as entrants without inspection or those with certain inadmissibility issues. Consular processing is usually faster for petition approval but requires an interview at a US consulate abroad and cannot be completed while inside the US. If you have any history of unlawful presence, visa overstay, or entry without inspection, consult an immigration attorney before choosing a path, because the wrong choice can trigger a 3-year or 10-year bar.
What is the 90-day rule for K-1 fiancé visa holders?
A K-1 visa holder must marry the US citizen petitioner within 90 days of entering the United States. The 90-day clock starts on the date of admission, not the date the visa was issued. If the marriage does not occur within 90 days, the K-1 holder is generally required to depart the United States. After the marriage, the K-1 holder must file Form I-485 to adjust status to lawful permanent residence. The K-1 route does not permit employment until the I-485-based Employment Authorization Document is approved or the green card is issued. A K-1 holder cannot adjust status through a different petitioner without leaving the US and starting a new petition.
When should I file Form I-751 to remove conditions on my green card?
You must file Form I-751 during the 90-day window before your 2-year conditional green card expires. Filing within this window extends your conditional residence under the receipt rule, meaning your status continues while the application is pending even if the card expires. If you file late, you must include a written explanation for the delay and request that USCIS excuse it. If you are no longer married to the petitioner due to divorce, abuse, or death, you may file a waiver of the joint filing requirement at any time, even before the 90-day window or after the card has expired. Keep evidence that the marriage was entered in good faith, such as joint financial records, insurance policies, and photographs spanning the relationship.
What documents best prove a bona fide marriage for I-130 or I-751?
USCIS looks for evidence of a shared life, not just a wedding ceremony. Strong evidence includes joint bank statements, lease or mortgage documents showing both names, insurance policies naming each other as beneficiaries, joint tax filings, utility bills, and dated photographs with locations spanning the relationship. If you have children together, birth certificates and medical records strengthen the case. A common mistake is submitting only wedding photos and love letters. If you lived apart for periods, explain why with supporting documents such as job offer letters or school enrollment records. For I-751, you must also show that the marriage was genuine at the time it was entered, not just that it is still ongoing.
Can I renew DACA in 2026?
Yes, if you currently hold DACA or previously held DACA that expired within the last year, you can file a renewal request in 2026. Renewals require Form I-821D (Consideration of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals), Form I-765 (Application for Employment Authorization), and Form I-765WS (Worksheet). You may file online or by mail. As of 2026, initial DACA requests are accepted by USCIS but are not being processed due to ongoing litigation. Form DS-160 — Online Nonimmigrant Visa Application
Form DS-160 is the online application that every nonimmigrant visa applicant must complete before scheduling a visa interview at a US consulate. The form collects biographical information, travel plans, employment history, educational background, and security-related questions. Once submitted, the form generates a confirmation page with a barcode that you must bring to your interview.
The DS-160 is not adjudicated on its own. It is a data-collection tool that gives the consular officer a structured overview of your background before the interview. The officer uses the DS-160 responses to ask targeted questions and to verify consistency between what you wrote and what you say in person. Discrepancies are one of the leading causes of visa refusal.
This guide explains what Form DS-160 is, who needs to file it, what information it collects, and how to avoid the most common mistakes that lead to interview problems or delays.
Who files this form
Form DS-160 is filed by anyone applying for a nonimmigrant visa to the United States. This includes F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, B-1/B-2 tourists, H-1B workers, and every other visa category except immigrant visas. Each applicant completes their own DS-160, including dependents. A parent may assist a minor child, but the responses must reflect the child's actual circumstances.
The form is completed online through the State Department's Consular Electronic Application Center. You do not mail a paper copy. After submission, you print the confirmation page and bring it to your visa interview. The DS-160 must be submitted before you can schedule the interview, and the information on the form should match your supporting documents exactly.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form DS-160 is to collect standardized biographical and background information from every nonimmigrant visa applicant. The State Department uses this information to screen applicants for security concerns, to verify identity, and to provide consular officers with a complete profile before the interview.
The form also serves as a legal record. By submitting the DS-160, you certify under penalty of perjury that the information is true and correct. Misrepresentation on the DS-160 can result in a permanent inadmissibility finding under INA §212(a)(6)(C)(i), which bars you from ever receiving a US visa. Accuracy is not optional — it is a legal requirement.
Key sections
Personal information: name, date and place of birth, passport details, and national ID number
Travel information: purpose of trip, intended dates of travel, and contact in the United States
Family information: parents, spouse, and children, including their US immigration status if applicable
Work and education: current and previous employers, schools attended, and field of study
Security and background: questions about criminal history, health, and prior immigration violations
Photo upload: a digital passport-style photograph that meets State Department specifications
Common mistakes
Inconsistencies between the DS-160 and supporting documents such as the I-20 or bank statements
Listing a travel date that has already passed or is unrealistically soon
Providing an incomplete employment history or omitting gaps between jobs
Answering the security questions incorrectly due to misunderstanding the question
Uploading a photo that does not meet the State Department specification
Not saving the confirmation page with the barcode — you cannot enter the interview without it

Form DS-2019 — Certificate of Eligibility for Exchange Visitor (J-1) Status
Form DS-2019 is not a form you fill out and mail to a government agency. It is a certificate issued by a designated program sponsor — a US university, research institution, hospital, or cultural organization that has been authorized by the Department of State to administer exchange visitor programs. The DS-2019 certifies that you have been accepted into a legitimate exchange program and that the sponsor has the resources and structure to support your participation.
Every J-1 exchange visitor receives a DS-2019 before applying for a J-1 visa at a US consulate. The document is also what you present to the Customs and Border Protection officer when you enter the United States. Once you are in the country, your program sponsor updates your DS-2019 whenever your program end date changes, when you transfer to a different sponsor, or when you need a travel signature for re-entry after international travel.
Unlike forms filed with USCIS, the DS-2019 is not fee-based. The program sponsor issues it as part of their sponsorship duties. However, sponsors may charge program fees, administrative fees, or insurance fees that are separate from the visa application fee paid to the Department of State. This guide explains what Form DS-2019 is, who issues it, what information it contains, and the most common mistakes exchange visitors make.
Who files this form
Form DS-2019 is not filed by the exchange visitor. It is issued by the program sponsor's Responsible Officer or Alternate Responsible Officer after the visitor has been accepted into a designated exchange program. The sponsor enters the visitor's information into the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System and generates the DS-2019 from the system. The visitor then uses the DS-2019 to apply for a J-1 visa at a US consulate.
After the visitor enters the United States, the Responsible Officer is responsible for maintaining the accuracy of the DS-2019. Any change to the visitor's program, funding, or personal information must be reported to the Responsible Officer, who updates SEVIS and issues a new DS-2019 if necessary. The visitor does not file anything with USCIS to update their DS-2019 — the sponsor does this through SEVIS.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form DS-2019 is to certify that a nonimmigrant has been accepted into a bona fide exchange visitor program administered by a Department of State-designated sponsor. The document serves as the foundation for the visitor's J-1 visa application, entry into the United States, and maintenance of lawful J-1 status throughout their program.
The DS-2019 also governs specific permissions and restrictions. The program start and end dates on the DS-2019 define the boundaries of the visitor's authorized stay. The category code on the form determines what type of exchange program the visitor is participating in — for example, student, research scholar, professor, intern, or trainee. The funding section documents how the visitor's expenses will be covered. And the form must be endorsed by the Responsible Officer before the visitor travels outside the United States and seeks re-entry.
Key sections
Box 1 — Name of program sponsor and sponsor number
Box 2 — Name of exchange visitor and date of birth
Box 3 — Exchange visitor category: student, research scholar, professor, intern, trainee, etc.
Box 4 — Program start and end dates
Box 5 — Funding sources: personal, government, institutional, or other
Box 7 — Travel validation: Responsible Officer endorsement for re-entry
Common mistakes
Letting the program end date pass without requesting an extension from the Responsible Officer
Traveling without a valid travel signature from the Responsible Officer — the signature is valid for 12 months
Assuming the DS-2019 expiration date is the same as the J-1 visa expiration date — they are independent
Failing to report a change of funding source or program objective to the Responsible Officer promptly
Not understanding that some J-1 categories require a two-year home residency requirement after program completion
Losing the original DS-2019 and not requesting a replacement from the sponsor before travel

Form I-129 — Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker
Form I-129 is the petition an employer files with USCIS to bring a foreign national worker to the United States in a temporary nonimmigrant status. It is not filed by the worker — it is filed by the employer, who is called the petitioner. The worker is called the beneficiary. The form covers multiple visa categories including H-1B for specialty occupations, L-1 for intracompany transferees, O-1 for individuals with extraordinary ability, and several lesser-known categories.
Each visa category has its own classification supplement that accompanies the I-129 — the H Classification Supplement for H-1B petitions, the L Classification Supplement for L-1 petitions, and the O and P Classifications Supplement for O-1 petitions. These supplements ask for category-specific information such as the job description, wage level, and evidence that the beneficiary meets the requirements.
The I-129 process is employer-driven from start to finish. The employer must demonstrate that the position qualifies for the requested visa category, that the beneficiary meets the requirements, and that the employer will pay the required wage. This guide explains what Form I-129 is, who files it, what the process involves, and the most common mistakes employers make.
Who files this form
Form I-129 is filed by a US employer who wants to employ a foreign national in a temporary nonimmigrant worker status. The employer is the petitioner, and the foreign national is the beneficiary. The form cannot be filed by the worker themselves, although the worker may need to provide documents and information to the employer for inclusion in the petition.
The employer must be a legitimate US entity with a tax identification number and the ability to pay the required wage. For H-1B specialty occupation petitions, the employer must also file a Labor Condition Application with the Department of Labor before filing the I-129. For L-1 intracompany transferee petitions, the employer must demonstrate a qualifying relationship between the US entity and a foreign parent, subsidiary, affiliate, or branch office. For O-1 extraordinary ability petitions, the employer or an agent may file on behalf of the beneficiary.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-129 is to allow USCIS to evaluate whether a US employer has a legitimate temporary need for a foreign worker and whether the proposed position and beneficiary meet the statutory and regulatory requirements for the requested nonimmigrant visa category. If approved, USCIS issues a Form I-797 Approval Notice, which the beneficiary can use to apply for a visa at a US consulate or, if already in the United States, to change or extend their status.
The I-129 petition is specific to the employer, the position, and the location. If any of these change significantly, the employer may need to file an amended petition. For H-1B workers, a change in work location may require a new Labor Condition Application and an amended I-129 if the new location is outside the existing labor condition application area. The petition does not grant the beneficiary permanent residence — it authorizes only temporary employment in the specified position.
Key sections
Part 1 — Petitioner information: employer name, address, EIN, and contact information
Part 2 — Beneficiary information: name, date and place of birth, country of citizenship, and passport number
Part 3 — Processing information: requested visa classification, requested action, and prior petitions
Part 4 — Supplemental information for the specific visa category: H-1B, L-1, O-1, etc.
Part 5 — Employer statement and signature
Common mistakes
Filing the I-129 without first obtaining an approved Labor Condition Application for H-1B petitions
Misclassifying the job title or wage level on the Labor Condition Application
Failing to demonstrate a qualifying corporate relationship for L-1 petitions
Submitting insufficient evidence of extraordinary ability for O-1 petitions
Not filing an amended I-129 when the beneficiary's work location changes significantly
Paying the wrong filing fee — check the current USCIS fee schedule for Form I-129 before submitting

Form I-130 — Petition for Alien Relative
Form I-130 is the petition a US citizen or lawful permanent resident files to establish a qualifying family relationship with a relative who wants to immigrate to the United States. It is the first step in most family-based immigration cases, but filing the I-130 does not grant the relative any immigration status or permission to enter the country. It merely establishes that a valid family relationship exists under the Immigration and Nationality Act.
The form is filed with USCIS and requires evidence of the petitioner's status, evidence of the claimed relationship, and the filing fee. The required evidence varies significantly depending on the relationship — a spousal petition requires a marriage certificate and evidence of a bona fide marriage, while a parent petition requires a birth certificate showing the biological or legal relationship. Step-parent and adoptive relationships require additional documentation.
After USCIS approves the I-130, the case moves to either consular processing at a US embassy abroad or adjustment of status inside the United States via Form I-485, depending on where the beneficiary currently lives and whether a visa number is immediately available. This guide explains what Form I-130 is, who files it, what evidence is required, and the most common mistakes petitioners make.
Who files this form
Form I-130 is filed by a US citizen or lawful permanent resident who wants to sponsor a qualifying relative for immigration to the United States. US citizens can petition for a spouse, unmarried children under 21, married children of any age, siblings, and parents. Lawful permanent residents can petition for a spouse and unmarried children, but not for parents, married children, or siblings.
The person filing the petition is called the petitioner. The relative being sponsored is called the beneficiary. The petitioner must prove both their own US citizenship or permanent resident status and the claimed relationship to the beneficiary. If the petitioner is a US citizen by naturalization, they must include their naturalization certificate. If they are a lawful permanent resident, they must include a copy of their green card.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-130 is to establish that a qualifying family relationship exists between a US citizen or lawful permanent resident and a foreign national relative. USCIS reviews the petition to verify the petitioner's status, the beneficiary's identity, and the claimed relationship through documentary evidence. The form does not grant the beneficiary any immigration benefit on its own — it is a prerequisite step.
Once approved, the I-130 petition creates a place in line for the beneficiary. For immediate relatives of US citizens — spouses, unmarried children under 21, and parents — visa numbers are always available, so the case can proceed immediately to the next step. For other family categories, the beneficiary must wait for their priority date to become current according to the Department of State Visa Bulletin before they can apply for a green card.
Key sections
Part 1 — Relationship: the specific family relationship you are petitioning for
Part 2 — Information about you: the petitioner's name, address, citizenship status, and A-number
Part 3 — Biographic information: ethnicity, height, weight, eye and hair color
Part 4 — Information about your relative: the beneficiary's name, address, date and place of birth
Part 5 — Information about the beneficiary's prior marriages and family
Part 6 — Address history and employment history for the beneficiary
Common mistakes
Filing for a relationship that is not eligible — for example, a lawful permanent resident cannot petition for a parent or sibling
Submitting a birth certificate or marriage certificate that is not translated into English by a certified translator
Failing to include evidence of the petitioner's US citizenship or permanent resident status
Submitting a photocopy of a vital record when the original or a certified copy is required
Not including evidence of a bona fide marriage for spousal petitions — joint accounts, leases, photos, and affidavits from friends
Paying the wrong filing fee — check the current USCIS fee schedule for Form I-130 before submitting
Official sources

Form I-20 — Certificate of Eligibility for F-1 Student Status
Form I-20 is not a form you fill out and mail to USCIS. It is a certificate issued by your Designated School Official — a staff member at your US educational institution who is authorized by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program to manage international student records. The I-20 certifies that you have been admitted to a full-time program of study, that you have demonstrated sufficient financial resources, and that the school has reported your enrollment in the SEVIS database.
Every F-1 student receives an I-20 before applying for a visa at a US consulate. The document is also what you present to the Customs and Border Protection officer when you enter the United States. Once enrolled, your DSO updates your I-20 whenever your program end date changes, when you apply for OPT, when you transfer schools, or when you travel and need a signature for re-entry.
This guide explains what Form I-20 is, who issues it, what information it contains, and how it governs your status as an F-1 student.
Who files this form
Form I-20 is not filed by the student. It is issued by the school's Designated School Official after the student has been admitted to a SEVP-certified institution and has demonstrated the ability to pay tuition and living expenses. The student then uses the I-20 to apply for an F-1 visa at a US consulate and to enter the United States.
After enrollment, the DSO is responsible for maintaining the accuracy of the I-20. Any change to your program, your funding, or your personal information must be reported to the DSO, who updates SEVIS and issues a new I-20 if necessary. You do not file anything with USCIS to update your I-20 — the DSO does this through the SEVIS system.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-20 is to certify that a nonimmigrant student has been admitted to a full-time academic or vocational program at a SEVP-certified school and has the financial means to complete that program. The document serves as the foundation for the student's F-1 visa application, entry into the United States, and maintenance of lawful status throughout their studies.
The I-20 also governs specific permissions and restrictions. The program start and end dates on the I-20 define the boundaries of your authorized stay. The I-20 must be endorsed by your DSO before you travel outside the United States and seek re-entry. And the OPT recommendation printed on page 2 of the I-20 is what authorizes you to file Form I-765 for work authorization after graduation.
Key sections
Page 1 — Student information: name, date of birth, country of citizenship, and SEVIS ID number
Page 1 — School information: name, address, and SEVP certification number
Page 1 — Program of study: degree level, major field, program start and end dates
Page 1 — Financial certification: estimated costs and funding sources
Page 2 — Employment authorization: DSO recommendation for OPT or CPT
Page 3 — Travel signature: DSO endorsement for re-entry after international travel
Common mistakes
Letting the I-20 program end date pass without requesting an extension from the DSO
Traveling without a valid DSO signature on page 3 — the signature is valid for 12 months for enrolled students, but only 6 months once you are on post-completion OPT
Assuming the I-20 expiration date is the same as the visa expiration date — they are independent
Failing to report a change of major or program level to the DSO promptly
Not understanding that the I-20 OPT recommendation must be dated within 30 days of filing Form I-765
Losing the original I-20 and not requesting a replacement from the DSO before travel

Form I-485 — Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status
Form I-485 is the application you file when you are already in the United States and want to become a lawful permanent resident — commonly known as getting a green card. Unlike consular processing, which happens at a US embassy abroad, adjustment of status happens entirely within the United States through USCIS. You do not leave the country during the process, and if your case is pending, you may be eligible for work authorization and advance parole while you wait.
The form is filed after an immigrant visa petition — such as Form I-130 for family-based cases or Form I-140 for employment-based cases — has been approved and a visa number is available. For immediate relatives of US citizens, the visa number is always available, so the I-485 can be filed concurrently with the I-130. For everyone else, the priority date must be current on the Department of State Visa Bulletin before filing.
The I-485 is one of the most document-intensive forms in the immigration system. It requires biometrics, a medical examination by a USCIS-approved civil surgeon, extensive background information, and evidence that you are admissible to the United States. This guide explains what Form I-485 is, who can file it, what the process involves, and the most common mistakes applicants make.
Who files this form
Form I-485 is filed by foreign nationals who are physically present in the United States and eligible to adjust their status to lawful permanent resident. The most common categories are immediate relatives of US citizens, family-sponsored preference immigrants with an approved I-130 and a current priority date, employment-based immigrants with an approved I-140, asylees who have been granted asylum and have waited one year, and refugees who have been admitted and have waited one year.
To be eligible, you must generally have been inspected and admitted or paroled into the United States, and you must not be inadmissible under any ground listed in INA section 212. Certain grounds of inadmissibility can be waived with Form I-601 or I-602, but not all. If you entered the United States without inspection, you are generally not eligible to adjust status unless you fall under a narrow exception such as section 245(i) or the LIFE Act.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-485 is to allow a foreign national who is already in the United States to become a lawful permanent resident without leaving the country. USCIS reviews the application to confirm that the applicant is eligible for adjustment of status, that they are not inadmissible, and that all required documents are present and authentic.
The application process includes a biometrics appointment for fingerprinting and background checks, a medical examination to screen for communicable diseases and required vaccinations, and potentially an interview where the applicant answers questions under oath about their application and eligibility. If approved, USCIS mails the green card to the applicant's address on file. If denied, the applicant may be placed in removal proceedings depending on the reason for denial.
Key sections
Part 1 — Information about you: name, address, A-number, date and place of birth, and nationality
Part 2 — Application type: the basis for your adjustment — family, employment, asylee, refugee, or other
Part 3 — Additional information about you: parents, marital history, and children
Part 4 — Address and employment history for the past five years
Part 5 — Information about your admission and criminal history
Part 6 — Biographic information and signature
Common mistakes
Filing before a visa number is available — check the Visa Bulletin before submitting
Failing to disclose a prior arrest, even if the charges were dismissed — USCIS will find it in background checks
Using a medical exam from a doctor who is not a USCIS-approved civil surgeon
Not updating your address with USCIS within 10 days of moving — this can cause you to miss important notices
Working without authorization before receiving an Employment Authorization Document
Paying the wrong filing fee — check the current USCIS fee schedule for Form I-485 before submitting

Form I-539 — Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status
Form I-539 is the document you file when you want to stay in the United States longer than your current nonimmigrant visa allows, or when you want to change from one nonimmigrant category to another without leaving the country. The most common filers are B-1/B-2 visitors extending a tourist stay, F-1 students requesting a program extension, and J-1 exchange visitors seeking a waiver or extension.
The form is filed with USCIS before your current authorized stay expires. Filing on time creates a period of authorized stay while the application is pending, but it does not guarantee approval. If you file after your status has already expired, you must demonstrate that the delay was due to extraordinary circumstances beyond your control.
This guide explains what Form I-539 is, who needs to file it, what the process involves, and the most common mistakes applicants make.
Who files this form
Form I-539 is filed by nonimmigrants who are already in the United States and need either an extension of their current status or a change to a different nonimmigrant category. Common filers include B-1/B-2 visitors whose travel plans have changed, F-1 students who need more time to complete their degree program, and J-1 exchange visitors who need additional time for research or training.
Dependents in certain visa categories also file Form I-539. For example, an F-2 dependent who wants to change status to F-1 student, or a B-2 dependent who needs to extend their stay along with the principal visa holder. Each category has different evidentiary requirements, and the burden of proof is on the applicant to show that they have maintained their current status and that the extension or change is warranted.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-539 is to request permission from USCIS to remain in the United States beyond the expiration date on your Form I-94, or to switch to a different nonimmigrant status without leaving the country and applying for a new visa at a consulate. If approved, USCIS updates your status in its records and issues a new I-94 with the extended or changed status.
For extensions, the key question is whether you still meet the requirements of your current visa category and whether your circumstances justify additional time. For changes of status, USCIS evaluates whether you are eligible for the new category and whether you have maintained lawful status up to the date of filing. A change of status is not available for every category — for example, changing from B-1/B-2 to F-1 is permitted but heavily scrutinized — you cannot begin studying until USCIS approves the change, and USCIS may deny it if your B visa was not annotated as a prospective student.
Key sections
Part 1 — Information about you: name, date of birth, country of birth, and passport information
Part 2 — Application type: extension of stay, change of status, or reinstatement
Part 3 — Processing information: current status, date of entry, and I-94 record number
Part 4 — Additional information about the applicant: explanation of why the extension or change is needed
Part 5 — Applicant statement and signature
Common mistakes
Filing after the I-94 expiration date without demonstrating extraordinary circumstances
Failing to include evidence of financial support for the extended or changed period
Requesting a change of status that is not permitted under USCIS rules
Omitting the I-94 record or submitting an expired I-94
Not explaining clearly why the extension or change is necessary
Paying the wrong filing fee — check the current USCIS fee schedule before submitting

Form I-765 — Application for Employment Authorization
Form I-765 is the document you file when you need permission to work in the United States as a noncitizen. Most F-1 students first encounter it when applying for Optional Practical Training after graduation, but the form is also used for other categories including asylum applicants, adjustment-of-status applicants, and certain dependents. The form is filed with USCIS, and approval produces an Employment Authorization Document — the physical card commonly called an EAD.
The form itself is deceptively short, but the supporting evidence and timing rules are where most filers stumble. A single wrong eligibility-category code, an expired I-20 recommendation, or a missing prior EAD can trigger a rejection that delays work authorization by weeks or months. Understanding what the form asks for, and what USCIS verifies behind the scenes, is the best way to avoid those delays.
This guide explains what Form I-765 is, who needs to file it, how the process works, and the most common mistakes filers make. For field-by-field review of your completed form, see the I-765 OPT review service.
Who files this form
Form I-765 is filed by noncitizens who are in the United States and need work authorization. The largest group of filers are F-1 students applying for post-completion OPT or the STEM OPT extension. Other filers include applicants for asylum, applicants adjusting status to lawful permanent resident, certain spouses of visa holders, and refugees.
For F-1 students specifically, the filing is tied to your academic stage. Pre-completion OPT filers are still enrolled; post-completion OPT filers have graduated or are about to graduate; STEM OPT extension filers have already been approved for post-completion OPT and hold a degree in a designated STEM field. Each stage uses a different eligibility-category code on the form, and choosing the wrong code is one of the most common rejection triggers.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-765 is to request permission to work in the United States. USCIS reviews the form to confirm that you belong to a category eligible for employment authorization and that your supporting documents prove your eligibility. If approved, USCIS issues an Employment Authorization Document that lists your photo, name, alien registration number, and the validity period of your work authorization.
For OPT filers, the EAD is what you show employers to prove you are legally authorized to work. The card is also what you use to complete the I-9 verification process when you start a job. Without an approved I-765 and a valid EAD, you cannot legally begin employment in the United States, even if you have a job offer in hand.
Key sections
Part 1 — Reason for applying: new application, renewal, or replacement of a lost or damaged EAD
Part 2 — Information about you: name, address, alien registration number, and USCIS online account number
Part 3 — Applicant statement and signature: declaration that the information is true and correct
Part 4 — Eligibility category: the three-letter code that determines which rule authorizes your work permission
Part 5 — Interpreter and preparer information: only completed if someone helped you fill out the form
Common mistakes
Selecting the wrong eligibility-category code — pre-completion, post-completion, and STEM OPT each have a different code
Filing outside the post-completion OPT window — the I-765 can be filed up to 90 days before your program end date and no later than 60 days after it
Forgetting to include the I-20 with the OPT recommendation dated within 30 days of filing
Submitting photos that do not meet the current USCIS passport-style specification
Omitting a prior EAD, which USCIS requires to verify your immigration history
Paying the wrong filing fee — check the current USCIS fee schedule before submitting

Form I-864 — Affidavit of Support
Form I-864 is the legally binding contract that a financial sponsor signs to promise that an immigrant will not become a public charge. It is required in most family-based immigration cases and some employment-based cases where the petitioner is a relative. The form creates a legal obligation for the sponsor to support the immigrant at 125 percent of the federal poverty guidelines until the immigrant becomes a US citizen, has worked 40 qualifying quarters, dies, or permanently leaves the United States.
The sponsor is typically the same person who filed the immigrant petition — for example, the US citizen spouse who filed Form I-130. However, if the petitioner does not meet the income requirement, a joint sponsor can also file a separate I-864. The joint sponsor does not need to be related to the petitioner or the beneficiary, but they must be a US citizen or lawful permanent resident, domiciled in the United States, and meet the income requirement independently.
The I-864 is one of the most legally consequential forms in the immigration process because it is enforceable in court. The sponsored immigrant, a federal agency, or a state agency that provides means-tested benefits can sue the sponsor to recover costs. This guide explains what Form I-864 is, who must file it, how the income requirement works, and the most common mistakes sponsors make.
Who files this form
Form I-864 is filed by the petitioner who sponsors an immigrant for lawful permanent residence. In family-based cases, the petitioner is usually the US citizen or lawful permanent resident who filed Form I-130. In employment-based cases where the petitioner is a relative, the relative may also need to file an I-864. The sponsor must be at least 18 years old, domiciled in the United States, and a US citizen, national, or lawful permanent resident.
If the petitioner's household income does not reach 125 percent of the federal poverty guidelines for their household size, a joint sponsor can file a separate I-864. A joint sponsor must meet the same eligibility requirements as the primary sponsor and must demonstrate sufficient income or assets independently. The beneficiary's own income cannot be used to satisfy the sponsor's obligation unless the beneficiary is the petitioner's spouse and the income will continue from the same source after the beneficiary becomes a permanent resident.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-864 is to satisfy the public charge ground of inadmissibility under INA section 212(a)(4). By signing the affidavit, the sponsor contractually obligates themselves to provide financial support to the immigrant at a level equal to or exceeding 125 percent of the federal poverty guidelines. The obligation continues until one of the terminating events occurs: the immigrant naturalizes, dies, permanently leaves the United States, or is credited with 40 qualifying quarters of work.
USCIS and consular officers use the I-864 to evaluate whether the immigrant is likely to need public assistance. If the sponsor's income and assets are insufficient, the officer may request additional evidence or deny the application. The form is also a legally enforceable contract — if the immigrant receives means-tested public benefits, the providing agency can sue the sponsor to recover the cost. Some states have used this provision to recover Medicaid and other benefits from sponsors.
Key sections
Part 1 — Basis for filing: the immigrant petition that triggers the I-864 requirement
Part 2 — Information about you: the sponsor's name, address, citizenship status, and household size
Part 3 — Household size: count yourself, your spouse, your dependents, the immigrants you are sponsoring, and any others you support
Part 4 — Income and employment: current annual income, employment status, and income from the prior tax year
Part 5 — Assets: bank accounts, real estate, stocks, and bonds that can supplement insufficient income
Part 6 — Contract and signature: the legally binding promise of support
Common mistakes
Using the wrong federal poverty guidelines table — the guidelines are updated annually and vary by household size and state
Including the beneficiary's income as the sponsor's own income when the beneficiary is not the spouse or the income will not continue
Failing to include the most recent federal tax return or transcript as required evidence
Not counting all household members correctly — for example, omitting a dependent child or an adult parent living in the home
Using assets without providing adequate documentation of ownership and valuation
Believing the I-864 obligation ends when the green card is issued — it continues until one of the statutory terminating events occurs
Official sources
Always verify the current form edition, fee, and instructions on the government site before filing. This guide is educational and not a substitute for your DSO or a licensed attorney.

Form I-94 — Arrival/Departure Record
Form I-94 is the official record of your admission to the United States. It is created electronically when you pass through Customs and Border Protection inspection at a port of entry — an airport, seaport, or land border crossing. The I-94 records your date of entry, the port of entry, your visa classification, and the date by which you must depart or change status. For most nonimmigrants, this date is what governs your authorized stay, not the visa expiration date in your passport.
You can retrieve your I-94 record online through the CBP I-94 website. The record is free to access and should be checked immediately after every entry to confirm that CBP recorded your admission correctly. Errors on the I-94 — such as the wrong visa class or an incorrect admission date — can cause problems with school enrollment, work authorization, and future visa applications.
This guide explains what Form I-94 is, how it works, why it matters, and what to do if the record contains an error.
Who files this form
Form I-94 is not filed by the traveler. It is created automatically by Customs and Border Protection when you are admitted to the United States. The CBP officer inspects your passport, visa, and supporting documents, determines your admissibility, and enters the admission data into the CBP system. The electronic I-94 record is then available for you to download and print.
Certain categories of travelers, including most F-1 and J-1 visa holders, are admitted for "duration of status" rather than a specific date. This means your I-94 shows "D/S" instead of a departure date. For these categories, your authorized stay is tied to your program end date on Form I-20 or DS-2019, not to a fixed date on the I-94.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-94 is to create an official record of every noncitizen's admission to the United States. The record documents when you entered, under what visa classification, and how long you are authorized to stay. USCIS, your school, and your employer all use the I-94 to verify that you were lawfully admitted and that you remain in valid status.
For F-1 students, the I-94 admission class should read "F1" and the admit-until date should read "D/S" for duration of status. If your I-94 shows a specific date instead of "D/S," or if the class of admission is incorrect, you must contact CBP to correct the record immediately. An incorrect I-94 can prevent you from enrolling in classes, applying for OPT, or changing status.
Key sections
Admission number: a unique 11-digit identifier assigned to each entry
Date of entry: the calendar date you were admitted to the United States
Class of admission: your visa category — F1, J1, B1, B2, H1B, etc.
Admit until date: the expiration of your authorized stay, or D/S for duration of status
Port of entry: the specific airport, seaport, or land border where you were inspected
Common mistakes
Not checking the I-94 immediately after entry — errors are easier to fix when caught early
Assuming the I-94 expiration date is the same as the visa expiration date
Not understanding that D/S means your stay is tied to your I-20 or DS-2019, not the I-94
Failing to correct an incorrect class of admission before filing for OPT or a status change
Losing the printed I-94 and not knowing how to retrieve it from the CBP website
Not realizing that each entry generates a new I-94 — the old one is replaced when you re-enter

How do I get my I-94? Visit the CBP I-94 website and enter your passport information. The record is free to access and can be printed immediately. If you entered before the electronic I-94 system was implemented, you may have a paper I-94 stapled in your passport. 
What does D/S mean on my I-94? D/S stands for "duration of status." It means your authorized stay is not limited to a specific calendar date. Instead, you remain in valid status as long as you maintain the requirements of your visa category — for F-1 students, this means maintaining full-time enrollment and a valid I-20. 
What if my I-94 has the wrong information? Contact the CBP Deferred Inspection office at the port of entry where you were admitted, or visit a deferred inspection site near you. Bring your passport, visa, I-20 or DS-2019, and any evidence showing the correct information. Corrections are usually made on the same day.

Form I-983 — Training Plan for STEM OPT Students
Form I-983 is the training plan that every STEM OPT extension applicant must complete with their employer. Unlike Form I-765, which is filed with USCIS, the I-983 is a bilateral agreement between you and your employer that documents how your practical training relates to your STEM degree. The form is signed by both you and your employer and is maintained in your school's records, not sent to USCIS.
The I-983 was introduced to ensure that STEM OPT employment is genuinely educational and not just a work permit. The form requires your employer to describe specific learning objectives, training methods, and supervision structures. It also requires the employer to commit to regular evaluations of your progress. These requirements are stricter than standard post-completion OPT and reflect the extended 24-month period that STEM OPT provides.
This guide explains what Form I-983 is, who needs to complete it, what the form requires, and how it fits into the STEM OPT extension process.
Who files this form
Form I-983 is completed by F-1 students who have been approved for post-completion OPT, hold a degree in a STEM field from a SEVP-certified institution, and are seeking a 24-month STEM OPT extension. The student and the employer must complete the form together. The student then submits the signed form to their Designated School Official, who creates a new I-20 with the STEM OPT recommendation.
The employer must be enrolled in E-Verify and must agree to the training plan's requirements, including the learning objectives, supervision structure, and evaluation schedule. The employer must also report any material changes to the training plan — such as a change in supervisor, a significant shift in duties, or termination of employment — to the student's DSO within five business days.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form I-983 is to document that your STEM OPT employment is a structured training experience that is directly related to your STEM degree. USCIS and SEVP use the form to verify that STEM OPT is being used for its intended purpose — practical training that enhances the student's academic knowledge — rather than as a generic work authorization.
The form creates accountability for both the student and the employer. The student must commit to the learning objectives and attend scheduled evaluations. The employer must provide supervision, training, and feedback, and must report material changes to the school. If the training plan is not followed, the DSO can terminate the student's STEM OPT recommendation, which invalidates the underlying I-765 and EAD.
Key sections
Section 1 — Student information: name, SEVIS ID, degree level, and CIP code
Section 2 — Employer information: name, address, E-Verify number, and number of employees
Section 3 — Training plan: specific learning objectives tied to the STEM degree
Section 4 — Employer oversight: name and qualifications of the supervisory official
Section 5 — Training methods: how the employer will provide the training and measure progress
Section 6 — Evaluations: schedule and criteria for formal performance assessments
Common mistakes
Writing generic learning objectives that do not clearly connect to the STEM degree field
Failing to list the employer's E-Verify number or using an employer that is not enrolled in E-Verify
Not understanding that the employer must report material changes to the DSO within five business days
Omitting the employer's commitment to regular evaluations with specific criteria
Assuming that self-employment or working for a staffing agency satisfies the I-983 requirements — it generally does not
Not keeping a copy of the signed I-983 for your own records

Form N-400 — Application for Naturalization
Form N-400 is the application a lawful permanent resident files to become a naturalized US citizen. Naturalization is the legal process by which a noncitizen voluntarily becomes a citizen of the United States. It is the final step in the immigration journey for most permanent residents, and it confers the full rights and responsibilities of US citizenship, including the right to vote, the right to run for most public offices, the ability to sponsor a wider range of family members for immigration, and protection from deportation.
To qualify for naturalization, you must meet several statutory requirements established by Congress. You must have been a lawful permanent resident for a specific period — generally five years, or three years if you are married to a US citizen. You must demonstrate continuous residence and physical presence in the United States. You must be a person of good moral character. You must demonstrate an attachment to the principles of the US Constitution. And you must pass an English test and a civics test covering US history and government.
The N-400 is a detailed application that asks about your residence history, employment history, marital history, children, travel outside the United States, criminal history, and affiliation with organizations. USCIS reviews every answer carefully, and discrepancies between the N-400 and prior immigration filings can raise concerns. This guide explains what Form N-400 is, who qualifies, what the process involves, and the most common mistakes applicants make.
Who files this form
Form N-400 is filed by lawful permanent residents who meet the statutory requirements for naturalization. The general requirement is five years of permanent residence, but the period is reduced to three years if you have been married to and living with a US citizen spouse for those three years. Certain military service members and their families may qualify under special provisions with reduced or no residence requirements.
To be eligible, you must also demonstrate continuous residence in the United States, meaning you have not taken trips abroad that are so long they break the continuity of your residence. You must meet the physical presence requirement — at least half of the required residence period physically in the United States. You must have lived in the state or USCIS district where you file for at least three months. And you must be a person of good moral character during the statutory period leading up to your application.
What this form is for
The purpose of Form N-400 is to allow USCIS to evaluate whether a lawful permanent resident meets all the statutory requirements for naturalization. USCIS reviews the application for completeness, consistency with prior immigration records, and any grounds that might disqualify the applicant. The review includes a background check, a biometrics appointment, and an in-person interview where the applicant is tested on English and civics.
If USCIS approves the application, the applicant is scheduled for a naturalization ceremony where they take the Oath of Allegiance to the United States. After taking the oath, they receive a Certificate of Naturalization and are immediately a US citizen. The process typically takes several months from filing to oath, but the timeline varies by USCIS field office and case complexity. Check the current USCIS processing times for the most accurate estimate.
Key sections
Part 1 — Information about your eligibility: the basis for your naturalization application
Part 2 — Information about you: name, A-number, date and place of birth, and social security number
Part 3 — Residence and physical presence: address history and trips outside the United States
Part 4 — Information about your parents and marital history
Part 5 — Information about your children and employment history
Part 6 — Moral character and criminal history: arrests, convictions, and affiliations
Common mistakes
Filing before meeting the full residence or physical presence requirement
Not disclosing a prior arrest or citation, even if the case was dismissed or expunged
Failing to account for all trips outside the United States, including short weekend trips to Canada or Mexico
Not updating USCIS after moving to a new address — the interview notice will be sent to your address on file
Studying the wrong civics questions — the test draws from a specific list of 100 questions published by USCIS
Paying the wrong filing fee — check the current USCIS fee schedule for Form N-400 before submitting
