Renewing or replacing a permanent resident card
A permanent resident card expires every ten years, and renewal requires Form I-90.
File well before the expiration date, since renewal processing can take several months.
Replacement for a lost, stolen, or damaged card also uses Form I-90, and you may need a temporary I-551 stamp in your passport if travel is urgent.
Renewal does not change your underlying status; it simply refreshes the physical document.
Conditional residents follow a different path through Form I-751, which you must file within the 90-day window before the card expires.
Missing that window can result in automatic termination of your status, so mark the date on your calendar the moment your conditional card arrives.
Travel and re-entry considerations
Leaving the U.S. while a green card application is pending can complicate your case, especially if you lack advance parole.
For approved permanent residents, short trips abroad are generally fine, but absences over six months may raise questions about your intent to reside permanently.
A re-entry permit, filed on Form I-131, protects extended travel of up to two years.
If you are in removal proceedings or have a criminal record, consult an attorney before any international travel, since re-entry may trigger secondary inspection or inadmissibility grounds.
Keep copies of your boarding passes and pay stubs from abroad to document that your U.S. residence remained your primary home.
Family members and derivative beneficiaries
Certain green card categories allow spouses and unmarried children under 21 to derive status from your application.
For employment-based petitions, derivatives file concurrently when a visa number is available, or later if priority dates differ.

02 Core rule: Marriage green card document prep must prove the legal marriage, bona fide relationship, sponsor eligibility, financial sponsorship, beneficiary admissibility, and the correct processing route. 
03 Documents: Marriage certificate, divorce decrees, passports, birth certificates, I-130 evidence, I-485 evidence if adjusting, I-864 tax and income records, medical exam, joint records, photos, affidavits, and civil documents. 
04 Timing: Choose adjustment or consular processing before finalising forms because medical timing, interview path, and document upload steps differ. 
05 Main risk: Weak bona fide marriage evidence, missing divorce records, wrong I-864 household size, stale medical timing, and undisclosed prior immigration history. 
06 Review status: Editorial review only. 
TL;DR — Preparation at a glance
The marriage green card document package has four parts, each with its own filing requirements and evidence standards the petition (I-130) proving the qualifying relationship, the adjustment or consular processing documents (I-485 or DS-260) proving admissibility, the affidavit of support (I-864) proving the sponsor meets the income threshold, and the supporting evidence file proving the marriage is bona fide. Each part is independently scrutinised. A weak file in any one area can delay the entire case by 6 to 12 months through RFEs, requests for additional evidence, or interview delays. A consistency check before mailing involves verifying that the names on all forms match the petitioner's and beneficiary's passports exactly, that the address listed on each form is the same physical address, that the I-864 household size matches the tax return filing status, and that the prior marriage history disclosed on the I-130 is consistent with the divorce decrees provided. A single inconsistency between forms can trigger an RFE that delays the entire case by three to six months, so checking every field before mailing saves significant time and reduces the risk of avoidable processing delays at the service centre.
Who this guide is for
Couples preparing a marriage-based green card application from scratch.
Applicants who received an RFE for the I-130, I-485, or I-864 and need to respond with additional evidence.
Applicants approaching the NVC stage who need to upload civil documents to the CEAC portal.
The controlling source
Primary source: USCIS I-130 Instructions | USCIS I-485 Instructions | USCIS I-864 Instructions | NVC CEAC Upload Portal 
Part 1: The I-130 petition evidence
The I-130 petition must prove the qualifying relationship between the US citizen (or permanent resident) petitioner and the beneficiary spouse. Required evidence:
Proof of petitioner's US citizenship or permanent residence: US birth certificate, naturalisation certificate, US passport, or green card copy.
Marriage certificate: Certified copy from the jurisdiction where the marriage was performed. If the marriage was outside the US, the certificate must be registered with the appropriate foreign authority and accompanied by a certified English translation.
Divorce decrees: Certified copies of final divorce decrees for ALL prior marriages of both spouses. Separation agreements are not sufficient — only final divorce decrees are accepted.
Two passport-style photos: One of each spouse.
Part 2: The I-864 affidavit of support
The I-864 is a legally enforceable contract. The sponsor agrees to support the beneficiary at 125% of the federal poverty guideline for the household size. Required documentation:
IRS tax transcripts or complete tax returns for the most recent 3 years.
W-2 forms or 1099 forms for each tax year.
Recent pay stubs covering at least the last 6 months.
Employment letter confirming current position, salary, and permanent or indefinite employment.
If income is insufficient: A joint sponsor (any US citizen or permanent resident who meets the income threshold) can file a separate I-864.
How to organise a complete marriage green card packet for USCIS review
A well-organised marriage green card packet is easier for USCIS to adjudicate and reduces the likelihood of a Request for Evidence. USCIS service centres process thousands of family-based applications each month, and a packet that presents documents in a clear, logical order with labelled section dividers signals to the officer that the applicant has prepared carefully and has nothing to hide. A sloppy, disorganised packet can create the impression that the applicant is not taking the process seriously, which may increase the scrutiny applied to the case.
Use the following tab-divider system to separate the packet into five clearly labelled sections. Place the check or money order for the filing fee on top of the entire packet with Form G-1145 e-notification request if desired. Use binder clips rather than staples where possible to make it easy for the officer to remove documents for scanning. Do not use plastic sleeves, three-ring binders, or spiral binding because USCIS will remove all documents from non-standard packaging during the intake process, which can cause documents to be lost or misordered.
Section divider one, I-130 petition for alien relative: Place the completed and signed Form I-130 first, followed by the evidence of the petitioner's US citizenship or permanent residence, the marriage certificate, divorce decrees from any prior marriages, and the two passport-style photos of each spouse. Include a cover sheet listing the contents of this section so the officer can verify at a glance that the core petition documents

TL;DR — N-400 documents in one minute
The N-400 naturalization application requires a document packet organised into six evidence categories: proof of identity and permanent residence (green card copy and passport), continuous residence evidence (complete travel history for the entire statutory period), good moral character evidence (tax transcripts, selective service registration, certified court dispositions), physical presence evidence (passport stamps and I-94 records), supporting documents for the specific rule you are applying under (marriage evidence for the three-year rule, military evidence for military naturalisation), and the application fee or fee waiver request. Each category is independently important, and a weakness in any one area can result in a Request for Evidence, a longer processing time, or a denial. Begin gathering documents three to four months before you plan to file so you have time to obtain certified copies of tax transcripts, request court dispositions, and compile the complete travel history.
Who this guide is for and who it is not for
This guide is for: Lawful permanent residents who are preparing to file Form N-400 for naturalisation, whether under the general five-year rule, the three-year marriage rule, or another eligibility basis such as military service. It is also for immigration attorneys and accredited representatives who advise naturalisation applicants on document preparation and for community-based organisations that assist permanent residents with the naturalisation process.
This guide is not for: Applicants who have already filed the N-400 and received an RFE for specific missing documents. Those applicants should follow the instructions in the RFE notice rather than this general checklist, because the RFE will specify exactly which documents USCIS needs. It is also not for applicants applying for a green card for the first time through family sponsorship or employment. Those applicants should read the marriage green card checklist guide or the employment-based green card guide instead.
The controlling source for N-400 document requirements
The primary controlling authority for N-400 document requirements is the USCIS Form N-400 Instructions, which are published on the USCIS website. The USCIS Policy Manual Volume 12 provides detailed guidance on the documentary requirements for naturalisation including what evidence is acceptable for each eligibility requirement. The specific requirements for travel history, good moral character evidence, and the three-year marriage rule are found in the Policy Manual Volume 12 Parts D and E. The IRS tax transcript requirement is established by USCIS policy requiring all naturalisation applicants to demonstrate compliance with federal tax law.

Complete document checklist for the five-year general rule

Present the documents with labelled section dividers so the USCIS officer can easily locate each category during the interview. A well-organised packet signals to the officer that you have prepared carefully and reduces the chance of additional document requests.
Copy of green card front and back. If the green card is lost or expired, include a copy of the Form I-90 receipt showing you have applied for a replacement, or explain in the application that the card is lost. USCIS can verify permanent residence through its own records even without the physical card.
All passports valid during the statutory period. Include every passport that was valid during the five-year statutory period, not just the most recent passport. The officer needs to see all entry and exit stamps for every trip taken during the period. If an old passport has expired, include it or provide certified copies of every page showing travel stamps.
Certified IRS tax transcripts for the five most recent tax years. Request these from the IRS using Form 4506-T. Transcripts can be ordered online at the IRS website or by mail. 03 Documents: Interview notice, green card, all passports, state ID, tax transcripts, selective service proof, court dispositions, marriage documents, updated address/employment. 
04 Timing: Start preparing when you receive the interview notice; update facts through the interview date. 
05 Main risk: Memorized answers contradicting the N-400, unlisted trips, undisclosed arrests, insufficient English practice, missing original documents. 
06 Review status: Basic review for N-400 interview available now; attorney-review tiers coming soon. 
What the N-400 naturalization interview covers
The N-400 interview is the stage after USCIS reviews the application and before the oath ceremony. A USCIS officer reviews the application under oath, tests English and civics knowledge, and determines eligibility through the interview date. The interview has three components: biographical verification, English test (reading and writing), and the civics test (up to 10 questions).
Thorough preparation is essential because changes between filing and the interview must be disclosed at the start. Failing to disclose changes can be treated as misrepresentation even if the original application was accurate.
Who this guide helps
This guide is for permanent residents who have filed N-400 and are preparing for the interview. It covers common questions, document requirements, and study strategies for the English and civics tests. It is relevant for applicants under both the 5-year general rule and the 3-year marriage rule.
The first step after receiving the interview notice
Review your N-400 thoroughly and note every changed fact: address, job, marital status, travel, law enforcement interactions. Prepare a written list of changes. Begin studying the 100 civics questions and practicing English reading and writing using USCIS study materials.
Document checklist for the interview
Appointment notice: Do not arrive without it.
Green card: Bring even if expired.
All passports: Valid and expired, all nationalities.
State ID: Showing current address.
Tax transcripts: 5 years (or 3 for marriage rule).
Selective service proof: If applicable.
Court dispositions: Certified copies of any arrests or citations.
Marriage/divorce documents: If applying under 3-year rule.
Risk triggers
The most common reason for a continued or denied interview is inconsistent travel history. USCIS cross-references with CBP records. Maintain a complete travel log. The second risk is undisclosed arrests, even those that did not result in conviction. The third risk is insufficient English proficiency during the speaking portion of the interview.
Worked example: Andre prepares for the interview
Andre, a permanent resident from Jamaica, filed N-400 under the 5-year rule. Since filing 8 months ago, he changed apartments and jobs and took a 2-week trip to Jamaica. He prepares by listing these changes, studying the civics flash cards, and practicing reading and writing sentences about US history. At the interview, he volunteers his changes and passes all tests. The officer approves his application and schedules the oath ceremony for 3 weeks later.
Related guides
The N-400 document checklist covers pre-filing documents. The civics test guide for 2026 provides a structured study plan. The naturalization overview explains the full path from filing through the oath ceremony.
Preparing for each section of the interview
The N-400 interview is divided into several sections, and understanding what each section covers allows the applicant to prepare more effectively. The first section is the application review, in which the USCIS officer reads through the entire N-400 line by line and asks the applicant to confirm each answer under oath. This section covers biographical information, residence history, employment history, travel history, marital history, and all the good moral character questions. The applicant should review their complete N-400 application before the interview so they can answer confidently without needing to read along with the officer.
The second section is the English test, which has three components. The speaking component is evaluated throughout the interview, because the officer assesses the applicant's ability to understand and respond to questions in English. The reading component requires the applicant to read one sentence aloud from a tablet or card that the officer presents. The writing component requires the applicant to write one sentence that the officer dictates. USCIS provides sample reading and writing vocabulary lists on its website, and applicants should practice reading and writing sentences that use words from those lists.
The third section is the civics test. The officer selects up to 10 questions from the official list of 100 questions, and the applicant must answer at least 6 correctly. The questions cover US history, government, geography, and symbols. The civics test is administered orally, so the applicant must speak the answers clearly. USCIS provides free study materials including flash cards, a practice test, and audio recordings of the questions and answers. The civics test is often the section that causes the most anxiety, but with consistent studying most applicants pass easily.
What happens after the interview
After the interview, the USCIS officer will inform the applicant of the decision or the next step. There are three possible outcomes. The first outcome is approval: the officer determines that the applicant meets all naturalization requirements and schedules the oath ceremony. The oath ceremony typically takes place two to six we

Eligibility requirements for Form N-400
To apply for naturalization, you must meet several baseline requirements set by Congress and administered by USCIS. The most common path requires you to be a lawful permanent resident, commonly called a green card holder, for at least five years. If you are married to a U.S. citizen, that timeline shortens to three years, provided you meet specific conditions.
General eligibility criteria
USCIS evaluates your application against a set of standard criteria. You must be at least 18 years old at the time you file the form. You must have lived continuously in the United States as a green card holder for the required period. You must also demonstrate good moral character for the statutory period, typically the three to five years immediately preceding your application.
The agency also requires you to take an English and civics test. This tests your ability to read, write, and speak basic English and your knowledge of U.S. history and government. Some applicants qualify for exemptions based on age and time as a permanent resident.
The three-year marriage exception
If you are married to a U.S. citizen, you may apply after three years instead of five. To use this exception, your spouse must have been a U.S. citizen for the entire three-year period. You must also have lived together as a married couple during that time, and your spouse must have been physically present in the United States for at least half of those three years.
Other qualifying categories
Several other categories allow for earlier or adjusted filing. If you obtained your green card through asylum, your continuous residence clock starts one year after your asylum approval date. This means you can apply for naturalization four years after receiving your green card, rather than the standard five.
Members of the U.S. military may qualify under special provisions under the Immigration and Nationality Act. If you served honorably during designated periods of hostility, you may be eligible without meeting standard residency requirements. You should consult with a military immigration assistance program or attorney if you believe you qualify under these provisions.
Continuous presence and physical presence rules
Two of the most common areas where applicants encounter issues involve the concepts of continuous presence and physical presence. These are two distinct legal requirements, and confusing them can lead to a denial.
Continuous residence
Continuous residence means you have maintained your primary home in the United States for the required statutory period. Trips abroad do not automatically break your continuous residence. However, a trip lasting six months or more raises a presumption that you have disrupted your residence.
If your trip lasts between six months and one year, USCIS may presume you broke your continuous residence. You can attempt to overcome this presumption by providing evidence that you maintained your life in the U.S., such as continuing to work, maintaining a home, and paying taxes. A trip lasting more than one year generally breaks your continuous residence entirely, resetting your clock unless you took steps to preserve it.
Physical presence
Physical presence is a strict mathematical calculation. You must be physically present in the United States for at least half of your required statutory period. For a five-year applicant, this means 30 months out of the 60 months preceding your application. For a three-year applicant, you need 18 months out of the 36 months.
USCIS counts the days you were in the country. You must account for every trip you took outside the United States during the statutory period. The form asks for your travel history, and you should gather your passport stamps and flight records to ensure accuracy.
Preserving residence for employment abroad
If your employer sends you abroad for work, you can file Form N-470 to preserve your continuous residence. This form does not excuse you from the physical presence requirement. It only prevents your cont

02 Core rule: O-1A is for individuals with extraordinary ability in science, education, business, or athletics who will continue work in their area of ability in the US temporarily. 
03 Documents: Awards, media coverage, judging evidence, original contributions, scholarly articles, high salary proof, critical role evidence, expert letters, consultation letter, itinerary, and contracts. 
04 Timing: Allow time for consultation letters, premium processing, and consular processing if the beneficiary is abroad. 
05 Main risk: Petitions fail when evidence shows employer praise without external recognition, weak consultation letters, or vague itineraries. 
06 Review status: Basic review for O-1A available now; attorney-review tiers coming soon. 
How the O-1A extraordinary ability visa works
The O-1A nonimmigrant visa, authorized under INA 101(a)(15)(O)(i), allows individuals with extraordinary ability in science, education, business, or athletics to work in the United States temporarily. Unlike the H-1B visa, O-1A has no annual cap, no lottery, and no prevailing wage requirement. It requires meeting at least 3 of 8 regulatory criteria or evidence of a one-time major achievement such as a Nobel Prize.
The petition must be filed by a U.S. petitioner and include a consultation letter from an appropriate labor organization or peer group. USCIS reviews evidence under a two-part framework: whether the beneficiary meets at least 3 criteria, and a final merits review of whether the totality of evidence demonstrates extraordinary ability.
The O-1A is distinct from the O-1B category for artists and entertainers. Applicants in creative fields should verify which category matches their work. The evidence standards differ materially between the two, and filing under the wrong category can result in denial.
Who should apply under O-1A
This guide is for individuals with verifiable achievements seeking U.S. work authorization without H-1B cap constraints. It is relevant for researchers with strong publication records, technology founders with industry recognition, athletes with national competition achievements, and business professionals at organizations with distinguished reputations.
This guide is not for individuals whose achievements are primarily internal to their employer without external recognition. It is not for artists or entertainers who should apply under O-1B. Applicants who cannot document 3 of 8 criteria should explore H-1B, L-1, or E-2 as alternatives.
The key strategic decision: O-1A versus EB-1A timing
If you qualify for O-1A, decide whether to apply for the O-1A first and pursue a green card later, or file EB-1A directly. O-1A allows starting work within weeks under premium processing. EB-1A requires more evidence but, if current, allows concurrent adjustment of status.
Many applicants choose O-1A first to demonstrate U.S. work history while preparing stronger EB-1A evidence. The O-1A evidence can be adapted for EB-1A, and the period of U.S. work provides additional evidence of sustained acclaim.
The controlling source for O-1A standards
USCIS adjudicates O-1A petitions under 8 CFR 214.2(o) and the USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 2, Part M. The consultation letter requirement is governed by 8 CFR 214.2(o)(5). USCIS must request consultation from an appropriate U.S. labor organization or peer group before approving an O-1A petition.
The most common RFE reasons include insufficient evidence of sustained acclaim, recommendation letters describing competence rather than extraordinary ability, and vague itineraries. Addressing each before USCIS issues an RFE significantly reduces processing time.
Document checklist for the O-1A petition
Organize the petition into sections by claimed criterion:
Criteria evidence: Cover sheet per criterion identifying the regulatory standard and explaining how the evidence satisfies it. Group evidence by criterion.
Recommendation letters: At least 4 to 6 letters from independent experts attesting to extraordinary ability. Each letter should describe specific achievements and their impact.
Consultation letter: Evidence that consultation was requested from an appropriate peer group, plus the response or evidence no appropriate organization exists.
Itinerary: Detailed schedule of U.S. activities including dates, locations, and the nature of each event.
Petitioner evidence: Employer registration documents, financial statements, and evidence of available work for the beneficiary.
Contract or offer letter: Written agreement describing the terms, compensation, and duration of the assignment.
Risk factors in the O-1A process
The consultation request should be sent at least 30 days before filing. Common refusal reasons include insufficient evidence that acclaim is sustained rather than a single achievement, recommendation letters that describe competence rather than extraordinary ability, and evidence primarily reflecting internal employer recognition.
Work with the petitioner to ensure the evidence narrative is coherent and focused on field-level recognition rather than employer-specific contributions. Premium processing is strongly recommended to obtain faster adjudication and to be able to respond quickly to any RFE.

Document Checklist: What to Gather Before Proofreading
Before a reviewer starts, assemble every file the review needs. Incomplete packages cause delays and missed errors.
Core documents: 
Final draft: Your completed paper in an editable format such as .docx or Google Docs.
Assignment prompt: The instructions from your professor or department.
Style guide: A current PDF or link to the required manual (APA, MLA, Chicago, IEEE, or another).
Reference list: Your bibliography or works cited page.
Supplementary files: 
Grading rubric: If your school provides one, include it so the reviewer can check formatting against stated criteria.
Instructor feedback: Prior comments help the reviewer understand recurring issues.
Specific concerns note: A short list of areas you want checked, such as quotations, tables, or headings.
Note: A proofreader can't review what they can't see. If your draft references a table in a separate file, include that file or paste the table into the main document.
Ready files speed up the review. Next, confirm which style rules apply.
Style Guide Compliance: APA, MLA, Chicago, and IEEE
Each academic style has distinct formatting rules. A proofreader checks your draft against the named guide, but you must tell the reviewer which one applies.
Common US style guides: 
Style Common Use Key Check Areas APA 7th edition Social sciences, education, nursing Title page, running head, parenthetical citations, reference list format MLA 9th edition Humanities, literature, arts In-text citations, works cited, margins, header Chicago 17th edition History, publishing, some social sciences Footnotes or endnotes, bibliography, title page IEEE Engineering, computer science Numbered citations in brackets, reference list formatting What the reviewer examines: 
Citation format: Each in-text citation matches the required style.
Reference entries: Every cited source appears in the reference list and vice versa.
Heading levels: Follow the hierarchy set by the style guide.
Numbers and units: Follow the style guide for abbreviations, dates, and measurements.
For instance, APA 7 requires a single space after sentence periods, while older APA 6 required two.
Reviewers familiar with the current edition catch this difference. Always confirm which edition your instructor requires before the review begins.
Common Mistakes Proofreading Catches Before Submission
Surface errors distract readers and can lower grades. A proofreader looks for the mistakes that are easy to miss when you wrote the draft yourself.
Frequent errors in academic papers: 
Inconsistent capitalization: Headings or terms spelled differently across sections.
Citation mismatches: A source cited in text but missing from the reference list, or the reverse.
Formatting drift: Font sizes, margins, or line spacing that change partway through the document.
Punctuation errors: Misplaced commas, missing periods, or incorrect quotation mark placement.
Number formatting: Inconsistent use of numerals versus spelled-out numbers.
What a proofreader flags but can't fix: 
Factual accuracy: The reviewer can't confirm your data or arguments.
Originality: The reviewer doesn't run plagiarism checks unless you request one separately.
Content quality: The reviewer doesn't rewrite weak arguments or add missing analysis.
Your proofreader returns a marked document. You decide which changes to accept and which to reject.
Reviewing the tracked changes yourself ensures the final paper still sounds like your work.
Turnaround Times and Rush Options
Review speed depends on document length, reviewer availability, and the scope you request. Standard academic proofreading turnaround ranges from 24 hours for short papers to several days for longer documents.

Word count: Longer drafts take more

Landlords must give advance written notice before raising rent.
Some cities cap rent increases; most areas do not.
Retaliatory rent increases after tenant complaints are illegal.
Check your lease and local rent control rules before responding.
State notice periods vary — verify against your state statute.
When a rent increase is legal
A landlord generally has the right to raise rent when a lease term ends or, for month-to-month tenancies, with proper advance notice. The notice requirement and any cap on the increase depend on your state and city.
In most of the US, there is no limit on how much a landlord can increase rent. The landlord must simply give the notice required by state law, which typically ranges from 30 to 60 days for month-to-month tenants. Some states require longer notice for larger increases.
A few cities have rent control or rent stabilization laws that cap annual increases. These laws typically apply to older buildings and require landlords to register the unit with a local housing agency. These cities include New York, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Washington DC, and others. If you live in a rent-controlled jurisdiction, your landlord must follow the local formula. Check your city housing department website for the current cap and any registration requirements that apply to your building.
How to respond to a rent increase — step by step
Step 1: Read the notice carefully. Check the effective date, the new rent amount, the percentage increase, and whether the notice meets your state's minimum advance notice requirement. Some states require 30 days, others require 60 days, and some require even longer notice for increases above a certain threshold. If the notice does not give you the required period before the increase takes effect, it is invalid and you can continue paying your current rent until proper notice is given.
Step 2: Check your lease. A fixed-term lease locks the rent until the term ends unless the lease includes a specific escalation clause. If you are on a month-to-month tenancy, the landlord can raise rent with proper notice, but the amount may still be limited by a local rent control ordinance. Look for the section titled "Rent" or "Payment Terms" in your lease to confirm whether any escalation clause exists and what conditions it requires.
Step 3: Verify local rules. If your city has rent control or just-cause eviction protections, the increase may be capped or require specific justification. Visit your city housing department website or call the local rent board to confirm whether your building is covered. In cities like Los Angeles, San Francisco, and New York, landlords must register rent-controlled units and provide tenants with annual notices about their rights. If your building is covered, the increase must follow the local formula, and you can file a complaint if the landlord exceeds the cap.
Step 4: Calculate whether you can afford the new rent. If not, start looking for alternatives and communicate with your landlord about your timeline. Some landlords prefer to keep a reliable tenant at a slightly lower increase rather than risk a vacancy. If you are planning to move out, confirm the notice period you must give under your lease or state law — typically 30 days for month-to-month tenancies — and provide written notice before the increase takes effect so you are not liable for the higher rent.
Step 5: Document everything. Keep the increase notice, your lease, and any correspondence with the landlord about the increase. If you believe the increase is illegal — because it violates notice requirements, exceeds a rent control cap, or is retaliatory — contact a local housing attorney or legal aid clinic before withholding rent or refusing to pay. Some jurisdictions require you to pay the old rent into an escrow account while challenging the increase, while others allow you to file a complaint with a rent board without withholding payment. Store all documents in a dedicated folder organized by date so you can produce them quickly if you need to file a complaint or appear in housing court.

Rent control and rent stabilization are local laws that limit how much a landlord can raise rent each year. These laws exist in a small number of cities and states, but they protect millions of tenants. The specific rules vary dramatically by jurisdiction — some cities cap increases at a flat percentage like 3%, while others use a formula tied to the Consumer Price Index plus an additional percentage.

International student renting in Austin: the rule in plain English
Renting in Austin as an international student means navigating Texas landlord-tenant law, city-level code compliance, and a rental market that revolves around the University of Texas academic calendar. The Texas Property Code Chapter 92 governs most landlord-tenant relationships, including the duty to repair, security deposit return rules, and eviction procedures.
Unlike states such as California or New York, Texas has no statewide rent control and no statutory limit on security deposits. The contract is king — but the Texas Property Code creates mandatory obligations that cannot be waived by lease language. Your lease cannot override the statutory habitability requirement, the 30-day deposit return deadline, or the landlord's duty to mitigate damages after a lease break.
For international students, the practical question is whether the apartment or house you are looking at is in a student-heavy area like West Campus, Hyde Park, or North Campus, or a more general rental area like Far West, Riverside, or South Austin. Each area has different lease types, utility setups, and landlord profiles.
Who this guide is for
International students renting near UT Austin or other Austin schools, including apartments, rooms, shared houses, and sublets. This guide covers leases signed directly with landlords or property management companies, as well as sublets from other students.
If you are a graduate student, a student with dependents, or a student on OPT or STEM OPT working in Austin, the same Texas Property Code rules apply but your documentation requirements may differ. You may need to show proof of income or OPT authorization instead of a guarantor.
Documents and evidence to prepare
Before you start looking at apartments, organise these documents. Having them ready speeds up the application process and strengthens your negotiating position. Texas is a landlord-friendly state for application processing, but a complete application packet signals that you know your rights and will use them.
Essential documents: Your passport bio page, current visa and I-94, Form I-20 or DS-2019, proof of enrollment or acceptance letter, bank statements or scholarship award letter showing sufficient funds, and a valid email address and US phone number for the application.
Move-in day documents: The fully executed lease with all riders and addenda, a copy of your deposit receipt or payment confirmation, and your move-in inspection checklist. Take date-stamped photos or a video walkthrough of every room before moving in your belongings. Texas law does not require the landlord to provide a written move-in inspection report — your own visual record is your primary evidence if a deposit dispute arises later.
Timing, deadlines, and sequencing
Austin's rental cycle follows the academic calendar at UT Austin. The busiest leasing period runs from March through August, with most leases starting in August and ending the following July. Many student-housing complexes begin showing units for the following academic year as early as October. Signing early can lock in lower rates and secure your preferred building but means you commit to a lease six to ten months in advance.
If you are arriving mid-year, the market is slower and prices tend to be slightly lower. Sublets from departing students are common in West Campus and Hyde Park. A sublet does not require landlord permission under Texas law in the same way a lease assignment does, but the original lease remains in force unless the landlord signs a release.
Payment sequence: Typically, the application fee is charged at application. If approved, you pay a holding fee within 24 to 48 hours to secure the unit. The holding fee is credited toward your security deposit at move-in. After the holding fee, you sign the lease and pay the first month's rent.

The first-in-time law applies equally to OPT workers, making Seattle one of the most accessible cities for international graduates starting their careers. These complexes are familiar with international student documentation and often offer per-bedroom leases that limit your liability to your own room. The UW Off-Campus Housing office publishes a list of complexes that accept international students without a US-based guarantor and can help you identify buildings that comply with the first-in-time ordinance.
Documents and evidence to prepare
Seattle landlords require a standardised application. The first-in-time law requires the landlord to publish screening criteria in advance, so you can check the requirements before paying an application fee. This transparency is one of the main advantages of renting in Seattle — you will know whether you qualify before you spend money on applications.
Application: Passport bio page, visa and I-94, I-20 or DS-2019, UW enrollment letter, two months of bank statements or scholarship letter, and proof of on-time rent payment from a previous landlord if available. If using a guarantor, include their credit authorization, two pay stubs, and signed guarantor agreement. Under Washington law, the application fee cannot exceed the actual cost of the tenant screening (typically $30–$50), and the landlord must provide a receipt for the fee.
Screening criteria: Ask for written screening criteria before paying any fee. The criteria must include the minimum credit score, income-to-rent ratio, rental history requirements, and any criminal history standards. If the criteria includes requirements you cannot meet — such as a minimum credit score of 700 or a US-based credit history — avoid the fee and move on to a building with more flexible requirements. The first-in-time law protects you from being skipped for arbitrary reasons, but it does not require a landlord to accept an applicant who does not meet the published screening criteria.
Move-in documents under Washington law: Washington requires the landlord to provide a written move-in inspection checklist, which you must complete and return within a reasonable time (typically 5 to 10 days). Take date-stamped photos of every room and upload them to a cloud service before moving your belongings in. Washington's 21-day deposit return deadline gives you a short window to challenge deductions, so having detailed move-in photos is essential for protecting your deposit.

UW's fall quarter starts in late September, and the rental market follows the academic calendar more closely than in many other US cities. Most student leases in the U-District begin in August or September, with the best selection available in April and May. 01 Joint and several liability means you can be held responsible for your roommate's unpaid rent — the landlord can demand the full amount from you alone. 
02 A written roommate agreement is separate from the lease and is enforceable in small claims court. It cannot override lease terms but helps prevent disputes before they start. 
03 If a roommate violates the lease, the landlord can evict all tenants on the lease, not just the violating one. Document your non-involvement.

Joint vs several liability: what every student tenant should know
When you sign a lease with roommates, the default legal structure in most US states is joint and several liability. This means all tenants on the lease are treated as a single group for rent payment, but each individual tenant is also personally responsible for the full amount. If your roommate cannot pay their share of the rent, the landlord can demand the difference from you. If neither of you pays, the landlord can evict everyone named on the lease — regardless of who actually owes what. An eviction filing appears on the credit and rental history of every tenant named in the lawsuit, even tenants who were paying their share consistently.
The liability structure is set by the lease, not by verbal agreements or informal splits. If the lease says "Tenant A and Tenant B jointly agree to pay $2,000/month," you are both individually on the hook for the full $2,000. A verbal agreement that "I pay $1,000 and you pay $1,000" is not binding on the landlord — it is an agreement between roommates only. Some leases, particularly for student housing complexes near universities, offer individual leases per bedroom. Under an individual lease, each tenant is responsible only for their own rent and the landlord collects separately. Individual leases are less common in off-campus rentals but are worth seeking if you are concerned about roommate liability. If you have a choice between a joint lease and individual leases, individual leases eliminate the financial risk of a non-paying roommate entirely.
Who this guide is for
This guide is for F-1 and other international students renting off-campus housing in the United States with roommates. It is also for domestic US students who are new to renting and want to understand roommate liability before signing a lease. If you are already in a roommate dispute — a roommate stopped paying, moved out early, or caused damage — this guide explains your legal options and how to protect yourself from liability.
This guide is not for tenants living in university dormitories or on-campus housing (those are governed by university housing policies, not standard landlord-tenant law), tenants in rent-controlled or subsidised housing with different eviction rules, or tenants who have already received an eviction notice or court summons — those situations require immediate legal advice from a local tenant attorney.
The roommate agreement: a contract that protects both of you
A roommate agreement is a written contract between co-tenants that covers issues the lease does not address: how rent and utility payments are split, how common expenses are shared, cleaning and chore schedules, guest policies, quiet hours, and how the security deposit will be divided when the lease ends. Unlike the lease, the roommate agreement is between you and your roommate — the landlord is not a party to it and has no obligation to enforce it. However, a well-written roommate agreement is enforceable in small claims court for financial disputes like unpaid rent shares or security deposit distributions.
Sign the roommate agreement before you move in together, not after a dispute arises. Cover the specific scenarios most likely to cause conflict: what happens if a roommate cannot pay rent for a month, what notice period is required if a roommate wants to move out early, how a replacement roommate will be selected and approved, and how shared damages (carpet stains, broken appliances) will be allocated at move-out. If a roommate refuses to sign a written agreement before moving in, that is a strong signal that disputes are likely. A refusal to document financial commitments is itself useful information before you commit to a joint lease. Most university legal services offices offer free roommate agreement templates tailored to your state's landlord-tenant laws — use them rather than downloading a generic template from the internet that may not address your state's specific rules on security deposits, notice periods, or small claims jurisdiction.
What to do when a dispute arises: a step-by-step approach
Step 1: Document everything. When a dispute arises — whether about unpaid rent, damages, noise, or guests — switch to written communication immediately. Emails and text messages create a record of the issue and your attempts to resolve it. Save copies of rent receipts, utility bills, bank transfers, and any communication with the landlord about the issue. If the dispute involves money, document every payment made and every amount owed with dates and amounts.
Step 2: Communicate directly and in writing. State the issue clearly, propose a resolution, and set a deadline. For example: "Your share of November rent was due on the 1st. It is now the 10th and I have covered the full amount myself. I need you to reimburse me $750 by the 15th. If you cannot pay the full amount by then, let me know what payment plan you can commit to." Keep a copy of this communication.

03 Documents: Signed lease showing deposit amount, payment receipt for the deposit, move-in and move-out condition photos, forwarding address in writing, and the landlord's itemized statement.

State law governs how long a landlord has to return your deposit.
You should request the return in writing before taking further action.
Small claims court is the usual next step if the landlord refuses.
Document every payment, receipt, and photograph from your tenancy.

What the law says about security deposits
State law governs every part of the security-deposit relationship between you and your landlord. There is no single federal rule that sets a maximum amount, a return deadline, or the deductions a landlord may take. Those details vary by state — check your state's landlord-tenant statute before you act. Some states cap the deposit at one month's rent; others allow a larger amount. Return deadlines range from two weeks to more than forty-five days. Interest rules also differ. Knowing your state's exact rule is the first step in deciding whether your landlord has broken the law. Some states also require landlords to hold deposits in a separate account or pay interest. Reviewing these rules now will tell you whether your landlord has already violated the law.
The absence of a federal rule means tenants cannot rely on a single source for deposit protections. A landlord who keeps a deposit for 45 days may be in full compliance with state law in some states but in violation in others. A tenant in New York has 14 days to receive the deposit or an itemised list; a tenant in Texas has 30 days; a tenant in California has 21 days. These differences matter when calculating whether the landlord has missed the deadline. Check the statute for the specific state where you rent, not a neighboring state or a general national guideline. Your state attorney general website or local housing court self-help center can direct you to the correct statute.
Common reasons landlords withhold deposits
Landlords most often withhold deposits for damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid rent, or cleaning costs. If your landlord keeps any portion of the deposit, state law usually requires an itemized statement that lists each deduction and the amount. Normal wear and tear — such as faded paint, minor carpet wear from ordinary living, or loose door handles — is not a valid basis for a deduction. Charges must be reasonable and supported by documentation. If the landlord cannot show receipts, repair estimates, or photographs, a small claims judge may reject the deduction and order the full deposit returned. You have the right to challenge any charge that looks inflated or unsupported.
The distinction between normal wear and tear and damage is one of the most frequently disputed issues in deposit cases. Normal wear and tear results from ordinary daily use over time — carpets become slightly worn in high-traffic areas, paint fades from sunlight exposure, and window blinds may need replacement after several years. Damage results from negligence, accidents, or abuse beyond normal use — such as a burn mark on the carpet from an iron, a hole in the wall from moving furniture, or a broken window from rough play. The landlord bears the burden of proving that a specific charge is for damage rather than wear and tear. If the landlord provides an estimate or receipt that includes both repair costs and routine maintenance, you should question whether the routine maintenance portion is being improperly passed on to you. A tenant who photographed the unit at move-in and move-out has a significant advantage in challenging inflated charges.
How to demand your deposit back — step by step
Step 1: Gather your lease, payment receipts, move-in and move-out photographs, and any written inspection reports. Organize everything by date so you can present a clear timeline. Step 2: Send a written demand letter to your landlord by certified mail or by email with a read receipt. Keep a copy for your records.
Step 3: Cite your state's landlord-tenant act in the letter. Request either the full deposit or a detailed, itemized accounting of every deduction. Step 4: Wait for the response period required by your state. The deadline varies by state — check your state's landlord-tenant statute for the exact number of days.
Step 5: If the landlord does not respond or refuses to return the money, file a claim in your local small claims court. The clerk can provide forms and filing instructions. Step 6: Bring all documentation to the hearing. Arrive early, dress neatly, and explain your case in plain language. Answer the judge's questions directly.

Client contracts or letters of intent to show business purpose
Proof of funds for your initial business bank deposit
Foreign address records if your US address is recent
Having these items ready makes the next phase, filing your registration, move faster.
How to file your LLC registration step by step
Filing your LLC means submitting paperwork to a state agency, usually the Secretary of State. Each state has its own portal and fee schedule, but the process follows a similar path across most jurisdictions.
Choose a business name. Search your state's business name database to confirm availability. Your name must include "LLC" or "Limited Liability Company" as a designator.
Appoint a registered agent. This person or company receives legal documents on behalf of your LLC. You can serve as your own agent in some states, but a professional service adds privacy.
File Articles of Organization. Submit this formation document through your state's online portal. Filing fees vary by state, so check the official schedule on your Secretary of State website.
Receive your approval. Processing times range from a few days to several weeks depending on the state. Wyoming and Delaware often approve filings within one to two business days, while California can take up to 15 business days.
Apply for your EIN. Once the state approves your LLC, visit the IRS online EIN application. The system issues your number immediately after you complete the form and save your confirmation notice.
Open a business bank account. Take your approved Articles, EIN confirmation, and photo ID to a bank. Separate your personal and business finances from day one to maintain your liability protection.
After filing, you move into the waiting period, where tracking your status keeps you ahead of deadlines.
What happens after you file: timelines and follow-up
Approval times depend on the state and the volume of filings at the time. Most states process standard LLC registrations within two to three weeks, though expedited options exist for an additional fee.
State confirmation: you'll receive a stamped copy of your Articles of Organization by mail or through the state portal. Keep this document in your records permanently, as banks and clients may request it.
EIN delivery: the IRS provides your EIN immediately after the online application. Save the official confirmation letter, CP 575, because replacing it later requires a phone call and a Form 147-C request.
Bank account opening: schedule your bank appointment within a week of receiving your EIN. Most national banks accept walk-ins, but booking ahead reduces wait time.
State tax registration: depending on your consulting services and location, you might need to register for state taxes. Check your state Department of Revenue website for franchise tax or sales tax obligations.
Note: Timelines shift based on state backlog and holiday schedules. Always check the current processing estimate on your state's official website before planning your launch date.
Common mistakes that trigger visa problems
Many visa holders assume that forming an LLC gives them automatic permission to work. It doesn't.
The most frequent error is signing client contracts and performing consulting services before holding valid work authorization.
Unauthorized employment: actively managing your LLC or delivering services counts as employment under US immigration law. Even unpaid work for your own company can violate your status if your visa restricts self-employment.
Commingling funds: mixing personal and business transactions weakens your liability protection. Open a dedicated business account immediately after receiving your EIN to keep finances clean.
Wrong business structure: an LLC is simple to form, but it may not suit every consultant.
If you plan to seek investor visas later, a C-corporation might align better with certain immigration pathways.

International student SSN: the rule in plain English
International students generally need authorised employment or another eligible basis before the Social Security Administration issues an SSN. The SSN is not automatically issued upon arrival in the US — it is tied to work authorisation. For F-1 students, this means having an on-campus job, CPT, or OPT permission before applying. For J-1 students, it means having a DS-2019 that authorises employment or an authorised internship. The SSA uses the SAVE (Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements) system to verify your immigration status and work authorisation with USCIS before issuing a number.
Why SSN matters for international students: The SSN is required for US employers to report wages to the IRS, open certain types of bank accounts or credit cards, file US tax returns (though an ITIN can substitute for this), obtain a driver's licence in some states, and rent an apartment (some landlords run credit checks requiring an SSN). However, an SSN is not required for: opening a basic bank account (use your passport and I-20 instead), obtaining health insurance through your school, or enrolling in classes.
The fundamental rule: You must have a valid, documented reason to need an SSN before you apply. The SSA will not issue an SSN simply because you are an international student in the US. You must demonstrate that you have authorised employment or another qualifying purpose. Applying without a valid work-authorisation basis will result in a denial and may complicate future applications.
Who this guide is for
F-1 students with on-campus employment (up to 20 hours per week during term, full-time during breaks) who need an SSN for payroll. F-1 students with Curricular Practical Training (CPT) authorisation who need an SSN for their internship or co-op employer. F-1 students with approved Optional Practical Training (OPT) or STEM OPT who need an SSN for their post-completion employment. J-1 students with employment authorisation on their DS-2019 or an authorised internship. International students who have been offered on-campus employment and need to complete the hiring process, which typically requires an SSN for payroll setup.
This guide is also for international students who already have an SSN but have lost their card and need a replacement. The replacement process is similar to the initial application but does not require re-verifying work authorisation if the SSN was previously issued. Students who changed their name (through marriage, for example) should apply for a corrected SSN card reflecting the new name.

Passport and visa: Valid passport with F-1 or J-1 visa stamp. If the visa in your passport has expired but you have a valid I-20 and I-94 indicating F-1 status, the SSA should accept this — the visa stamp is an entry document, and your status is evidenced by the I-20 and I-94.
I-94 admission record: Print the most recent I-94 arrival record from the CBP website (i94.cbp.dhs.gov). The SSA uses the I-94 to verify your lawful admission, visa class, and authorised period of stay. Do not rely on the paper I-94 issued at the airport — use the online printout.
I-20 or DS-2019: Current, valid form with DSO endorsement within the last 12 months (6 months if on OPT or STEM OPT). The I-20 must reflect your current program and status. For OPT students, the endorsed I-20 with the OPT recommendation on page 2 is critical — without it, the SSA cannot verify your work authorisation.

How to weigh rent against commute time
Cheap rent far from campus can cost you missed classes. Late arrival is a school problem, not a landlord problem.
Map three zones. Walkable, one-transfer transit, and car-only. Write the door-to-door minutes for each.
Price the hour. If a cheaper unit adds 90 minutes a day, you lose study time. Recalculate weekly, not just monthly rent.
Test the route. Ride the bus at 8 a.m. once. Apps hide transfers and weather delays.

Rain, snow, and transfer waits change the real door-to-door number.
Write three columns on one page: monthly rent, weekly minutes, and how many early classes you'd miss. That sheet is the decision tool.
If two units look equal on rent, pick the one with fewer transfers. Transfers fail more often than a single train.
Campus shuttles sometimes close the gap for outer units. Confirm the shuttle calendar for breaks, not only fall term.
Night labs and Saturday exams change the picture. A cheap unit with no Sunday bus can strand you after a review session.
Count walking minutes from the stop to the building door. That last stretch often adds ten minutes that apps omit.
Ask current tenants about elevator waits and building lockouts. Those delays sit on top of the street commute.
If you'll hold CPT or on-campus work, add the work site as a second pin. One address isn't enough when your week has two hubs.
Note: HUD explains rental assistance programs at hud.gov/topics/rental_assistance . Many student rentals don't qualify.

Landlords want identity, income, and a U.S. contact. Immigration papers prove lawful presence. They don't replace a credit file.
Passport and visa page: Clear copies. Keep originals for in-person checks.
I-20 or DS-2019: Shows school and program dates. Don't alter SEVIS data to match a rental agreement.
I-94 printout: Confirms admission. Officers, not landlords, control that record.
Proof of funds: Bank letter, sponsor affidavit, or assistantship letter. Match names to the contract.

Scan every page in color. Name files by document type so a leasing office can open them on a phone.
If a sponsor pays rent, put the sponsor name on the funds letter exactly as it'll appear on any guarantor form.

Optional packet extras SSN or ITIN if you have one. Never invent a number.
U.S. guarantor form if the building requires one.
Prior landlord reference, even from your home country.
Renter insurance quote some buildings demand at move-in.

In 60 seconds
Landlord-tenant law in the US is state-specific, not federal.
Every state has rules on deposits, leases, repairs, and evictions.
International students have the same tenant rights as US citizens.
Your school's housing office and legal aid can point you to state resources.
Always verify the current rule against your state statute before acting.
Why landlord-tenant law is state-by-state
The United States does not have a single national landlord-tenant statute. Each state writes its own laws, and some cities add local rules on top. This means the deposit limit, notice period, repair deadline, and eviction process that apply in one state may be completely different in the next.
For international students, this patchwork creates confusion. A lease clause that is illegal in California might be enforceable in Texas. A 30-day notice requirement in one state could be 60 days in another. The only safe approach is to check the specific statute for the state where you rent.
Your state attorney general website, local housing court, and school housing office are the best starting points for the current rule.
Key tenant rights every state protects
Despite the differences, every state protects a core set of tenant rights. These include the right to a habitable home, the right to privacy with reasonable notice before landlord entry, the right to a return of your security deposit with an itemized deduction list, and protection against retaliatory eviction.
The details vary. Some states cap security deposits at one month's rent; others allow two or three months. Some states require 24 hours' notice for landlord entry; others use a "reasonable" standard. Some states let tenants repair and deduct; others do not.
The consistent principle is that tenants have rights, and landlords cannot override them in the lease. Any clause that tries to waive habitability, allow unlimited landlord entry, or force you to give up your deposit without cause is likely unenforceable.
The right to a habitable home is the foundation of all tenant protections. It means the landlord must provide working heat in winter, running water, electricity, a structurally safe building, and pest control. If the landlord fails to maintain these basic conditions, the tenant has legal remedies — but those remedies differ by state. Some states allow tenants to withhold rent through a court-supervised escrow account, while others require tenants to continue paying rent and then sue the landlord for damages later. The right to privacy means the landlord cannot enter your apartment without proper notice — typically 24 hours in most states — except in emergencies such as a fire or gas leak. The right to a security deposit return with an itemised statement means the landlord must provide a written list of deductions, including receipts or repair estimates, within a deadline set by state law. The right to protection against retaliatory eviction means the landlord cannot evict you for reporting a habitability violation or exercising any other legal tenant right.
How to check your state's rules — step by step
Step 1: Identify your state. This sounds obvious, but some students live near state lines or attend school in a different state from their permanent address. The law of the state where the rental property sits controls your rights. If you attend school in Massachusetts but your permanent address is in New York, the Massachusetts landlord-tenant statute applies to your campus rental, not the New York statute you may be familiar with.
Step 2: Find your state landlord-tenant statute. Search for "[your state] landlord tenant act" or visit your state legislature's website. Most statutes are available online. You can also search for "[your state] security deposit law" or "[your state] eviction notice requirements" to find the specific statute that applies to your situation. State attorney general websites often publish plain-language summaries of landlord-tenant laws with links to the full statutes.
Step 3: Check your city or county rules. Some cities have rent control, just-cause eviction rules, or additional tenant protections. Search for "[your city] tenant rights" or visit the city housing department website. Cities like San Francisco, New York, Los Angeles, and Seattle have local tenant protection ordinances that provide stronger rights than the state law. If you live in a rent-controlled city, your rent increase limits and eviction protections may be significantly greater than what state law provides.
Step 4: Contact your school's housing office or legal aid clinic. Many universities have resources specifically for international students dealing with housing issues. The international

US student visas: F-1, CPT, OPT, and STEM OPT
US student immigration is not one form — it is a sequence of status rules, school reporting duties, and work authorizations that must stay consistent with your SEVIS record. This hub orients you to the F-1 cluster: how status is maintained, when CPT or OPT is the right authorization, how STEM OPT extends post-completion OPT, and what to do when SEVIS or travel creates risk. Every linked guide is written for international students and graduates; controlling sources are USCIS, ICE/SEVP (Study in the States), and the Code of Federal Regulations. This page is orientation and routing — not a substitute for your DSO or individual legal advice.
Whether you are applying for your first F-1 visa, already studying in the US and planning OPT, or facing a status violation, the guides below walk through the rules, documents, and deadlines that apply to your situation. The cluster covers the full lifecycle: initial F-1 entry, maintaining status through enrollment and reporting, work authorization through CPT and OPT, the STEM OPT extension, SEVIS transfer and reinstatement, and the transition to H-1B or other work visas.
Last updated 2026-07-14 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
Who reviews this cluster
The US student-visas guides linked from this hub are reviewed for legal accuracy by Denise Platter Cabrera, Esq. (CA Bar #298948), a California immigration attorney who has been certified as a specialist in Immigration & Nationality Law by the State Bar of California. Review is independent: she is paid for review time, not for case outcomes. Each guide is reviewed against the controlling regulations (8 CFR 214.2), USCIS policy memos, and SEVP guidance to confirm substantive accuracy. The review status on each guide indicates whether it has received attorney review or remains editorial-only.
One guide in this cluster ( LLC on OPT ) remains editorial-only because it spans business-formation topics outside the core F-1/OPT procedure review scope — pair it with the attorney-reviewed STEM OPT self-employment guide for work-authorisation rules. Guides marked as "editorial-only" have been checked for factual accuracy against published sources but have not received individual attorney review.
Author profile: /authors/denise-platter-cabrera/ · attorneydpc.com 
The 5 most important things to know
F-1 status is maintained through a valid I-20, full course of study (unless authorized reduced load), and school reporting in SEVIS — not only through a visa stamp in your passport. See 8 CFR 214.2(f) and Study in the States . Maintaining status also requires reporting address changes within 10 days, keeping your passport valid, and extending your I-20 before it expires. Falling out of status can trigger unlawful presence accrual and bars on re-entry.
On-campus work, CPT, and OPT are different authorizations with different approval paths. Working without the correct authorization is a status violation that can affect future benefits and may permanently bar OPT at that education level. Start with the CPT vs OPT comparison, then follow the specific checklist for your path. Never start work before confirming the authorization is in place.
Post-completion OPT has an unemployment clock of 90 calendar days. STEM OPT adds 60 days for a total of 150 days across both periods. The clock starts on the EAD start date and counts every day you are not employed, including weekends and holidays. Track your working days in a spreadsheet or log from day one. Exceeding the cap results in SEVIS termination and loss of F-1 status.
Travel while an OPT EAD is pending, or with a SEVIS problem, is high risk. CBP officers may question your intent to return if your status or authorization is unresolved. Confirm travel signatures on your I-20 are current (12 months for standard F-1, 6 months for OPT/STEM OPT), carry your EAD card and employer letter if employed, and consult your DSO before booking international travel during a pending OPT application.
SEVIS termination is not always permanent — but timelines are short and documentation matters. If your record shows termination or your DSO flags a problem, read the termination and reinstatement guide before you travel or change plans. Reinstatement under Form I-539 is available within 5 months of the violation if the cause was beyond your control. After 5 months, departure and re-entry on a new I-20 may be the only option.
Choose your path
Pick the guide that matches your current situation. If you are still in full-time study, start with F-1 rights and CPT. If you are graduating, start with OPT. If something already went wrong with SEVIS or a refusal, jump to recovery guides. § Key takeaways
01 Four required elements of CPT authorization on the I-20: employer name and address, start and end dates, full-time or part-time designation, and DSO signature and date. 
02 CPT cannot be back-dated; the start date on the I-20 controls when work may legally begin. 
03 Twelve months or more of full-time CPT at the same education level disqualifies the student from OPT at that level permanently. 
04 Part-time CPT does not count against the 12-month OPT cap, but full-time CPT is over 20 hours per week. 
05 Common DSO mistakes include authorizing CPT before a written job offer exists, authorizing for an elective rather than integral course, and failing to update SEVIS within 21 days of the start date. 
06 An attorney reviews the offer letter, the I-20 CPT page, and the course syllabus together to confirm the integral-curriculum requirement is documented. 
Last updated 2026-05-09 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(i) ; SEVP CPT policy guidance.
Core rule: CPT must be an integral part of an established curriculum and authorised by the DSO on the I-20 before any work begins.
Documents: signed I-20 with CPT page, employer offer letter, course syllabus tying the work to the curriculum.
Timing: CPT cannot start before the date on the I-20 and must end on or before the date on the I-20.
Main risk: 12 months or more of full-time CPT at the same education level disqualifies you from OPT entirely at that level.
Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera, Esq. (CA Bar #298948, Certified Specialist — Immigration & Nationality Law).
The rule in plain English
Curricular Practical Training is employment authorised by the DSO as an integral part of a degree program. The controlling source is 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(i) . Unlike OPT, CPT does not require USCIS adjudication — the DSO authorises it directly on the Form I-20. That speed is the appeal; the cost is that almost all errors are made at school level and only become visible later.
The integral-curriculum requirement is the most important and most misunderstood element of CPT. For CPT to be valid, the practical training must be an integral part of an established curriculum — not merely beneficial or related to the field of study. This means the CPT must be tied to a specific course for which the student receives academic credit, or be a required component of the degree program (such as a mandatory internship for a hospitality management programme). Courses described as "elective," "optional," or "available" rather than "required" or "integral" create a weak CPT basis. A DSO who authorises CPT for a course that is only tangentially related to the program puts both the student and the school at regulatory risk under SEVP oversight.
Read Form I-765 OPT application: the eight common mistakes that get it denied for the parallel OPT rules and F-1 visa status violation: what happens, what to do, and when to call an attorney if you have already worked outside the dates on your I-20.
Who this guide is for
Likely fit
You are an F-1 student in good standing, you have completed at least one academic year, and your degree program requires or permits practical training as an integral part of the curriculum.
Needs review
Your program does not name CPT in the curriculum but offers an internship course. The DSO must confirm the work is an integral part of the program before any authorisation is valid.
Usually not a fit
You have used 12+ months of full-time CPT at the same level, you are in your first academic year, or your degree program does not include practical training in any form.
CPT vs OPT
CPT is school-authorised, employer-specific, and tied to a specific course or curriculum requirement. OPT is USCIS-authorised, not employer-specific, and follows program completion. Both consume work-authorisation entitlement but differently: CPT is unlimited in duration unless and until 12 months of full-time CPT is reached, at which point OPT is barred at that level. Read STEM OPT self-employment and startups for the STEM-extension rules that follow OPT.
The practical difference matters for students who plan to use both CPT and OPT during their academic career. Part-time CPT (20 hours or fewer per week) can be used during the academic year without affecting OPT eligibility at all. Full-time CPT during summer or vacation periods is also safe for OPT as long as the aggregate across all full-time CPT authorisations at the same education level stays under 12 months. A student who uses 11 months of full-time CPT across two summers and a semester break can still qualify for 12 months of post-completion OPT. A student who crosses the 12-month full-time threshold loses OPT permanently at that degree level — even one day over the cap triggers the bar.
Four required elements of CPT authorisation on the I-20
Employer name and address. Specific to one employer per authorisation. The employer name must match the offer letter and the entity that will issue the pay statement. A parent company name is not sufficient if a subsidiary or franchise will actually employ you.
Start and end dates. Inclusive. Work outside these dates is unauthorised employment, regardless of whether the DSO later corrects the dates in SEVIS. The start date must be after the DSO enters the authorisation — CPT cannot be retroactive.
Full-time or part-time designation. Full-time is over 20 hours per week. Part-time CPT during the academic year is limited to 20 hours or fewer. Full-time CPT during the academic year requires a specific curriculum exception.
DSO signature and date. CPT cannot be back-dated to cover a period that has already passed. The DSO signs the I-20 on the date they enter the authorisation in SEVIS, and work may not begin before that date regardless of what the employer

§ Key takeaways
01 CPT must be an integral part of an established curriculum, or a required practicum or internship — 'it would be a good experience' is not a qualifying basis. 
02 The employer offer letter must state: job title, specific duties tied to the degree, employer legal name and address, start and end dates, hours per week, worksite, and supervisor name and title. 
03 A faculty member, program director, or academic advisor must confirm the position is in the student's degree field and the training is curriculum-integral before the DSO can authorize CPT. 
04 The DSO must endorse CPT on the I-20 before the first workday; starting work before endorsement is unauthorized employment under 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(i). 
05 A material change in duties, hours, worksite, or employer requires a new offer letter and a new DSO endorsement on a revised I-20. 
06 An offer letter that says 'general assistant — various duties as assigned' with no degree-field connection gives the DSO no basis for endorsement.

Primary authority: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(i)
CPT must be an integral part of an established curriculum, or a required practicum or internship.
The employer offer letter must state: job title, specific duties tied to the degree, employer name and address, start and end dates, hours per week, and worksite.
Faculty or program director must endorse the CPT request before the DSO can authorize it on the I-20.
