This page is part of the OPT and STEM OPT — complete guide cluster. For the downstream risk that full-time CPT use creates for OPT, read CPT vs OPT — which applies to you . For the specific risk profile of Day 1 CPT programs, read Day 1 CPT — risk assessment .
Who this is for
An F-1 student preparing the CPT authorization request and the employer offer letter required for the DSO endorsement on Form I-20.
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(i) .
The integral-curriculum test
CPT is authorized only when the practical training is an integral part of an established curriculum. The practical training must satisfy one of two conditions:
The student receives academic credit for the work.
The practical training is a required component of the program (an established practicum, internship requirement, or co-op that every student in the program must complete).
"It would be a good experience" is not a qualifying basis. The integral-curriculum tie must be documentable.
What the offer letter must state
The DSO cannot authorize CPT without an offer letter that contains all of the following elements:
Job title — the specific role, not a generic description.
Specific duties — the actual tasks, tied to the technical skills of the degree program. A letter that says "general assistant" or "various duties" is insufficient.
Degree tie — an explicit statement linking the duties to the student's field of study.
Employer legal name and address — matching the employer's official registration.
Start and end dates — exact dates, not open-ended. These dates flow directly to the I-20 CPT endorsement and cannot exceed the academic term or the program requirement dates.
Hours per week — part-time (20 hours or fewer) or full-time. Full-time CPT use has OPT consequences; see CPT vs OPT — which applies to you .
Worksite — physical address or remote work confirmation.
Supervisor name and title — the person responsible for the student's day-to-day supervision.
Faculty or program endorsement
Before the DSO can authorize CPT, a faculty member, program director, or academic advisor must confirm:
The position is in the student's degree field.
The training is an integral part of the curriculum or a required program component.
The student is enrolled in (or will enroll in) the associated course or practicum if credit is the basis.
Some schools require a formal faculty approval form. Others accept an email from the advisor. Confirm your school's requirement with the DSO before requesting the offer letter from the employer.
DSO authorization process
Once the offer letter and faculty endorsement are in hand, submit the CPT authorization request to your DSO. The DSO must update SEVIS and issue a new I-20 with the CPT endorsement before the first workday. Do not begin work, accept compensation, or perform services for the employer before the CPT-endorsed I-20 is in your hands.
Timeline
Before accepting the offer: request exact duty language in the offer letter — do not accept and then try to retrofit the letter.
Before the first workday: DSO must have endorsed CPT on the I-20.
At any CPT extension: update the CPT authorization before the old end date; do not continue working on an expired CPT authorization.
At any change in duties, worksite, or hours: obtain a new or amended offer letter and DSO endorsement before the change takes effect.
Part-time vs full-time CPT and the downstream effect
CPT is authorised in two forms: part-time (20 hours or fewer per week) and full-time (more than 20 hours per week). Part-time CPT during the academic year allows the student to continue a full course load simultaneously. Full-time CPT is common during summer break or when the program requires an internship as a graduation condition. The distinction matters beyond the immediate work schedule: full-time CPT used for 12 months or more at the same education level permanently bars OPT at that level. Part-time CPT does not count toward the 12-month bar. Keep a running tally of full-time CPT weeks across all authorisations at each degree level. body:
Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com
Source URL: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com/us/student-visas/f1-cap-gap/

F-1 Cap-Gap Extension Guide — H-1B Bridge to October 1 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates

§ Key takeaways
01 Cap-gap extends both F-1 status and OPT employment authorization from the OPT end date to October 1, when the selected H-1B takes effect. 
02 Cap-gap applies only if the H-1B was cap-selected, a timely change-of-status petition was filed before OPT expired, and the petition is still pending or approved. 
03 Consular processing does not trigger cap-gap; if the H-1B was filed for consular processing, the student must depart and re-enter on H-1B status after October 1. 
04 Departure during cap-gap typically abandons the change-of-status petition and ends the cap-gap extension; re-entry usually requires an H-1B visa from a consulate after October 1. 
05 The DSO updates the I-20 to reflect the cap-gap extension; the cap-gap I-20 is the document that proves continuous F-1 status during the bridge period. 
06 If the H-1B is denied during cap-gap, F-1 status and employment authorization end at the point of denial, though a grace period may allow time to depart or change status. 
Last updated 2026-07-14 · Reviewed by Attorney reviewed 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(5)(vi)
Cap-gap extends both F-1 status and OPT employment authorisation from the OPT end date to October 1, when the selected H-1B takes effect.
Applies only if: H-1B was cap-selected, a timely change-of-status petition was filed before OPT expired, and the petition is still pending or approved.
Critical rule: do not travel outside the U.S. during cap-gap. Departure typically ends the cap-gap extension and the change-of-status path.
This page is part of the F-1 visa rights: the international student's complete guide cluster. For OPT travel rules outside of cap-gap, read OPT travel and re-entry rules . For the STEM OPT timeline that precedes cap-gap, read STEM OPT 24-month extension checklist .
Who this is for
An F-1 student whose OPT or STEM OPT authorization ends before the H-1B October 1 start date, with a pending or approved H-1B change-of-status petition filed before the OPT EAD expired. This includes students currently on their initial 12-month OPT period and students on the 24-month STEM OPT extension, as long as the H-1B petition with change of status was timely filed. The cap-gap extension bridges the gap between the end of OPT work authorization and the October 1 start date, ensuring continuous employment eligibility and F-1 status during this critical transition period.
If your H-1B petition was filed for consular processing instead of change of status, the cap-gap extension does not apply to you. Consular processing requires you to leave the US, obtain the H-1B visa at a US consulate abroad, and re-enter after October 1. This page covers the change-of-status scenario only. If you are unsure whether your petition was filed as change of status or consular processing, check the I-129 petition form or ask your employer's immigration attorney before making any travel or employment plans.
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(5)(vi) . This regulation authorises automatic extension of F-1 status (and related OPT employment authorisation when applicable) for students who are the beneficiaries of timely filed, cap-subject H-1B petitions requesting change of status to begin on October 1. Cap-gap is not a separate USCIS application — it is a status bridge that depends on petition type (change of status vs consular processing), timely filing, and continued petition viability. Confirm current SEVP/USCIS guidance with your DSO when the H-1B lottery and petition receipts are issued.
What the cap-gap extension does
The cap-gap automatically extends F-1 status and OPT employment authorisation from the date the OPT EAD expires until September 30 of the H-1B fiscal year — provided the conditions below are met. This means you can continue working for your H-1B sponsoring employer without interruption during the bridge period between your OPT end date and the October 1 H-1B start date. The extension is automatic — no separate application to USCIS is required for the status extension itself.
The DSO updates the I-20 with a cap-gap notation showing the extended F-1 status end date. The cap-gap I-20 is the critical document that proves continuous F-1 status during the bridge period. Without it, you cannot verify your work authorization with your employer or demonstrate lawful status if asked by immigration authorities. Request the updated I-20 from your DSO as soon as USCIS confirms receipt of the H-1B petition. The DSO can issue the cap-gap I-20 once the petition is receipted, not only after it is approved.
Conditions for cap-gap to apply
The H-1B petition was cap-selected in the current fiscal year's lottery and assigned to a cap-subject category.
A change-of-status petition was filed with USCIS before OPT expired — not a consular processing petition. The change-of-status request (I-129, Part 2, question 4, box b) is what triggers the cap-gap extension.
The petition is still pending or approved as of the OPT end date. If the petition is denied before the OPT end date, no cap-gap protection begins. If the petition is denied during the cap-gap period, the extension ends immediately and any ongoing employment must stop.
Consular processing does not trigger cap-gap. If the H-1B was filed for consular processing, the student must depart and re-enter on H-1B status after October 1. Check the I-129 petition form filed by your employer to confirm whether change of status or consular processing was selected. If your employer's attorney filed for consular processing and you are currently in the US on OPT, ask whether the petition can be amended to change of status before a decision is made — this may be possible in some cases.

body:
Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com
Source URL: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com/us/student-visas/f1-document-checklist-2026/

F-1 Visa Document Checklist 2026 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
§ Key takeaways
01 Eight core documents in officer-review order: passport, DS-160 confirmation page, appointment confirmation, photo, Form I-20 (signed §11), I-901 SEVIS fee receipt, financial proof, and academic credentials. 
02 Financial proof must include a sponsor letter dated within the last 30 days and bank statements in the sponsor's name showing average balance — a sudden large deposit days before the application is a recognized refusal pattern. 
03 If funding is shared across multiple sources, document each one separately; officers refuse on 'funds insufficient' when one component is undocumented, even if the total is adequate. 
04 In the first 60 seconds the officer cross-checks DS-160 against I-20, confirms SEVIS fee paid, and reads the financial proof to verify the funded amount equals or exceeds the I-20 cost-of-attendance. 
05 Both §11 (student signature) and §3 (DSO signature) must be present on the I-20; an unsigned I-20 is a common mistake. 
06 A DS-160 typo in the school name must be corrected before the interview; resubmitting the DS-160 and verifying the new confirmation with the post is required. 
Last updated 2026-06-09 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
F-1 document checklist at a glance
Eight core documents, in the order a consular officer reviews them: passport, DS-160, appointment confirmation, photo, Form I-20 (signed §11), I-901 SEVIS fee receipt, financial proof, academic credentials.
Financial proof is the most frequently weak item: sponsor letter dated within 30 days + bank statements in the sponsor's name showing average balance, not a single peak deposit.
DS-160 and I-20 must agree on every fact: school name, program, dates, funding number. A single typo can trigger a 221(g) administrative return.
If you were previously refused, the same document set is not sufficient — you must add new material evidence that addresses the refusal ground.
This page is part of the F-1 visa rights: the international student's complete guide cluster. It exists to answer the document-assembly decision only; for interview strategy, read the F-1 visa interview prep checklist .
Why document order matters
Consular officers at most posts process 80 to 120 interviews per day. The officer has approximately two to three minutes per applicant in a non-immigrant visa interview. Within the first 60 seconds, the officer has already formed a preliminary impression based on three rapid cross-checks: the DS-160 against the I-20, the SEVIS fee status, and the financial summary. If all three align, the remaining two minutes are routine. If any one fails, the entire interview pivots to the failed item.
Presenting your documents in the order an officer expects them reduces cognitive friction. The officer should not have to ask twice for the same document. A folder organised with labelled dividers — DS-160, I-20, financial proof, academic credentials — signals preparedness and reduces the chance of a 221(g) administrative processing request for a document that is in the folder but not visible.
Who this is for
A first-time F-1 applicant preparing for the consular interview.
A reapplicant rebuilding a document set after a 214(b) refusal.
A DSO advising an admitted international student through pre-departure.
Who this is not for
M-1 vocational visa applicants — different SEVIS sub-program and document set.
J-1 exchange visitors — DS-2019, not I-20.
Students already inside the U.S. who only need a new I-20 for transfer or extension.
The controlling source
Department of State 9 FAM 402.5 (Students and Exchange Visitors).
USCIS Form I-20 instructions (issued to the school by SEVP).
I-901 SEVIS fee regulation (8 CFR 214.13).
The eight core documents
In the order a consular officer reviews them. Present the folder in this sequence and label each section clearly:
# Document What it proves Notes 1 Passport Identity; travel-document validity ≥ 6 months past intended stay Bring old passports if any prior U.S. visas were issued 2 DS-160 confirmation page Visa application of record One bar-coded confirmation per applicant; ensure the post on the DS-160 matches the I-20 school 3 Appointment confirmation The interview slot Print from the appointment booking system 4 Photo Biometric standard, 2"×2", recent (within 6 months) Some posts retain the photo; bring two. No glasses, no head coverings unless religious 5 Form I-20 (signed §11) School certification and SEVIS ID Bring the original; sign §11 in ink; §3 must carry the DSO signature 6 I-901 SEVIS fee receipt SEVIS fee paid Print from fmjfee.com; without it the interview will not proceed 7 Financial proof Ability to fund the first academic year Sponsor letter + bank statements; see detailed section below 8 Academic credentials Admission rationale: transcripts, degree certificates, English scores Officers ask about the program, not just the campus Financial proof: the detail that matters
Financial proof is the document set most frequently flagged as weak or insufficient. A refusal based on "funds" is almost never because the total amount is too low. It is because the documentation does not convince the officer that the funds are genuinely available, belong to the stated sponsor, and will remain available for the duration of study.
A strong financial proof set has three components, each essential:
Sponsor letter dated within the last 30 days. The letter must name the student, state the relationship, specify the exact amount the sponsor will cover, and commit to paying the I-20 cost of attendance. A letter that says "I will support my child" without naming the amount is not sufficient. The letter should be on the sponsor's business letterhead if employed, or include their contact details and ID number.
Bank statements in the sponsor's name. The statements should show

body:
Source site: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com
Source URL: https://legal.yousafeconsultancy.com/us/student-visas/f1-interview-prep-checklist/

F-1 Visa Interview Prep Checklist 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
§ Key takeaways
01 The 14 days before the appointment are for auditing the DS-160 against the I-20, refreshing financial proof, and removing contradictions — not for memorising scripts. 
02 Two yes-or-no questions before walking in: (1) Do my DS-160, I-20, and financial proof agree on every fact? (2) Can I state my study purpose, funding, and return plan in two short sentences each, in my own words? 
03 The interview typically lasts 90 seconds to 4 minutes; the shortest interviews often end in approval, while the longest end in refusal or 221(g). 
04 Consular officers are trained to detect scripted responses; rehearse facts, not phrasing, so you can answer in two sentences without filler. 
05 A parent or friend may be present in the waiting area but does not participate at the interview window; officers expect adults to answer for themselves. 
06 Over-explaining or adding context the officer did not ask for invites follow-up questions on new ground and can weaken the case. 
Last updated 2026-07-14 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
Interview prep at a glance
The 14 days before your appointment are not for memorising scripts — they are for auditing your DS-160 against your I-20, refreshing financial proof, and removing contradictions before the officer finds them.
Two yes-or-no questions before you walk in: (1) Do my DS-160, I-20, and financial proof agree on every fact? (2) Can I state my study purpose, funding, and return plan in two short sentences each, in my own words?
If either answer is no, the interview is not yet realistic.
This page is part of the F-1 visa rights: the international student's complete guide cluster. For the document list itself, read the F-1 visa document checklist 2026 first.
Who this is for
An F-1 applicant 14–30 days from a scheduled consular interview.
A reapplicant who has rebuilt the case after a 214(b) refusal and is preparing for the second attempt.
A parent or sponsor wanting to support realistic preparation.
Who this is not for
An applicant whose I-20 has not yet been issued — prep is wasted until the actual SEVIS-stamped I-20 is in hand.
An applicant who has not paid the I-901 SEVIS fee — start there.
An applicant looking for a script of "winning answers" — these do not exist, and officers detect them.
The controlling source
INA 214(b): officers presume immigrant intent until you overcome the presumption with evidence and credibility.
9 FAM 402.5: the consular adjudication manual section that frames F-1 review.
Department of State appointment guidance (post-specific).
Documents to audit
You should already have the eight documents from the F-1 visa document checklist 2026 . Prep specifically audits:
Document What to audit DS-160 Names, addresses, sponsor relationship, prior travel, prior refusals, work history I-20 School, program, level, start date, cost-of-attendance, funding source Sponsor letter Date within 30 days, sponsor name, relationship, dollar amount, signature Bank statements Sponsor's name, average balance (not a single peak), 3–6 months of activity Academic credentials Transcripts, degree certificates, English scores, prior degree progression Print each. Place them side by side. Read line by line. Any fact on more than one document must read the same on each.
14-day prep timeline
Days −14 to −10. Document audit. Check DS-160 vs I-20 field by field. Correct DS-160 errors by submitting a new DS-160; the corrected confirmation must reach the post before the interview.
Days −9 to −5. Sponsor and funding audit. Refresh the bank letter if it is dated more than 25 days before the appointment. Confirm the sponsor letter names you, the school, the dollar amount, and is signed.
Days −4 to −2. Verbal rehearsal. Speak each answer aloud in two sentences. Have a friend listen for filler words and contradictions. Do not write a script.
Day −1. Logistics. Reconfirm appointment time and location, print all documents in interview order, plan transport, pack a folder.
What the officer checks first
The officer's screen shows the DS-160. They open with two or three short questions:
School / program. A two-sentence answer naming the school, the degree, and one reason you chose it.
Funding. Who pays. How much. Where the money lives. Offer the documents.
Return plan. What you intend to do after the program ends.
If your answers track the DS-160 and I-20 in two sentences, the officer's screen turns to other queues. If they conflict or stall, the interview probes the weakest point.
Handling unexpected and difficult interview questions
Not all interview questions follow the standard script of school, funding, and return plan. Consular officers may ask unexpected questions to test your credibility and assess non-immigrant intent. Common curveball questions include: "What will you do if your visa is denied?", "Why didn't you apply to universities in your home country?", "How does this US degree help your career in your home country?", and "Do you have relatives in the United States?" Prepare for these questions by thinking through your answer before the interview. For the relatives question, be honest — if you have a sibling or cousin in the US, disclose it on the DS-160 and explain how your ties to your home country are stronger. For the denial consequence question, a straightforward answer like "I will reapply with stronger evidence or pursue my education in another country" shows you understand the process. Do not invent answers or contradict your DS-160 — the officer has the document on their screen and will compare.
Memorised scripts
Officers are trained to detect them. Rehearse facts, not phrasing.
DS-160 contradictions
A different school spelling, sponsor name, or date is a 60-second question you may not be ready for.

F-1 Visa Interview Questions 2026 — Answer Map 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home

Following

Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
§ Key takeaways
01 INA 214(b) creates a presumption of immigrant intent that the applicant must overcome; each of the seven question types tests a sub-element of that presumption. 
02 The seven question types are: school choice, program fit, funds, sponsor, academic history, return plan, and prior immigration history. 
03 The recommended answer structure is two sentences: the direct answer, then the document or fact that proves it. 
04 A vague or evasive answer on any of the seven areas signals the officer to probe further, while long scripts create inconsistencies. 
05 A study gap should be addressed directly with a credible explanation backed by a document; evasive answers or minimisation are credibility concerns. 
06 For the return-plan question, the stronger answer names the most concrete tie — a job offer, family business, professional license, or property — rather than uncertainty. 
Last updated 2026-06-09 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: INA 214(b); Department of State 9 FAM 402.5
Core rule: The officer presumes immigrant intent. Each question type tests a sub-element of that presumption. Answer in two sentences: the direct answer, then the document that proves it.
Seven question types: school choice, program fit, funds, sponsor, academic history, return plan, prior immigration history.
Long scripts create inconsistencies. A vague or evasive answer on any of the seven areas signals the officer to probe further. Know your own facts, not a memorised script.
This page is part of the F-1 visa rights: the international student's complete guide cluster. It exists to answer the interview-question decision only. For document assembly, read the F-1 visa document checklist 2026 . For the 14-day preparation routine, read the F-1 visa interview prep checklist .
Who this is for
An F-1 applicant who wants the canonical answer-map for the seven question types consular officers actually ask, not a script to memorise.
Who this is not for
Students already inside the U.S. managing status — read the F-1 visa rights: the international student's complete guide .
Applicants looking for scripted sample answers, success rates, or legal advice. What works for one applicant may hurt another.
Readers who need country-specific consular practice; local embassy pages must be verified separately before relying on them.
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: INA 214(b); Department of State 9 FAM 402.5 . INA 214(b) establishes the presumption that every non-immigrant visa applicant is an intending immigrant until they prove otherwise. 9 FAM 402.5 provides the specific framework officers use to evaluate F-1 applicants, including the five factors for determining whether a student's intent is genuinely non-immigrant.
The INA 214(b) framework — how officers decide
Every non-immigrant visa applicant is presumed to be an intending immigrant under INA 214(b). The applicant must overcome this presumption by convincing the officer of three things: that the proposed stay in the United States has a specific, time-limited purpose (study); that the applicant has a residence abroad they have no intention of abandoning; and that they will depart the U.S. when their authorised stay ends.
For F-1 applicants specifically, 9 FAM 402.5 directs officers to evaluate five factors: the applicant's academic preparation and intent to study, financial capacity to cover the full cost of attendance, ties to the home country, prior immigration history, and credibility. An F-1 refusal under 214(b) typically fails on one or more of these five factors — most commonly financial documentation or home-country ties.
Understanding this framework changes how you prepare. Instead of memorising answers, prepare evidence for each of the five factors. When the officer asks about your return plan, they are testing factor three — home-country ties. When they ask about your sponsor, they are testing factor two — financial capacity. Know which factor each question targets, and answer with the evidence that addresses that factor. Preparing your evidence for each of the five factors before the interview is more effective than memorizing sample answers because the officer can ask follow-up questions that a script cannot handle. Evidence-based preparation means organizing your financial documents, academic credentials, home-country ties, and prior immigration history into a folder the officer can reference. When the officer asks about your sponsor, you do not just say “my parents are paying” — you hand them the sponsor letter and bank statements showing the average balance over the past six months. When the officer asks about your return plan, you reference a specific job offer, property document, or family business registration. This document-forward approach demonstrates credibility because the officer can verify each claim immediately against the documents you have provided, reducing the likelihood of follow-up questions that might expose inconsistencies in a memorized script.
The seven question types
Most F-1 interviews test these seven areas. Each maps to one or more of the 214(b) factors:
School choice. Why this school, not a closer or cheaper one. Tests academic intent (factor one). Answer by naming a specific program feature, faculty research area, or lab that is unique to this school.
Program fit. How the program connects to prior study or future work. Tests academic intent and credibility (factors one and five). Answer by showing a logical academic progression, not a disconnected leap.
Funds. Whether the total funded amount equals or exceeds the I-20 cost of attendance. Tests financial capacity (factor two). Answer with the exact funded amount and the source, cross-referenced to the financial documents.
Sponsor.

title: F-1 Visa Refused — 30-Day Recovery Plan (214(b))
body:

F-1 Visa Refused — 30-Day Recovery Plan (214(b)) 
Skip to main content MyCaseworks 
Home 
Library 
Profile 
Your stats 
Following 
Discover 
Get weekly immigration updates
Join 
§ Key takeaways
01 There is no statutory wait after a 214(b) refusal, but reapplying without a materially stronger case typically produces the same outcome. 
02 The material-change test asks: What is materially different now that the officer did not see before? A new appointment date alone is not a stronger case. 
03 Prior refusals are on record and are considered; a reapplication without a materially different file signals the same result. 
04 The four refusal categories are: funds, study plan, ties/return plan, and credibility. Each requires a different fix. 
05 Within 48 hours of refusal, the applicant should write down the exact questions and answers; in week one, identify which category was tested. 
06 A stale bank letter older than 30 days signals that nothing changed since the refusal and weakens the reapplication. 
Last updated 2026-06-09 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: INA 214(b); 9 FAM 302.1; 9 FAM 504.4
Core rule: Do not rebook without a materially stronger case. The question is not how soon — it is whether the evidence changed.
Four refusal categories: funds, study plan, ties/return plan, or credibility. Identify which one applies before you prepare new evidence.
Timeline: write down questions within 48 hours, identify the refusal category in week one, correct the evidence before rebooking.
This page is part of the F-1 visa rights: the international student's complete guide cluster. It exists to answer the refusal-recovery decision only. For interview preparation, read the F-1 visa interview prep checklist .
Who this is for
An F-1 applicant refused under INA 214(b) within the last 30 days, deciding when and whether to reapply.
Who this is not for
Applicants refused under a ground other than 214(b) — different analysis applies. Read the refusal notice carefully.
Readers looking for approval rates, guarantees, or legal advice. No page on the internet can promise a visa outcome.
Country-specific consular guidance — local post practices vary and must be verified separately.
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: INA 214(b); 9 FAM 302.1 (Visa Ineligibilities); 9 FAM 504.4 (Reapplication after refusal) . Under 9 FAM 504.4, a reapplication after a 214(b) refusal must present new facts that overcome the specific ground of ineligibility identified — or reasonably inferred from — the previous refusal.
First 48 hours: capture the interview while it is fresh
Within 48 hours of the refusal, write down every question the officer asked and every answer you gave. Be as precise as possible — exact wording matters because the difference between "My father will support me" and "My father, a civil engineer with 15 years at Shell, has held 60,000 USD in a savings account at Access Bank for the past 14 months" is the difference between a vague answer and a verifiable claim.
Separate your notes into the four refusal categories below. A refusal that appears to be about funds may actually be a credibility issue — the officer did not believe the sponsor letter because the bank statements showed a sudden large deposit. Writing down the exact exchange helps you distinguish surface question from underlying concern.
Documents that prove the case at rebooking
The single most important document is the one that addresses the specific reason for the initial refusal. If the officer refused because the bank statements showed a sudden large deposit, bring statements showing the average balance over six months along with a source-of-funds letter explaining the deposit. If the refusal was based on a weak study plan, bring a written academic progression statement that connects your prior degree, work experience, and the US program in a logical sequence. If the refusal turned on ties to your home country, bring a letter from a home-country employer confirming a role available after graduation, or documentation of property, a family business, or a professional license that requires your return. Each piece of new evidence should be dated within 30 days of the rebooking date and should be clearly labelled with a cover sheet explaining what it is and how it addresses the prior refusal ground.
If the prior refusal was for a category the student is unsure about, a free initial consultation with a US immigration attorney can help identify the specific weakness in the file and suggest the most effective new evidence to assemble before rebooking. Many attorneys offer a short consultation specifically for this purpose, and the investment of time and money is worthwhile if it prevents a second refusal that would make future applications more difficult to approve.
The material-change test
Before rebooking, answer one question honestly: what is materially different now that the officer did not see before? 
A stronger file includes new evidence that specifically addresses the refusal ground. A new sponsor letter with source-of-funds documentation, a corrected DS-160, a clarified academic progression statement, or a fixed inconsistency between documents qualifies as a material change. A new appointment date by itself is not a material change.
This is the single most important concept in refusal recovery. Most refusals at the second interview happen because the applicant rebooked without fixing anything. The officer sees the same file and reaches the same conclusion in under two minutes.
The four refusal categories — and how to fix each
1. Funds
What it looks like. The officer asked about who is paying, how much is available, and where the money comes from. The refusal sheet may not specify "funds" — the officer may simply state 214(b) without elaboration.
Common problems. The total documented amount is below the I-20 cost of attendance. The bank statements are in a relative's name without a spons

This page is part of the F-1 visa rights: the international student's complete guide cluster. For status violations connected to a transfer, read F-1 status violation — emergency triage .
Who this is for
An F-1 student transferring SEVIS from one SEVP-certified institution to another mid-program. This includes students moving between associate, bachelor's, and master's programs at different schools, as well as students transferring between English language programs and degree-granting institutions at the same school or between different schools.
This guide is for students who are currently in valid F-1 status and are planning a transfer to a new SEVP-certified school before completing their current program of study. If you have already violated your F-1 status or your SEVIS record has been terminated, the reinstatement process differs from a standard transfer — read the SEVIS termination and F-1 reinstatement guide page for guidance on the reinstatement or new initial I-20 options. A transfer is only available while your F-1 status is currently active and your SEVIS record is in valid status at your current school.
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(8) .
What the SEVIS release date is
The SEVIS release date is the date the current school releases your SEVIS record to the receiving school. This is a date entered into the SEVIS system by your current DSO, and once the release date passes, the current school loses all ability to edit the SEVIS record. Only the new school can make changes after the release date.
Until you enrol at the new school, your F-1 status depends on the transfer-pending I-20 issued by the receiving school. The transfer-pending I-20 shows that your SEVIS record is in transit between the two schools and that you are authorized to remain in the US during the transfer period. This I-20 does not authorize employment or travel — it simply documents your continued F-1 status during the transition. Once you enrol full-time at the new school, the new DSO updates the SEVIS record to "active" status and issues a new I-20 reflecting the current program of study.
Release-date test
Do not ask the current school to set a release date until all three conditions are confirmed. Setting the release date too early — before the new school is ready to process your transfer — creates a gap where no school has full control of your SEVIS record, which can lead to status complications.
Final admission received from the receiving school. Conditional admission is not sufficient — the receiving school must have issued a final acceptance letter. If admission is conditional on completing courses at the current school or meeting language proficiency requirements, wait until all conditions are satisfied before initiating the transfer.
Funding confirmed for the first term at the receiving school. You must demonstrate sufficient financial resources to cover tuition, living expenses, and other costs for at least the first academic year. Your bank statements, scholarship letter, or sponsor letter must meet the receiving school's documented funding requirement as shown on the I-20.
Start date confirmed and a transfer-pending I-20 can be issued by the receiving school immediately after release. Confirm with the new DSO that they can issue the transfer-pending I-20 on the same day the SEVIS release date passes. A delay in issuing the transfer-pending I-20 can leave you without documentation of valid F-1 status during the transfer period.
Timeline
Before release (2 to 4 weeks before your planned transfer date): Secure final admission and confirm the start date with the receiving school. Confirm that your funding documents meet the receiving school's documented requirements. Request the transfer-pending I-20 from the receiving school's DSO and confirm they can issue it immediately after the SEVIS release date passes. Notify your current DSO of your intent to transfer and agree on a transfer release date that aligns with your last day of attendance at the current school.
After release (within 15 days of the release date or program start date, whichever comes first): Enrol full-time at the next available term at the receiving school. Complete the check-in process with the new DSO within 15 days. Failure to enrol after release terminates the SEVIS record and yo

§ Key takeaways
01 The triage matrix has five categories: paperwork error, enrolment error, employment error, transfer error, or SEVIS termination. Identify the category before acting. 
02 Employment error — off-campus work without CPT, OPT, or other authorization — creates a permanent OPT bar at that education level. 
03 Dropping below full course load without reduced-course-load approval is a status violation from the date of non-compliance. 
04 Unlawful presence above certain thresholds triggers 3- or 10-year bars on re-entry. 
05 Same-day rule: speak to the DSO before travelling or working; do not depart the U.S. without understanding the unlawful-presence risk. 
06 Documents to gather: current I-20, I-94, SEVIS status from DSO, course-load record, employment records, DSO emails, and travel history. 
Last updated 2026-05-14 · Reviewed by Attorney reviewed 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: 8 CFR § 214.1(e)–(g); 8 CFR § 214.2(f)
Triage matrix: paperwork error, enrolment error, employment error, transfer error, or SEVIS termination. Identify the category before acting.
Documents: current I-20, I-94, SEVIS status from DSO, course-load record, employment records, DSO emails, travel history.
Same-day rule: speak to the DSO before travelling or working. Do not depart the U.S. without understanding the unlawful-presence risk.
This page is part of the F-1 visa rights: the international student's complete guide cluster. It exists for emergency triage only. For SEVIS termination and the reinstatement vs re-entry decision, read SEVIS termination and F-1 reinstatement guide .
Who this is for
An F-1 student who has just learned, or fears, that they are out of F-1 status — emergency triage page. This includes students who have dropped below a full course load, accepted work without proper authorisation, let their I-20 expire, missed a transfer deadline, or received a notice from their DSO that their SEVIS record has been or may be terminated. If you are a DSO or immigration adviser helping a student navigate a status violation, the triage matrix and recovery path guidance below will also help structure the response.
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: 8 CFR § 214.1(e)–(g); 8 CFR § 214.2(f) .
8 CFR § 214.1(e)–(g) establishes the general rules for maintenance of status across all nonimmigrant categories, including when a violation triggers unlawful presence accrual. Section 214.2(f) sets out the specific F-1 student conditions, including the full-course-of-study requirement, work authorisation limits, and the grounds for SEVIS termination. A status violation occurs when any of these conditions are not met — from the date of non-compliance, not from the date the DSO discovers it. Understanding which subsection was violated determines the available recovery path.
Triage matrix
Identify the violation category before choosing a recovery path:
Paperwork error. I-20 expired, wrong name, missing DSO signature. May be correctable without a formal status violation if caught early and corrected before the DSO reports it in SEVIS. Contact the DSO immediately to correct or reissue the I-20. Paperwork errors discovered within 30 days are typically the easiest category to resolve.
Enrolment error. Dropped below full course load without reduced-course-load (RCL) approval. This is a status violation from the date of non-compliance, not from the date the school discovers it. Even if the DSO does not immediately terminate SEVIS, the violation exists and must be addressed. Options include requesting retroactive RCL approval (if grounds exist), reinstatement, or departure.
Employment error. Off-campus work without CPT, OPT, or other authorisation. Creates a permanent OPT bar at that education level. Unauthorised employment is the most serious category because it cannot be retroactively authorised. Even one day of unauthorised work can permanently bar OPT at that level and may trigger unlawful presence accrual.
Transfer error. Failed to enrol at the new school within the required window after SEVIS release. If the 15-day enrolment window passes without the new school completing the transfer-in, the SEVIS record becomes terminated. The student may need reinstatement or a new initial I-20 and re-entry.
SEVIS termination. DSO has already terminated the SEVIS record. At this point, the student is out of status and must either reinstate under I-539 or depart and re-enter on a new I-20. Read SEVIS termination and F-1 reinstatement guide for the full comparison between these two paths.
Same-day actions
Speak to the DSO before travelling or working. The DSO is your first point of contact. They can confirm whether SEVIS is still active, whether a correction is possible, and what documentation you will need for the next step. Do not rely on speculation — confirm the facts directly with the DSO.
Do not depart the U.S. without understanding whether unlawful presence has accrued. Departure can convert a status problem into a multi-year bar. If you have accrued 180 or more days of unlawful presence, departing triggers a 3-year bar on re-entry under INA § 212(a)(9)(B). If you have accrued 365 or more days, the bar is 10 years.
Gather your documents. Collect your current I-20, I-94, SEVIS status printout, course-load records, employment records, and any DSO communications. Having these organised before meeting with the DSO or an attorney saves critical time.
Do not sign or agree to anything without understanding the consequences. If the DSO asks you to sign a voluntary departure or status-termination acknowledgement, ask to take the document away for review before signing.
Documents to gather
Current I-20 — check the program end date, DSO signature validity, and the SEVIS ID. If the I-20 is expired, note the expiry date and whether an extension

F-2 is for spouses and unmarried children under 21 of F-1 students. Each dependant needs a separate I-20 and DS-160.
F-2 restrictions: spouses cannot work in any capacity. Children can attend school up to grade 12 without separate permission. Neither can enrol in a full-time degree program without separate status.
Documents: principal F-1 I-20, dependent I-20, marriage or birth certificate, passport, DS-160, financial proof, proof of relationship.
This page is part of the F-1 visa rights: the international student's complete guide cluster. It exists to answer the F-2 dependant visa decision. For the F-1 applicant's own documents, read the F-1 visa document checklist 2026 .
Who this is for
An F-1 student bringing a spouse or unmarried minor children to the U.S. on F-2 dependant visas. This page is also relevant for F-2 dependants already in the U.S. who want to understand their status restrictions, and for F-1 students approaching graduation who need to plan how a transition to H-1B or another status affects their dependants’ F-2 status.
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(15); 22 CFR § 41.61 .
8 CFR § 214.2(f)(15) establishes the F-2 classification for spouses and unmarried children under 21 of F-1 students. It defines the scope of what F-2 dependants may and may not do in the United States, including the work prohibition and the limits on study. 22 CFR § 41.61 governs the consular processing of F-2 visa applications abroad, including the documentary requirements and the dependency proof test. Together, these two regulations create the legal framework for every F-2 application — whether filed as a change of status inside the U.S. or as a visa application at a consulate abroad.
What F-2 allows and does not allow
F-2 spouses: 
May accompany the principal F-1 student in the U.S. for the duration of the F-1’s authorised stay.
May study part-time in a vocational or recreational program that does not constitute a full course of study. This includes language courses, hobby classes, and certificate programs that are less than a full-time academic load.
Cannot work in any capacity — no employment authorisation is available on F-2 status, including remote work for a foreign employer, freelance projects, unpaid internships with for-profit companies, or self-employment of any kind. Any compensated activity, regardless of the source or location of the employer, is prohibited.
Cannot enrol in a full-time degree program without changing to F-1 or another qualifying status. Full-time enrollment while on F-2 is a status violation.
F-2 children (unmarried, under 21): 
May attend elementary or secondary school (through grade 12) in the United States without a separate student visa. The F-2 child’s I-20 serves as the basis for school enrollment.
Cannot enrol in post-secondary education (college, university, or vocational training beyond high school) without changing to F-1 status.
Cannot work in any capacity during F-2 status, including part-time or summer employment.
Age-out at 21 — must change status to F-1 or another qualifying category, or depart the U.S., before their 21st birthday. US Citizenship and Immigration Services uses the date the change-of-status application is filed (or the date of admission) to determine whether the child is under 21, so filing a timely change-of-status application before the 21st birthday can preserve eligibility.
Documents that prove the case
Principal F-1 I-20 — the dependent I-20 is issued by the same school and ties to the principal student’s SEVIS record. The school must issue a separate I-20 for each dependant. This is the most critical document — without it, the consular officer cannot process the F-2 application.
Separate dependent I-20 for each dependant. Request these from the DSO after the F-1 student’s own I-20 is current and active. Each dependant receives their own SEVIS ID and I-20.
Marriage certificate (for spouse) or birth certificate (for children) — translated into English by a certified translator if the original is not in English. The translation must include the translator’s certification of accuracy.
Passport for each dependant, valid for at least six months beyond the intended stay.
Separate DS-160 for each dependant, with the correct SEVIS ID from their dependent I-20. Each dependant pays the visa application fee separately.
Financial proof showing the F-1 student can support both themselves and the dependants for the full I-20 cost period. Bank statements, sponsorship letters, or scholarship awards showing sufficient funds for the first year of study are typically sufficient. USCIS and consular officers look for evidence that the dependant will not need to work to support themselves.
Proof of relationship — official civil registry documents, joint bank account statements, or correspondence spanning the relationship period may be required if the marri

01 F-1 status is conditional on full-course-load enrolment, work only as authorized, timely transfers, and maintaining a valid I-20. 
02 On-campus work is permitted up to 20 hours per week during term and full-time on official school breaks without additional authorization. 
03 Any unauthorized employment, even one day, creates a permanent OPT bar at that education level. 
04 SEVIS transfer to a new school must occur within 15 days of the new school's start date. 
05 Re-entry on F-1 requires a valid passport, valid F-1 visa stamp (or automatic revalidation), an I-20 with travel signature within 12 months (6 for OPT/STEM OPT), and proof of enrolment or employment. 
06 Part-time enrolment generally breaks F-1 status except in the final term or with specific medical or academic DSO authorization. 
Last updated 2026-05-09 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: 8 CFR § 214.2(f) ; SEVP policy guidance; USCIS work-authorisation forms (I-765, I-983).
Core rule: F-1 is conditional on full-course-load enrolment, work only as authorised, timely transfers, and a valid I-20.
Documents: I-20, I-94, passport, F-1 visa stamp, EAD where applicable, transcripts.
Timing: 60-day grace after program completion; 30 days within I-20 endorsement for I-765 OPT filing; 15 days for school transfers.
Main risk: any unauthorised employment, even one day, creates a permanent OPT bar at that level.
Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera, Esq. (CA Bar #298948, Certified Specialist — Immigration & Nationality Law).
The rule in plain English
F-1 status grants permission to study full time in the United States, with limited work authorisation tied to specific authorisations. The controlling source is 8 CFR § 214.2(f) and the SEVP policy guidance issued to Designated School Officials. The core bargain of the F-1 visa is straightforward: you are admitted to pursue a legitimate academic program at a SEVP-certified school, and in exchange you agree to maintain a full course of study, work only within authorised categories, and depart the US or change status upon completion of your academic objectives. Violating any of these core conditions — even inadvertently — can result in SEVIS termination, loss of F-1 status, and removal proceedings.
This page serves as the pillar guide for the F-1 visa cluster. Each topic below links to a dedicated page with detailed guidance. Use this guide to understand the overall framework, then follow the links to the specific page that matches your situation.
Who this guide is for
Likely fit
You are admitted to a SEVP-certified school, you hold a valid I-20, you have entered or will enter on F-1 status.
Needs review
You are between programs; you are on a J-1 considering a switch; you are on a dependent F-2.
Usually not a fit
You are out of status with no reinstatement filed; your visa was cancelled at port of entry.
Maintaining status
Maintaining F-1 status requires compliance with several basic rules throughout your stay:
Full course of study every fall and spring (summers are optional unless the first term). For undergraduates, this typically means at least 12 credits per semester; for graduate students, at least 9 credits, though specific requirements vary by school and program.
Work only as authorised: on-campus up to 20 hours per week during term, full-time on breaks; CPT before program completion; OPT after; STEM OPT for designated degrees. Any work outside these categories is a status violation.
Transfer SEVIS to a new school within 15 days of the start date there. The transfer process requires acceptance at the new school and coordination between the current and new DSO.
Apply for I-20 extension before the program end date. DSOs cannot extend retroactively — if your I-20 expires before you complete your program, you are out of status.
Update your address with your DSO within 10 days of any move. Report a new U.S. address to the DSO through the school’s reporting system.
Maintain a valid passport at all times. If your passport expires, renew it through your home country’s embassy or consulate and provide the updated information to your DSO.
Read F-1 visa status violation: what happens, what to do, and when to call an attorney if status has slipped.
Work authorisation routes
F-1 students have four main work authorisation categories, each with different requirements and limitations:
On-campus employment. No additional permission needed. You may work up to 20 hours per week during the academic term and full-time during official school breaks. The position must be on the school’s premises and provide direct services to students. This is the only work category available without DSO or USCIS authorisation.
CPT (Curricular Practical Training). School-authorised, employer-specific, and must be an integral part of an established curriculum. CPT can begin at any point in the program, including day one if the program qualifies. Part-time CPT does not affect OPT eligibility; full-time CPT beyond 12 months permanently bars OPT at that level. Read CPT authorization letters: what your DSO writes, what an attorney checks .
OPT (Optional Practical Training). USCIS-authorised, available before or after program completion. Standard OPT provides 12 months of work authorisation per education level. Pre-completion OPT uses the same 12-month pool at a reduced rate. Post-completion OPT requires filing within 30 days of the DSO recommendation and allows up to 90 days of unemployment. Read Form I-765 OPT application: the eight common mistakes that get it denied .
STEM OPT extension. 24-month extension available for STEM Designated Degrees. Requires E-Verify enrolled employer, signed I-983 training plan, and ongoing reporting obligations. Read STEM OPT self-employment and startups .

§ Key takeaways
01 Five common violation patterns: dropping below full course load without DSO authorization; unauthorized employment; failing to extend the I-20 before program end; failing to transfer SEVIS within 15 days; and criminal conviction triggering visa revocation. 
02 Reinstatement on Form I-539 is generally available only within five months of the violation and requires showing the violation was beyond the student's control or due to a school error. 
03 Travel-and-re-entry on a new I-20 restarts the clock on OPT and CPT eligibility, but departure before filing reinstatement removes the I-539 option. 
04 For F-1 students admitted for 'duration of status' (D/S), unlawful presence usually starts only after USCIS or an immigration judge formally finds a violation. 
05 Reinstatement decisions currently average four to eight months, and premium processing is not available for I-539. 
06 The visa stamp is not automatically cancelled by SEVIS termination, but it cannot be used for re-entry while the termination is in place. 
Last updated 2026-05-09 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: 8 CFR § 214.1(g) and (h) ; 8 CFR § 214.2(f) ; SEVP reinstatement policy guidance.
Core rule: F-1 status is maintained by full-course-load enrolment, work only as authorised, and timely transfers/extensions. Any of these can be broken.
Documents: Form I-20, I-94, SEVIS record, transcripts, prior I-797s, any termination notice, employer letters.
Timing: reinstatement under Form I-539 is generally available only within five months of the violation. Beyond that, departure and re-entry on a new I-20 may be the only route.
Main risk: continuing to work or attend on a terminated SEVIS record. Each day is a separate violation and accrues unlawful presence.
Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera, Esq. (CA Bar #298948, Certified Specialist — Immigration & Nationality Law).
The rule in plain English
F-1 status is conditional. To maintain it you must enrol in a full course of study, work only as authorised by your DSO or USCIS, transfer to a new school under the proper procedure, and apply for any extension before your program end date. The controlling sources are 8 CFR § 214.1(g) and (h) and 8 CFR § 214.2(f) .
A violation does not automatically lead to deportation. It does end work authorisation immediately, may end SEVIS enrolment, and starts the clock on potential unlawful presence. Unlawful presence for F-1 students admitted for Duration of Status (D/S) typically starts only after USCIS or an immigration judge formally finds a violation — it does not begin automatically when a status violation occurs. However, once SEVIS is terminated and the violation is recorded, USCIS may back-date the unlawful presence finding. Accruing more than 180 days of unlawful presence triggers a 3-year bar on re-entering the US under INA 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(I); more than 365 days triggers a 10-year bar. Do not depart the US without understanding your unlawful presence exposure. Read Form I-765 OPT application: the eight common mistakes that get it denied for the OPT-specific paths back.
Who this guide is for
Likely fit
Your DSO or USCIS has confirmed a violation; you are still in the United States; the violation occurred within the past five months.
Needs review
You suspect a violation but have not received written confirmation. Request your SEVIS record before filing anything.
Usually not a fit
You have already accrued more than 180 days of unlawful presence; you have a prior order of removal; you have a criminal arrest unrelated to the status violation.
What counts as a violation
Five common patterns: dropping below a full course load without DSO authorisation; unauthorised employment (any work for pay before EAD start date); failing to extend the I-20 before the program end date; failing to transfer SEVIS to a new school within 15 days of the start date at the new school; and any criminal conviction that triggers visa revocation.
The 15-day and 60-day grace rules
After a properly completed program, F-1 students have 60 days to depart, transfer, or change status. After OPT ends, the same 60-day grace applies. After a SEVIS termination for cause, there is no 60-day grace — you are expected to depart immediately. The 15-day rule applies to school transfers and to re-entry timing on a new I-20.
Reinstatement vs. re-entry on a new I-20
Reinstatement is filed on Form I-539 with USCIS, typically within five months of the violation. The application asks USCIS to treat the violation as if it had not happened. Approval restores F-1 status. The bar is high: you must show the violation was beyond your control or due to a school error.
Travel-and-re-entry on a new I-20 is the alternative. You depart the United States, your DSO issues a new I-20 with a new SEVIS ID, and you re-enter on a new admission. This restarts the clock on OPT and CPT eligibility. Read CPT authorization letters: what your DSO writes, what an attorney checks before assuming a fresh CPT clock applies.

US Student Visa FAQ
Attorney-reviewed answers about F-1 status, OPT and STEM OPT rules, CPT traps, travel during pending applications, and SEVIS termination. This FAQ aggregates the most common decision points from our US student visa articles.
This FAQ is for F-1 students preparing for OPT or STEM OPT, navigating CPT limits, managing SEVIS compliance, or dealing with a status violation. The questions reflect the most common situations we see from international students in USCIS forums and from our document review clients. Each answer has been reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera, a licensed California attorney (CA Bar #298948), and is grounded in the Immigration and Nationality Act, 8 CFR regulations, SEVP policy guidance, and current USCIS adjudication practices as of mid-2026.
F-1 regulations around STEM OPT employer monitoring, CPT accumulation, and unemployment caps remain areas of frequent confusion and compliance failure. The 2026 policy landscape includes continued USCIS scrutiny of staffing-agency STEM OPT placements, evolving E-Verify requirements, and strict enforcement of the 90-day and 150-day unemployment limits — areas where adjudication standards have tightened measurably since 2024. The answers below reflect the current published rules and guidance.
The question list below covers the most urgent student-visa compliance topics. For deeper guidance on each subject, the linked articles at the bottom of this page give full step-by-step instructions, form references, and the specific regulatory citations that govern each area.
OPT and STEM OPT compliance requirements have received increased enforcement attention from USCIS in the 2024-2026 period, particularly around worksite verification, employer-employee relationship requirements for staffing agency placements, and electronic I-983 signature validity. The 90-day unemployment cap for post-completion OPT and the 150-day aggregate cap for STEM OPT remain areas where students unintentionally fall out of status by underestimating gaps between jobs or failing to report qualifying employment promptly through their DSO or the SEVP Portal.
CPT accumulation continues to be a frequent source of post-completion OPT ineligibility. The 12-month full-time CPT threshold under 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(i) eliminates OPT eligibility permanently, not just for the current degree level. Students who have used part-time CPT do not accumulate time toward the 12-month limit, but any week in which more than 20 hours of CPT are authorized counts as a full-time week. DSOs are not required to proactively warn students that they are approaching the 12-month limit, making self-tracking the only reliable safeguard.
The H-1B cap-gap extension described in one of the questions below remains one of the most consequential automatic benefits available to F-1 students, but it contains several traps: the cap-gap ends immediately if the H-1B petition is denied or withdrawn, travel during cap-gap terminates the change-of-status component, and the cap-gap does not apply to consular-notification H-1B petitions (those filed for consular processing rather than change of status). Understanding which type of H-1B petition your employer has filed is essential before relying on the cap-gap extension for continued work authorization through September 30.
How this FAQ is organised
The questions are grouped by topic area. OPT and STEM OPT questions cover travel while an I-765 is pending, verifying employer E-Verify enrollment, job change reporting requirements, self-employment structures for solo founders, unemployment cap tracking across both OPT and STEM OPT periods, and staffing agency placement compliance. CPT questions focus on the 12-month full-time CPT trap under 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(i) and how cumulative CPT hours affect post-completion OPT eligibility. SEVIS and compliance questions address the immediate steps to take after a termination notice, the legal distinction between an F-1 visa stamp and F-1 status, and cap-gap extension mechanics.
Each answer follows the same structure: the regulatory or statutory rule, the practical application for a current F-1 student, and the specific documents or evidence the rule requires. Where multiple interpretations exist — such as whether a staffing agency can sponsor STEM OPT or whether a solo-owned LLC satisfies the self-employment requirements — the answer explains the conditions under which each interpretation applies rather than giving a blanket yes or no.
If your specific situation is not represented below, the linked articles at the bottom of this page provide deeper treatment of each topic with full regulatory citations, step-by-step document checklists, and worked examples for common scenarios. For applicants who need a structured review of their OPT packet before filing, our flat-fee document checklist review and SOP review services can verify your forms, evidence, and compliance posture before submission to USCIS.
All answers reference the Immigration and Nationality Act, 8 CFR Part 214, USCIS adjudicator guidance, and SEVP policy documents as of July 2026. Rules published on agency blogs, third-party forums, or university international office websites may not reflect current enforcement practice — always cross-reference responses here against the official regulatory sources cited in each answer before taking action.

body:

§ Key takeaways
01 Form I-765 must be filed within 30 days of the DSO's OPT endorsement on the I-20; filing before endorsement rejects the application and the fee is not refunded. 
02 You can file no earlier than 90 days before your program end date and no later than 60 days after; USCIS counts from the receipt date at the lockbox, not the postmark. 
03 Wrong (c)(3) eligibility category code produces a Request for Evidence at best and a denial at worst. 
04 USCIS rejects passport photos that are not exactly 2×2 inches, more than 30 days old, or taken by phone — even if printed at 2×2. 
05 Twelve months of full-time CPT at the same education level permanently bars OPT at that level. 
06 Post-completion OPT requires directly related employment; self-employment is allowed only if the business is properly established with an EIN and license before the EAD start date. 
Last updated 2026-05-09 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: USCIS Form I-765 instructions, 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10), and SEVP Optional Practical Training policy guidance.
Core rule: OPT requires a SEVIS recommendation from your DSO and Form I-765 filed within strict windows tied to the program end date.
Documents: Form I-765, signed Form I-20 with OPT recommendation (within 30 days), passport bio page, all prior I-94s, prior EADs, two passport photos, Form G-1145, filing fee.
Timing: file no earlier than 90 days before the program end date, no later than 60 days after, and within 30 days of your DSO's I-20 endorsement.
Main risk: Form I-765 filed before the I-20 OPT recommendation is rejected outright. The fee is not refunded.
Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera, Esq. (CA Bar #298948, Certified Specialist — Immigration & Nationality Law).
The rule in plain English
USCIS denies Form I-765 OPT applications for procedural reasons more often than substantive ones. The controlling sources are the USCIS Form I-765 instructions , 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10) , and the SEVP policy guidance issued to Designated School Officials.
Optional Practical Training is a benefit, not an entitlement. To receive an Employment Authorization Document, an F-1 student must have a Designated School Official recommend OPT in SEVIS, receive an I-20 endorsed with that recommendation, and file Form I-765 with USCIS within a window tied to the program end date. Missing any link in that chain is the most common reason applications fail.
Who this guide is for
Likely fit
You are an F-1 student in lawful status, you have completed at least one academic year, your DSO has agreed to recommend OPT, and your filing window is open or about to open.
Needs review
You have a gap in your I-20 history, a prior period of unauthorised employment, a prior CPT authorisation that exceeded 12 months full-time at the same level, or an arrest record.
Usually not a fit
You are out of status, you missed the 60-day filing window after program end date, or you previously used 12 months of OPT at the same education level.
Mistake 1 — filing before the DSO recommends OPT in SEVIS
Form I-765 must be filed within 30 days of the date your DSO endorsed the OPT recommendation on your Form I-20. The endorsement date is printed on page 2 of the I-20 in the OPT section. If you file before the DSO recommends OPT — even by one day — USCIS rejects the application as procedurally defective. The filing fee is not refunded.
Mistake 2 — filing outside the 90/60 window
You can file Form I-765 for post-completion OPT no earlier than 90 days before your program end date, and no later than 60 days after. USCIS counts from the receipt date stamped at the lockbox, not the postmark date. Allow at least seven business days for transit if filing by mail.
Mistake 3 — wrong eligibility category code
The "eligibility category" on Form I-765 Part 2, Item 27 tells USCIS what kind of work permission you are requesting. The OPT codes are (c)(3)(A) for pre-completion OPT, (c)(3)(B) for post-completion OPT, and (c)(3)(C) for the STEM OPT 24-month extension. Putting (c)(3)(B) on a pre-completion application produces a Request for Evidence at best, a denial at worst.
Mistake 4 — sending the wrong filing fee
Filing with the wrong amount — including being short by one dollar — causes USCIS to reject the application. Check the USCIS fee schedule on the day you are mailing the packet. Pay by personal check, money order, or credit card via Form G-1450.
Mistake 5 — incomplete or incorrect Form I-94 history
Item 18 on Form I-765 asks for your most recent I-94 number and arrival information. Item 19 asks for the place of last entry. USCIS cross-references these against CBP records. Pull your current I-94 from the CBP I-94 website, print the record-of-admission, and include a copy in your packet. Read F-1 visa status violation: what happens, what to do, and when to call an attorney if your I-94 history has gaps because of a SEVIS issue.
Mistake 6 — passport photos that do not meet specification
USCIS rejects photos that are not exactly 2×2 inches, that are more than 30 days old, or that do not show a clear front view of the face against a plain white background. Sending photos taken by phone — even printed at 2×2 — is a common rejection reason.

body:

LLC on F-1 OPT: Rules & Steps (2026)

Home

§ Key takeaways
01 Forming an LLC is legal in every US state for non-citizens, including F-1 students; owning membership interests is investment, not work. 
02 The work-vs-investment line controls everything: performing services for the LLC is work and requires OPT authorization. 
03 Post-completion OPT requires work be directly related to the degree; a one-page memo documenting the relationship is standard. 
04 The IRS issues an EIN to any LLC, including foreign-owned ones; F-1 students with valid SSNs can use them, otherwise an ITIN or international applicant procedure applies. 
05 A single-member LLC owned by a foreign national is a disregarded entity for federal tax; income flows to the member, who files Form 1040 or 1040-NR. 
06 You can form the LLC before the OPT EAD is issued, but you cannot begin work for the LLC before the EAD start date. 
Last updated 2026-05-09 · Editorial review by MyCaseworks Editorial 
This guide is editorial-only . It covers LLC formation capacity and the work-vs-investment line for F-1/OPT students. For attorney-reviewed STEM OPT self-employment and employer-structure rules, read STEM OPT self-employment and startups . See the MyCaseworks Editorial profile .
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: USCIS OPT self-employment guidance; IRS Form SS-4 instructions; the Secretary of State filing rules in your state of formation.
Core rule: an F-1 student can form an LLC in any state. Whether you can work for the LLC depends on OPT authorisation, not on the formation itself.
Documents: Articles of Organization, Operating Agreement, EIN, registered agent appointment, business bank account paperwork, OPT EAD.
Timing: form the LLC any time. Begin work for the LLC only on or after the OPT EAD start date and only if the work is directly related to your degree.
Main risk: working on the LLC before the EAD start date or in roles unrelated to your degree. Both are status violations.
The rule in plain English
Forming an LLC as an international student is legal in every US state. Owning shares is investment, not work. The two facts you can rely on are: yes, you can be a member of an LLC; and yes, you can hold an EIN. The question that controls everything else is whether what you do day to day is "work" under USCIS rules, and if so, whether OPT authorises it.
The controlling guidance is the USCIS OPT self-employment policy, the IRS Form SS-4 instructions, and the Secretary of State filing rules in your state of formation. Read STEM OPT self-employment and startups for the parallel STEM OPT rules.
Who this guide is for
Likely fit
You are an F-1 student with an approved EAD for post-completion OPT, your degree is directly related to the LLC's intended business, and you intend to work for the LLC after the EAD start date.
Needs review
Your degree is loosely related to the business; the LLC will be a mix of work and passive ownership; you have co-founders who are US citizens or permanent residents.
Usually not a fit
You are pre-OPT; you are an undergraduate in your first academic year; the work is unrelated to your degree.
Legal capacity to form
Every US state allows non-citizens, including non-residents, to form LLCs. Delaware, Wyoming, and your home study state are common choices. Filing requires Articles of Organization, the appointment of a registered agent, and payment of the state filing fee. None of these requires US citizenship or residency.
EIN as a foreign national
The IRS issues an Employer Identification Number to any LLC, including those owned by foreign nationals. Form SS-4 requires either a Social Security Number or an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) of a "responsible party" — the individual who owns or controls the LLC. F-1 students with valid SSNs can use them as the responsible party. Without an SSN you may need an ITIN or to apply by fax/mail using the international applicant procedure. The IRS processes EIN applications immediately for online filers, so you can apply for the EIN on the same day you file the Articles of Organization. Apply as soon as the LLC is formed, but do not begin working for the LLC until the OPT EAD start date arrives. The EIN confirmation letter (CP 575) serves as proof that the business exists for tax purposes and is required for opening a business bank account.
The work-vs-investment line
Holding LLC membership interests is investment. Receiving distributions from those interests is investment income, not employment. Performing services for the LLC — writing code, designing, selling, managing operations — is work, and work requires authorisation. The line is not always clean: a passive investor who writes a brief is a passive investor who has just done work. If in doubt, document the activity and treat it as work.

body:
