§ Key takeaways
01 Four replacement paths exist: lost or damaged (applicant fault), stolen (police report), or USCIS production error. 
02 The replacement fee is waived only for USCIS production errors documented on the issued card, provided the original error card is returned. 
03 Do not file a USCIS-error EAD as a lost card; that changes the fee and evidence path and may delay the correct replacement. 
04 Do not assume work authorization while waiting for the replacement; if the employer requires the physical EAD for I-9, you cannot work until it arrives. 
05 For a stolen card, obtain a police report before filing with USCIS. 
06 Address an uncorrected USCIS error within 30 days of card receipt to avoid complications at I-9 or port of entry. 
Last updated 2026-05-14 · Reviewed by Attorney reviewed 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: USCIS Form I-765 instructions; 8 CFR § 274a.13(d)
Four replacement paths: applicant-fault loss, damage, theft (police report), or USCIS production error.
Fee is waived only when USCIS issued a card with a documented error (wrong name, wrong dates, wrong category) and you return the original card.
Do not assume work authorization while waiting — if the employer requires the physical card for I-9, you cannot work until the replacement arrives.
This page is part of the OPT and STEM OPT — complete guide cluster. For filing errors that affect the replacement path, read Form I-765 OPT application: the eight common mistakes that get it denied .
Who this is for
An F-1 OPT or STEM OPT holder whose EAD card was lost, stolen, damaged, or issued with a USCIS production error. This includes students on standard post-completion OPT, STEM OPT extension holders, and students with pending OPT applications where the issued card arrived with incorrect information. Employers of OPT holders whose employees have lost or damaged their EAD cards will also find the I-9 compliance guidance relevant.
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: USCIS Form I-765 instructions; 8 CFR § 274a.13(d) .
8 CFR § 274a.13(d) governs the replacement of employment authorisation documents. It provides that an individual whose EAD has been lost, stolen, or damaged may apply for a replacement by filing a new Form I-765 with the required fee. For USCIS-issued cards that contain a Service error — such as an incorrect name, date of birth, category code, or validity period — the same regulation permits a fee-exempt replacement provided the original card is returned. The regulation does not create a separate right to employment authorisation during the replacement period; the student’s underlying OPT authorisation remains valid even if the physical card is lost, but the employer may still require a physical document for I-9 compliance.
Four replacement paths
Identify the path before filing. Each path has different evidence requirements and may have different fees.
Lost or damaged — applicant fault
File a new Form I-765 with the same category code as the original EAD. Include identity documents (passport biographic page, I-94, most recent I-20) and a signed written explanation of when and how the card was lost or damaged. A filing fee applies — check the current USCIS fee schedule on the Form I-765 webpage before preparing the payment. Processing times for replacement EADs are typically 3 to 6 months, comparable to an initial OPT application. If the card was lost while travelling abroad, you may need to apply for a transportation letter (carrier document) from the nearest US consulate to re-enter the US while the replacement is pending.
Stolen — police report
Obtain a police report documenting the theft before filing the I-765 replacement packet. File the police report in the jurisdiction where the theft occurred — this could be a local police department, campus security, or airport police if the card was stolen during travel. Include the police report case number and a copy of the report with the replacement packet. A filing fee applies. Filing without the police report may result in an RFE, delaying the replacement by 2 to 3 additional months. If the card was stolen along with other identity documents (passport, other cards), report all stolen documents to both the police and the relevant issuing authorities.
USCIS production error
If the issued card contains an error that is USCIS’s fault — wrong legal name, wrong date of birth, wrong category, wrong dates of validity — the replacement fee is waived. You must return the original error card with the replacement request. Compare every field on the issued card against your I-20, DS-160, and Form I-765 receipt notice before concluding that the error is USCIS’s. If the error originated in your application (e.g., you entered the wrong date on the I-765), it is not a USCIS error — you must file a paid replacement. Include a cover letter that identifies each error on the card, shows the correct information from your supporting documents, and confirms that the error is not in your original application. Do not file as a lost card if the problem is an error on the face of the issued card; that changes the fee and evidence path.
Document checklist
Copy of the old EAD if available — front and back. Even a photocopy or photo of the card helps establish the original authorisation period and category code. Keep a digital scan of your EAD card in a secure location for this reason.
Police report for a stolen card — include the case number, the issuing agency, and the date reported. A police report serves as independent third-party evidence of the theft and reduces the risk of an RFE.
Original error card to return for USCIS-error replacement — USCIS requires the original physical card. Do not destroy or discard it. Include a cover letter listing each error and the correct informati

§ Key takeaways
01 Pre-completion OPT requires one full academic year in F-1 status before filing; confirm how your school defines the academic year. 
02 During academic sessions, pre-completion OPT is limited to 20 hours per week. During official school breaks, full-time is allowed if enrolled for the next term. 
03 Pre-completion OPT draws from the same 12-month aggregate pool as post-completion OPT at the same education level. 
04 Part-time pre-completion OPT counts at half-rate: two days of part-time use generally equal one day deducted from the aggregate. 
05 Heavy pre-completion OPT use may affect STEM extension eligibility because STEM OPT requires maintaining a full 12-month post-completion OPT period. 
06 The correct I-765 category code for pre-completion OPT is (c)(3)(A). 
Last updated 2026-07-14 · Reviewed by Attorney reviewed 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(A)
Requires one academic year in F-1 status before filing.
During school sessions: limited to 20 hours per week. During official school breaks: full-time is allowed.
Two days of part-time pre-completion OPT generally count as one day deducted from the 12-month aggregate at the same education level.
Any days used now reduce post-completion OPT availability at the same degree level.
This page is part of the OPT and STEM OPT — complete guide cluster. To compare pre-completion OPT against CPT for the same role, read CPT vs OPT — which applies to you .
Who this is for
An F-1 student considering OPT during program enrollment — before graduation — and needing to understand how that use affects future OPT availability. This guide is for students who have a part-time or internship opportunity during their degree program and want to evaluate whether pre-completion OPT is the right authorisation type, and for students who have already been offered a full-time summer internship and need to apply for pre-completion OPT to accept it. If you are a graduate student whose program involves both coursework and thesis or dissertation research, the timing of when you complete the one-year academic requirement and when you can start pre-completion OPT may differ from undergraduate schedules — confirm your program's structure with your DSO before filing.
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(A) . Pre-completion OPT is employment authorisation before program completion, filed on Form I-765 under category (c)(3)(A). It draws from the same 12-month OPT pool at the education level as post-completion OPT. Hours limits during academic sessions (generally 20 hours/week) and full-time allowance on official breaks are set by regulation and school policy. Always confirm your school’s academic-year definition and break calendar with the DSO before filing.
Eligibility requirements
One full academic year in F-1 status must be completed before pre-completion OPT begins. Confirm how your school defines the academic year, as it varies by institution. Some schools define it as two semesters or three quarters; others count credit hours rather than time enrolled.
The employment must be directly related to the student's major area of study. The DSO reviews this connection before recommending the OPT, and USCIS may verify it when adjudicating the I-765. If the role involves duties that are not clearly connected to your degree field, the DSO may reject the recommendation.
DSO must recommend the OPT in SEVIS before USCIS will accept the I-765. The DSO enters the OPT recommendation into SEVIS and prints a new I-20 with the recommendation noted on page 2. The I-20 must be signed within 30 days of the date you file the I-765.
The I-765 must be filed with USCIS and approved before the employment start date. Unlike post-completion OPT, pre-completion OPT does not have a 90-day advance filing window — the timing is tied to when the DSO enters the recommendation and when the employment period begins. File as soon as the DSO enters the recommendation to allow enough processing time before the intended start date.
Hours limits
During academic sessions: maximum 20 hours per week. The 20-hour cap applies to all pre-completion OPT employment combined, not per employer. If you have two part-time pre-completion OPT positions, the total hours across both must stay at or below 20 hours per week during the academic year. Each job requires its own DSO recommendation and I-20 endorsement, but the hours count together toward the same weekly limit. Any hour worked beyond 20 in a week is a status violation that can trigger SEVIS termination and affect future immigration benefits, including post-completion OPT and H-1B eligibility.
During official school breaks: full-time employment (more than 20 hours per week) is allowed if the student is enrolled for the next term. Confirm your school's break dates and enrollment requirements. Official school breaks include summer vacation, winter break, and spring break. The full-time allowance applies only during the official break dates published in your school's academic calendar — not during reading days, exam periods, or other unofficial breaks. Some schools have different break definitions for graduate programs, so check with your DSO if you are enrolled in a non-semester program such as a quarter system or continuous enrollment program.
The consumption rule
Pre-completion OPT draws from the same 12-month aggregate pool as post-completion OPT at the same education level. Full-time pre-completion OPT days count one-for-one. Part-time pre-completion OPT days count at half-rate: two days of part-time use generally equal one day deducted from the aggregate.

§ Key takeaways
01 The STEM OPT employer must be enrolled in E-Verify under the specific EIN that employs the student. 
02 The worksite must be covered by the employer's E-Verify enrollment; a different worksite may require separate enrollment verification. 
03 The employer-identity test requires the same entity to employ the student, be E-Verify enrolled, provide training and supervision, and have authority to terminate. 
04 Staffing-agency placements at a client company that controls training and supervision create employer-identity risk, even if the agency is E-Verify enrolled. 
05 If the client company signs Form I-983 instead of the staffing employer, the employer-identity test fails. 
06 Verify E-Verify enrollment through the E-Verify employer search tool at e-verify.gov before filing the STEM OPT extension. 
Last updated 2026-07-14 · Reviewed by Attorney reviewed 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C)(2)
The STEM OPT employer must be enrolled in E-Verify under the specific EIN that employs the student.
The worksite must be covered by the employer's E-Verify enrollment — a different worksite may require a separate enrollment verification.
The employer that signs Form I-983 must be the employer providing training and supervision, not a client or third party.
Staffing-agency placements at a client that is not the I-983 signatory create employer-identity risk.
This page is part of the OPT and STEM OPT — complete guide cluster. For the full STEM OPT filing checklist including E-Verify verification steps, read STEM OPT 24-month extension checklist .
Who this is for
An F-1 student or employer evaluating whether an employer's E-Verify enrollment qualifies for STEM OPT supervision before signing Form I-983. This page is also for staffing-agency placements, multi-entity corporate groups with multiple EINs, and remote/multi-site worksites where enrollment may not cover the training location.
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C)(2) . STEM OPT requires the employer to be enrolled in E-Verify and to provide structured training under Form I-983. SEVP and USCIS treat the employer that pays, supervises, and evaluates the student as the STEM OPT employer — not a related brand name, parent company, or client site that merely hosts the student. Re-check e-verify.gov and the current SEVP STEM OPT Hub guidance before every filing or employer change.
The employer-identity test
The employer that signs Form I-983 must be the same employer that:
Employs the student under a direct employment relationship (pays wages under its own EIN).
Is enrolled in E-Verify under that same EIN.
Provides the training and supervision described in the I-983 training plan.
Has authority to evaluate and terminate the student.
All four elements must align. A company that is E-Verify enrolled but does not supervise the day-to-day training fails the test.
Worksite coverage
E-Verify enrollment is tied to specific employer locations. If the student works at a worksite that is not covered by the employer's E-Verify enrollment, the worksite condition may not be satisfied. Verify the employer's E-Verify company ID and confirm it covers the specific worksite before training begins. Check the E-Verify employer search tool and any SEVP guidance on multi-site employers.
Staffing-agency and third-party placement risk
A staffing company may sign Form I-983 only if it is:
The direct employer of record (pays the student under its own EIN).
E-Verify enrolled.
The entity providing genuine training and supervision — not merely placing the student at a client site where the client controls daily work.
If the staffing company places the student at a client company, and the client company controls the training and supervision, the employer-identity test may fail regardless of the staffing agency's E-Verify enrollment.
Document checklist
Employer legal name (exact match to EIN registration).
EIN used on Form I-983.
E-Verify company ID (confirm through the E-Verify employer search before filing).
Worksite address and confirmation it is covered by the enrollment.
Form I-983 — employer section completed and signed by an authorized signatory.
Supervisor name and title confirmed as an employee of the signing employer.
Timeline
Before filing the STEM OPT extension: verify E-Verify enrollment and worksite coverage.
At any change of worksite: confirm whether the same employer E-Verify enrollment still covers the new location.
At STEM OPT validation (6- and 12-month reviews): keep E-Verify enrollment evidence current in the file.
How to confirm an employer E-Verify enrollment
The E-Verify employer search tool at e-verify.gov allows students and DSOs to confirm enrollment by employer name, EIN, or E-Verify company ID. If the employer appears in the search results, verify that the enrolled name matches the legal name on the Form I-983. A mismatch between the enrolled name and the signatory name is a common RFE trigger. If the employer does not appear in the search results, they may not be enrolled or may have enrolled under a different legal entity. Ask the employer for their E-Verify company ID and a copy of their E-Verify Memorandum of Understanding, which confirms their enrollment date and obligations. Some employers operate under multiple EINs for different business lines — confirm that the specific EIN paying the student is the one enrolled in E-Verify.
Multi-site and remote work considerations
Large employers may have E-Verify enrollment that covers multiple worksites, but not all locations are automatically covered. Three-part test: STEM Designated Degree Program (correct CIP code) + E-Verify employer (correct employer identity) + signed Form I-983 training plan before training begins.
Filing deadline: I-765 must be received by USCIS while the post-completion OPT EAD is still valid. Filing after expiry makes you ineligible.
Documents: current OPT EAD, STEM degree evidence with CIP code, I-20 with STEM recommendation, Form I-765 (c)(3)(C), Form I-983, E-Verify employer information.
This page is part of the OPT and STEM OPT — complete guide cluster. It exists to answer the STEM OPT extension checklist decision. For E-Verify employer verification, read STEM OPT E-Verify requirements . For job changes during STEM OPT, read STEM OPT job change rules .
Who this is for
An F-1 OPT holder filing the 24-month STEM OPT extension (Form I-765 category (c)(3)(C)). This applies whether you are currently on standard post-completion OPT and approaching the EAD expiry date, or if you received your STEM degree and are planning ahead to ensure all three eligibility requirements are met before you start the filing process. Employers sponsoring STEM OPT employees will also find this page relevant for understanding their obligations under the I-983 training plan and E-Verify requirements.
If you need a broader overview of STEM OPT rather than the filing checklist, start with OPT and STEM OPT — complete guide . For employer-specific E-Verify verification, see STEM OPT E-Verify requirements .
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C); § 214.2(f)(11) .
Section 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C) establishes the STEM OPT extension framework, authorising the 24-month extension for F-1 students who have completed a STEM designated degree program and are employed by an E-Verify enrolled employer. Section 214.2(f)(11) sets out the training plan requirements, reporting obligations, and the employer responsibilities that govern the extension period. Together, these regulations create a three-part test that must be satisfied before filing: a qualifying STEM degree, an E-Verify employer, and a signed I-983 training plan.
The three-part test
All three must be satisfied before filing:
STEM Designated Degree Program with correct CIP code. The degree must appear on the STEM Designated Degree Program List with a matching CIP code. The CIP code on the I-20 must match. A STEM subject degree from a non-listed CIP code does not qualify.
E-Verify employer. The employer that signs the I-983 must be enrolled in E-Verify under the correct employer name and EIN. A staffing agency that places the student at a non-E-Verify client typically does not qualify. Read STEM OPT E-Verify requirements for the employer-identity test.
Form I-983 training plan signed by both parties before training begins. The plan must include learning objectives, supervision structure, evaluation schedule, and compensation. Do not begin training before the plan is signed.
Documents that prove the case
Assemble the following before filing the I-765. USCIS may issue an RFE if any document is missing or inconsistent.
Current OPT EAD — must still be valid at the time of I-765 receipt by USCIS. USCIS uses the receipt date, not the postmark date. If the EAD expires before USCIS receives your application, the STEM OPT extension is not available and you must depart or find another immigration option.
STEM degree evidence — diploma or transcript showing the conferred degree and CIP code. If your degree program has changed CIP codes since you enrolled, confirm with the DSO which CIP code appears in SEVIS. The code on the I-20 must match the STEM Designated Degree Program List.
I-20 with STEM recommendation from the DSO, issued within 30 days of the I-765 filing. The recommendation is entered in SEVIS by the DSO, and the page 2 printout includes the STEM OPT start date calculation and employer information.
Form I-765 with category (c)(3)(C), properly completed with the correct eligibility code. Ensure the current EAD expiry date, the STEM degree information, and the employer details are correctly entered. A typo in the EAD expiry date can cause a rejection.
Form I-983 signed by both student and qualifying supervisor before training begins. The supervisor must be an employee of the E-Verify-enrolled employer with direct oversight of the student’s training. A human resources representative may countersign, but the direct supervisor who completes the evaluations must also sign.
E-Verify employer information — company legal name, EIN, and E-Verify company ID. Confirm these details by searching the employer’s name in the E-Verify database or ask the employer for their E-Verify enrollment confirmation letter. Using an incorrect EIN or company name can lead to an RFE or denial.

Report all employer changes, address changes, and material training-plan changes within 10 days via the SEVP Portal.

Material changes to job duties, supervisor, or worksite at the same employer may also require a new or amended I-983.

This page is part of the OPT and STEM OPT — complete guide cluster. For the E-Verify requirement that must be confirmed before a new I-983 is signed, read STEM OPT E-Verify requirements .
Who this is for
An F-1 STEM OPT holder changing employers or experiencing a material change in job conditions during the 24-month extension period. This includes students who have accepted a new position with a different employer, students whose current job duties or reporting structure has changed significantly, and students who are considering a job change and need to understand the reporting requirements and unemployment cap implications before making the transition. Understanding your reporting obligations before you accept a new position helps you plan the transition timeline and avoid unemployment gaps between roles.
This guide covers the reporting obligations specific to STEM OPT job changes. The rules differ from standard OPT because STEM OPT requires a formal training plan (Form I-983), an E-Verify enrolled employer, and structured evaluations. If you are on standard OPT and changing employers, the requirements are simpler — update your DSO within 10 days through the SEVP Portal, but no new Form I-983 is required. Read the OPT and STEM OPT — complete guide for a full comparison of OPT and STEM OPT reporting obligations.
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(12)(ii); 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(11) .
Change types and what each requires
New employer
Changing to a new employer triggers the most comprehensive set of reporting obligations. You must complete a new Form I-983 signed by the new employer before training begins at the new position. The new employer must be E-Verify enrolled under the specific EIN that will employ you — not just the parent company or a related entity. Report the employer change in the SEVP Portal within 10 days of the change. Do not begin work at the new employer before the new I-983 is signed by both you and the employer and reviewed by your DSO. Starting work before the I-983 is processed can result in a finding of unauthorized training, which may lead to SEVIS termination and loss of STEM OPT eligibility.
The new I-983 must include updated training objectives, a detailed description of the new role's connection to your STEM degree, and the new employer's E-Verify credentials. Submit the new I-983 to your DSO for review and SEVIS update at least two weeks before your intended start date to allow time for processing. If the new employer is not yet E-Verify enrolled, they must enroll before you can begin work — the enrollment process typically takes 3 to 5 business days but can take longer if the employer has compliance issues.
Same employer — material change in duties, supervisor, or worksite
A change in job title, primary duties, reporting supervisor, or physical worksite at the same employer may constitute a material change to the training plan. Material changes require a new or amended Form I-983 before the new conditions begin. The key test is whether the change affects the training objectives, the degree-related skills being developed, or the supervision structure outlined in the original I-983. A promotion that involves the same technical skills and the same supervisor, for example, may not be material, while a move to a completely different department or function almost certainly is.
Minor administrative changes that do not affect the training relationship or training objectives may not require a new I-983, but always confirm with your DSO what counts as a material change under current SEVP guidance. When in doubt, submit an amended I-983 — having an updated training plan on file is safer than facing a compliance finding during a future immigration filing. Your DSO can advise on whether the change requires a new SEVIS entry or can be handled through a note in the existing SEVIS record. Document the change in the SEVP Portal within 10 days regardless of whether a new I-983 is required.
Address change
Student address changes must be reported in the SEVP Portal within 10 days. Worksite address changes that affect the employer's E-Verify worksite coverage may also require verification before the change takes effect.
Document checklist
Old I-983 final evaluation — complete any required periodic evaluation before the change. If you are at the 6-month or 12-month evaluation point, complete the evaluation for the current position before starting the new I-983.

01 STEM OPT requires a bona fide employer-employee relationship with independent supervision. 
02 The founder-risk test asks: can someone other than the student supervise, train, evaluate, and terminate the student? 
03 A sole-founder LLC where the student is the only officer and signs their own I-983 typically fails both the employer-employee and supervision requirements. 
04 A startup may qualify if a co-founder with genuine supervisory authority signs the I-983, the company is E-Verify enrolled, and the student receives salary.

Last updated 2026-07-14 · Reviewed by Attorney reviewed 
In 60 seconds
Primary authority: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C); § 214.2(f)(11)
Core rule: STEM OPT requires a bona fide employer-employee relationship with independent supervision. A sole founder who signs their own I-983 typically fails both requirements.
The test: can someone other than the student supervise, train, evaluate, and terminate the student?
Documents: ownership records, independent supervisor evidence, E-Verify employer details, I-983 training plan, pay records, board or manager oversight documentation.
Compensation rule: W-2 wages through payroll are required. Equity-only or unpaid founder work does not satisfy STEM OPT compensation requirements.
This page is part of the OPT and STEM OPT — complete guide cluster. For LLC ownership questions during OPT (not STEM OPT), read Forming an LLC as an international student on OPT: a legal walkthrough . For E-Verify employer requirements, read STEM OPT E-Verify requirements .
Who this is for
An F-1 STEM OPT holder considering founding or working at a startup the student also owns or controls. This includes students who have already started a company before entering STEM OPT and want to use the startup as their qualifying employer, students who are considering a co-founder arrangement and need to structure the supervisory relationship, and students who have been offered equity in a startup and need to determine whether the arrangement qualifies as STEM OPT employment. This page is also for co-founders, investors, and DSOs evaluating whether a proposed I-983 structure has independent supervision. Standard post-completion OPT LLC questions (not STEM OPT) belong on Forming an LLC as an international student on OPT: a legal walkthrough .
The controlling source
Primary controlling source: 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C); § 214.2(f)(11) . STEM OPT is training with a qualifying employer — not a general self-employment visa. The regulations and SEVP STEM OPT guidance expect a bona fide employer-employee relationship, E-Verify enrollment under the correct employer identity, and a Form I-983 training plan with a supervising official who is not the student.
The key interpretive guidance comes from SEVP’s STEM OPT policy guidance, which clarifies that the employer-employee relationship is evaluated based on the totality of circumstances, not on the student’s ownership percentage alone. SEVP looks at whether the entity can actually hire, pay, supervise, and terminate the student. In a startup context, this means examining the governance documents, board structure, and actual supervisory arrangements rather than simply the percentage of equity held. A student who owns 100% of a startup with no employees and no board likely cannot establish the required relationship. A student who owns 30% with a co-founder CEO who has genuine supervisory authority may be able to. The analysis is fact-specific and requires careful documentation.
The founder-risk test
SEVP requires a bona fide employer-employee relationship and structured training with independent supervision. Before accepting founder or startup work on STEM OPT, answer this question:
Can someone other than the student supervise, train, evaluate, and terminate the student? 
If the answer is no — because the student is the sole owner, sole officer, or has no genuine supervisor above them — the structure typically fails the STEM OPT requirement. Paper titles without real authority do not fix the problem. The supervisor must be able to set training goals, review progress, and end the employment relationship if training fails.
What might work
A startup structure may qualify if:
The company has a board of directors or co-founder with genuine supervisory authority over the student’s work. The supervisor should have the practical ability to assign tasks, review performance, and make employment decisions independent of the student. A board resolution or co-founder agreement documenting this authority is essential.
That person signs the I-983 as the supervising official — not the student signing their own training plan. The supervising official’s name and title must appear in the appropriate fields of the I-983, and they must be an employee of the E-Verify-enrolled entity.
The company is enrolled in E-Verify under the correct employer identity (EIN). The employer name on the I-983 must match the E-Verify enrollment. If the company uses a parent company’s E-Verify, the student must confirm that the entity signing the I-983 is the E-Verify-enrolled entity.
The student receives wages or salary through payroll — not just equity distributions. Payroll must be on the company’s payroll system with proper tax withholdings. A single paystub or quarterly distribution does not establish an ongoing employment relationship.
Training objectives on the I-983 map to the STEM degree and can be evaluated at the required intervals. The training plan should include specific, measurable learning objectives

02 Core rule: Subletting does not release you from the original lease — you remain liable for rent and damages even if the subtenant defaults on payments or causes damage. 
03 Documents: Original lease, written sublet agreement, landlord consent correspondence, subtenant screening documents, and move-in condition photos. 
04 Timing: Request landlord consent in writing before the sublet begins; some states require landlords to respond within a reasonable timeframe (typically 7 to 14 days).

In 60 seconds
Most leases require landlord consent before subletting.
Subletting without permission can breach your lease.
You remain liable for rent and damage even after subletting.
A written sublet agreement protects you from common disputes.
State rules on subletting vary — check your state statute.
When your lease allows subletting
Most residential leases in the US address subletting in one of three ways: they prohibit it entirely, they allow it with the landlord's written consent, or they say nothing at all. The rule that applies depends on your lease and your state law.
If your lease prohibits subletting, doing it anyway is a lease violation that can lead to eviction. Even if the landlord has allowed informal sublets in the past, the written lease controls your legal obligations. If your lease allows it with consent, you must request permission in writing and wait for the landlord's response. Some states require landlords to be reasonable when withholding consent — California, New York, and Massachusetts are among the states that impose a reasonableness standard, meaning a landlord cannot arbitrarily block a qualified subtenant.
If your lease is silent on subletting, state law controls. Some states give tenants a right to sublet unless the lease explicitly prohibits it. Others default to requiring landlord consent. Check your state landlord-tenant statute before proceeding, and request any required consent in writing so you have a record of the landlord's decision. If you live in a rent-controlled or rent-stabilized unit in cities like New York, San Francisco, or Los Angeles, local rent ordinances may provide additional subletting protections that override your lease language — including a statutory right to sublet as long as the tenant continues to occupy the unit as their primary residence.
Reading the sublet clause in your lease. Look for a section titled "Assignment and Subletting" or "Transfer of Interest." The clause will typically state that you cannot sublet without the landlord's prior written consent and that consent may not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed. If the clause says the landlord can withhold consent arbitrarily, that clause may still be enforceable in states without a reasonableness requirement — but in states that impose a reasonableness standard by statute, the lease clause cannot override the law. Read this clause carefully before signing the lease, not after you need to sublet. If the sublet clause is ambiguous, ask the landlord in writing what their standard process is for approving subtenants and what documentation they require.
How to sublet safely — step by step
Step 1: Read your lease. Look for clauses about subletting, assignment, or transferring possession. Note whether the landlord must consent and whether consent can be withheld arbitrarily. Highlight the specific requirements — some leases require the subtenant to meet the same screening criteria you met, including credit score and income thresholds.
Step 2: Request landlord consent in writing if required. Send an email or letter with the proposed subtenant's name, contact information, and the sublet terms. Attach the subtenant's application documents (ID, proof of income, reference) with your request. Keep a copy of your request and the landlord's response. If the landlord does not respond within a reasonable time — typically 7 to 14 days — follow up in writing and note the lack of response.
Step 3: Draft a written sublet agreement. The agreement should state the rent amount, the sublet period, who pays utilities, and what happens if the subtenant damages the property or fails to pay rent. Do not rely on verbal agreements. Include a clause that the subtenant agrees to follow all terms of your original lease, including quiet hours, guest policies, and pet restrictions. Sign and date the agreement with the subtenant and keep a copy for your records.
Step 4: Document the apartment condition. Take dated photos or videos of every room, including closets, cabinets, and windows, before the subtenant moves in. Upload the photos to a cloud service with a date stamp. This protects you from false damage claims when the subtenant moves out and provides evidence if you need to deduct from the subtenant's security deposit.
Step 5: Keep paying rent to the landlord. You remain legally responsible for the full rent even if the subtenant pays you. If the subtenant stops paying, you must cover the shortfall or face eviction yourself. Set a reminder to confirm that the subtenant's payment has arrived before the rent due date each month. If the subtenant is late, you have time to step in before the landlord issues a late notice.

01 Primary authority: USCIS TN USMCA Professionals guidance, 8 CFR 214.6, Department of State TN visa guidance, and CBP admission guidance 
02 Core rule: TN classification permits qualified Canadian and Mexican citizens to work temporarily in the United States in listed USMCA professional occupations. The classification falls under the nonimmigrant category — it requires the applicant to demonstrate nonimmigrant intent (a temporary stay with a foreign residence) unless an exemption applies. The list of eligible professions includes accountants, engineers, computer systems analysts, scientists, and approximately 55 other occupational categories, each with specific educational and credential requirements. 
03 Documents: Proof of citizenship: Valid Canadian or Mexican passport. Canadian citizens may also use a NEXUS card at some ports of entry, but a passport is the safest document. Mexican citizens must have a valid passport with a U.S. TN visa stamp. 
04 Timing: Canadians may often apply at a port of entry or preflight inspection; Mexicans generally need a TN visa from a U.S. consulate before admission. 
05 Main risk: Unlisted occupations. The most common TN refusal reason is an occupation that does not appear on the USMCA professions list. Job titles like "Business Analyst," "Project Manager," "Marketing Specialist," or "Management Consultant" are not listed professions. If the role is not on the list, it cannot be classified as TN regardless of the applicant's qualifications. Consider the H-1B visa for roles that do not fit any listed TN profession. 
06 Review status: Basic review for TN visa for Canadian and Mexican professionals available now; attorney-review tiers coming soon. 
TN visa: the rule in plain English
TN classification permits qualified Canadian and Mexican citizens to work temporarily in the United States in listed USMCA professional occupations. The classification falls under the nonimmigrant category — it requires the applicant to demonstrate nonimmigrant intent (a temporary stay with a foreign residence) unless an exemption applies. The list of eligible professions includes accountants, engineers, computer systems analysts, scientists, and approximately 55 other occupational categories, each with specific educational and credential requirements.
The TN process differs significantly by nationality. Canadian citizens can apply for TN status at a U.S. port of entry (land border or pre-flight inspection) without filing a petition with USCIS first. They need only the employer support letter, proof of citizenship, and evidence of qualifications at the time of admission. Mexican citizens, by contrast, must obtain a TN visa from a U.S. consulate before traveling to the United States. The consular process requires a Form DS-160, an interview at the consulate, and a visa stamp in the passport before the applicant can seek admission at a port of entry. Canadians cannot obtain a TN visa at a consulate — they must apply at the border or pre-flight.
The TN classification is employer-specific but not petition-specific (unlike H-1B). A new employer requires a new TN application. TN status is granted in increments of up to three years with no hard limit on renewals, but indefinite renewal without changing employers may trigger scrutiny under the temporary intent requirement. The application timing depends on whether the applicant is a Canadian (apply at the border on the day of travel) or Mexican (schedule a consular interview, typically 2-8 weeks wait).
Who this guide is for
Canadian citizens with a job offer in a USMCA listed profession who plan to apply for TN status at a U.S. port of entry or pre-flight inspection. Mexican citizens with a job offer who need to obtain a TN visa from a U.S. consulate before traveling to the United States. Professionals already working in the U.S. on TN status who are changing employers, renewing their status, or have questions about transitioning to lawful permanent residence.
This guide is also for employers who hire Canadian or Mexican professionals and need to prepare the employer support letter, verify the occupation code, and understand the document requirements for TN applications. If you are an H-1B worker considering a switch to TN, check whether your occupation is on the USMCA list and whether your educational credentials meet the TN requirements — TN has stricter education-to-occupation matching rules than H-1B does.
Documents and evidence to prepare
Proof of citizenship: Valid Canadian or Mexican passport. Canadian citizens may also use a NEXUS card at some ports of entry, but a passport is the safest document. Mexican citizens must have a valid passport with a U.S. TN visa stamp.
Employer support letter: A letter from the U.S. employer addressed to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (for Canadians) or to the consular officer (for Mexicans). The letter must describe the professional capacity, the job duties (mapped to the USMCA profession), the duration of employment, the salary and benefits, and the employer's business address. For Canadians applying at the border, the letter should be on company letterhead and signed by an authorized representative with a wet signature or digital signature that CBP can verify.
Educational credentials: Degree certificate and official transcripts from the post-secondary institution that qualifies the applicant for the USMCA profession. For engineers licensed in Canada or Mexico, professional engineering (P.Eng.) certification may be accepted. For computer systems analysts, a post-secondary diploma or degree in a related field is required — work experience alone does not satisfy the educational requirement for most TN professions.
Credentials and licenses: State or provincial professional license if required for the occupati

§ Key takeaways
01 TPS beneficiaries must re-register during country-specific periods to maintain TPS and may file Form I-765 for employment authorization. 
02 Core documents include Form I-821, Form I-765 if requesting EAD, proof of identity and nationality, prior TPS approval, EAD, address history, country-specific evidence, fee or fee waiver request, and travel authorization documents if needed. 
03 Check the country-specific TPS page and Federal Register notice before filing because dates and EAD extension language differ by country. 
04 Do not write a generic TPS deadline; teach readers to find the specific designation, extension, and re-registration window. 
05 Pitfalls include using the wrong country deadline, missing EAD extension proof, travelling without I-512T, late re-registration without good-cause explanation, and fee errors. 
How TPS renewals work in 2026
Temporary Protected Status under INA 244 allows nationals of designated countries to remain in the US when conditions in their home country make safe return impossible. Designations are based on armed conflict, environmental disasters, or extraordinary conditions. TPS is not a path to permanent residence.
Approximately 16 countries maintain active TPS designations in 2026. Each requires filing Form I-821 and Form I-765 during specific re-registration periods announced in Federal Register notices. Check the USCIS country-specific page before filing.
Understanding TPS re-registration requirements
Temporary Protected Status re-registration requires submitting Form I-821, Application for Temporary Protected Status, during the designated re-registration period for the applicant's country. The re-registration period is announced in a Federal Register notice published by the Department of Homeland Security. The notice specifies the exact start and end dates of the re-registration period, the fee amounts required, the edition of Form I-821 to use, and the filing address based on the applicant's location. Re-registration periods are typically open for 60 to 180 days, and filing outside this window without good cause results in loss of TPS.
In addition to Form I-821, applicants who need employment authorization must file Form I-765, Application for Employment Authorization, with the required fee. Some country designations bundle the I-765 fee with the I-821 fee, while others require separate payments. The Federal Register notice for each country specifies the fee structure. Applicants who cannot afford the fee may file Form I-912, Request for Fee Waiver, with supporting evidence of financial hardship. Fee waivers are discretionary, and applicants should provide thorough documentation of their financial situation.
TPS re-registration requires proof of continuous physical presence in the United States since the date of the most recent designation for the applicant's country. Supporting documents include lease agreements, utility bills, bank statements, school records, employment records, and medical records showing the applicant's presence during the relevant period. The burden is on the applicant to establish continuous physical presence by a preponderance of the evidence. If the applicant has not maintained continuous physical presence, they must demonstrate that any absence was brief, casual, and innocent. Absences without advance parole are presumptively not authorized and may break the continuous presence requirement.
Country-specific deadlines in 2026
Each TPS designation has its own re-registration calendar. Venezuela's designation runs through September 2026 with a re-registration period that typically opens 60 days before the expiration date. Haiti's designation was extended through August 2026 following the most recent Federal Register notice. Ukraine's designation, granted after the 2022 invasion, has been extended multiple times and the current re-registration period runs through early 2027 for beneficiaries who registered during the initial designation or a previous extension. Burma and Cameroon both have designations that extend into 2027, but the re-registration periods for each country are announced separately and may not align with the designation end date.
Country designations change frequently due to litigation, new Federal Register notices, and changes in home country conditions. Applicants should verify their country's current designation status on the USCIS TPS page rather than relying on previous renewal notices or guidance from prior years. A TPS designation can be terminated by the Secretary of Homeland Security at any time if the conditions that justified the designation no longer exist. When a designation is terminated, beneficiaries receive a wind-down period of at least 120 days to prepare for departure or seek alternative immigration status. During the wind-down period, beneficiaries retain their TPS status and work authorization until the termination date specified in the Federal Register notice.

Who Needs a US Embassy Interview? Visa Types & Eligibility
Most applicants for a US visa interview must appear in person at a US embassy or consulate.
Exceptions exist for children under 14, applicants over 79, and renewals of certain visas within 12 months of expiry.
The following common visa categories require a consular interview :
F-1 and M-1 student visas. International students coming to study in the US.
J-1 exchange visitor visas. Scholars, researchers, au pairs.
H-1B work visas. Specialty occupation workers.
B-1/B-2 visitor visas. Tourism, business, medical treatment.
K-1 fiancé(e) visas. To marry a US citizen.
Immigrant visas (green card). Including family-sponsored and employment-based petitions.
Eligibility depends on demonstrating that you qualify for the visa category and that you intend to return to your home country after the temporary stay (for nonimmigrant visas). For immigrant visas, the green card interview at US embassy requires a petition approved by USCIS first.
Typically, The us embassy eligibility criteria vary by visa type.
For a student visa, you need acceptance to a SEVP-certified school, proof of sufficient funds, and a valid I-20.
For an H-1B visa, you need an approved I-129 petition and evidence of a specialty occupation role.
For a B-1/B-2 visitor visa, you need to show tourism or business purpose and strong ties to your home country.
Meanwhile, The us embassy requirements also include a valid passport (six months beyond your intended stay), a completed DS-160 form, and the visa application fee. Some visa categories require additional forms such as the I-20 for students or the I-797 approval notice for work visas.
Note: Schedule your interview at the embassy or consulate with jurisdiction over your place of residence, not necessarily where you want to travel. Check the us embassy website for your region.
How to Find and Book a US Embassy Interview Near You
Finding the correct embassy appointment location is the first step. Use the US Department of State's embassy locator to identify the consular district that covers your home address.
Locate your embassy. Go to travel.state.gov and select your country. Each embassy page lists available appointment slots.
Pay the application fee. The Machine Readable Visa (MRV) fee must be paid before booking. Fees vary by visa type (e.g., $185 for most nonimmigrant visas in 2026).
Complete Form DS-160. The online nonimmigrant visa application. Save the barcode confirmation page.
Schedule the interview. Log into the embassy's appointment system with your DS-160 confirmation number. Choose a date and time. Some posts use third-party call centers.
Print your appointment letter. Bring it to the interview along with the DS-160 confirmation and fee receipt.
Wait times for appointments vary by embassy and season. During peak periods (May to August for student visas), delays can exceed 30 days.
Check the embassy website for current us embassy timeline estimates. Apply early.
It is possible to schedule a priority or emergency appointment for urgent travel (medical, funeral).
How to apply for us embassy interview appointments depends on your country of residence.
Some embassies use an online portal, while others require a call center booking.
If you are applying from a country where you do not hold citizenship, you may still be eligible to apply there if you have legal residency.
In 2026, visitor visa appointments in high-demand posts (India, Mexico, Philippines) can exceed 100 days.
Student visa appointments are typically faster from March to June. Check the State Department's visa appointment wait time tool before booking.

The checklist covers your passport, Form I-20, SEVIS I-901 receipt, DS-160 confirmation, MRV fee receipt, financial evidence, and academic records.
Most F-1 and M-1 applicants ages 14 to 79 must appear in person at a US embassy or consulate for the interview.
Pay the SEVIS I-901 fee at least three days before your interview so the system reflects the payment.
Rehearse short, factual answers about your program, funding, and ties to your home country to address Section 214(b).

Rehearsing answers for the 214(b) tie test
Consular officers deny most F-1 cases under Section 214(b) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which requires you to prove you intend to return home after your studies.
Your document folder alone will not carry the interview; your spoken answers must reinforce the same story.
Practice aloud until your responses sound natural, not memorised.
Start with the three questions almost every officer asks: why this school, why this programme, and what you plan to do after graduation.
Tie each answer to concrete evidence. If you studied computer science as an undergraduate, explain how the US master's curriculum fills a specific gap.
When asked about post-graduation plans, name a role, an employer type, or an industry that exists in your home country, not a vague "maybe a job."
Prepare two or three examples of family, property, or employment ties.
A letter from a parent's employer, a property deed, or a return job offer carries weight when you mention it naturally.
Do not volunteer documents the officer did not request; keep them organised in labelled tabs so you can produce them in seconds.
Finish each answer in under one minute. Officers interview dozens of applicants daily, and rambling responses read as evasive.
If you do not understand a question, ask the officer to repeat it. A calm pause beats a rushed guess.
F-2 dependents: documents and interview notes
Spouses and unmarried children under 21 accompany F-1 students on F-2 visas, and their interviews follow a separate track.
The primary student must already hold a valid F-1 visa or be applying simultaneously.
Each F-2 applicant needs their own DS-160 confirmation, passport, and visa fee receipt, plus a marriage certificate for a spouse or a birth certificate for a child.
Financial evidence matters more for F-2 cases because the officer must see funds covering the dependent's living costs, not just tuition.
Bring bank statements showing available balance for at least one academic year, and if the student has an assistantship or scholarship, include the award letter.
The I-20 for an F-2 dependent is issued by the same school and lists the student's SEVIS ID; verify the name and date of birth match the passport exactly.
Interview questions for dependents usually focus on the student's programme and the family's intent to return.
Rehearse basic answers about the student's school and graduation timeline.
Children under 14 may qualify for an interview waiver in some posts, but check the specific embassy page because rules vary by country.
Consulate scheduling logistics and regional differences
Interview wait times vary sharply by post, from a few days in some cities to several months in high-demand ones.
Check the current visa appointment wait time published on the US Department of State website before you book flights or pay non-refundable deposits.
Schedule your interview as soon as you receive your I-20, because the SEVIS record does not guarantee a fast slot.
Some consulates require you to collect your passport at a designated courier location rather than the embassy itself.
Confirm the delivery method when you pay the visa fee, and note that the DS-160 location code must match the post where you interview.
If you plan to apply outside your home country, verify that the post accepts third-country nationals; many do, but some restrict F-1 processing to residents.
Arrive at least 30 minutes before your appointment, and leave electronics, large bags, and food at home or in your hotel.
Security screening adds time, and a missed slot means rescheduling with a new wait.
Bring a printed copy of your appointment confirmation, because some posts will not admit you without it.

US work visas fall into three broad groups: temporary employment visas (H-1B, L-1, TN, O-1A, E-2), employment-based green cards (EB-1A, EB-2 NIW), and the cap-gap bridge for students transitioning from OPT to H-1B. The right visa depends on your qualifications, employer type, nationality, and whether you seek temporary status or permanent residence. The 5 most important things to know
H-1B lottery selection is not approval. Selection only permits the employer to file Form I-129. The petition must still prove specialty occupation, wage, and maintenance of status. See USCIS H-1B guidance.
H-1B portability under INA § 214(n) may allow starting work for a new employer upon USCIS receipt of a non-frivolous petition, but travel and paystub gaps create significant risk. Many attorneys advise waiting for the receipt notice before starting.
The EB-1A extraordinary ability classification is self-petitioning — no job offer or PERM required — but the standard is high. You must show sustained national or international acclaim and membership in the small percentage at the very top of your field.
The EB-2 National Interest Waiver requires proving substantial merit, national importance, and that you are well positioned to advance the proposed endeavor under the Dhanasar framework. Personal career benefit alone is insufficient.
Canadians and Mexicans apply for TN visas differently. Canadians often use port-of-entry or preflight inspection without a prior visa; Mexicans generally need a consular visa first. The TN is not a dual-intent visa, and pursuing a green card while in TN status can create complications.
Choose your path
Pick the guide that matches your current situation. If you are a professional with a US job offer, start with the H-1B or L-1 guide. If you have extraordinary ability or a nationally important endeavor, the EB-1A or EB-2 NIW guides explain the self-petition process. If you are Canadian or Mexican, the TN guide covers the USMCA professional route. This FAQ is for professionals and employers navigating US work visas: the H-1B lottery and transfer process, L-1 intracompany transfers, EB-1A extraordinary ability and EB-2 National Interest Waiver green cards, TN status for Canadian and Mexican professionals, and E-2 treaty investor visas. The questions reflect the most common complexities we see from applicants in USCIS forums and from our document review clients. Each answer has been reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera, a licensed California attorney (CA Bar #298948), and draws on the Immigration and Nationality Act, 8 CFR regulations, and current USCIS adjudication guidance as of mid-2026.
Employment-based immigration rules continue to shift, with periodic H-1B cap registration changes, updated EB-2 NIW policy guidance from January 2025, and ongoing USCIS scrutiny of specialty occupation qualifications and staffing arrangements. The answers below reflect the current published rules. Processing times, fee schedules, and form editions change periodically, so you should verify the latest requirements on uscis.gov before filing.
The question list below covers the most frequently asked work-visa topics. For a deeper dive into any subject, the full articles below provide step-by-step filing guidance, document checklists, and the regulatory references that apply to each visa category.
How to use this FAQ

Students bridging OPT to H-1B should also read the cap-gap guide and F-1 / OPT hub .

Last updated 2026-07-14 · Reviewed by Denise Platter Cabrera 
Is H-1B lottery selection the same as visa approval?
No. Lottery selection means your employer is permitted to file a Form I-129 petition on your behalf. It does not mean USCIS will approve the petition or that you will receive an H-1B visa. After selection, the employer must prove three things: that the job qualifies as a specialty occupation, that you meet the educational or experiential requirements for that occupation, and that the employer will pay the required wage. USCIS may issue a Request for Evidence (RFE) or deny the petition if any of these elements is not adequately documented. Selection is only the first step in a multi-stage process that includes petition review, possible RFE response, and, if abroad, consular visa issuance.
Can I start working for a new employer before my H-1B transfer is approved?
Under INA § 214(n), H-1B portability allows you to begin working for the new employer as soon as USCIS receives a non-frivolous I-129 petition, provided you were lawfully admitted, the new petition is filed before your current H-1B expires, and the new job is in the same or a similar specialty occupation. However, starting work before receipt confirmation is risky because you have no proof the petition was received. Travel while the transfer is pending is also risky; if you leave the US and the petition is denied, you may not be able to return. Many attorneys advise waiting for the receipt notice or even the approval notice before starting, especially if you have any history of status gaps or prior denials.
What is the difference between an L-1A and an L-1B visa?
The L-1A visa is for executives and managers being transferred to a US parent, subsidiary, affiliate, or branch office. The L-1B visa is for employees with specialized knowledge of the company's products, services, research, or procedures. Both require that you have worked for the foreign entity for at least one continuous year within the three years immediately preceding your admission to the US. L-1A holders can stay for up to 7 years, while L-1B holders are limited to 5 years. The L-1A is also a direct path to an EB-1C green card for multinational managers, whereas L-1B holders usually must go through PERM labor certification unless they qualify for a National Interest Waiver.
Do I need a job offer or labor certification for an EB-1A green card?
No. The EB-1A classification for aliens of extraordinary ability is a self-petitioning category. You do not need a job offer, labor certification (PERM), or employer sponsor. You must demonstrate sustained national or international acclaim in your field through evidence such as major awards, membership in selective associations, published material about you, original contributions of major significance, authorship of scholarly articles, high remuneration, or directing critical roles for distinguished organizations. The standard is high — you must show that you are in the small percentage at the very top of your field. Generic recommendation letters from colleagues are weak evidence; objective, third-party recognition carries more weight.
What is the Dhanasar framework for an EB-2 National Interest Waiver?
The Dhanasar framework, established in Matter of Dhanasar, sets out three prongs for an EB-2 National Interest Waiver: (1) the proposed endeavor has both substantial merit and national importance, (2) you are well positioned to advance the proposed endeavor, and (3) on balance, it would be beneficial to the United States to waive the job offer and PERM requirements. National importance is not the same as personal career benefit; your work must have potential prospective impact in a field of substantial intrinsic merit, such as public health, technology, or educ

Australia Student Visa Fee Increase: 2026 Budget Guide | YouSafe 
Skip to main content Core answer: A student visa fee increase changes what you pay at ImmiAccount lodgement, not your university course quote.
Who it hits: Most Subclass 500 primary applicants, plus partners or children listed on the same form (each has their own charge line).
What to check: Open the Student visa (subclass 500) page — or the Visa Pricing Estimator — on the day you pay.
Next step: Separate visa money from tuition, OSHC, English tests, and living costs, then keep a small FX and health-exam buffer.
Table of contents
What the fee increase means in 2026 
Current Subclass 500 charges 
Who may pay a reduced charge 
How to check before you lodge 
Estimate the full study budget 
Worked example: Priya's lodgement budget 
Frequently asked questions 
Sources 
Educational disclaimer 
What the fee increase means in 2026
A visa fee increase is a government charge change, not a university discount and not a processing-speed upgrade. Study Australia reports that the Student visa application charge (VAC) moved from AUD $2,000 to AUD $2,500 from 1 July 2026 for most applicants. Temporary Graduate (subclass 485) charges also rose in the same cycle — keep that product separate when you budget a student lodgement.
Headlines from the 2025 fee cycle can be stale. Always re-read the live Home Affairs listing on the morning you submit. Paying sooner does not buy a faster decision. Genuine student (GS) assessment, enrolment (CoE), health, and character rules still sit with Home Affairs regardless of the amount you transfer.
Use this lodgement-charge checklist before you click pay:
Fee line: Primary applicant plus any dependants listed on the form.
Documents line: Passport, CoE, and other evidence your course and GS statement need.
Buffer line: Health exam, biometrics, and currency conversion.
Mistake to avoid: Lodging from a blog screenshot or a social post instead of the official table.
Current Subclass 500 charges
Home Affairs sets the visa application charge you pay in ImmiAccount. Published guidance for applications lodged on or after 1 July 2026 commonly lists these planning figures for the standard Student pathway — treat them as a starting point only and confirm on the official listing or Visa Pricing Estimator before you pay:
Applicant Typical VAC (AUD) Main applicant $2,500 Additional applicant aged 18 or over $1,530 Additional applicant under 18 $500 Verify before you pay. Subsequent temporary application charges, concessions, and indexation can change the total. The Student 500 listing and Home Affairs pricing tools are the source of truth — not this article.
Item Who sets it Where you verify Lodgement charge Home Affairs Student 500 listing / pricing estimator Course fees Your provider Offer letter and CoE OSHC Insurer Current policy quote 
Who may pay a reduced charge
Study Australia notes that some students are not subject to the full AUD $2,500 step-up. Eligible primary applicants may continue on the prior base charge plus an annual CPI adjustment. Categories commonly cited include:
Primary applicants holding passports from ASEAN member countries (for example Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam).
Primary applicants holding passports from listed Pacific Island countries and Timor-Leste.
Students applying for independent ELICOS or Non-Award courses only — recognising shorter program lengths.
If the primary applicant qualifies, accompanying dependants are often assessed at the related lower rate in the ImmiAccount payment step. Eligibility is driven by passport and course details you enter — you do not "claim" a discount with a separate form. Confirm your exact total in the Visa Pricing Estimator before you freeze funds.
How to check before you lodge
Treat the fee check as a short planner, not a hunt for a bargain. Pay only when the form is complete enough to lodge.
Open the Student visa (subclass 500) listing.
Find the visa application charge for the primary applicant.
Add charges for partners or children if they are on the same form.
Run the Home Affairs Visa Pricing Estimator for your scenario.
Confirm payment methods ImmiAccount accepts that day.
Save a dated screenshot or PDF for your file — then pay from the live form.
The student visa cost line is only the Home Affairs charge. Tuition, OSHC, flights, and living money sit elsewhere. Study Australia publishes high-level living-cost guidance on studyaustralia.gov.au , but it does not replace the lodgement table.
Estimate the full study budget
Build three buckets you can actually fund — then keep them separate so a fee headline never empties your rent or OSHC line.
Government charges. Use the Student 500 listing on the day you pay. Count the primary applicant and any partner or children on the same form. Do not reuse a screenshot from last year.
Course and insurance. Tuition comes from your offer and CoE. Get a current OSHC quote that covers the visa period you intend to request.
Living and extras. Use Study Australia living-cost guidance as a planning floor, then add your city, rent, and dependants. Put English tests, translations, currency conversion, and a small contingency on their own lines.
Faster payment does not buy a faster decision. Re-check the Student 500 page the morning you submit. If you later compare work or skilled visas, keep study charges separate from those pathways — for example, a points-tested skilled visa is a different product from Subclass 500.
Worked example: Priya's lodgement budget
Priya, 24, holds a CoE for a Melbourne master's and is budgeting a Subclass 500 lodgement with no dependants. Her goal is a complete, decision-ready payment — not a promised visa outcome.
Government charge: Copied from the live Student 500 listing / pricing estimator on the day she lodges (she ignores visitor and partner fee rumours).

Banking in Canada for International Students: Accounts, Credit & SIN (2026) | YouSafe 
Skip to main content Step 1: Get your Social Insurance Number first
A Social Insurance Number (SIN) is a 9-digit number issued by Service Canada. You need it before a bank can open an interest-bearing account or before any employer can pay you. Apply in person at a Service Canada Centre — bring your study permit, passport, and proof of enrolment. The SIN is issued on the spot and is free. You can also apply online or by mail, but in-person is fastest. Once you have the SIN, provide it to your bank when opening your account so that interest earned is properly reported to the CRA. Without a SIN on file, your bank may withhold tax on interest at the highest marginal rate.
Your SIN is confidential. Do not carry the card (Service Canada no longer issues plastic cards — you receive a paper confirmation). Store the number securely and provide it only to employers, financial institutions, and government agencies that have a lawful reason to request it. Do not provide your SIN to landlords, phone companies, or as general identification — they do not need it.
Step 2: Choose a student bank account
All five major Canadian banks — RBC, TD, Scotiabank, BMO, and CIBC — offer student accounts with no monthly fees. Most also offer a sign-up bonus (typically $50–$100) for new student accounts. You will need your passport, study permit, and proof of enrolment to open the account. The bank will ask for your Canadian address and phone number — a temporary address is fine, but update it when you move.
Student accounts typically include unlimited debit transactions and Interac e-Transfers, which is how most Canadians pay rent and split bills.
International student accounts at Scotiabank and RBC are specifically marketed to newcomers — Scotiabank's StartRight programme and RBC's Newcomer Advantage offer additional perks such as no-fee international money transfers for the first year and a dedicated newcomer advisor.
Online-only banks such as Tangerine and Simplii also offer no-fee accounts but may require a Canadian credit history to open — they are better as a second account after you have established a relationship with a major bank.
Step 3: Start building Canadian credit history
Canadian credit history does not transfer from your home country. You start from zero, and building credit takes time. The fastest way to start is a secured credit card: you deposit $500–$1,000 with the bank as collateral, and the bank issues a credit card with a limit equal to your deposit. After 6–12 months of on-time payments, you can apply for an unsecured card and the deposit is returned. Use the card for one small recurring purchase each month (a phone bill or a streaming subscription), pay the balance in full by the due date, and never use more than 30% of the credit limit. This pattern builds a positive payment history that Equifax and TransUnion report to lenders.
Avoid applying for multiple credit cards in your first year — each application triggers a hard credit inquiry, and multiple inquiries in a short period signal risk to lenders. If your first application is declined, wait 6 months before trying again rather than applying at a different bank immediately.
Step 4: Set up for part-time work
As an international student with a valid study permit that authorises off-campus work, you can work up to 24 hours per week during academic sessions (as of the policy change confirmed by IRCC) and full-time during scheduled breaks. When your employer hires you, they will ask for your SIN and a void cheque or direct deposit form from your bank — this is why opening the account before you start job hunting saves time. The employer will deduct income tax, CPP, and EI from your paycheque. File a tax return by April 30 each year even if your income is below the tax threshold — filing triggers GST/HST credit payments and other benefits, and creates a record of Canadian income that may support future immigration applications.

Banking setup that supports immigration evidence later
Canadian student banking is not only convenience — statements may later support rent, status, or PGWP life logistics. Choose an account you can open with passport + study permit + enrollment proof, and keep clean records of large international transfers.
Avoid mixing personal and sponsor funds without labels. When family wires tuition, keep remittance advices. Unexplained cash deposits recreate the same funds problems that cause study-permit refusals.

How Canadian study actually feeds CRS and PNP
Canadian study can improve Express Entry competitiveness through Canadian education points, Canadian work experience after a PGWP, and provincial nomination pathways — but none of these are automatic. Program length, language scores (IELTS/CELPIP/TEF), age, and arranged employment still dominate CRS math. A one-year certificate rarely substitutes for a multi-year degree plus skilled work in a TEER-eligible occupation.
Sequence matters: finish an eligible program → secure PGWP if eligible → obtain skilled work → raise language scores → enter the pool or pursue PNP. Students who reverse the order (creating an Express Entry profile with no work history and weak language) burn time without invitations. Category-based draws add another layer: healthcare, STEM, trades, and French-language categories change which profiles get invited below all-program CRS cutoffs.
Documents to collect while you still have school access
Request official transcripts, completion letters, and co-op evaluations before accounts lock after graduation. Keep contracts, pay stubs, and T4s from any authorized work. For Express Entry later you will need educational credential assessment where required, police certificates, and medicals on a short clock after an ITA — starting early reduces scramble risk.
Language scores, TEER mapping, and category draws
Language is often the cheapest CRS lever after graduation. Plan IELTS/CELPIP/TEF attempts before your PGWP is half gone. Retakes are normal; leaving language to the final months is how strong work experience still misses cutoffs.
Map your job duties to the correct TEER/NOC carefully. Title inflation without matching duties fails both CRS claims and future employer-sponsored work. Keep offer letters and pay records that match the occupation you claim.
Category-based draws mean healthcare, STEM, trades, or French proficiency can matter more than all-program scores. Watch IRCC notices, but do not enroll in a weak program solely because a category “might” open later — program eligibility for PGWP still comes first.
A simple post-graduation Express Entry timeline
Month 0–3 after completion: lock PGWP filing if eligible, request transcripts and completion letters, and book language tests. Month 3–12: accumulate skilled work evidence and re-test language if scores are soft. Month 12+: enter the pool or pursue PNP only when your CRS factors are competitive enough to justify the fees and medicals.
If your program was not PGWP-eligible, stop assuming Canadian study alone will carry Express Entry. Rebuild the plan around foreign work experience, language, or a different lawful pathway — do not pay for “CRS boost” marketing that ignores status reality.
